title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text: Before reading: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry, Model restrictions and efficiency, and From an influence function to an estimator. This application reuses the capstone’s nuisance-bias and held-out empirical-term arguments for a covariance target.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
1 The problem this page solves
The Model restrictions and efficiency page introduced an asymptotic efficiency benchmark and showed how its influence function can depend on unknown nuisance quantities. Here the nuisance is a regression function: how a gene’s mean, or variance, depends on covariates such as cell composition, age, batch, or an interferon score. The estimand here is the average conditional covariance between two genes after removing their conditional means given Z, rather than a causal or conditional-independence claim. We do not want to assume the regressions are linear, so we estimate them flexibly, and then we need to know how the error in those flexible estimates propagates into the estimand. For this target, an orthogonal residual-product equation removes the first-order population nuisance error. Its exact remaining bias and its empirical fluctuation still need control.
This transfer application reuses Neyman orthogonality and cross-fitting for a different target. The task is to determine which derivatives and remainder terms change for covariance.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
2 The efficient influence function, briefly
The Model restrictions and efficiency page defines the EIF as the canonical gradient in the model’s tangent space. Its variance is the asymptotic variance bound for regular estimation under the relevant conditions; an estimator still needs an expansion and a variance argument to attain it. For nondegenerate plain correlation in the unrestricted model, the sample correlation has the canonical first-order expansion under suitable moments (finite fourth moments are sufficient here). Nuisance estimation creates additional work for adjusted targets.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
2 The conditional covariance, two ways
Let Z be a covariate (say, a cell-composition score), and let m_X(z) = E[X \mid Z = z] and m_Y(z) = E[Y \mid Z = z]. The estimand is the average conditional covariance

\psi = E\big[\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y \mid Z)\big].

This is the covariance between two genes after removing what each shares with Z, averaged over the population. There are at least two correct formulas for it:

\psi = E\big[(X-m_X(Z))(Y-m_Y(Z))\big]


\psi = E[XY]-E[m_X(Z)m_Y(Z)]

The first is the residual form and the second the difference form. Both are exactly right if m_X and m_Y are the true regression functions. Both can be turned into estimators by plugging in estimates \hat m_X and \hat m_Y and averaging. They behave completely differently when the estimates are imperfect.
To verify their equality, expand the residual product. The tower property gives E[Xm_Y(Z)]=E[m_X(Z)m_Y(Z)], and the same identity holds with X and Y reversed. Two subtractions and one addition of that mean-product term leave the difference form. Algebraic equivalence at the truth does not imply equal sensitivity to estimated inputs.
Write W=(X,Y,Z) for one person’s record. Throughout, P f=E[f(W)] denotes a population average, P_n f=n^{-1}\sum_i f(W_i) a sample average, and \|f\|_2=\{E[f(W)^2]\}^{1/2} the population root-mean-square size. Existence of the covariance needs second moments of X and Y. A CLT for their residual product needs the product itself to have finite variance; suitable fourth moments are a convenient stronger condition.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
3 Neyman orthogonality
We want a formula whose population value changes little when a fitted conditional mean is slightly wrong. Write the trained errors as \delta_X=\hat m_X-m_X and \delta_Y=\hat m_Y-m_Y. A fitted residual is U_X-\delta_X, so the exact expansion is

\begin{aligned}
E[(U_X-\delta_X)(U_Y-\delta_Y)]&=\psi-E[U_X\delta_Y]-E[U_Y\delta_X] +E[\delta_X\delta_Y]\\
&=\psi+E[\delta_X\delta_Y].
\end{aligned}

The two single-error terms vanish because each error is a function of Z and each true residual has conditional mean zero given Z. Only their product remains. In contrast, plugging into the difference form leaves -E[m_X\delta_Y+m_Y\delta_X+\delta_X\delta_Y], including single-error terms. This exact comparison motivates the derivative definition that follows.
Hold the population law P fixed and write the population estimating map as M(m), with nuisance arguments m and true pair m_0=(m_X,m_Y) satisfying M(m_0)=\psi. The target is fixed; we are varying the nuisance arguments supplied to the formula. Perturb them along an admissible direction h. The equation is Neyman orthogonal when

\frac{\partial}{\partial\varepsilon}M(m_0+\varepsilon h)
\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}=0.

The derivative is taken at the true nuisance for the permitted directions. A quadratic remainder additionally needs smoothness and norm controls; a zero derivative alone is not a universal rate theorem. For the residual product below, the second-order term follows from exact algebra.
Residual form. Write U_X=X-m_X(Z) and U_Y=Y-m_Y(Z) for the true conditional-mean residuals. Perturb m_X by \varepsilon h_X(Z):

\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\varepsilon}E[(U_X-\varepsilon h_X)U_Y]\Big|_0&=-E[h_X(Z)U_Y]\\
&=-E[h_X(Z)E(U_Y\mid Z)]\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}

because E[Y - m_Y(Z) \mid Z] = 0 by definition of m_Y. The same holds for m_Y. The residual form is orthogonal. Its second-order term is E[h_X(Z) h_Y(Z)]\,\varepsilon^2: the product of the two nuisance errors.
Difference form. Perturb m_X:

\frac{\partial}{\partial\varepsilon} \{E[XY]-E[(m_X+\varepsilon h_X)m_Y]\}\Big|_0=-E[h_X(Z)m_Y(Z)],

This derivative is generally nonzero, so the difference-form plug-in is not generally orthogonal. Particular directions can still give zero derivative; orthogonality requires the condition for every relevant direction.
Here it is numerically. Inject a known error into the nuisance (inflate the true regression function by a factor 1 + \varepsilon) and watch the two formulas.


Code
set.seed(1)
n <- 20000
z <- runif(n); e1 <- rnorm(n); e2 <- rnorm(n)
x <- z + e1                 # m_X(z) = z
y <- z + 0.5 * e1 + e2      # m_Y(z) = z;  Cov(X, Y | Z) = 0.5 exactly
m_x <- z; m_y <- z          # the true nuisances

Residual   <- function(mx, my) mean((x - mx) * (y - my))
Difference <- function(mx, my) mean(x * y) - mean(mx * my)

eps <- c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4)
out <- sapply(eps, function(e) c(residual_form = Residual((1 + e) * m_x, (1 + e) * m_y),
                                 difference_form = Difference((1 + e) * m_x, (1 + e) * m_y)))
colnames(out) <- paste0("eps=", eps)
round(out, 3)


                eps=0 eps=0.05 eps=0.1 eps=0.2 eps=0.4
residual_form   0.494    0.495   0.498   0.508   0.548
difference_form 0.493    0.459   0.423   0.346   0.173


With m_X = m_Y = Z and Z uniform, the residual form’s error is \varepsilon^2 E[Z^2] = \varepsilon^2/3 (about 0.003 at \varepsilon = 0.1) and the difference form’s is -2\varepsilon/3 - \varepsilon^2/3 (about -0.07 at \varepsilon = 0.1). Those are population biases for this perturbation. The displayed sample averages also contain Monte Carlo fluctuation; these numerical biases are specific to the perturbation.


Code
grid <- seq(-0.3, 0.3, length.out = 201)
matplot(grid, cbind(residual = grid^2/3, difference = -(2*grid + grid^2)/3),
        type = "l", lty = c(1, 2), col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00"),
        xlab = "Nuisance perturbation epsilon", ylab = "Population bias")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "gray70")
legend("topright", c("Residual form", "Difference form"), lty = 1:2,
       col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00"), bty = "n")








Figure 1: Exact population bias in the stated synthetic perturbation. The residual formula changes quadratically; the difference formula has a nonzero first-order slope. These curves are not sampled estimates.





The remainder of the residual form is a product of the two nuisance errors, so it also vanishes when either regression function is exactly right. Keep m_X exact and make m_Y badly wrong:


Code
m_y_wrong <- 3 * z + 1                                   # a badly wrong nuisance function
round(c(residual_form   = Residual(m_x, m_y_wrong),      # still near 0.5 (Monte Carlo SE about 0.02)
        difference_form = Difference(m_x, m_y_wrong)),   # far from 0.5
      3)


  residual_form difference_form 
          0.488          -0.675 


The important condition is on the product of nuisance errors, not on the name of the learning algorithm. For root-n inference centered at the target, a usual sufficient condition here is

\|\delta_X\|_2\,\|\delta_Y\|_2=o_p(n^{-1/2}),

along with moment, consistency, and sampling conditions. Errors of exactly order n^{-1/4} each give a product of order n^{-1/2}, which need not be negligible; both being o_p(n^{-1/4}) is sufficient, and faster convergence of one can compensate for slower convergence of the other. Orthogonality removes the first-order population term, while cross-fitting helps control the empirical term. Neither promises valid inference for arbitrary nuisance fits. Chernozhukov et al. develop this distinction.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
section: 4 The connection to the efficient influence function
text:
4 The connection to the efficient influence function
Efficient influence functions provide a systematic route to orthogonal equations. Orthogonality to nuisance scores is a model-geometric statement; Neyman orthogonality concerns derivatives of the chosen estimating equation in its nuisance arguments. For a valid influence-function construction these properties are connected under regularity conditions. We can verify the nuisance derivative directly for this residual-product equation. For \psi above, the EIF is

\operatorname{EIF}(X,Y,Z)=U_XU_Y-\psi,

and setting its sample average to zero gives the residual form. The naive difference-form plug-in has first-order nuisance sensitivity. It is not automatically an estimator with a different valid influence function: its behavior also depends on how the regressions are estimated. So the recipe for an orthogonal estimator is: find the EIF, and estimate by solving its empirical mean equals zero. The one-step estimator adds an estimated influence-function correction to an initial estimate. Writing P_n for a sample average,

\hat\psi_{\rm step}=\hat\psi_{\rm initial} +P_n\phi(W;\hat\psi_{\rm initial},\hat m).

Here the centering parameter is included in the estimated influence function. For this residual-covariance equation the initial centering cancels algebraically, leaving the residual-product average. Equivalence to an estimating-equation solution must be checked for the particular target and construction, including how the initial target estimate enters the estimated EIF.
Why is this the influence function of a target that itself contains conditional means? Along a smooth path with score s, differentiating E_t[U_{X,t}U_{Y,t}] gives a law-change term E[U_XU_Ys] and two mean-change terms. Each mean-change term vanishes by conditional residual centering, just as in the calculation above. Since E[s]=0, the derivative is E[(U_XU_Y-\psi)s]. In the unrestricted model this identifies the canonical gradient. It is a derivative of the whole functional, including its changing conditional means, rather than a calculation that assumes those means are known.
Deriving EIFs is a skill; Hines et al. (2022) teach it with the Gateaux-derivative method from the Influence functions page, and Kennedy (2022) catalogs common examples. Residual correlation requires a further normalization step below.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
5 Cross-fitting
Cross-fitting separates a held-out observation from its own training fit. It does not make nuisance predictions correct or all held-out contributions jointly independent: different folds share training observations.
One more problem. If \hat m_X is fit on the same observations it is then evaluated on, the fit absorbs some of each observation’s own noise. The residual X_i - \hat m_X(Z_i) is then too small, and because Y_i - \hat m_Y(Z_i) is shrunk in a correlated way, the residual product is biased. For a fixed common linear smoother S, an error-covariance contribution is scaled by \operatorname{tr}\{(I-S)^\top(I-S)\}/N; a projection fit loses its rank in this trace. A smoothing spline is not generally a projection, and adaptive fits need their own analysis. The direction and size of the total finite-sample bias also depend on approximation error.
Cross-fitting prevents a held-out outcome from being used to train its own prediction. Split the sample into K folds. For each fold, fit the nuisances on the other K - 1 folds and evaluate the residuals on the held-out fold. Average the residual products over all folds. Each observation’s residual now uses a nuisance fit that never saw it.


Code
set.seed(2)
# Nonlinear nuisance so that a smoother is needed. Cov(X, Y | Z) = 0.5 again.
OneRep <- function(n, df = 15, K = 5) {
  z <- runif(n); e1 <- rnorm(n); e2 <- rnorm(n)
  m <- sin(2 * pi * z)
  x <- m + e1; y <- m + 0.5 * e1 + e2
  Fit <- function(zt, xt, ze) predict(smooth.spline(zt, xt, df = df), ze)$y
  in_sample <- mean((x - Fit(z, x, z)) * (y - Fit(z, y, z)))
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = n))
  r <- numeric(n)
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    tr <- fold != k; te <- fold == k
    r[te] <- (x[te] - Fit(z[tr], x[tr], z[te])) * (y[te] - Fit(z[tr], y[tr], z[te]))
  }
  c(in_sample = in_sample, cross_fit = mean(r))
}

# Bias is measured against the truth (0.5) and compared with the SD of the estimator.
Summarize <- function(n, R = 150) {
  res <- replicate(R, OneRep(n))
  bias <- rowMeans(res) - 0.5
  sd_hat <- apply(res, 1, sd)
  data.frame(n = n, estimator = rownames(res), bias = round(bias, 3),
             bias_mcse = round(sd_hat / sqrt(R), 4),
             sd = round(sd_hat, 3), bias_over_sd = round(bias / sd_hat, 2), row.names = NULL)
}
do.call(rbind, lapply(c(200, 800, 3200), Summarize))


     n estimator   bias bias_mcse    sd bias_over_sd
1  200 in_sample -0.042    0.0070 0.086        -0.48
2  200 cross_fit  0.044    0.0083 0.102         0.43
3  800 in_sample -0.008    0.0036 0.044        -0.19
4  800 cross_fit  0.013    0.0038 0.047         0.27
5 3200 in_sample -0.002    0.0017 0.021        -0.09
6 3200 cross_fit  0.004    0.0017 0.021         0.17


Read bias against its Monte Carlo SE and the estimator’s sampling SD. The common-smoother trace can explain downward in-sample noise absorption. Cross-fitting can leave positive bias because the two estimated regression errors are correlated through shared training noise.
This experiment does not prove root-n inference. Keeping the spline’s nominal degrees of freedom fixed does not generally make its approximation error vanish for every nonlinear mean. Three sample sizes do not establish an asymptotic rate, and changing the fold count need not decrease bias monotonically. Tuning, approximation, moments, and the full remainder still matter.

5.1 A counterexample: separated folds with a bad nuisance learner
Here both true conditional means are zero and the true residual covariance is 0.5. A one-nearest-neighbor fit interpolates its training outcomes, giving zero in-sample residual products. Out of fold, it predicts a different person’s noise. Because the same neighbor supplies both predictions, their errors have covariance 0.5: the cross-fitted residual product has expectation 1, not 0.5. The learner’s nuisance error does not vanish. A training-set mean is a consistent nuisance fit in this deliberately flat model.


Code
set.seed(22)
BadLearner <- function(n = 250, K = 5) {
  z <- runif(n); x <- rnorm(n); y <- 0.5*x + rnorm(n)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = n))
  nearest <- constant <- numeric(n)
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    tr <- which(fold != k); te <- which(fold == k)
    neighbor <- tr[max.col(-outer(z[te], z[tr], "-")^2, ties.method = "first")]
    nearest[te] <- (x[te]-x[neighbor])*(y[te]-y[neighbor])
    constant[te] <- (x[te]-mean(x[tr]))*(y[te]-mean(y[tr]))
  }
  c(in_sample_1NN = 0, cross_fit_1NN = mean(nearest), cross_fit_mean = mean(constant))
}
bad_fit <- replicate(120, BadLearner())
boxplot(t(bad_fit), names = c("In-sample\n1NN", "Cross-fit\n1NN", "Cross-fit\nmean"),
        col = c("gray80", "#D55E0033", "#2F80C833"), ylab = "Estimated residual covariance")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2)








Figure 2: An interpolation counterexample with 120 independent synthetic datasets. Separating folds removes own-outcome reuse, but a one-nearest-neighbor nuisance still leaves population bias. A training mean works here because the true means are zero.





A finite-sample spread in the plot does not change the exact expectation argument. To see the mechanism directly, the held-out person and their selected training neighbor have independent residual pairs, each with covariance 0.5. Expanding (X_i-X_{\rm neighbor})(Y_i-Y_{\rm neighbor}) leaves two covariance terms, totaling 1, because predicting with one neighbor retains its noise even as the training set grows. Predicting with a training mean instead adds only 0.5/n_{\rm train} in expectation. That extra term vanishes as the training set grows. Cross-fitting removes self-use in both cases, but only the second learner estimates the zero conditional means consistently in this example.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
section: 6 The fold includes the fitting pipeline
text:
6 The fold includes the fitting pipeline
For an independent-subject analysis, put all observations from one subject in the same fold. Estimate outcome-dependent preprocessing, feature selection, tuning, and nuisance regressions within the training data when they belong to the fitting pipeline; then apply those fitted operations to held-out observations. A fixed transformation chosen independently of the analysis can be applied consistently across folds. Shared preprocessing learned from all observations needs its own justification and can otherwise leak evaluation information into training.
For this average covariance, the held-out contribution and estimator are

\begin{aligned}
R_i&=\{X_i-\hat m_X^{(-k)}(Z_i)\} \times\{Y_i-\hat m_Y^{(-k)}(Z_i)\},\\
\hat\psi&=n^{-1}\sum_iR_i.
\end{aligned}

The estimated influence contributions are R_i-\hat\psi. For a residual correlation, estimate the covariance and both residual variances jointly; averaging stratum-specific correlations is a different target. Put v_X=E[U_X^2], v_Y=E[U_Y^2], and \rho=\psi/\sqrt{v_Xv_Y}, with both variances positive. The delta method gives

\phi_\rho=\frac{U_XU_Y-\psi}{\sqrt{v_Xv_Y}} -\frac{\rho}{2}\left\{ \frac{U_X^2-v_X}{v_X}+\frac{U_Y^2-v_Y}{v_Y}\right\}.

The first term tracks covariance uncertainty; the second tracks uncertainty in both normalizers. Replace all components by held-out estimates, then take the SD of the resulting influence values divided by \sqrt n under the inference conditions below. Reusing only the covariance SE would omit denominator uncertainty. Also, an exact m_X alone does not repair the Y variance: its population bias is E[\delta_Y^2]. The covariance’s either-mean-correct property therefore does not automatically transfer to correlation.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
section: 7 Conditions connecting the formula to an SE
text:
7 Conditions connecting the formula to an SE
Let D_0=(X-m_X)(Y-m_Y), and for fold k let H_k=D_{\hat m_k}-D_0. With w_k=n_k/n,

\hat\psi-\psi=(P_n-P)(D_0-\psi) +\sum_k w_k(P_{n,k}-P)H_k +\sum_k w_kE[\Delta_{X,k}\Delta_{Y,k}].

For i.i.d. units and a fixed number of nonvanishing folds, require 0<\operatorname{Var}(D_0)<\infty, \|H_k\|_2=o_p(1), and the product bias o_p(n^{-1/2}) in every fold. Conditional variance within each held-out fold controls the middle term; the proof in From an influence function to an estimator shows that step. Do not assume joint conditional independence across all folds.
Under these controls, averaging the true contributions gives a CLT and the sample SD of the estimated contributions divided by \sqrt n consistently estimates the SE. L2 consistency of mean fits alone need not imply L2 consistency of their products. Bounded outcomes/fits plus L2 nuisance consistency are one sufficient setup; suitable L4 moments and L4 nuisance consistency are another route. See Estimating nuisance functions for inference for a concrete learning-rate calculation.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
section: 8 Putting it together: the recipe we use
text:
8 Putting it together: the recipe we use
For an estimand with nuisances, the group’s estimators are built in this order.

Write the estimand as a functional \psi(F) and derive its efficient influence function.
Estimate the nuisances flexibly, with cross-fitting.
Construct the orthogonal formula or EIF estimating equation. Verify any claimed equivalence with a one-step or targeted construction for this particular target.
Standard error: for independent units and valid remainder conditions, use the sample standard deviation of estimated EIF values divided by \sqrt n. With clustered observations, aggregate contributions and use a design-appropriate variance calculation. Orthogonality alone does not establish these conditions.

For sample-specific network summaries, define the population quantity and derive the relevant correction before assigning an observation-level interpretation. The Jackknife pseudo-values page explains why simply recentering a cohort-derived score is not by itself an inferential argument.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
9 Words you will meet

Double robustness. A separate robustness property of some estimating equations with two nuisances (an outcome regression and a propensity or censoring model) where the estimator is consistent if either nuisance is correct. The residual form of \psi has this property: its remainder is the product E[h_X h_Y], so it is zero when either m_X or m_Y is exactly right, whatever the other is (see the check above). This same either-correct guarantee does not generally transfer to residual correlation: its two residual-variance denominators each have a squared-error remainder for their own mean fit.
Targeted learning, TMLE, double machine learning (DML). Related frameworks that can use orthogonal estimating constructions and sample splitting. Targeted learning emphasizes distributional updates, while DML emphasizes orthogonal moments with learned nuisances; neither label alone specifies a complete algorithm or proof. Some valid procedures avoid splitting by imposing different empirical-process conditions. For the same target and efficiency conditions, particular estimators can share an efficient first-order expansion. The frameworks are not interchangeable in every model or finite sample.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
11 Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Show that the variance \sigma^2 = E[(X - \mu)^2], viewed as a formula with nuisance \mu, is Neyman orthogonal in \mu. Then show that the formula E[X^2] - \mu^2 is not. Check both numerically by inflating \mu by 1 + \varepsilon.
In the orthogonality simulation, replace the inflation error with an additive error m + \varepsilon(Z - 1/2) and predict, before running, the leading term of each formula’s bias.
Change df in the cross-fitting example to 5 and to 40 and re-run at N = 200. How do the two biases change, and which grows faster with df? Then replace the smoothing spline with an average of 20 deep regression trees, each grown on a bootstrap resample (rpart is a recommended R package; use rpart.control() with cp=0, minsplit=5, and minbucket=3). Compare the in-sample and cross-fit biases. Why does a deep tree fit its own noise?
The residual correlation is \psi / \sqrt{\psi_{XX}\,\psi_{YY}} with \psi_{XX} = E[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)]. Write the orthogonal estimators of the three pieces and combine them. What does the delta method say about the standard error?

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
11 Reading
The DML paper and Kennedy review provide the formal conditions behind the constructions.

Hines, O., Dukes, O., Diaz-Ordaz, K., and Vansteelandt, S. (2022). Demystifying statistical learning based on efficient influence functions. The American Statistician, 76(3), 292 to 304. An introductory derivation-focused treatment.
Kennedy, E. H. (2022). Semiparametric doubly robust targeted double machine learning: a review. arXiv:2203.06469. Influence-function construction, remainder decomposition, and efficiency conditions.
Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., Duflo, E., Hansen, C., Newey, W., and Robins, J. (2018). Double/debiased machine learning for treatment and structural parameters. The Econometrics Journal, 21(1), C1 to C68. Section 2 for Neyman orthogonality and cross-fitting.
Vansteelandt, S. and Dukes, O. (2022). Assumption-lean inference for generalised linear model parameters. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 84(3), 657 to 685. Asks what a regression coefficient estimates when the model is wrong, defines an estimand that does not depend on the model being right, and builds the orthogonal estimator for it. The target remains defined independently of the correctness of the working regression model.
Tsiatis, A. A. (2006). Semiparametric Theory and Missing Data. Springer. Chapters 3 and 4 for the geometry, when you want the full version.

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
text: Before reading: Network inference from omics data, Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error, and Multiple testing when the tests are not independent. The residual-covariance page supplies the derivative, nuisance remainder, and inference conditions used here.

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
section: 1 A question about co-variation after adjustment
text:
1 A question about co-variation after adjustment
Do two measured features co-vary differently between groups after removing their conditional means given recorded covariates? A marginal correlation can change because a shared predictor varies or predicts the features differently. Here we define the adjusted association before choosing a network algorithm.
This complete synthetic analysis uses 600 independent people, one fully observed assay per person, six continuous features, a binary group A, and covariate Z. Feature values represent a fixed log2-intensity scale. All IDs and measurements are invented. There is no molecular-interaction ground truth: the generator supplies statistical covariance truth for checking an estimator. The case study does not model assay detection, annotation, normalization estimation, or biological causality.
The downloadable base-R script contains data generation, alignment, cross-fitting, all edge tests, a failure-aware simulation, and output writing. It runs without additional packages. An end-to-end expression analysis is the complementary example with missingness and a standardized mean contrast.

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
section: 2 Define the population edge and its contrast
text:
2 Define the population edge and its contrast
For feature j and group g, let m_{jg}(z)=E[Y_j\mid Z=z,A=g]. Define

\begin{aligned}
U_{jg}&=Y_j-m_{jg}(Z),\\
\psi_{jk,g}&=E[U_{jg}U_{kg}\mid A=g],\\
\Delta_{jk}&=\psi_{jk,1}-\psi_{jk,0}.
\end{aligned}

The edge is an average conditional covariance, averaging over the covariate distribution within group g. Its units are the product of the two outcome units. It is not a correlation, a coefficient from a precision matrix, conditional independence, or a causal interaction. Rescaling a feature rescales its incident edges.
If conditional covariances vary with Z, the contrast can reflect both their differences and the groups’ different covariate distributions. A common-population standardized covariance contrast is a different estimand and requires a different estimation/identification argument. In this generator the conditional covariance is constant within group, making the truth simple. Both groups have the same covariate distribution, but this convenience is not an assumption silently imposed on arbitrary data.
Six features yield 15 unordered pairs. Prespecify all 15 as the testing family; do not select promising pairs from the same outcomes and then report ordinary p-values as if prespecified. Each null is H_{0,jk}:\Delta_{jk}=0, not a null that either group has zero covariance.

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
section: 3 Derive the contribution before implementing it
text:
3 Derive the contribution before implementing it
Write W=(A,Z,Y_1,\ldots,Y_6) for one person’s complete record. Let \pi_g=P(A=g)>0 and R_{jk,g}=U_{jg}U_{kg}. For the nonparametric observed-data model, a mean-zero influence function for \psi_{jk,g} is

D_{jk,g}(W)=\frac{1\{A=g\}}{\pi_g}
            \{R_{jk,g}-\psi_{jk,g}\}.

To see the nuisance cancellation, differentiate the residual product along a smooth distributional path. Its mean-function derivative has terms involving E[U_{jg}\mid Z,A=g] or E[U_{kg}\mid Z,A=g], both zero. The remaining distribution derivative is the group-conditional mean derivative, including its group-probability denominator. Thus D_{jk}=D_{jk,1}-D_{jk,0} represents the contrast derivative. In the unrestricted observed-data model this is the efficient gradient when square integrable. Efficiency here refers to a regular-estimation asymptotic bound for this target and model.
The group factor can also be understood as the influence function of a ratio: \psi_{jk,g}=E[1\{A=g\}R_{jk,g}]/\pi_g. Changing the numerator alone would miss the change in the group probability. Differentiating both gives the centered residual product multiplied by 1\{A=g\}/\pi_g. People outside the group contribute zero to that group’s first-order term; people inside it represent the group through the inverse probability factor.
There is also an exact population remainder. For fixed trained mean estimates, put e_{jg}=\widehat m_{jg}-m_{jg}, and let \widehat R_{jk,g} denote the product of their two fitted residuals. Conditional mean-zero residuals give

\begin{aligned}
E[\widehat R_{jk,g}\mid A=g]&=\psi_{jk,g}+E[e_{jg}e_{kg}\mid A=g],\\
|E[e_{jg}e_{kg}\mid A=g]|&\leq\|e_{jg}\|_{2,g}\|e_{kg}\|_{2,g}.
\end{aligned}

The contrast bias is the group-1 product remainder minus the group-0 remainder. A small held-out prediction error is useful evidence, but does not alone establish the little-o product condition needed at the inference scale. The Orthogonality and cross-fitting page gives a counterexample where splitting fails to remove population bias.

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
section: 4 Data, alignment, and held-out residual products
text:
4 Data, alignment, and held-out residual products
The generator has group-specific quadratic conditional means. Residual variances are one. Three disjoint feature pairs have covariance 0.2 in group 0. In group 1, those covariances are 0.65, −0.35, and 0.2. All other conditional cross-covariances are zero. The block matrices are positive definite. Hence only F1–F2 and F3–F4 have nonzero contrasts, 0.45 and −0.55.


Code

study <- GenerateResidualNetwork()
fit <- EstimateResidualNetwork(study$assay, study$metadata)
fit$group_counts

1 person_0001     0    1

4 person_0004     0    5
5 person_0005     1    1
6 person_0006     0    5


The assay has features in rows and person IDs in columns. The metadata are deliberately shuffled. The estimator matches IDs, rejects duplicate/mismatched IDs or nonfinite values, and checks group counts and training-design rank. Simulation truth is a separate object and is never passed to the estimator.
Five folds are formed within groups. For each held-out fold and group, the script fits all six means using only the other people in that group, with basis (1,Z,Z^2). It then multiplies pairs of held-out residuals. The group average of these products is \widehat\psi_{jk,g}, and their difference is \widehat\Delta_{jk}. Each person has one held-out product per edge. Training sets overlap; this does not make the fitted residual products independent finite-sample data.
For one edge, follow the calculation in this order: predict both features from other people; subtract those predictions from the held-out values; multiply the two residuals; average the products separately by group; subtract group 0 from group 1. The product can be negative even though both residual variances are positive: it records whether the two features depart from their fitted means in the same or opposite directions. The estimator averages these signed products, rather than fitting a separate biological network to each person.
The influence calculation justifies their first-order variance under further conditions. Require nonvanishing group probabilities, independent people, fixed feature family and fold count, finite/nonzero influence variances, negligible fold-weighted product remainders, and held-out score differences converging in L2. Suitable L4/moment control on residuals and fits can ensure the latter; nuisance L2 consistency by itself need not control every product. In this fixed-dimensional, correctly specified quadratic generator, the regular least-squares fits have the requisite moments/rates asymptotically. This is a teaching case, not a proof for an arbitrary machine learner.

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
section: 5 Estimate uncertainty for the actual target
text:
5 Estimate uncertainty for the actual target
The asymptotic variance separates by group:

\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Delta_{jk})\approx\frac{\operatorname{Var}(R_{jk,1}\mid A=1)}{n_1} +\frac{\operatorname{Var}(R_{jk,0}\mid A=0)}{n_0}.

The implementation substitutes sample variances of held-out products and observed group counts. These finite-sample degrees-of-freedom conventions are asymptotically equivalent to the full influence-function variance. They do not establish an exact t distribution for learned residuals. Normal p-values and 95% intervals are asymptotic and pointwise.
To see the scale, a bivariate-normal residual pair with unit variances and covariance c has product variance 1+c^2. For F1–F2 the oracle product variances are therefore 1.04 and 1.4225 in groups 0 and 1. With 300 people per group, the oracle SE of the difference is about \sqrt{1.04/300+1.4225/300}=0.091. The actual group counts and fitted residuals vary, so the implementation estimates this quantity. The spread of the individual residual products is roughly one; averaging over independent people reduces estimation uncertainty to roughly a tenth in this example.

BY adjusts over the 15 prespecified tests. It handles arbitrary dependence among valid marginal p-values; our normal p-values have asymptotic justification under the conditions above. With a fixed finite family, that supports an asymptotic error guarantee, not exact finite-sample control. Pointwise 95% intervals are neither simultaneous intervals nor intervals with automatic post-selection coverage.
A raw 95% interval can exclude zero while BY does not declare a discovery, because these are different decision rules. BY applies the step-up procedure at 0.05/H_{15}, with H_{15}\approx3.32, to the entire family. The table retains all edges so the reader can distinguish effect size, pointwise uncertainty, and the family-level reporting rule. In real data the number of false discoveries is unknown; only the generator makes the realized FDP available for the evaluation below.

section: 6 Check why marginal and residual networks disagree
text:
6 Check why marginal and residual networks disagree

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
section: 7 Challenge the estimator with a paired simulation
text:
7 Challenge the estimator with a paired simulation
Use 200 independently generated datasets at each of n=300 and 900. Within each dataset, compare the correct quadratic nuisance basis with an intercept-only basis, using the same folds. The misspecified fits leave covariate mean structure in the residuals; cross-fitting still separates training people but does not repair that remainder.
The script retains every attempted dataset/model fit and its error message. Summaries report successes and failures. If any fail, performance conditional on success is not the whole procedure’s performance; investigate the failure pattern before making a claim. The reference run below has no failures.


Code

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
section: 8 Reproduce the analysis and audit the claim
text:
8 Reproduce the analysis and audit the claim
Download residual-network.R, save it in a project, and run the command below in a terminal. It writes the synthetic assay, shuffled metadata, separate truth, folds, all 15 edge results, simulation attempts, evaluation edge records/summaries, and R session information. The fixed data and fold seeds are visible in the script. The default evaluation uses 200 replicates per sample size/model; replace the final argument with 3 for a workflow smoke test, not a precision evaluation.
Rscript residual-network.R results 200
A defensible report says: “We compared average group-specific conditional covariances of the defined log2-intensity features, adjusting their means for Z, over all 15 prespecified pairs. We used person-level cross-fitting, influence-based pointwise uncertainty, and BY-adjusted asymptotic p-values.” It also states the measurement limitations and simulation scope. It does not call the discoveries physical interactions or claim that nonsignificance proves equality.
For repeated specimens, first define whether the target averages people, visits, scheduled times, or within-person changes. The contribution and weights must match that choice. Keep all records from a person in a fold, and use whole-person contributions under independent-person sampling. Simply plugging repeated row products into this script’s SE does not implement that extension; the Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference page provides the necessary framework.

title: An end-to-end residual-network analysis
text:
9 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · NETCASE-01 — Derive the residual-edge contrast and its contribution
Task type: Derivation and interpretation.
For one prespecified pair, define ψ_g and Δ, derive D_g including its group-probability factor, and derive the exact nuisance product remainder. Explain why this is neither a partial-correlation edge nor necessarily a common-covariate-population comparison.
Ready to continue when: you can connect the edge definition, centering, nuisance cancellation, and remainder to the estimator actually implemented.
Transfer: How would multiplying F1 by ten change the edge and its SE?


Hint

Differentiate the conditional group average, then use the zero conditional means of the true residuals.



Solution outline — open after trying

ψ_g=E[(Y_j−m_jg)(Y_k−m_kg)|A=g] and Δ=ψ_1−ψ_0. D_g=1(A=g)(R_g−ψ_g)/π_g, and D=D_1−D_0. Expanding trained residual products leaves E[e_jg e_kg|g] after the two cross terms vanish. Average conditional covariance is not precision-matrix partial correlation. The outer covariate law is group-specific; standardizing both groups to a common law changes the target.





Checkpoint · NETCASE-02 — Audit uncertainty and reproduce a failure case
Task type: Implementation and diagnosis.
Rerun the script, check ID alignment and all 15 family members, and locate the pointwise intervals, BY decisions, failure log, and MCSEs. Compare the quadratic and intercept-only fits for the sentinel null edge. State the independent unit and what must change for repeated specimens.
Ready to continue when: you can trace each conclusion to its target, inputs, conditions, and evaluation record rather than relying on a plot of discoveries.
Transfer: If no edge is significant after BY, what evidence would you need before claiming the two covariance networks are equivalent?


Hint

Compare a study SE with a simulation MCSE, and compare training separation with population remainder control.



Solution outline — open after trying

The implementation matches metadata by unique person IDs and evaluates all 15 pairs. Pointwise intervals do not give simultaneous or post-selection coverage. BY needs valid marginal p-values; normal approximations here are asymptotic. Monte Carlo SEs quantify estimated simulation metrics. Intercept-only means leave a nonvanishing product remainder despite cross-fitting. Repeated specimens need a newly specified person/visit target, cluster contributions and person-level folds, rather than treating extra rows as independent.




Additional practice (optional)

Derive the sentinel F1–F3 marginal covariance contrast under the generator and compare it with the simulation bias.
Change the random seed and report changes in point estimates, intervals, and BY discoveries without changing the tested family.
Design a separate estimator for a common-population standardized covariance contrast; identify its additional nuisance functions before coding.
Prespecify an equivalence margin for one edge and explain how its inferential question differs from testing Δ=0.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
text: Before reading: Read Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated, From a research question to an identified estimand, and From an influence function to an estimator. The target and data-audit sections can be read before completing all the proofs.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
section: 1 One research argument, from measurements to a reported contrast
text:
1 One research argument, from measurements to a reported contrast
We will analyze 24 synthetic expression features from independently sampled people. Group membership is associated with a recorded covariate and technical batch. Some whole-assay measurements are missing. The question is: how do the groups differ on the supplied log2 expression scale after standardizing to a common covariate distribution?
This extended worked application follows one argument: define the target, audit the data, construct its estimator and uncertainty, then assess the reported family of claims. Simulation checks specific predictions of that argument. The From an influence function to an estimator page supplies the proof pattern; here we combine group standardization with missing outcomes.
Everything in this example is synthetic. Feature IDs are invented. The generator supplies known truth for evaluation, while the estimator receives only the observed assay and metadata. No clinical or biological finding is being asserted.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
section: 2 Define the population, scale, and target
text:
2 Define the population, scale, and target
Let A be group (0 or 1), C=(Z,B) the recorded covariate and batch, and Y_g a feature’s calibrated log2 intensity. Define

\begin{aligned}
\mu_{ag}(c)&=E[Y_g\mid A=a,C=c],\\
\psi_g&=E_C[\mu_{1g}(C)-\mu_{0g}(C)].
\end{aligned}

The outer distribution is that of all eligible people in the source population, estimated using everyone’s recorded C, including people with missing assays. We do not condition on the realized covariate values as a fixed population. Variation in the sampled covariate mix therefore contributes to the influence function.








Decision
Specification in this case




Independent unit
One person, one specimen, one assay occasion


Population
The source population sampled by the synthetic generator


Measurement
Supplied calibrated log2 intensity; no learned normalization


Contrast
Mean conditional group difference standardized over the source population’s C distribution


Missingness
One recorded indicator R for a missing whole assay; all covariates remain observed


Family
All 24 prespecified feature hypotheses H_{0g}:\psi_g=0


Interpretation
A standardized association; no causal interpretation is assumed




A log2 contrast exponentiates to a ratio of geometric means of the two standardized intensity distributions. It is not a ratio of arithmetic mean expression or an absolute molecules-per-cell contrast. The Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated page explains those distinctions. Real count data would need their own measurement and normalization argument before this analysis could be reused.
Group contrasts can vary with C. We do not impose a constant coefficient or a common regression slope across groups. Nor does adjustment alone turn this association into an intervention effect. A causal interpretation would need a well-defined intervention and additional identification assumptions.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
text:
3 Reconstruct the observation process
We observe W=(C,A,R,RY_1,\ldots,RY_G). Algebraically RY_g contributes zero when R=0; the stored assay uses NA for those outcomes. Treating those outcomes as measured zeros would change the analysis.
Assume E[|Y_g|]<\infty, outcome missingness at random given (A,C), and positive group and observation probabilities on the target support:

\begin{aligned}
e(c)&=P(A=1\mid C=c),\\
\pi_a(c)&=P(R=1\mid A=a,C=c),\\
q_a(c)&=P(A=a,R=1\mid C=c).
\end{aligned}

Thus q_1=e\pi_1 and q_0=(1-e)\pi_0. MAR identifies \mu_{ag} from the observed outcomes within group a. Positive q_a provides data for each required group/covariate combination. Stronger lower bounds will support the simple variance and remainder argument below.
The missingness assumption is known in this generator. In real assays, failure to detect a low-abundance feature can depend on its unobserved value; that mechanism is not automatically MAR. Feature-specific non-detection, missing covariates, repeated specimens, and perfect group–batch confounding each require a revised analysis. See Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target and Units of analysis, replication, and study design.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
text:
4 Generate and audit the study
The complete R functions use base R. Start from a fresh R session; each random operation has an explicit seed.


Code
source("../examples/adjusted-expression.R")
config <- ExpressionStudyConfig()
study <- GenerateExpressionStudy(config$n, config$genes, config$data_seed)
aligned <- AlignExpressionStudy(study$assay, study$metadata)
d <- aligned$metadata
c(features = nrow(study$assay), specimens = ncol(study$assay),
  people = length(unique(d$id)))


 features specimens    people 
       24       800       800 


Code
with(d, table(group = a, assay_observed = r))


     assay_observed
group   0   1
    0 132 221
    1 236 211


The assay has features in rows and person IDs in columns. Metadata are intentionally shuffled. AlignExpressionStudy() checks unique IDs, an exact match of specimen sets, and explicit column alignment. It rejects nonfinite observed outcomes and nonmissing values on rows declared unobserved. No complete-case sample exclusion is used to define the covariate distribution. Every person remains in the analysis.
The generator uses Z\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(-1,1) and B\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2) independently, with

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}e(C)&=-0.1+Z+0.5B,\\
\operatorname{logit}\pi_A(C)&=0.6-0.6A +0.5Z-0.3B.
\end{aligned}

Here \operatorname{logit}(p)=\log\{p/(1-p)\}; applying its inverse expit turns each linear predictor into a probability. This is a convenient factorization of the joint distribution, not a claim that technical batch causes group status. The conditional outcome mean is

\mu_{ag}(Z,B)=b_g+c_gZ+d_g(Z^2-1/3) +t_gB+a(\delta_g+h_gZ).

A shared bounded person-level noise component and independent bounded feature noise induce correlated features. Their conditional means are zero. Since E[Z]=0, the population standardized contrast is \psi_g=\delta_g. The first six features have nonzero \delta_g; the remaining eighteen have zero standardized contrasts, even though their conditional group contrasts vary with Z.
The generator returns these oracle values in a separate truth table. EstimateExpressionContrast() has no truth argument and does not receive the complete missing outcomes.


Code
g <- 12; z_grid <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 201)
conditional <- study$truth$psi[g] + study$truth$heterogeneity[g] * z_grid
plot(z_grid, conditional, type = "n", xlab = "Covariate Z",
     ylab = "Conditional group contrast (log2 units)")
for (side in list(z_grid <= 0, z_grid >= 0)) {
  polygon(c(z_grid[side], rev(z_grid[side])),
          c(conditional[side], rep(0, sum(side))),
          col = if (all(z_grid[side] <= 0)) "#D55E0033" else "#2F80C833", border = NA)
}
lines(z_grid, conditional, lwd = 2, col = "#2F80C8")
abline(h = study$truth$psi[g], lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Conditional contrast", "Population standardized contrast"),
       col = c("#2F80C8", "black"), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)








Figure 1: A zero standardized contrast can coexist with nonzero conditional contrasts. For synthetic gene_12, the positive and negative areas cancel under the uniform population distribution of Z. This is an association, not a causal curve.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
section: 5 Derive the contribution before fitting a model
text:
5 Derive the contribution before fitting a model
The influence function in the unrestricted observed-data model, under identification and square integrability, is

\phi_g(W)=\mu_{1g}(C)-\mu_{0g}(C)-\psi_g +\frac{AR}{q_1(C)}\{Y_g-\mu_{1g}(C)\} -\frac{(1-A)R}{q_0(C)}\{Y_g-\mu_{0g}(C)\}.

The first line captures variation in the population’s covariate mix. The second uses observed group-1 residuals; the third subtracts observed group-0 residuals. Conditional centering gives mean zero. In an inner product with an outcome-law score, the joint observation weight cancels the probability of observing that group’s outcome. Scores changing group assignment or observation alone have zero derivative for this functional. Covariate-distribution scores pair with the first line. This follows the derivation in From an influence function to an estimator separately for the two standardized means.
The uncentered contribution starts with the two predicted means for everyone’s C. An observed group-1 person then adds their weighted prediction error; an observed group-0 person subtracts theirs. Someone with a missing assay contributes only the predicted contrast, but remains part of the target covariate population. For example, suppose a held-out person’s predictions are 6.5 and 6.0. If they are observed in group 1 with outcome 7.0 and fitted joint probability 0.25, their contribution is 0.5+(7.0-6.5)/0.25=2.5. That is a weighted statistical contribution, not their measured or causal individual contrast.
Why the joint probability? Among people with the same C, only a fraction q_1(C) both belong to group 1 and have an observed assay. Multiplying by AR/q_1(C) makes that subgroup’s residual correction represent its conditional population average. Weighting by the group probability alone would leave assay selection uncorrected; weighting by observation alone would leave the unequal group distribution of C uncorrected.
For held-out person i, estimate all nuisances on other people, construct the uncentered contribution \hat D_{ig}=\hat\phi_{ig}+\hat\psi_g, and average it.






NoteAlgorithm: cross-fitted standardized expression contrast



Inputs: the aligned observed assay, all people’s covariates and observation indicators, and prespecified fitting choices.

Randomly assign independent people to five folds. All features for a person stay together.
On each training set, fit group membership using a ~ z + batch and observation using r ~ a + z + batch.
Fit a quadratic outcome regression separately in each group, using only its observed training outcomes. All genes use the same design, but have separate coefficients.
Predict both group means, both observation probabilities, and the group probability on held-out covariates.
Add residual corrections only where the corresponding outcome is observed, then combine all held-out contributions.

Output: one contribution per person and feature, and their feature-wise means. Uncertainty additionally requires the remainder and sampling conditions below.


The residual correction uses q_a, not just the group probability or just the assay observation probability. It never multiplies an NA residual by zero. In code, the group-1 update is:


Code
observed_1 <- a == 1 & r == 1
score[observed_1, ] <- score[observed_1, , drop = FALSE] +
  sweep(y[observed_1, , drop = FALSE] - m1[observed_1, , drop = FALSE],
        1, q1[observed_1], "/")


This is the same code used in the downloadable function. For repeated specimens, splitting arbitrary columns would leak person-level information and the independent-person SE below would be inappropriate.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
section: 6 Name the remainder and the inferential conditions
text:
6 Name the remainder and the inferential conditions
Hold one training fit fixed. Let \Delta\mu_{ag}=\hat\mu_{ag}-\mu_{ag}. Its exact population bias is

P\hat D_g-\psi_g=E\!\left[\frac{\hat q_1-q_1}{\hat q_1}\Delta\mu_{1g}\right] -E\!\left[\frac{\hat q_0-q_0}{\hat q_0}\Delta\mu_{0g}\right].

If each fitted joint probability is at least a fixed \kappa>0, its magnitude is bounded by

\kappa^{-1}\big\{\|\hat q_1-q_1\|_2\|\Delta\mu_{1g}\|_2 +\|\hat q_0-q_0\|_2\|\Delta\mu_{0g}\|_2\big\}.

Both correct outcome regressions can make this bias vanish with controlled, incorrect weights. Correct joint probabilities can do so with controlled, incorrect outcome regressions. These are consistency statements. They do not automatically justify the same estimated influence-function SE under misspecification.
For the efficient first-order argument used here, require i.i.d. people; fixed fold count with nonvanishing fold proportions; MAR; true and fitted joint probabilities bounded below; bounded outcomes and fitted means; L2 consistency of all nuisances; each displayed product o_p(n^{-1/2}); and finite nonzero influence variance. The fold-wise conditional proof in From an influence function to an estimator controls the empirical remainder. The bias bound controls the other remainder. Then

\begin{aligned}
\hat\psi_g-\psi_g&=(P_n-P)\phi_g+o_p(n^{-1/2}),\\
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_g&=\frac{\operatorname{SD}(\hat D_{ig}-\hat\psi_g)}{\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}

The default generator and correctly specified finite-dimensional fits provide a transparent setting for these conditions. This does not demonstrate that those nuisance models are adequate in a real cohort. Nor does the fixed-24-feature argument establish uniform validity when the number of features grows rapidly with sample size.
The SE formula uses variation in the constructed contributions across all sampled people, including those with missing assays. It is not the raw expression SD divided by the square root of the observed assay count. Cross-fitting contributions share training fits; their dependence becomes negligible at first order only through the displayed expansion. The proof, rather than treating fitted scores as new independent data, justifies this variance calculation.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
text:
8 Address the family of claims
Use the two-sided asymptotic Wald p-value for H_{0g}:\psi_g=0. All 24 tests belong to the prespecified family. Shared noise and nuisance fitting induce dependence. We use Benjamini–Yekutieli (BY) as the primary FDR adjustment because its multiplicity result permits arbitrary dependence among valid null p-values. This does not remove the need for valid individual tests; here those are asymptotic approximations.
The calculation takes all 24 raw p-values, sorts them, and applies the BH step-up rule at 0.05/H_{24}, where H_{24}\approx3.78. It then maps the decisions back to feature IDs. This is the BY algorithm in Multiple testing when the tests are not independent; selecting just the displayed or smallest-p-value features first would change the family and the guarantee. Each null concerns the standardized contrast, so a gene with varying conditional contrasts can still be a true null in this family.
With a fixed family and jointly adequate marginal approximations, the argument supports asymptotic FDR control at 0.05. It is not an exact finite-sample guarantee. BH can be less conservative under appropriate dependence conditions, but positive feature correlations alone do not establish the required condition for these two-sided tests. See the Multiple testing when the tests are not independent page and R’s adjustment documentation.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
section: 9 Challenge the analysis in repeated samples
text:
9 Challenge the analysis in repeated samples
Evaluate all features on the same synthetic datasets under four prespecified fitting choices: both model families correct; only outcome models correct; only weight models correct; both wrong. Incorrect models are intercept-only fits. Repeat at n=400 and 1200. The two singly correct cases investigate double-robust consistency; the efficient-SE theorem above requires all nuisance functions consistent and does not promise interval calibration in those cases.


Code
records <- EvaluateExpressionStudy(B = config$simulation_replicates,
  ns = config$simulation_n, genes = config$genes, folds = config$folds,
  seed = config$simulation_seed, alpha = config$alpha,
  probability_bounds = config$probability_bounds, mean_bounds = config$mean_bounds)
performance <- SummarizeExpressionEvaluation(records)

}








Figure 4: Mean estimation error for the prespecified null gene_12. Bars are plus/minus two MCSEs for the simulated bias, not SEs of an individual gene estimate. Each scenario uses the same datasets and folds. Small horizontal offsets separate scenarios at each sample size. Only two sample sizes are shown; the asymptotic claims come from the remainder analysis.





For interval and multiplicity summaries, first compare the fully specified setup with the deliberately wrong setup:



Code
performance[performance$scenario %in% c("Both correct", "Both wrong"),
  c("n", "scenario", "coverage", "coverage_mcse", "fdr", "fdr_mcse", "true_positive_fraction")]


     n     scenario   coverage coverage_mcse         fdr    fdr_mcse
1  400 Both correct 0.95833333   0.005772288 0.005595238 0.003296084
4  400   Both wrong 0.12833333   0.015036898 0.737973926 0.017038970
5 1200 Both correct 0.95125000   0.008185880 0.010714286 0.004439868
8 1200   Both wrong 0.01666667   0.003792085 0.803885440 0.002060112
  true_positive_fraction
1              0.9783333
4              0.6800000
5              1.0000000
8              0.7216667



Within each replicate, coverage is the fraction of the 24 fixed targets covered, and FDP is false rejections divided by all rejections (zero when no tests reject). We average those replicate summaries. Their MCSEs use variation across independent datasets; genes within a dataset are not independent simulation replicates. A plug-in MCSE can be zero if every observed FDP is zero; that does not prove true FDR is zero.
Each attempt is retained with seeds, success status, and any error. Metrics are conditional on successful complete-family fits, so report success counts alongside them; do not interpret conditional performance as unconditional reliability when fits fail. One hundred replicates make this a runnable teaching experiment, with visibly reported Monte Carlo uncertainty. A research benchmark should plan its replicate count from the precision needed.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
section: 10 Reproduce the inputs, run, and report
text:
10 Reproduce the inputs, run, and report
Download the complete project, which includes the R functions, editable configuration, runner, observed synthetic assay/metadata, truth stored separately for evaluation, diagnostics, contributions, all simulation attempts, manifests, software information, Quarto report source, and rendered report. You can also read the standalone report.
The archive’s results/ is the supplied reference run. From the unpacked project root, rebuild into a new directory so the reference run remains available:


Code
Rscript run.R rerun-results
quarto render report.qmd -P results_dir:rerun-results


The runner refuses to overwrite a populated output directory. It records input/output identity and code/configuration checksums for local change tracking. Analysis needs base R; rendering the report additionally needs a working Quarto R/knitr installation. The report reads explicit result files and has freezing disabled. It can be regenerated without an interactive workspace.
A methods paragraph should state the scale, population, independent unit, target distribution, missingness assumptions, nuisance models, folds, clipping, family, uncertainty calculation, and inferential limits. For example, the following is generated from this run:

Code
s <- results[1, ]; a <- fit$diagnostics
cat(sprintf(paste0(
  "In this synthetic study, %d independently sampled people supplied covariates, ",
  "and %d supplied the whole expression assay. We standardized group contrasts ",
  "to the source-population covariate distribution using all people. ",
  "For gene_01, the cross-fitted augmented estimate was %.3f log2 units ",
  "(SE %.3f; pointwise approximate 95%% interval %.3f to %.3f). ",
  "The prespecified family contained %d features; BY at 0.05 rejected %d nulls. ",
  "Fitted probabilities and means required clipping for %.1f%% and %.1f%% ",
  "of their predictions. These are standardized associations under the stated ",
  "MAR, overlap, sampling, and nuisance-rate conditions; they do not establish ",
  "causal or absolute-abundance effects.\n\n"),
  a$n, a$observed, s$estimate, s$se, s$lower, s$upper,
  nrow(results), sum(results$reject_BY), 100 * a$probability_clipped, 100 * a$mean_clipped))

In this synthetic study, 800 independently sampled people supplied covariates, and 432 supplied the whole expression assay. We standardized group contrasts to the source-population covariate distribution using all people. For gene_01, the cross-fitted augmented estimate was 0.670 log2 units (SE 0.050; pointwise approximate 95% interval 0.572 to 0.767). The prespecified family contained 24 features; BY at 0.05 rejected 6 nulls. Fitted probabilities and means required clipping for 0.0% and 0.0% of their predictions. These are standardized associations under the stated MAR, overlap, sampling, and nuisance-rate conditions; they do not establish causal or absolute-abundance effects.
The scientific interpretation is bounded by the target and assumptions, even when execution is reproducible and the synthetic answer is close to truth. Return to Reporting a statistical methods study for the full claim/evidence checklist.

title: An end-to-end expression analysis
text:
11 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · CASE-01 — Specify and identify the expression contrast
Task type: Interpretation and derivation.
Write the independent observation, measurement scale, population distribution, estimand, and tested family for this case. Derive why the generator gives \psi_g=\delta_g. Explain how a feature can have \psi_g=0 with conditional contrasts that vary with Z, and state the missingness/support assumptions needed to identify the full-population contrast.
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish the standardized target from a complete-case crude contrast, a constant regression coefficient, and a causal effect.
Transfer: If the target covariate distribution were that of group 1, would the same delta remain the target? Explain what changes in estimation and uncertainty.


Hint

Average the conditional contrast over the specified population, then identify which outcome laws are actually observed.



Solution outline — open after trying

One independent observation is a person’s covariates, group, observation indicator, and observed assay vector. The outcome is calibrated log2 intensity, and the family contains all 24 feature-wise standardized-contrast nulls. The conditional contrast is \delta_g+h_gZ; since the population has E[Z]=0, its average is \delta_g. A zero average need not imply zero contrast at every covariate value. MAR within group/covariates identifies the outcome regressions from observed outcomes; positive group and observation probabilities are needed throughout the target support, and covariates must be observed for the target population. None of these statements alone gives a causal or absolute-abundance interpretation.





Checkpoint · CASE-02 — Reconstruct the estimator and its remainder
Task type: Derivation and implementation.
Derive the conditional expectation of each residual correction, then the two-term exact bias displayed in this page. Explain why the weight uses the joint probability q_a. Reconstruct the fold procedure without accessing simulation truth or unobserved outcomes, and identify the conditions needed before using the estimated influence-function SE.
Ready to continue when: you can connect every correction and condition to an observed-data quantity and explain what double-robust consistency does and does not establish.
Transfer: If observation probabilities depend on the unobserved expression even after conditioning on group and C, which step of the argument fails?


Hint

Hold a training fit fixed. For group a, the expected observed residual is q_a times the difference between the true and fitted conditional mean.



Solution outline — open after trying

The group-a correction has fresh-observation expectation E[q_a(\mu_{ag}-\hat\mu_{ag})/\hat q_a]. Combining it with each plug-in mean yields the displayed signed product remainders. Weighting only by group or observation probability fails to cancel the joint observation process. Fit all nuisance functions on other people, evaluate both group predictions on all held-out covariates, and correct residuals only on observed rows of the matching group. For efficient inference, check nuisance consistency, lower probability bounds, product little-o rates, the held-out empirical term, finite variance and sampling/moment conditions. A wrong but controlled nuisance can permit consistency while invalidating that efficient-SE argument.





Checkpoint · CASE-03 — Interpret discoveries and uncertainty correctly
Task type: Interpretation and computation.
Explain the difference between a pointwise 95% interval, BY FDR control for the 24-feature family, a realized FDP in one simulation, and MCSE for estimated FDR. State the assumptions left after selecting BY and explain why you cannot treat 24 genes in each of 100 datasets as 2,400 independent replicates.
Ready to continue when: you can label each uncertainty quantity and error criterion, including the conditions multiplicity adjustment cannot repair.
Transfer: If you display only the twelve prespecified plot features, does the tested family shrink to twelve? What if those twelve were chosen after inspecting significance?


Hint

Ask whether the expectation is over people, repeated datasets, or the feature family.



Solution outline — open after trying

A pointwise interval targets one feature’s population contrast across samples. BY targets the expected FDP across repeated analyses of a stated family, allowing arbitrary p-value dependence but requiring valid null p-values; the Wald p-values here are asymptotically justified under the estimator’s conditions. One simulated FDP is known only because truth is supplied. Its average estimates FDR; its MCSE is the SD of replicate FDPs divided by the square root of the number of independent successful datasets. Within-dataset genes share people, noise, and fits. BY does not create simultaneous confidence intervals or repair missingness, target, or sampling errors.





Checkpoint · CASE-04 — Reproduce and challenge the complete analysis
Task type: Execution and diagnosis.
Unpack the project, regenerate it in a new results directory, render its report, and compare target estimates and simulation records with the reference run. Audit the input alignment, missing-outcome conventions, seeds, code/configuration identities, warnings, clipping, and attempted/successful counts. Before examining the four scenario summaries, predict which cases support consistency and which support the efficient-SE theorem.
Ready to continue when: you can rebuild the result, trace a claim to its inputs and assumptions, and diagnose a failed condition without silently discarding failures.
Transfer: Change only the number of folds or one model class, record a new run, and distinguish stochastic changes from a changed target or invalid theorem.


Hint

Use a fresh session and retain the reference directory. Derive the exact bias prediction before looking at the simulation plot.



Solution outline — open after trying

The documented runner sources explicit functions and configuration, writes observed inputs separately from oracle truth, and records results, diagnostics, attempts, manifests, and software information. With the tested environment and seeds the statistical outputs reproduce; session metadata can differ across environments. Correct outcomes or correct joint weights can remove population bias under the stated controls. The fully consistent, sufficiently fast nuisance case supports the efficient-SE argument; single-model correctness alone does not. Both wrong leaves a generally nonzero remainder. Inspect failures and their denominators rather than assuming missing rows succeeded.




Additional practice (optional)

Extend the generator to feature-specific missingness and derive the corresponding observation probabilities; do not silently reuse the whole-assay indicator.
Use an external target covariate sample. Derive the new target and account for its sampling variation instead of treating the current influence function as unchanged.
Compare the four scenarios across more sample sizes and choose replicate counts from a prespecified MCSE goal. Treat singly correct nuisance cases as a separate inference problem.
Construct a simultaneous interval procedure for the prespecified family and explain how its claim differs from the plotted pointwise intervals.

Kennedy, review of influence-function estimation: standardized means, estimator construction, and remainder analysis.
