13 Continue through the guide
Return to the Omics analysis problems overview, compare with the Differential expression and abundance page, or assess the four case-study tasks in the Completion checkpoints page.

title: Differential expression and abundance
text:
Before reading: The relevant assay primer in Omics data and measurement, basic regression, and the distinction between an estimand and a model coefficient. The worked examples use gene expression; transferring the design and contrast ideas to another assay requires its own measurement and variance assumptions.
For a population-standardized contrast with covariate-varying group differences and missing assays, see An end-to-end expression analysis. Its target and assumptions differ from a constant linear-model contrast; the examples are not a blanket ranking of procedures.

title: Differential expression and abundance
text:
1 Start with a feature-level contrast
For a feature g measured on a stated scale, an unadjusted group contrast is \Delta_g=E[Y_g\mid A=1]-E[Y_g\mid A=0]. If adjustment is needed, define the conditional contrast or specify a common covariate distribution Q over which to average it. The corresponding standardized contrast is \int\{E[Y_g\mid A=1,Z=z]-E[Y_g\mid A=0,Z=z]\}\,dQ(z). These targets need not equal a coefficient in an arbitrary regression.
Decide which units are independent, which design supports the contrast, and which preprocessing created Y_g. Here the worked method is limma for log-expression, with a common linear contrast across the modeled covariates. Applying a similar workflow to proteins, metabolites, or relative microbial abundances requires assay-appropriate measurement and observation models. A difference on the log scale is not a difference in mean abundance on the original scale.
The What is your estimator actually estimating? page explains interpretation under misspecification; the Omics data and measurement overview compares the available assay primers and the assumptions that differ across them.

title: Differential expression and abundance
text:
2 One regression per gene
The standard analysis of an expression matrix fits the same linear model to every gene. For gene g with expression y_{gi} in sample i (on the log scale),

\begin{aligned}
y_{gi}&= \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol\beta_g + \varepsilon_{gi},\\
\varepsilon_{gi}&\sim N(0, \sigma_g^2),
\end{aligned}

where independent-person errors are assumed in this unweighted teaching model. The vector \mathbf{x}_i records sample i’s group and covariates. It is the same row of the design matrix for every gene; the coefficient vector \boldsymbol\beta_g and residual variance \sigma_g^2 are gene-specific. With 15,000 genes this is 15,000 regressions sharing one design, not 15,000 independent people.
Let X have N rows and r linearly independent columns. Choose a fixed contrast vector c: for example, a vector that selects the patient coefficient, or subtracts the control mean coefficient from the patient mean coefficient. The model contrast and ordinary least-squares uncertainty are

\begin{aligned}
\theta_g&=c^\top\boldsymbol\beta_g,\\
\hat\theta_g&=c^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_g,\\
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_g\mid X)
&=\sigma_g^2\,c^\top(X^\top X)^{-1}c,\\
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_g
&=s_g\sqrt{c^\top(X^\top X)^{-1}c}.
\end{aligned}

The design factor describes how much information this study provides about the chosen contrast. The residual SD s_g describes feature-specific noise after fitting the mean. Their product is the contrast’s SE; neither alone is the SE. Dividing \hat\theta_g-\theta_{g,0} by that SE gives an ordinary t-statistic for the specified null value. Under this Gaussian, constant-variance, independent-error model its reference has N-r residual degrees of freedom.
Everything you know about linear regression applies, per gene. What is new is that the number of samples is small (often 10 to 50), the number of genes is large, and the questions are asked across genes. Those three facts are what limma (Smyth 2004; Ritchie et al. 2015) is built around.

title: Differential expression and abundance
section: 3 The design matrix is the analysis
text:
3 The design matrix is the analysis
Students arriving from a regression course know lm(y ~ group). In expression work you write the design matrix explicitly, once, and hand it to every gene.


Code
group <- factor(rep(c("control", "patient"), c(6, 10)))
batch <- factor(rep(c("b1", "b2"), 8))
sex   <- factor(replace(rep("F", 16), c(4, 11), "M"))   # two males, fixed so the page renders the same every time
X <- model.matrix(~ group + batch + sex)
head(X)


  (Intercept) grouppatient batchb2 sexM
1           1            0       0    0
2           1            0       1    0
3           1            0       0    0
4           1            0       1    1
5           1            0       0    0
6           1            0       1    0


Code
colnames(X)


[1] "(Intercept)"  "grouppatient" "batchb2"      "sexM"        


Reading it: the intercept is the control, batch 1, female baseline; grouppatient is the patient-minus-control difference at fixed batch and sex under the stated common-contrast model; batchb2 and sexM are adjustments. Adding a covariate to the design is what “adjusting for” means in practice, and the What is your estimator actually estimating? page says what that buys: the coefficient on group is the group difference within levels of the covariates, which is the estimand you want only if the covariates are the right ones and enter correctly (a continuous composition score entered linearly is a linear adjustment; the group’s research on cell-composition adjustment is about what that leaves behind).
Two design decisions that come up constantly:

Group-means parameterization. model.matrix(~ 0 + group) gives one column per group and you then form contrasts (patient - control). Equivalent fits, often clearer when there are three or more groups.
Interactions. ~ group * sex lets the group difference differ by sex. Use interactions when the target permits group differences to vary across the covariate. Without them, a common-contrast assumption is being imposed; their value is not decided by available degrees of freedom alone.

For a continuous covariate Z, a model containing A, Z, and AZ has conditional group contrast \beta_{A,g}+\beta_{AZ,g}z. The coefficient on A alone is the contrast at z=0. Averaging over a specified covariate population gives \beta_{A,g}+\beta_{AZ,g}E[Z]. These coincide only in special cases. Always translate the proposed contrast into words before fitting it.
The inverse above also needs full column rank. If every patient is in batch 2 and every control is in batch 1, separate group and batch effects cannot be learned from this design. Software cannot recover the missing comparison by adding both columns. Even with full rank, limited overlap can make the contrast imprecise or dependent on extrapolation of the mean model.


Code
stopifnot(qr(X)$rank == ncol(X))
image(seq_len(ncol(X)), seq_len(nrow(X)), t(X[nrow(X):1, ]),
      col = c("white", "#2F80C8"), zlim = c(0, 1), xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n",
      xlab = "Design column", ylab = "Specimen")
axis(1, at = 1:4, labels = c("Intercept", "Patient", "Batch 2", "Male"), cex.axis = 0.8)
axis(2, at = 1:16, labels = 16:1, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.65)








Figure 1: The shared design has 16 specimens and four columns. Group and batch overlap, and both groups contain the sex categories; the rank check matters more than the visual appearance alone. Rows are not automatically independent people.





The design matrix specifies mean contrasts; the covariance model and variance calculation specify how dependence is handled. An ordinary independent-error fit with one row per specimen is inadequate when repeated specimens from one subject remain correlated. The repeated-measures section below discusses alternatives.

title: Differential expression and abundance
section: 4 What limma adds: borrowing strength across genes
text:
4 What limma adds: borrowing strength across genes
With N=16 and four linearly independent design columns, fitting the mean uses four dimensions, leaving 16-4=12 residual degrees of freedom. The estimate is s_g^2=\mathrm{RSS}_g/12. Across hypothetical repetitions, a gene’s variance estimate can be too small or too large relative to its true variance. An accidentally small denominator can inflate a t-statistic, although a large statistic can also reflect a large numerator; the top-ranked genes need not have the smallest absolute variances.
limma’s empirical Bayes step assumes the true variances across genes are drawn from a common prior, a scaled inverse chi-square with d_0 degrees of freedom and scale s_0^2, and forms a moderated variance estimate

\tilde s_g^2 = \frac{d_0\, s_0^2 + d_g\, s_g^2}{d_0 + d_g}.

Each gene’s variance is pulled toward the common value s_0^2, by an amount that depends on how informative the prior is (d_0) relative to the data (d_g). In the ideal known-prior model, the moderated t uses \tilde s_g in the denominator and has a marginal t_{d_0+d_g} reference. This is calibration over the stated hierarchical variance distribution, not an exact conditional-on-every-fixed-variance theorem. In the implementation the hyperparameters are estimated, residual degrees of freedom can vary, and the total degrees of freedom are also constrained by available information. The formula is the simple constant-prior teaching case. d_0 and s_0^2 are estimated from the spread of the observed s_g^2 across genes (Smyth 2004, Section 6), so the shrinkage is data-driven: if gene variances really vary a lot, d_0 is small and little shrinkage happens.
The formula is a weighted average: the prior scale gets weight d_0/(d_0+d_g) and the observed variance gets weight d_g/(d_0+d_g). With d_0=4, d_g=12, and s_0^2=1, an observed variance of 2 becomes 1.75, while an observed variance of 0.1 becomes 0.325. Moderation can move a variance up or down. The added prior degrees of freedom represent information borrowed through the variance model, not four additional people.
The moderated statistic replaces s_g by \tilde s_g in the SE formula above; it leaves the fitted contrast in the numerator unchanged. This is why understanding the ordinary regression calculation first makes moderation easier to interpret.
Here is the effect with a known prior, which is a simplified version of what eBayes() estimates. This separate simulation uses only two group means and no batch/sex adjustment, so its design has rank 2 and residual degrees of freedom 16-2=14, rather than the earlier design’s 12.


Code
set.seed(1)
G <- 5000; n1 <- 8; n2 <- 8; d_g <- n1 + n2 - 2
sigma2 <- 1 / rgamma(G, shape = 2, rate = 2)        # inverse-chi-square scale 1, df 4; mean 2
Y1 <- matrix(rnorm(G * n1, sd = sqrt(sigma2)), G)   # control; no true differences
Y2 <- matrix(rnorm(G * n2, sd = sqrt(sigma2)), G)   # patient
diff <- rowMeans(Y2) - rowMeans(Y1)
s2 <- (rowSums((Y1 - rowMeans(Y1))^2) + rowSums((Y2 - rowMeans(Y2))^2)) / d_g
se_factor <- sqrt(1 / n1 + 1 / n2)
t_ord <- diff / (sqrt(s2) * se_factor)

d0 <- 4; s0_2 <- 1                                   # true prior scale here; limma estimates it
s2_mod <- (d0 * s0_2 + d_g * s2) / (d0 + d_g)
t_mod <- diff / (sqrt(s2_mod) * se_factor)

# Assess noise relative to each gene's own known variance, not absolute s2.
top_ord <- order(-abs(t_ord))[1:20]
rbind(all_genes = quantile(s2 / sigma2), top_ordinary_t = quantile((s2 / sigma2)[top_ord]))


                      0%       25%       50%       75%     100%
all_genes      0.1372922 0.7155509 0.9485540 1.2208810 3.160393
top_ordinary_t 0.2766340 0.4472796 0.4822695 0.5507113 0.639766


Code
# The moderated reference here is marginal under this known-prior generator.
c(ordinary = mean(2 * pt(-abs(t_ord), d_g) < 0.05),
  moderated = mean(2 * pt(-abs(t_mod), d0 + d_g) < 0.05))


 ordinary moderated 
   0.0570    0.0548 


Moderation borrows information about variances; it does not shrink the fitted group coefficient in this workflow. It can improve power and stability under suitable variance models, but cannot guarantee superiority for every feature or population. Compare the simulated rejection fractions with binomial MCSEs if assessing calibration across independently generated genes; that calculation is specific to this simulation.


Code
observed_s2 <- seq(0.05, 5, length.out = 200)
residual_df <- c(4, 14, 60)
curves <- sapply(residual_df, function(d) (4 + d * observed_s2)/(4 + d))
matplot(observed_s2, curves, type = "l", lty = 1:3,
        col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00", "#009E73"),
        xlab = "Observed residual variance", ylab = "Moderated variance")
abline(0, 1, col = "gray65"); abline(h = 1, lty = 3, col = "gray65")
legend("topleft", paste("Residual df", residual_df), lty = 1:3,
       col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00", "#009E73"), bty = "n")








Figure 2: Known-prior variance moderation toward scale 1. Smaller residual degrees of freedom give more shrinkage. The horizontal reference is a prior scale, not a known variance for every gene or the prior mean.






4.1 Run the actual log-expression workflow
This executable example uses synthetic log2 expression and the design above. It requires limma and its dependencies. Normalization is not learned in this generator. Feature and sample identifiers remain explicit.


Code
set.seed(81)
G_demo <- 600
beta <- rbind(rep(6, G_demo), c(rep(0.7, 40), rep(0, G_demo - 40)),
              rep(0.2, G_demo), rep(-0.1, G_demo))
variance_demo <- 1 / rgamma(G_demo, shape = 3, rate = 2)
rownames(X) <- paste0("sample_", seq_len(nrow(X)))
logexpr <- t(beta) %*% t(X) +
  matrix(rnorm(G_demo * nrow(X), sd = sqrt(variance_demo)), G_demo)
dimnames(logexpr) <- list(paste0("gene_", seq_len(G_demo)), rownames(X))
stopifnot(identical(colnames(logexpr), rownames(X)), qr(X)$rank == ncol(X))
fit <- limma::lmFit(logexpr, design = X)
fit <- limma::eBayes(fit, trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE)
limma::topTable(fit, coef = "grouppatient", number = 6, sort.by = "none",
                adjust.method = "BH", confint = TRUE)

The output is a six-row display from the full 600-feature family. number = 6 limits printing; it does not mean that only six hypotheses received the multiplicity adjustment. The model contrast is the constant patient–control difference at the same batch/sex levels. Report logFC, its scale, uncertainty, and the hypothesis family. The moderation and estimated hyperparameters are part of the inference model. BH still needs valid individual tests and the appropriate dependence conditions; its adjusted p-values do not make the displayed intervals simultaneous or selection-adjusted. See the Multiple testing when the tests are not independent page.


4.2 A separate raw-count example with voom
Do not feed raw counts into the unweighted log-expression model. This separate synthetic count example uses edgeR’s filtering and normalization factors, then voom’s observation-level precision weights. The resulting modeled scale and assumptions must be stated; it is not an absolute-abundance analysis or a validation of every real RNA-seq pipeline.


Code
set.seed(82)
expected_counts <- 2^(t(beta) %*% t(X)) *
  outer(rep(1, G_demo), exp(seq(-0.4, 0.4, length.out = nrow(X))))
counts <- matrix(rnbinom(length(expected_counts), mu = as.vector(expected_counts), size = 10),
                 G_demo, dimnames = dimnames(logexpr))
dge <- edgeR::DGEList(counts)
keep <- edgeR::filterByExpr(dge, design = X)
dge <- dge[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
dge <- edgeR::calcNormFactors(dge)
v <- limma::voom(dge, design = X, plot = TRUE)
count_fit <- limma::eBayes(limma::lmFit(v, design = X))
c(tested_features = nrow(v), independent_people = ncol(v))


   tested_features independent_people 
               600                 16 








Figure 3: The voom mean–variance trend in a separate synthetic count example. The fitted trend generates observation-level precision weights; it does not change the number of independent biological units.





Filtering defines the tested feature set and needs the workflow’s null-calibration justification. Keep the original counts and record filtering, normalization, design, and weighting decisions. trend=TRUE moderates variances with an intensity trend; voom models observation-level precision. They are not identical operations. The official limma documentation and voom paper describe the implementations.
A voom weight is approximately an inverse variance for a log-expression observation: a noisier observation receives less weight in fitting its gene’s mean model. It is not a count of additional biological replicates. Normalization factors address the modeled library scale, precision weights address variability on that scale, and variance moderation borrows information about residual variances. Understanding their separate roles helps diagnose which part of a workflow needs attention.

title: Differential expression and abundance
section: 5 What limma assumes, and when it breaks
text:
5 What limma assumes, and when it breaks
The empirical Bayes step buys power with assumptions. Know them.
One residual variance per gene, shared across groups. The linear model has a single \sigma_g^2 for all samples, so patients and controls are assumed equally variable. When they are not, the moderated t inherits the behavior of the pooled-variance t-test, which depends on which group is more variable and which is larger. The simple unweighted variance model has the same vulnerability as a pooled two-sample t-test. Welch addresses unequal variances for independent observations; it does not repair dependence from cohort-derived pseudo-values or network scores. See the variance issue on independently generated observations:


Code
set.seed(2)
Level <- function(n1, n2, sd1, sd2, R = 2000) {
  p <- replicate(R, {
    a <- rnorm(n1, sd = sd1); b <- rnorm(n2, sd = sd2)
    c(pooled = t.test(a, b, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value, welch = t.test(a, b)$p.value)
  })
  rate <- rowMeans(p <= 0.05)
  data.frame(n1, n2, sd1, sd2, method = rownames(p), rejection = rate,
             MCSE = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / R), row.names = NULL)
}
rbind(`5 vs 15, small group more variable` = Level(5, 15, 2, 1),
      `5 vs 15, small group less variable` = Level(5, 15, 1, 2),
      `10 vs 10, unequal variances`        = Level(10, 10, 2, 1))


                                     n1 n2 sd1 sd2 method rejection        MCSE
5 vs 15, small group more variable.1  5 15   2   1 pooled    0.1475 0.007929179
5 vs 15, small group more variable.2  5 15   2   1  welch    0.0490 0.004826956
5 vs 15, small group less variable.1  5 15   1   2 pooled    0.0100 0.002224860
5 vs 15, small group less variable.2  5 15   1   2  welch    0.0430 0.004536022
10 vs 10, unequal variances.1        10 10   2   1 pooled    0.0570 0.005184159
10 vs 10, unequal variances.2        10 10   2   1  welch    0.0515 0.004942052


Check the simulated rates and their Monte Carlo uncertainty. The pooled test is anti-conservative when the smaller group is more variable and can be conservative in the reverse configuration. Balance reduces this particular distortion but does not establish exact validity under unequal variances. Welch usually improves calibration here; very small samples still require scrutiny. The result concerns this synthetic configuration. Weighted limma models instead allow \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{gi})=\sigma_g^2/w_{gi} for supplied or estimated precision weights. arrayWeights() and voomWithQualityWeights() address particular sample/observation precision structures. The weights and correlation model still need justification for the assay and design; the unweighted example does not describe every weighting option.
Genes share a variance distribution. Borrowing variance information trades conditional bias against variability under the variance model. A feature far from the bulk can be affected differently from a typical feature. trend=TRUE allows an intensity-dependent prior scale, and robust=TRUE robustifies hyperparameter estimation against outlying variances; neither proves that every feature satisfies the model.
Normality on the log scale, and independence across samples. A transformation does not prove normality or control extreme tails. The exact small-sample reference uses its distributional assumptions; residual diagnostics and suitable large-sample arguments have their own scope. Dependence across samples requires a design-appropriate covariance calculation. Correlated genes do not by themselves create additional independent people.

title: Differential expression and abundance
text:
6 Repeated samples per subject
Longitudinal cohorts give several samples per subject. For a between-person contrast with positive within-person correlation, an independent-row analysis can understate uncertainty. For a within-person contrast, ignoring pairing can instead discard precision (the Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests page shows the same failure in a different setting). limma has two tools.
Block as a fixed effect. Put subject in the design matrix. Useful for specified within-person contrasts under its mean/error assumptions, but it uses person-level parameters and renders a group main effect that is constant within person (patient versus control) inestimable, since subject is nested in group.
duplicateCorrelation(). Estimates a single within-subject correlation shared across genes, then fits each gene by generalized least squares with that correlation. Keeps subject-level contrasts estimable and borrows strength for the correlation the way eBayes does for the variance. It assumes the within-subject correlation is the same for every gene and every pair of samples from a subject, which should be assessed against the visit structure and biological heterogeneity rather than assumed suitable for every cohort.


Code
set.seed(83)
subject_id <- rep(seq_len(12), each = 2)
visit <- rep(0:1, 12)
group_r <- factor(rep(rep(c("control", "patient"), each = 6), each = 2),
                  levels = c("control", "patient"))
X_r <- model.matrix(~ group_r + visit)
U <- matrix(rnorm(200 * 12, sd = 0.6), 200, 12)
y_r <- 6 + U[, subject_id] + matrix(rnorm(200 * 24, sd = 0.6), 200, 24) +
  outer(c(rep(0.7, 15), rep(0, 185)), as.numeric(group_r == "patient")) +
  outer(rep(0.2, 200), visit)
corfit <- limma::duplicateCorrelation(y_r, design = X_r, block = subject_id)
repeated_fit <- limma::lmFit(y_r, design = X_r, block = subject_id,
                            correlation = corfit$consensus.correlation)
repeated_fit <- limma::eBayes(repeated_fit)
c(people = length(unique(subject_id)), specimens = ncol(y_r),
  estimated_consensus_correlation = corfit$consensus.correlation)


                         people                       specimens 
                     12.0000000                      24.0000000 
estimated_consensus_correlation 
                      0.4989482 


In this generator the residual for a specimen is its person’s shared random intercept plus its own noise. Both have variance 0.6^2=0.36. Two visits from the same person therefore have covariance 0.36 and marginal residual variance 0.36+0.36=0.72, giving within-person correlation 0.5. Visits from different people share no random intercept. This explains why compound symmetry matches this example and why 24 specimens still represent only 12 independent people. It does not establish that one consensus correlation fits every longitudinal assay.
Gene-specific mixed models, including dream in variancePartition, can model richer correlation structures under their own assumptions. Unequal visit counts also affect target weighting and selection, not only covariance. Choose the target and design before the fitting engine; see Units of analysis, replication, and study design.

title: Differential expression and abundance
section: 7 Check the inference before interpreting the list
text:
7 Check the inference before interpreting the list
Check whether the design matrix is full rank and the desired contrast is estimable; perfect group–batch confounding cannot be removed by adding both columns. Examine residuals, mean–variance trends, influential samples, and whether repeated measurements were handled at the correct level. Report the estimated contrast and uncertainty on the stated scale, alongside the multiple-testing procedure and the family of features tested.
The weighted limma workflow can accommodate modeled precision differences; the simple unweighted example above has a narrower variance model. Consult the limma introduction and user guide for the implemented weighting and correlation options. Variance moderation improves variance estimation under its assumptions; it does not identify a confounded contrast or correct a scientifically inappropriate adjustment set.

title: Differential expression and abundance
text:
8 Where this connects

The What is your estimator actually estimating? page: the design matrix is where “adjusting for Z” happens, and the coefficient’s target is the within-covariate difference only when the adjustment is correct and complete.
The Jackknife pseudo-values page: comparing per-sample network edges between groups is a limma or t-test on the edges as if they were expression values. Check the dependence introduced by estimating those summaries from the shared cohort as well as the mean and variance models; ordinary independent-observation testing is not automatically justified.
The Orthogonality and cross-fitting page: a misspecified linear adjustment can change the coefficient’s target. An orthogonal, cross-fitted construction is an alternative when its target, model, and nuisance-rate conditions fit the question; it is not an automatic repair for every design or measurement problem.
The Multiple testing when the tests are not independent page: the output of limma is 15,000 p-values, and what you do with them is the subject of that shared inference guide.

title: Differential expression and abundance
text:
9 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · DE-01 — Write an estimable contrast
Task type: Construction and interpretation.
Use a group-means design with columns (A,B,C,Z) for three groups and one continuous covariate. Write contrast vectors for B minus A and the average of B and C minus A. State the scale and common-slope assumption needed to interpret these contrasts as adjusted feature differences. Explain what must be checked before claiming the contrasts are estimable.
Ready to continue when: you can connect a design/contrast calculation to its population interpretation and check rank and confounding.
Transfer: If the group difference varies with Z, which additional design terms and reference values would you need?


Hint

A contrast takes a weighted sum of the coefficients; a common covariate term cancels in a same-Z difference.



Solution outline — open after trying

In the stated column order, the vectors are (-1,1,0,0) and (-1,1/2,1/2,0). Interpretation is on the feature scale modeled, such as log-expression. Without interactions the design assumes a common covariate slope and a group difference constant in Z. Check the design rank and whether the contrast lies in its estimable space; perfect confounding or absent groups can prevent identification. More generally, a standardized group contrast can differ from a coefficient in a misspecified model.





Checkpoint · DE-02 — Explain what variance moderation changes
Task type: Derivation and interpretation.
In the known-prior teaching model, take d_0=4, s_0^2=1, d_g=4, and observed s_g^2=0.2. Compute the moderated variance and compare it with the result at d_g=40. State whether the fitted group coefficient is shrunk. Explain what is averaged over in the known-prior moderated-t calibration and what remains to check in an actual weighted, repeated-measures limma analysis.
Ready to continue when: you can separate the target contrast, variance borrowing, hierarchical calibration, and the independent-unit/weighting assumptions.
Transfer: Would changing a batch-confounded design become identifiable after stronger variance moderation? Why?


Hint

Use the weighted variance formula; the hyperprior scale is not every gene’s true variance.



Solution outline — open after trying

The moderated variance is (4+4(0.2))/8=0.6 at four residual df, and (4+40(0.2))/44=12/44 at forty df. More residual information reduces shrinkage toward the prior scale. This variance moderation does not shrink the fitted group coefficient in the displayed workflow. The ideal moderated-t reference integrates over the specified gene-variance distribution; it is not an exact conditional-on-every-fixed-variance guarantee. Estimated hyperparameters, mean specification, precision weights, within-person covariance, contrast estimability, marginal p-values, and the tested family still need checking.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

In the shrinkage simulation, add a true difference of 1 to the first 200 genes and compare the number of true positives at a Bonferroni threshold for the ordinary and moderated statistics. Then set d0 <- 50 and d0 <- 0.5 and explain what happens.
Extend the Level() simulation so that the two groups also differ in shape (one normal, one a t_3 scaled to the same SD). Does Welch still hold its level? At what sample size?
Simulate 20 subjects with 3 samples each and a within-subject correlation of 0.5, no group effect. Fit lm(y ~ group) ignoring subjects and record the level over 2000 simulated genes. Then fit with subject as a random effect (lme4::lmer) and compare.

title: Orthogonality and cross-fitting
text: Before reading: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target, Influence functions, and stochastic orders from Large-sample reasoning for methods research.

title: Orthogonality and cross-fitting
section: 1 Keep the target fixed while learning nuisances
text:
1 Keep the target fixed while learning nuisances
The target is the eligible-population feature mean \mu=E[Y]. We observe independent records W=(Z,R,RY): Z is recorded for everyone, and R=1 means the outcome is observed. The product RY encodes an unrecorded outcome when R=0; it does not say that person’s outcome equals zero.
Assume an integrable outcome, missing at random (MAR), R\perp Y\mid Z, and positive observation probability over the target population. Then

\begin{aligned}
m_0(z)&=E[Y\mid Z=z,R=1],\\
\pi_0(z)&=P(R=1\mid Z=z),\\
\mu&=E[m_0(Z)].
\end{aligned}

The subscript 0 marks the true population functions; hats will mark estimates. MAR connects the observed-outcome regression to the full-population conditional mean. The outer expectation uses the covariate distribution of all eligible people. Neither learning nor cross-fitting supplies this identifying assumption.
Write Pf=E[f(W)] and P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(W_i). For a function of Z, \|f\|_2=\sqrt{E[f(Z)^2]}, averaging over the eligible population. A fitted function is random across training datasets; when we hold a fit fixed, P averages over a fresh observation with that fit unchanged.
Averaging fitted means alone can be sensitive to regression error. An augmented contribution combines a prediction with an observed residual:

\begin{aligned}
D_\eta(W)&=m(Z)+\frac{R}{\pi(Z)}\{Y-m(Z)\},\\
\eta&=(m,\pi).
\end{aligned}

Every person contributes a prediction m(Z). A person with an observed outcome also contributes a residual, weighted by the inverse observation probability. At the true functions, E[R(Y-m_0)\mid Z]=0, so PD_{\eta_0}=\mu. If m=3, \pi=1/2, and an observed outcome is 5, the contribution is 3+2(5-3)=7; a person with the same covariates and a missing outcome contributes 3. These are estimation contributions, not imputed individual outcomes, so they need not stay within the outcome’s range.
The centered function \phi_0=D_{\eta_0}-\mu is the observed-data influence function derived in From an influence function to an estimator. The mean-zero equation D_\eta-\mu is an estimating function; D_\eta is not a likelihood score. This page explains why estimating its nuisance arguments requires both bias control and careful training/evaluation separation.

title: Orthogonality and cross-fitting
section: 2 Orthogonality concerns the supplied nuisance functions
text:
2 Orthogonality concerns the supplied nuisance functions
Hold the population law and target fixed. Change only the nuisance arguments supplied to M(\eta)=PD_\eta. Neyman orthogonality means that the first derivative of this map is zero at the true nuisances along the permitted perturbations. This differs from a score-path derivative, where the distribution and target can change, and from independence of two random variables. Here it says that a small nuisance error has no first-order effect on the population estimating equation.
To see the cancellation, fix fitted functions with \widehat\pi\ge c>0. Conditioning on Z gives

\begin{aligned}
E[R(Y-\widehat m)\mid Z]&=\pi_0(m_0-\widehat m),\\
E[D_{\widehat\eta}\mid Z]-m_0&=(\widehat m-m_0) \left(1-\frac{\pi_0}{\widehat\pi}\right).
\end{aligned}

The first term in the contribution introduces prediction error; the residual correction subtracts the part scaled by \pi_0/\widehat\pi. Averaging the remaining difference gives the exact identity

PD_{\widehat\eta}-\mu
=E\left[\frac{\widehat\pi-\pi_0}{\widehat\pi}
(\widehat m-m_0)\right].

Write a perturbation as m_0+\varepsilon h_m, \pi_0+\varepsilon h_\pi, keeping probabilities admissible. Its bias is

\varepsilon^2E\left[\frac{h_\pi h_m}{\pi_0+\varepsilon h_\pi}\right].

Under the needed integrability and denominator bounds, dividing by \varepsilon and taking \varepsilon\to0 gives derivative zero. The first surviving change is a product of the two perturbations. By comparison, the regression-only contribution has population change \varepsilon E[h_m], generally first order. Augmentation removes that term. The exact identity shows which product remains; a zero formal derivative alone is not a general rate theorem.
For a numerical check, take \pi_0=0.5, \widehat\pi=0.6, and \widehat m-m_0=0.2 everywhere. The exact bias is (0.1/0.6)0.2=1/30, compared with 0.2 for prediction alone. Halving both errors gives (0.05/0.55)0.1=1/110, approximately a quarter as large. The denominator also changes, so the finite change need not be exactly quadratic.

title: Orthogonality and cross-fitting
section: 3 Consistency and root-n inference are different claims
text:
3 Consistency and root-n inference are different claims
Cauchy–Schwarz yields

\begin{aligned}
|PD_{\widehat\eta}-\mu|
&\le E\left[\frac{|\widehat\pi-\pi_0|}{c}|\widehat m-m_0|\right]\\
&\le c^{-1}\|\widehat\pi-\pi_0\|_2\|\widehat m-m_0\|_2.
\end{aligned}

If either supplied function is exactly correct, this population bias is zero. For learned functions, one nuisance converging to truth can make the bias vanish if the other error stays bounded in the required norm and the denominator remains controlled. With a vanishing empirical error, this gives double-robust consistency. “Double” refers to two opportunities for this consistency property; it does not mean robustness to MAR failure or to arbitrary errors in both functions.
Consistency asks only that the estimation error vanish. A centered root-n limit asks for the nuisance bias to be negligible compared with the leading n^{-1/2} sampling fluctuation. The efficient-inference argument using \phi_0 here assumes both nuisances converge, a product o_p(n^{-1/2}), and the empirical and variance conditions below. These are sufficient conditions for this proof. A different limit with one incorrect nuisance needs its own expansion and variance analysis.
If the two L2 errors are O_p(n^{-a}) and O_p(n^{-b}), their product is O_p(n^{-(a+b)}). Multiplication by \sqrt n leaves order O_p(n^{1/2-a-b}). Thus a+b>1/2 is sufficient through this bound.








L2 exponents (a,b)
Product order
Root-n bias guarantee from the bound




(1/3,1/5)
O_p(n^{-8/15})
Negligible: 8/15>1/2


(1/4,1/4)
O_p(n^{-1/2})
Boundary: big-O alone is insufficient


(1/5,1/5)
O_p(n^{-2/5})
No negligibility guarantee



At the boundary, stronger little-o control of at least one factor can suffice. If the bound is too large, the actual signed expectation might still cancel; failing a sufficient condition is not itself proof of bias. Faster convergence of one nuisance can compensate for slower convergence of the other. Estimating nuisance functions for inference connects these exponents to regression learning.

title: Orthogonality and cross-fitting
section: 4 Cross-fitting controls reuse of evaluation noise
text:
4 Cross-fitting controls reuse of evaluation noise
Split independent people into a fixed number K of folds, using a split independent of their measurements. Fit nuisance functions outside each validation fold and evaluate the contribution inside it. In a two-fold example:



Contributions being evaluated
Data allowed to train those fits




People in fold A
Fold B


People in fold B
Fold A



Every person is evaluated once and can help train the fit used for other people. Cross-fitting recovers use of the full sample for evaluation; it does not train any one fit on the full sample. Train learned preprocessing, selection, and tuning inside the relevant training set. For repeated specimens, keep an entire person together and adapt the variance argument to the independent unit.
Let I_k be validation fold k, n_k its size, P_{n,k} its average, and \widehat\eta_k the fit trained outside that fold. The subscript k labels the held-out fold, not data used for training. The estimator is

\widehat\mu=\sum_{k=1}^K\frac{n_k}{n}
P_{n,k}D_{\widehat\eta_k}.

Fold-size weights make this exactly the average of the n held-out contributions. A simple unweighted average of fold estimates would generally give different person weights when fold sizes differ.
For validation fold k, condition on its training data. Its fitted functions are then fixed, while the validation observations are fresh independent draws. This permits a conditional-variance argument for the fitted-minus-true empirical term. Conditioning on all fitted functions simultaneously would be a different step: the fits use observations from other validation folds, so the full set of contributions is not jointly independent.
Cross-fitting does not identify an unsupported target, make a bad learner consistent, or remove the product bias. For example, constant nuisance errors of order n^{-1/5} can leave a bias of order n^{-2/5}, which grows after root-n scaling. Separated folds do not change that population calculation.

title: Orthogonality and cross-fitting
text:
5 Locate the two remainders
Let H_k=D_{\widehat\eta_k}-D_{\eta_0} and w_k=n_k/n. Add and subtract the true contribution, and then its population average. The error decomposes exactly as

\widehat\mu-\mu=(P_n-P)\phi_0 +\sum_k w_k(P_{n,k}-P)H_k +\sum_k w_kPH_k.

The first term averages the same fixed, mean-zero \phi_0 over everyone. With finite nonzero variance it has a CLT. The middle term is a centered empirical remainder: how much the evaluation sample’s average fitted error differs from its fresh-population average. Conditional on training, its scaled variance is at most PH_k^2, so \|H_k\|_2=o_p(1) makes it negligible. The last term is the population bias remainder, the exact product derived above. Cross-fitting does not shrink that product by itself.
To obtain the usual limit, both remainders must be o_p(n^{-1/2}). Then the leading contribution determines the limiting law. A feasible SE still needs consistent contribution-variance estimation and finite nonzero limiting variance; a small computed SE is not evidence that the bias remainder is small.
From an influence function to an estimator completes the derivation, conditional-Chebyshev proof, implementation, and uncertainty argument for this same target. Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error is a network-analysis transfer with its own gradient and remainder, rather than another name for the missing mean.

title: Orthogonality and cross-fitting
text:
6 Exercises
The checkpoint is a completion target. Additional practice is optional.


Checkpoint · SP-11 — Bound the nuisance-bias remainder
Task type: Derivation and rate reasoning.
Fix nuisance fits trained independently of a fresh observation. Under the missing-mean identification assumptions, derive PD_{\widehat\eta}-\mu. Assume \widehat\pi\ge c>0 and square-integrable nuisance errors. Bound the bias using Cauchy–Schwarz. If the L2 errors are O_p(n^{-a}) and O_p(n^{-b}), give a sufficient condition for a negligible root-n bias. Check exponent pairs (1/3,1/5), (1/4,1/4), and (1/5,1/5). Explain which additional random term this calculation does not control.
Ready to continue when: you can derive the exact product remainder, distinguish big-O from little-o, and identify the additional empirical and variance arguments needed for inference.
Transfer: Compare this weighted product with the residual-covariance product in the application page. What role does the denominator bound play?


Hint

Condition on Z: E[R(Y-\widehat m)\mid Z]=\pi_0(m_0-\widehat m). Combine the prediction and residual terms before applying the norm bound.



Solution outline — open after trying

The bias is E[(\widehat\pi-\pi_0)(\widehat m-m_0)/\widehat\pi], bounded by c^{-1} times the two L2 errors. An exponent sum greater than 1/2 guarantees little-o through this bound. The first pair satisfies it, equality at (1/4,1/4) is insufficient from big-O alone, and (1/5,1/5) gives no negligible-bias guarantee. Failing a sufficient bound alone is not proof of actual failure, since a particular inner product may cancel. The fitted-function empirical remainder and variance consistency remain to be controlled. Cross-fitting addresses the former under its own conditions, not the population bias.




Additional practice (optional)

Set one nuisance equal to truth and derive the remaining population bias.
Use bounded perturbation directions to verify the zero first derivative directly.
Draw the fitting/evaluation scheme for repeated specimens from independent people.

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text: Before reading: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target, Influence functions, Orthogonality and cross-fitting, Estimating nuisance functions for inference, and Large-sample reasoning for methods research.
crumbs: From an influence function to an estimator

title: From an influence function to an estimator
section: 1 One target, a complete estimation argument
text:
1 One target, a complete estimation argument
The target is the eligible-population mean \mu=E[Y] when some outcomes are missing. We observe i.i.d. records W=(Z,R,RY) with covariates recorded for everyone. Assume E[|Y|]<\infty, missing at random (MAR), R\perp Y\mid Z, and \pi_0(Z)>0 almost surely in the target population. The Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target page explains why these conditions identify the mean as E[m_0(Z)], where m_0(z)=E[Y\mid Z=z,R=1] and \pi_0(z)=P(R=1\mid Z=z).
Write Pf=E[f(W)] under the true observed-data law and P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(W_i). For fitted functions, P means expectation over a fresh record while holding the training fit fixed. The L2 norm is \|f\|_2=\sqrt{P f^2}. When f depends only on Z, this averages over all eligible people’s covariates. Positivity and MAR identify the target; stronger bounds and learning conditions will be imposed separately for the inference proof.
This is an extended capstone. First follow the derivation, then inspect the implementation, and finally reconstruct the proof through the checkpoints. The same pattern transfers to residual covariance and partially linear coefficients, but their gradients and remainders must be derived for their own targets.
crumbs: From an influence function to an estimator

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text:
2 Derive the observed-data influence function
An observed-data density factors into the distribution of Z, the observation mechanism given Z, and the outcome distribution among observed units. Writing w=(z,r,ry) for an observed record value and p_1(y\mid z) for the last density, its form is

p(w)=p_Z(z)\pi(z)^r\{1-\pi(z)\}^{1-r} \times p_1(y\mid z)^r.

The outcome factor appears only when r=1; the notation does not evaluate an unrecorded y. A smooth path has total score

s(W)=s_Z(Z)+s_{R\mid Z}(R,Z) +Rs_Y(Y,Z),

where s_Y abbreviates the observed conditional-outcome score. Density normalization gives E[s_Z]=0, E[s_{R\mid Z}\mid Z]=0, and E[s_Y\mid Z,R=1]=0. These are the three sets of permitted local directions whose target derivatives must be represented.
Differentiate the identified functional \mu(P)=E_P[m_P(Z)]. Changing the covariate distribution contributes E[(m_0-\mu)s_Z], because its score is centered. At a fixed z, differentiating the outcome mean contributes E[(Y-m_0(z))s_Y\mid Z=z,R=1]. Averaging over target covariates gives

E_Z\!\left[E[(Y-m_0(Z))s_Y\mid Z,R=1]\right].

Changing the observation probability alone does not change the identified functional: its expression uses p_Z and p_1, not \pi. This does not make missingness irrelevant to precision; fewer observed outcomes can still mean less information. A candidate gradient representing these derivatives is

\phi_0(W)=m_0(Z)-\mu +\frac{R}{\pi_0(Z)}\{Y-m_0(Z)\}.


2.1 Verify each score component
Conditioning first on (Z,R) gives E[\phi_0\mid Z,R]=m_0(Z)-\mu: when R=1, the observed residual has mean zero; when R=0, its weighted term is absent. Averaging gives E[\phi_0]=0.
For covariate scores, the same centering gives E[\phi_0s_Z]=E[(m_0-\mu)s_Z]. For observation-mechanism scores,

\begin{aligned}
E[\phi_0s_{R\mid Z}]
&=E[(m_0-\mu)E[s_{R\mid Z}\mid Z]]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

For outcome scores, the m_0-\mu term vanishes because the conditional score is centered. The remaining product has R^2=R, so

\begin{aligned}
E[\phi_0 R s_Y]&=E\left[\frac{R}{\pi_0}(Y-m_0)s_Y\right]\\
&=E_Z\!\left[E[(Y-m_0)s_Y\mid Z,R=1]\right].
\end{aligned}

The inner conditioning contributes a factor \pi_0(Z) that cancels the inverse weight. Thus the same \phi_0 represents the derivative for each score component, and hence their sums and limits under the required differentiability and integrability conditions.


2.2 Interpret the efficiency bound
In the unrestricted observed-data model the tangent space is L_2^0(P). When the candidate has finite second moment, its representation of all these derivatives makes it the unique gradient, the efficient influence function (EIF). To compute its variance, note that E[\phi_0\mid Z]=m_0(Z)-\mu and

E\left[\left.\left\{\frac{R}{\pi_0}(Y-m_0)\right\}^2\right|Z\right]=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid Z,R=1)}{\pi_0(Z)}.

One factor of \pi_0 cancels the squared inverse weight, leaving one in the denominator. Conditional centering makes the cross term zero. The total-variance calculation gives

V_0=\operatorname{Var}(m_0(Z)) +E\left[\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid Z,R=1)}{\pi_0(Z)}\right].

V_0 is the variance of one influence contribution, or the limiting variance of the root-n scaled estimator error. The estimator-variance bound is V_0/n, and its SE bound is \sqrt{V_0/n}. Dividing by n accounts for averaging; taking the square root expresses uncertainty on the outcome scale.
The first component reflects between-covariate differences in the mean. The second reflects within-covariate outcome noise, inflated by incomplete observation. For example, if \pi_0=1/2, \operatorname{Var}(m_0)=1, and every conditional outcome variance is 4, then V_0=1+4/(1/2)=9. If every outcome were observed, the variance bound would instead be (1+4)/n=5/n. Missingness doubles the conditional-noise contribution here, rather than doubling every part of the variance. These compare two different observation experiments at the same full-data law.
crumbs: From an influence function to an estimator

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text:
3 Construct the augmented estimator
For fitted nuisances \hat\eta=(\hat m,\hat\pi), define

D_{\hat\eta}(W)=\hat m(Z) +\frac R{\hat\pi(Z)}\{Y-\hat m(Z)\}.

A plug-in starts with an average prediction P_n\hat m. Adding the empirical residual correction gives the augmented inverse-probability estimator. With fixed fits, the equation P_n(D_{\hat\eta}-\mu)=0 has the explicit solution \widehat\mu=P_nD_{\hat\eta}. This is why the EIF suggests the augmentation. Solving a sample equation does not itself show that the resulting estimator is centered at the population target.
For cross-fitting, split independent units into a fixed number K of folds independently of their data. In fold k, learn both functions on the other folds and evaluate D_{\hat\eta_k} on held-out units. The label k names the excluded validation fold. Average all held-out contributions with fold-size weights. Every row is evaluated once using a fit that did not train on that row. Repeated observations of one person need grouped folds and an appropriate cluster-level variance; the implementation below assumes independent people with one row each.
Only observed-outcome rows receive a residual correction. Missing-outcome rows still contribute their predicted means. In code, multiplying 0 * NA gives NA; the implementation constructs the correction on observed rows rather than treating the unobserved outcome as zero.

title: From an influence function to an estimator
crumbs: From an influence function to an estimator

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text:
5 Decompose the full estimation error
Let I_k be fold k, n_k its size, w_k=n_k/n, and P_{n,k} its empirical average. The estimator is \widehat\mu=\sum_k w_kP_{n,k}D_{\hat\eta_k}. Put D_0=\mu+\phi_0 and H_k=D_{\hat\eta_k}-D_0. Add and subtract D_0 inside each validation average, then add and subtract PH_k. Because the folds partition the sample, \sum_k w_kP_{n,k}D_0=P_nD_0. Exactly,

\hat\mu-\mu=(P_n-P)\phi_0 +\sum_k w_k(P_{n,k}-P)H_k +\sum_k w_kPH_k.

The first term has a fixed-function CLT. The last is the population bias remainder just calculated. The middle is the centered empirical error from evaluating a learned function. A fixed-function CLT cannot simply be applied to it as if the fits were prespecified, because those fits are random and use part of the same overall dataset.

5.1 Bound one validation fold, then combine folds
Define T_k=\sqrt{n_k}(P_{n,k}-P)H_k. Conditional on fold k’s training data, H_k is fixed and its validation observations are independent. Thus E[T_k\mid\text{training}_k]=0 and

\operatorname{Var}(T_k\mid\text{training}_k)\le PH_k^2.

If PH_k^2=o_p(1), the variance bound is small with high probability. This does not require its training-sample expectation to converge to zero. For fixed \epsilon,\delta>0, separate the event where the bound exceeds \delta, and apply conditional Chebyshev on its complement:

\Pr(|T_k|>\epsilon)
\le\Pr(PH_k^2>\delta)+\frac{\delta}{\epsilon^2}.

First let n grow; the first probability tends to zero. Then let \delta decrease to zero. This proves T_k=o_p(1). For the overall empirical remainder,

\begin{aligned}
\sqrt n\sum_k w_k(P_{n,k}-P)H_k&=\sum_k\sqrt{w_k}\,T_k\\
&=o_p(1).
\end{aligned}

There are only finitely many folds, and every weight is bounded. Their training sets overlap, so joint conditional independence of all contributions is not assumed. A fixed finite sum of negligible terms is enough. A growing number of folds, including a leave-one-out scheme, would need a further argument rather than automatic reuse of this proof.
crumbs: From an influence function to an estimator

title: From an influence function to an estimator
section: 6 A tractable sufficient set of conditions
text:
6 A tractable sufficient set of conditions
One sufficient teaching setup uses the following conditions:

The units are i.i.d.; K is fixed; the split is independent of the data; and every fold’s size fraction stays bounded away from zero.
MAR holds, and true and fitted observation probabilities are at least a fixed c>0.
Outcomes and fitted means are bounded in absolute value by a fixed B<\infty.
Both nuisances are L2-consistent, and their L2 error product is o_p(n^{-1/2}) in every fold.
The influence variance satisfies 0<V_0<\infty.

To see why nuisance consistency controls H_k, suppress the fold label and expand exactly:

H=(\widehat m-m_0)\left(1-\frac R{\widehat\pi}\right) +R(Y-m_0)\left(\frac1{\widehat\pi}-\frac1{\pi_0}\right).

The first multiplier is bounded by 1+c^{-1}. For the second, |Y-m_0|\le2B and the inverse-probability difference is at most c^{-2}|\widehat\pi-\pi_0|. The triangle inequality therefore gives

\|H\|_2\le(1+c^{-1})\|\widehat m-m_0\|_2 +2Bc^{-2}\|\widehat\pi-\pi_0\|_2.

Both errors tending to zero makes H L2-small. The conditional-variance argument now controls the empirical remainder, while the product rate controls the population remainder. The fixed-function CLT and Slutsky’s theorem give

\begin{aligned}
\widehat\mu-\mu&=P_n\phi_0+o_p(n^{-1/2}),\\
\sqrt n(\widehat\mu-\mu)&\xrightarrow{d}N(0,V_0).
\end{aligned}


6.1 Justify the estimated variance
For i\in I_k, write \widehat D_i=D_{\widehat\eta_k}(W_i) and \widehat\phi_i=\widehat D_i-\widehat\mu. Their sample mean is exactly zero. The sample variance and SE are

\begin{aligned}
\widehat V&=\frac1{n-1}\sum_i\widehat\phi_i^2,\\
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}&=\sqrt{\widehat V/n}.
\end{aligned}

The learned contributions share training data, so the justification is not that they are all independent. For each fold, conditioning on training gives E[P_{n,k}H_k^2\mid\text{training}_k]=PH_k^2. Conditional Markov and the same small-probability-event argument above show that the average squared difference between \widehat D_i and D_0(W_i) tends to zero. Cauchy–Schwarz then controls the difference of their empirical second moments. The LLN for the fixed true contributions and consistency of \widehat\mu give \widehat V\xrightarrow{p}V_0.
Consequently (\widehat\mu-\mu)/\widehat{\operatorname{SE}} converges in distribution to a standard normal, and \widehat\mu\pm1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}} is an asymptotic 95% interval. Coverage concerns repeated datasets under the stated conditions. Bounded outcomes simplify this proof; unbounded outcomes need appropriate moment and uniform-integrability controls.

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text:
7 Implement the complete teaching example
Here Z is uniform on [-1,1], m_0(Z)=2+Z+Z^2, \pi_0(Z)=\operatorname{expit}(-0.3+Z), and the outcome error is independently uniform on [-1,1]. The simulator draws R using only Z, so MAR holds by construction. Since E[Z]=0 and E[Z^2]=1/3, the population mean is \mu=2+0+1/3=7/3. Conditional outcome variance is 1/3.
The regression and observation models below are correctly specified: the outcome fit includes both Z and Z^2, and the observation fit uses a linear logit. Under their regular finite-dimensional conditions, both can attain root-n rates, giving a product of order n^{-1}, negligible on the root-n scale. This is a transparent verification case; flexible learners would need their own accuracy conditions.
The observed dataset does not retain missing outcome values. The simulator constructs them only to generate the observation process and then returns NA for missing rows. Prespecified probability bounds (0.1,0.9) contain the true probability range, approximately (0.21,0.67); the outcome/prediction bounds (0,6) also contain the truth. These teaching constraints are not learned from unavailable outcomes. Clipping to bounds containing the truth does not increase the distance from that truth. All reported inference concerns the cross-fitted augmented estimator.
Within each training set, lm uses only observed outcomes and glm uses everyone’s observed R. Predictions are made for the excluded fold, then assembled in original row order. score stores \widehat D_i; phi stores \widehat\phi_i. These names denote contributions, not likelihood scores. Centering and dividing their SD by \sqrt n implements the variance formula just justified.
The functions are also available as a downloadable R script.


Code
# Self-contained bounded-outcome teaching example; independent rows are people.
SimulateMissingMean <- function(n = 800, seed = 51) {
  set.seed(seed)
  z <- runif(n, -1, 1)
  prob <- plogis(-0.3 + z)
  full_y <- 2 + z + z^2 + runif(n, -1, 1)
  r <- rbinom(n, 1, prob)
  list(data = data.frame(id = seq_len(n), z = z, r = r,
                         y = ifelse(r == 1, full_y, NA_real_)), truth = 7 / 3)
}

CrossFitMissingMean <- function(d, K = 5, seed = 52,
                                probability_bounds = c(0.1, 0.9),
                                outcome_bounds = c(0, 6)) {
  n <- nrow(d)
  stopifnot(n >= 20, K >= 2, K <= n, !anyDuplicated(d$id),
            all(is.finite(d$z)), all(d$r %in% c(0, 1)),
            all(is.finite(d$y[d$r == 1])),
            all(is.na(d$y[d$r == 0])),
            length(probability_bounds) == 2,
            0 < probability_bounds[1], probability_bounds[1] < probability_bounds[2],
            probability_bounds[2] < 1, length(outcome_bounds) == 2,
            outcome_bounds[1] < outcome_bounds[2],
            all(d$y[d$r == 1] >= outcome_bounds[1]),
            all(d$y[d$r == 1] <= outcome_bounds[2]))
  set.seed(seed)
  fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = n))
  mhat <- phat <- raw_p <- raw_m <- numeric(n)
  for (k in seq_len(K)) {
    train <- d[fold != k, ]; test <- d[fold == k, ]
    observed <- train[train$r == 1, ]
    if (nrow(observed) < 6 || length(unique(train$r)) < 2) {
      stop("Training fold has inadequate observed outcomes or observation classes")
    }
    outcome_fit <- lm(y ~ z + I(z^2), data = observed)
    probability_fit <- glm(r ~ z, family = binomial(), data = train)
    if (!isTRUE(probability_fit$converged)) stop("Observation fit did not converge")
    raw_m[fold == k] <- predict(outcome_fit, newdata = test)
    raw_p[fold == k] <- predict(probability_fit, newdata = test, type = "response")
  }
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(raw_m)), all(is.finite(raw_p)))
  mhat <- pmin(outcome_bounds[2], pmax(outcome_bounds[1], raw_m))
  phat <- pmin(probability_bounds[2], pmax(probability_bounds[1], raw_p))
  score <- mhat
  observed <- d$r == 1
  # Do not multiply zero by NA: construct residual corrections on observed rows.
  score[observed] <- mhat[observed] + (d$y[observed] - mhat[observed]) / phat[observed]
  estimate <- mean(score); phi <- score - estimate
  se <- sd(phi) / sqrt(n)
  list(summary = data.frame(estimate = estimate, se = se,
                            lower = estimate - 1.96 * se, upper = estimate + 1.96 * se,
                            observed = sum(observed), n = n,
                            probability_clipped = mean(phat != raw_p),
                            mean_clipped = mean(mhat != raw_m)),
       contributions = data.frame(id = d$id, fold = fold, r = d$r, z = d$z,
                                  mhat = mhat, phat = phat, score = score, phi = phi))
}


Before running the next chunk, predict why the complete-case mean may differ from 7/3 even though observation depends only on recorded Z. Under this mechanism, the complete-case limit is E[\pi_0(Z)m_0(Z)]/E[\pi_0(Z)]: it weights covariates by their observation probabilities. MAR does not make that covariate mix match the full population. The cross-fitted estimate should be close to the truth on the scale of its SE, not identical to it.


Code
example <- SimulateMissingMean()
fit <- CrossFitMissingMean(example$data)
fit$summary

  mean_clipped
1            0

complete_case         truth

Code
# Exact observed-data bound in this known simulation, not a real-data oracle.
V0 <- integrate(function(z) ((1/3) / plogis(-0.3 + z) +
                            (2 + z + z^2 - 7/3)^2) / 2, -1, 1)$value
c(theoretical_SE = sqrt(V0 / nrow(example$data)), estimated_SE = fit$summary$se)


theoretical_SE   estimated_SE 
    0.04006777     0.04003445 




Code
a <- fit$contributions
plot(a$z, a$phi, pch = 16, cex = 0.55,
     col = ifelse(a$r == 1, "#2F80C8", "#D55E00"),
     xlab = "Observed covariate Z", ylab = "Estimated influence contribution")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Outcome observed", "Outcome missing"),
       col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00"), pch = 16, bty = "n")








Figure 1: Cross-fitted contributions in one synthetic sample. Large values can arise from weighted observed residuals; missing-outcome units contribute predicted means.





The integral uses the known functions and conditional variance 1/3 to compute V_0, then reports \sqrt{V_0/n}. Compare this theoretical SE with the estimated SE; neither is the SD of individual outcomes. One estimate can be above or below the truth and one estimated SE can be above or below the asymptotic benchmark. Such differences in a single sample do not establish bias, inefficiency, or improved efficiency.
In the figure, missing-outcome units have \widehat\phi_i=\widehat m(Z_i)-\widehat\mu. Observed units also receive the weighted residual, so their contributions can be more spread out, especially where estimated observation probability is small. The plot displays the terms used in the estimator and SE; it is not a check of MAR.
The code records clipping fractions and stops on inadequate training folds or nonfinite fits. A production evaluation should retain those failures rather than silently omit them. One interval containing the truth does not establish coverage; Evaluating a statistical method explains repeated-sampling assessment.

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text:
8 An introduction to targeting (optional)
This optional comparison introduces a different construction. It updates an initial regression to solve an empirical EIF equation, then reports the target evaluated at the updated regression. For a Gaussian working squared-error loss, take a one-dimensional fluctuation m_\epsilon=\widehat m+\epsilon a, where a(Z)=1/\widehat\pi(Z) is the specified update direction.
Minimizing observed-outcome squared loss gives the equation P_n[Ra(Y-m_\epsilon)]=0. Its solution, when the denominator is positive, is

\widehat\epsilon
=\frac{P_n[Ra(Y-\widehat m)]}{P_n[Ra^2]}.

Now report the plug-in mean \widetilde\mu=P_nm_{\widehat\epsilon}. The mean of its prediction-minus-target term is zero by definition, and the weighted residual term is zero by the update equation. Hence the updated empirical EIF mean is zero. This is the algebra behind targeting the update toward the final parameter.
This illustrates a targeting step. A complete targeted-learning procedure must choose a suitable loss/submodel, preserve relevant bounds, handle fitted nuisances and folds, and establish its own remainder conditions. The proof and interval implementation above are for the cross-fitted augmented estimator; the illustration does not transfer that proof automatically to every targeting algorithm.
crumbs: From an influence function to an estimator

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text:
9 Diagnose the failed condition
If a positive-probability stratum has \pi_0=0, no outcomes are observed there. Two full-data populations can have the same observed law and different means in that stratum, giving different \mu. The full mean is therefore not identified without extra information. More data from the same observation mechanism do not resolve that ambiguity.
If \pi_0(Z)>0 almost surely but approaches zero, identification can remain while EIF variance diverges. For Z uniform on (0,1), \pi_0(Z)=Z, and conditional outcome variance 1, the variance contains

\begin{aligned}
E[1/Z]&=\int_0^1\frac{1}{z}\,dz\\
&=\infty.
\end{aligned}

Every stratum has some observation support, but the rare observations near zero carry too much inverse-probability variation for the finite-variance root-n argument. This is a precision/regularity failure, distinct from the previous identification failure.
Slow nuisance learning can leave first-order bias even with perfectly separated folds. Let \pi_0=1/2 and take constant errors \widehat\pi-\pi_0=n^{-1/5} and \widehat m-m_0=n^{-1/5} for sufficiently large n that the probabilities are admissible. The exact bias and its scaling are

\begin{aligned}
b_n&=\frac{n^{-2/5}}{1/2+n^{-1/5}}\\
&\longrightarrow0,\\
\sqrt n\,b_n&=\frac{n^{1/10}}{1/2+n^{-1/5}}\\
&\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{aligned}

Both learners converge and the estimator can be consistent, yet its bias overwhelms root-n uncertainty. This constructs an actual noncanceling remainder; merely failing a sufficient norm bound would not establish such failure. Cross-fitting leaves this population calculation unchanged.
Optional transfer beyond the missing-mean target. A unique median with F(y)-1/2\approx cy^3, c>0, near zero remains a defined and identified target, but its population derivative cannot be inverted by a positive density. Balancing CDF noise of order n^{-1/2} with c\widehat q^3 suggests \widehat q has order n^{-1/6}. Quantiles and local expansions explains the regular positive-density comparison. This failure belongs to the target’s local behavior, not to a missingness model or a nuisance learner.
Identification, finite influence variance, nuisance-bias control, and local differentiability are separate parts of an inference argument. A denominator cutoff cannot supply missing information about an unobserved stratum, and an SE formula cannot remove persistent bias.

title: From an influence function to an estimator
text:
10 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets. Additional practice is optional. Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · SP-12 — Control the cross-fitted empirical-process term
Task type: Proof.
Assume i.i.d. observations and a fixed number of folds with nonvanishing validation fractions. Let H_k be the fitted-minus-true contribution, fixed conditional on fold k’s training data, with PH_k^2\to_p0. Define T_k=\sqrt{n_k}(P_{n,k}-P)H_k, where n_k is its validation size. Derive the conditional-variance bound for T_k. Use conditional Chebyshev to show the scaled validation average is negligible, then explain how a fixed number of folds are combined without assuming their fitted contributions are jointly independent. Identify the additional empirical-process condition needed if fitting and evaluation use the same sample.
Ready to continue when: you can show exactly which random term cross-fitting controls and what it does not control.
Transfer: Would the same proof work if the number of folds grew without bound? Which finite-sum argument would need replacement?


Hint

For any \delta>0, separate the event PH_k^2>\delta before applying the conditional variance bound.



Solution outline — open after trying

Conditional on the training data, the validation observations are independent fresh draws. Thus E[T_k\mid\mathrm{training}]=0 and \operatorname{Var}(T_k\mid\mathrm{training})=\operatorname{Var}_P(H_k)\leq PH_k^2. For fixed \epsilon>0, the unconditional tail probability is bounded by

P(PH_k^2>\delta)+\frac{\delta}{\epsilon^2}.
 Take the large-sample limit and then \delta\downarrow0. Multiplying each fold’s o_p(1) term by its bounded root-size weight and summing a fixed number of folds remains o_p(1); no joint fold independence is required. Without splitting, one must justify that the data-dependent empirical term is o_p(1), for example through suitable stochastic-equicontinuity/Donsker conditions and L2 consistency. Cross-fitting leaves the population bias term to be bounded separately.





Checkpoint · SP-13 — Complete the missing-outcome mean capstone
Task type: Derivation, implementation, and inference.
Starting from W=(Z,R,RY) and the full-population mean target, state identification assumptions, derive the EIF through the score components, construct cross-fitted contributions, and derive their exact bias. Give conditions controlling both remainders and a feasible standard error. Run the example without using unobserved outcomes, and explain what a comparison with the observed-data efficiency bound can establish.
Ready to continue when: you can reproduce the chain from target and assumptions through estimator, proof, uncertainty, and interpretation.
Transfer: Replace the outcome regression by a misspecified line. Which consistency and efficient-inference claims remain justified, and which require rechecking?


Hint

Organize the argument as identification, derivative, estimator, error decomposition, and variance.



Solution outline — open after trying

MAR and positivity identify \mu=E[Y] as E[m_0(Z)]. Score decomposition gives the centered EIF m_0-\mu+R(Y-m_0)/\pi_0. Average its estimated uncentered version out of fold. Its training-conditional bias is E[(\widehat\pi-\pi_0)(\widehat m-m_0)/\widehat\pi]. A lower probability bound, L2 consistency, a product o_p(n^{-1/2}), finite nonzero EIF variance, and the stated sampling/moment controls yield an asymptotic linear expansion: SP-12 controls the empirical term and the product controls bias. The SD of estimated influence values divided by \sqrt n gives the SE under those conditions. Double-robust consistency alone does not establish efficiency. An oracle simulation bound benchmarks repeated-sampling variance in this model; one interval or a smaller observed SE does not prove attainment.





Checkpoint · SP-14 — Distinguish identification, variance, and remainder failures
Task type: Diagnosis and derivation.
Diagnose three settings for the missing-outcome mean: (a) observation probability zero in a stratum of positive target mass; (b) \pi_0(Z)=Z for uniform Z on (0,1), with conditional outcome variance 1; and (c) constant positive nuisance errors n^{-1/5} in both models when \pi_0=1/2. State what fails and whether identification can remain.
Ready to continue when: you can name the failed condition or term instead of treating every problem as insufficient sample size.
Transfer: For each setting, propose what additional data, assumptions, changed target, or different asymptotic analysis would be needed.


Hint

Evaluate the unobserved stratum, the inverse-probability variance integral, and the exact bias times \sqrt n.



Solution outline — open after trying


The missing stratum mean is not identified without extra restrictions. (b) Positivity holds almost surely, so MAR identification can hold, but the EIF variance includes the divergent integral of 1/Z; the finite-variance root-n argument fails. (c) The exact bias is n^{-2/5}/(1/2+n^{-1/5}); its \sqrt n scaling grows, so centering at the scientific target is wrong at first order.





Additional practice (optional)

Repeat the synthetic analysis over at least 200 independent datasets; report bias, empirical SD, mean SE, coverage, failures, and MCSE.
Change only the outcome model and then only the observation model; separate consistency experiments from efficient-inference claims.
Derive the variance formula using conditional variance and compare it with the hypothetical complete-data variance.
For the optional median example with F(y)-1/2\approx cy^3, balance the population CDF drift against noise of order n^{-1/2}. Explain the resulting rate and compare the failed condition with the regular case in Quantiles and local expansions.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
1 The measurement question
This is the gene-expression branch of the Omics data and measurement overview. The transferable task is to identify the biological unit, the feature, the scale, and the measurement process. RNA counts and fluorescence intensities are not interchangeable; neither directly reports an absolute molecule count per cell without further calibration.
For a later feature comparison, write the target on the scale actually analyzed, for example E[Y_g\mid A=1]-E[Y_g\mid A=0] for log-expression Y_g in two specified populations. For a network edge, specify which population and adjustment define the association. Different filtering, normalization, or cell-composition choices can change that interpretation. Several specimens from one person remain clustered measurements even if they occupy separate columns.
The other assay primers develop parallel measurement questions. The biological and lupus examples here illustrate expression data; they are not prerequisites for the statistical guides. This page builds toward two conclusions: an expression value describes a particular assay representation, and a bulk association can reflect measurement noise or cell mixtures as well as within-cell regulation.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
2 RNA and the central dogma
Every analysis of gene expression starts from a table of numbers, one per gene per sample. This section assumes no biology and explains where those numbers come from.
Think of a cell as a workshop with one very long instruction manual. The workshop never works from the manual itself. It photocopies the pages it needs right now, and the machinery that builds things reads the photocopies. A gene expression experiment measures the pile of photocopies.
DNA is the manual. DNA is a very long string over a four-letter alphabet (A, C, G, and T). A typical nucleated human cell carries two sets of 23 chromosomes. Different cell types share broadly the same genome but use different parts of it. A gene is a stretch that can be transcribed into RNA. About 20,000 human genes code for proteins; many other genes produce RNAs that are not translated.
RNA is the photocopy. RNA is a chain of letters like DNA, with U in place of T, and is usually single stranded. A cell can make many RNA copies from a gene. Their abundance at a moment depends on both production and breakdown; RNA lifetimes vary widely. Slower degradation can increase RNA abundance even if the production rate stays fixed. An abundance measurement therefore does not by itself measure a transcription rate.
The central dogma says how information moves: from DNA to RNA to protein (Figure 1).

Figure 1: The familiar DNA–RNA–protein pathway: transcription produces messenger RNA, and translation reads it three letters at a time to build a protein. The toy coding sequence ATG GCA TTC becomes AUG GCA UUC; these triplets specify methionine, alanine, and phenylalanine. The dashed RNA-to-DNA arrow is reverse transcription, used in RNA-seq and also occurring naturally, for example in retroviruses. The diagram illustrates a protein-coding transcript, not every RNA’s fate.




Transcription copies a gene from DNA into RNA. An enzyme, RNA polymerase, reads the gene and builds the RNA copy. In human cells the copy is then edited: splicing cuts out stretches called introns and joins the remaining pieces (exons), and most finished copies receive a tail of repeated A’s, the poly-A tail.
Translation reads the finished RNA three letters at a time. A ribosome links together the amino acids those triplets specify, and the chain folds into a protein. Proteins do most of the cell’s work: they are the enzymes, the structural parts, and the signaling machinery.

The arrow can run backward in the lab (the dashed arrow in Figure 1). Retroviruses carry an enzyme, reverse transcriptase, that copies RNA into DNA, and RNA sequencing borrows it.
Not all RNA is the same. The RNA that carries a protein’s instructions is messenger RNA (mRNA). Most of the RNA in a cell is something else, mainly ribosomal RNA (rRNA), a structural part of the ribosome, along with transfer RNAs, microRNAs, and long non-coding RNAs. Sequencing protocols either capture the mRNA by its poly-A tail or remove the rRNA, because otherwise most of the reads would be spent on rRNA.
Why measure RNA? An expression assay provides a broad view of transcript abundance across many genes in one experiment. It complements measurements of proteins and other molecular layers. RNA abundance is an imperfect proxy for protein abundance because translation, protein turnover, and other regulation intervene. A transcript contrast and a protein contrast are related scientific questions, not the same measurement.
Same DNA, different pages. A neutrophil and a T cell express different sets of genes. Transcription factors and signaling pathways can coordinate many genes. Interferon signaling, often prominent in lupus, can raise a set of interferon-stimulated transcripts together. Such shared activity is one source of co-expression, statistical co-variation across the sampled people. Cell composition and technical effects can produce co-variation too. A co-expression edge therefore does not establish that one gene directly regulates another.

2.1 How RNA-seq turns RNA into numbers
In a common short-read RNA-seq workflow, RNA is converted to a DNA library, fragments are sequenced, and their origins are inferred from reference sequences. The resulting count summarizes assigned reads or fragments. It is an indirect measurement shaped by capture, library preparation, and mapping. Figure 2 illustrates this workflow; direct-RNA and other protocols differ.

Figure 2: How RNA-seq turns a blood sample into one column of the count matrix. Colors mark which gene a molecule came from (genes A, B, and C). The reads in step 4 are gray because the sequencer does not know where they came from; they take on a gene’s color only when they are aligned in step 5. The counts are toy numbers.



An aligner such as STAR or HISAT2 can map reads, and a tool such as featureCounts can summarize assignments. Transcript quantifiers such as Salmon and kallisto estimate abundances using their own mapping and statistical procedures; estimated counts can be fractional. Paired-end reads may be counted as one fragment, and UMI-based protocols can count deduplicated captured molecules. Record what the provided entries count, rather than inferring it from the file’s name.

A count is a sample, not a census. Conditional on a fixed read budget and assignment probabilities, a gene count has binomial sampling variation; a rare-feature Poisson approximation is useful in some settings. Variation across people and preparation can add dispersion. The negative-binomial model below summarizes extra variation rather than counting all cellular molecules.
Read depth is not total cellular RNA. The library total (12 and 8 in the toy table) reflects sequencing allocation, library yield, and processing. A larger total alone does not establish more RNA per cell. Between-specimen comparisons need exposure and normalization assumptions.
Counts share a finite budget. If one feature takes a larger share, other shares can fall at unchanged absolute amounts. TMM and related methods estimate useful reference-based corrections under stability assumptions; they do not identify every global absolute change.

Every step in the picture is also a place where technical differences creep in: RNA quality, the day the library was made, the sequencing lane. Those differences are the batch effects described below.
