title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
3 The matrix
A gene-expression matrix usually puts features in rows and specimens in columns. A feature can be a gene, transcript, or array probe, and entry (g,i) records its assay value in specimen i. Annotation and filtering determine the number of rows; study design determines the number of columns. The operational quantity is a count, intensity, or derived representation, with an additional measurement argument needed for absolute RNA abundance.
Two more pieces of context will matter throughout: what a sample is, and the disease used as the running example.

A bulk specimen, such as blood or tissue, contains many cells. Its RNA combines their contributions. The weights for a relative RNA measurement depend on RNA amount and recovery, not only cell counts: equal numbers of two cell types need not contribute equal RNA. A change in mixture can change many measured genes without changing expression within either cell type.
Lupus (SLE) is the running example for several expression datasets. Blood studies often report elevated interferon-stimulated transcripts such as IFI44L, RSAD2, and IFI27, with substantial patient heterogeneity. The pattern depends on tissue, disease state, treatment, and assay; it is useful biological context rather than a compulsory pattern for every patient or dataset.

For an ideal relative bulk measurement, write q_g^{\mathrm{bulk}}=\sum_c w_cq_{gc}, where q_{gc} is gene g’s RNA fraction within cell type c and w_c is that cell type’s share of the assayed RNA. If two cell types contribute equal cell numbers but one contributes four times as much RNA per cell, their RNA weights are 1/5 and 4/5 under equal recovery. This is why a cell-count proportion is not automatically the right RNA mixture weight. Deconvolution needs assumptions connecting the reference and bulk measurement.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
section: 4 Two technologies, two kinds of numbers
text:
4 Two technologies, two kinds of numbers
Microarrays. Probes bind labeled target material, and a scanner records fluorescence. Intensities are continuous; preprocessing such as RMA on suitable Affymetrix platforms commonly produces log2 summaries. The protocol and processing record determine the scale, not an assumed numerical range. Several probes may map to one gene, and a probe may have ambiguous or outdated mapping. Check the platform-specific annotation and the summary supplied.
RNA sequencing. Direct read/fragment counts are nonnegative integers; abundance estimators can produce noninteger estimated counts. Low-abundance features often have zeros. A count model can use the original counts while accounting for effective library exposure through an offset; it need not first log-transform them. Transformed matrices serve different tasks, such as exploratory plots or explicitly defined correlations.
A common working model has conditional mean \mu_{gi} and dispersion \alpha_g:

\operatorname{Var}(C_{gi})=\mu_{gi}+\alpha_g\mu_{gi}^2.

The first term resembles Poisson sampling variance; the second allows extra variation. Dividing by \mu_{gi}^2 gives squared relative SD 1/\mu_{gi}+\alpha_g. More counts reduce the first component, but a dispersion floor remains. An appropriate design still needs independent biological replication to estimate population differences.


Code
# What RNA-seq counts look like: a negative binomial with mean-dependent overdispersion.
set.seed(1)
mu <- 2^seq(0, 14, length.out = 2000)                 # gene means, from 1 to ~16000
counts <- rnbinom(2000, mu = mu, size = 1 / 0.1)      # dispersion 0.1 (moderate; human cohorts are often higher)
plot(log2(mu), log2(counts + 1), pch = ".", xlab = "log2 true mean", ylab = "log2(count + 1)")
abline(0, 1, col = "grey")








Figure 3: One simulated negative-binomial count at each of 2,000 specified means, with dispersion 0.1. The reference line is y = x on the displayed log2 scales; it is not a fitted regression. Low means produce zeros and discrete counts, while relative variation remains at high means.





Each dot is one negative-binomial draw at its specified mean, not a repeated-measures estimate of a gene’s variance. At low means, integer sampling and zeros strongly affect the log plot. At high means the relative dispersion remains; the points do not collapse onto the reference line. The plot illustrates the measurement model, not an empirical claim about every cohort.
A dataset’s technology and supplied processing stage determine the appropriate next steps. Public archives contain both array and sequencing cohorts; publication date or the word “expression” does not establish the data scale.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
section: 5 From counts to something you can correlate
text:
5 From counts to something you can correlate
For an RNA-seq correlation analysis on a defined transformed scale, work through four decisions. A count-model differential-expression analysis instead uses its count likelihood, design, and offsets; the transformed values below are not replacements for its count input.
Filter with the design in mind. Very sparse features can provide little information for the intended contrast and unstable transformed correlations. A feature expressed mainly in one group is a different case from one barely measured anywhere. edgeR’s filterByExpr() uses library sizes and the supplied group/design to determine adequate expression across relevant samples, with additional total-count and large-group rules. Its thresholds are parameters, not a universal number of retained genes. Record the rule and resulting family. The edgeR reference manual gives its exact definition.
Define the exposure and reference. Plain counts per million use \mathrm{CPM}_{gi}=10^6C_{gi}/L_i, where L_i is the column’s library total. TMM estimates a factor f_i and uses effective library size L_i^{\mathrm{eff}}=L_if_i. It can enter a count model as an offset or a log-CPM calculation without overwriting the raw matrix. The factor is estimated from relative feature behavior under reference/stability assumptions. DESeq2’s median-of-ratios factors also use a reference-based construction; neither alone identifies a shared absolute increase in all RNA.
TPM and FPKM/RPKM additionally account for feature length and use different denominators. TPM is a length-adjusted composition whose within-sample sum is one million. Between-sample comparisons of such values concern that relative representation and its assumptions. They are not interchangeable with integer counts in a count-model likelihood, and length correction alone does not provide molecules per cell. Importing transcript-quantifier output needs the relevant method’s handling of estimated counts and effective lengths.
Specify a transformation. \log_2(\mathrm{CPM}+c) gives an observed log-scale variable when the offset c>0 is fixed. It keeps zeros finite and changes the low end most strongly; it does not turn a zero into evidence of biological absence. The next chunk adds c in CPM units. edgeR’s prior.count uses a library-scaled count addition with a corresponding library-size adjustment, so it is not the same operation as adding the same integer to every cell. DESeq2’s vst and rlog provide other transformations aimed at reducing mean-dependent variance under their models.
A transformation need not make all genes identically noisy or all observations normally distributed. For correlation, the target is the correlation of the specified representation. Recovering latent biological correlation from noisy measurements needs additional assumptions. The simulation below isolates one way noise affects that comparison.
Check the mean-variance relationship after transforming. Plot per-gene standard deviation against per-gene mean on the transformed scale. A strong trend means the noise level depends on how highly a gene is expressed, and your correlations will inherit that. The next chunk runs steps 2 to 4 by hand in base R on a simulated count matrix, so you can see the plot before you have real data. The edgeR version for real data follows it.


Code
# Steps 2 to 4 by hand: 20,000 genes x 20 samples, with sample depths that differ several-fold.
set.seed(2)
n <- 20
mu <- 2^runif(20000, -3, 13)                                  # gene means: many low, a few high
depth <- exp(rnorm(n, 0, 0.4))                                # per-sample depth factors
counts <- matrix(rnbinom(20000 * n, mu = outer(mu, depth), size = 1 / 0.16), nrow = 20000)
lib_size <- colSums(counts)                                   # library sizes, in reads
cpm <- t(t(counts) / lib_size * 1e6)                          # normalize: counts per million
offset <- 1                                                   # try 0.1 and 5
log_cpm <- log2(cpm + offset)                                 # transform
gene_mean <- rowMeans(log_cpm)
gene_sd <- apply(log_cpm, 1, sd)
plot(gene_mean, gene_sd, pch = ".",
     xlab = "mean of log2(CPM + offset)", ylab = "SD of log2(CPM + offset)")
lines(lowess(gene_mean, gene_sd), col = "red")








Figure 4: Across-specimen SD versus mean of log2(CPM + 1) for 20,000 simulated genes in 20 specimens, with a red smooth trend. At the lowest abundances, the offset compresses both the mean and SD toward zero. This is a simulation of the chosen representation, not a universal mean–variance curve.





The plot summarizes simulated across-specimen SD for each gene after normalization and transformation. With offset 1 CPM, nearly unobserved genes are often mapped close to \log_2(1)=0, so their SD can be small because the offset dominates. A small SD here does not imply precise measurement of a biological abundance. Changing the offset can alter both this pattern and correlations at the low end. Compare offsets in optional practice rather than treating the displayed curve as a universal property.
Now consider correlations. The next chunk gives two latent log-expression variables correlation 0.6, exponentiates them to obtain count means, and generates conditionally independent negative-binomial noise. It repeats this experiment at five mean-count levels. The reported correlation is between \log_2(\mathrm{count}+1) values, so its target differs from correlation of the latent log variables.


Code
# Observed correlation between two genes with the same underlying correlation, by mean count.
ObsCor <- function(m, n = 200, rho = 0.6, reps = 200) {
  mean(replicate(reps, {
    z1 <- rnorm(n)
    z2 <- rho * z1 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)               # correlated latent expression
    x <- rnbinom(n, mu = m * exp(0.4 * z1 - 0.08), size = 1 / 0.16)
    y <- rnbinom(n, mu = m * exp(0.4 * z2 - 0.08), size = 1 / 0.16)
    cor(log2(x + 1), log2(y + 1))
  }))
}
set.seed(3)
means <- c(1, 5, 20, 100, 1000)
round(setNames(sapply(means, ObsCor), means), 2)


   1    5   20  100 1000 
0.07 0.16 0.24 0.27 0.29 


The latent log correlation stays fixed while the average observed correlation rises from roughly 0.07 at mean count 1 to roughly 0.29 at 1,000. In this experiment, weaker observed edges at low counts arise without a change in the latent dependence. At high means, negative-binomial dispersion still adds noise, so more counts do not recover the latent log correlation exactly. Exponentiating also changes Pearson correlation; the latent abundances themselves need not have correlation 0.6.
A simpler additive-error model explains the attenuation idea. If X=U+e and Y=V+d, with centered errors independent of the latent variables and each other, then \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(U,V) while both variances increase. Consequently

\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\frac{\operatorname{Corr}(U,V)} {\sqrt{(1+\sigma_e^2/\sigma_U^2)(1+\sigma_d^2/\sigma_V^2)}}.

Here \sigma_U^2,\sigma_V^2>0 are latent variances and \sigma_e^2,\sigma_d^2 are error variances. This exact identity uses the additive independent-error assumptions; it is an analogy, not the formula for the transformed negative-binomial experiment. Correlated technical errors or normalization can create associations as well as weaken them.
On real data, the standard path uses edgeR, which normalizes with TMM instead of plain library-size scaling. Here count_matrix and sample_group stand for your data.


Code
# The standard path with edgeR (install from Bioconductor: BiocManager::install("edgeR"))
library(edgeR)
y <- DGEList(counts = count_matrix, group = sample_group)
keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = sample_group)
y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
y <- calcNormFactors(y, method = "TMM")
logcpm <- cpm(y, log = TRUE, prior.count = 2)     # genes x samples, log2 scale


For arrays, verify scale and preprocessing from the platform and processing record before transforming again. Numerical ranges and boxplots are diagnostic clues, not proof: matching distributions can be imposed by quantile normalization, and differing distributions can have biological causes. A gene-level summary needs a prespecified probe-mapping and aggregation rule, including treatment of ambiguous or discordant probes. Keeping probe-level features is another defined analysis. Selecting whichever probe gives the largest group difference is not an innocuous annotation step.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
6 Things that will bite you

Batch effects. Inspect processing dates, sites, chips, and runs, and cross-tabulate them with group. PCA colored by batch can reveal structure, but association with a principal component does not identify its cause. Batch covariates, ComBat, and removeBatchEffect() serve different modeling/preprocessing roles; check the intended design and preserve the contrasts of interest. Perfect group–batch confounding prevents their direct separation without additional information. A correction can also change covariance, so a network analysis needs to assess the resulting representation.
Cell composition. Blood cell mixtures vary with disease and treatment. In an ideal mixture, two genes enriched in the same cell type can co-vary as that type’s contribution changes, even with fixed within-type expression. Reference-based deconvolution estimates composition under measurement and reference assumptions. Measured blood counts provide other information but need specimen matching and an argument connecting cell counts to RNA contributions. Estimated composition is not an exact confounder or a cell-type-specific outcome.
Sex and age. Check their distributions by group and their role in the intended contrast. XIST and Y-chromosome transcript patterns can help investigate sample identity, but expression depends on tissue, assay, and biology; they are not infallible classifiers. Investigate discrepancies using the original records instead of automatically overwriting metadata.
Outliers and failed samples. PCA or clustering can reveal unusual specimens. Determine whether they reflect assay failure, a metadata error, or genuine heterogeneity. Prespecify defensible exclusion rules where possible and report their consequences for the analyzed population. Maximizing group separation is not a QC criterion.
Scale. Always ask: counts, CPM, log-CPM, TPM, or array intensities, and on which base of logarithm? GEO deposits are inconsistent, and “normalized” in the submitter’s description can mean any of several things.
Repeated samples. Longitudinal cohorts have several samples per subject. Choose the independent unit using Units of analysis, replication, and study design; retain all visits from one person together when people are the independent draws. Check the metadata for subject identifiers; they are sometimes only in the sample title string. GSE65391 has a subject field; in GSE49454 the patient appears only in the title (C2PL28V2 is patient C2PL28 at visit 2).
crumbs: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
7 Where the data come from
Public repositories supply real gene-expression datasets for research and practice. The examples below explain how to obtain and inspect them. Elsewhere, controlled methods examples use synthetic data so that population truth is known; keep that distinction when interpreting a result.
GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus, NCBI). Three identifiers matter: GSE identifies a series, GSM a deposited sample record, and GPL a platform. A GSM can represent a specimen, technical measurement, or multiplexed pool; it is not automatically one independent person. A series can provide processed matrices, supplementary files, and links to raw data. Read the file descriptions and processing fields before importing. RNA-seq supplementary files can hold counts, RPKM, or another representation, so downloading the right study is not enough to establish the scale.


Code
# Pull a GEO series in R. install.packages("BiocManager"); BiocManager::install("GEOquery")
library(GEOquery)
dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
gse <- getGEO("GSE65391", GSEMatrix = TRUE, destdir = "data/raw")   # a list; inspect its platforms before selecting
eset <- gse[[1]]
expr <- exprs(eset)                                  # genes/probes x samples
meta <- pData(eset)                                  # one row per sample: title, characteristics, etc.
anno <- fData(eset)                                  # probe annotation, including gene symbols
dim(expr); head(meta[, head(grep("characteristics", names(meta)), 5)])   # the first five metadata columns
stopifnot(identical(colnames(expr), rownames(meta)))   # verify specimen alignment
summary(as.vector(expr[, 1]))                        # inspect range; establish scale from processing metadata


Metadata in GEO are free text in “characteristics” columns and need cleaning every time. Each cell holds text of the form key: value, so strip the key first (for example with sub("^[^:]*: ", "", x)). Write the cleaning as a script, never by hand, so that anyone can rerun it.
For this RNA-seq example, the deposit supplies a specifically named RPKM file. Select it explicitly rather than reading whichever supplementary file happens to appear first; another file could be an archive or another assay. This example inspects a processed representation, not input for the count-model path above.


Code
supp <- getGEOSuppFiles("GSE72509", baseDir = "data/raw")   # returns the paths of the files it saved
paths <- rownames(supp)
chosen <- paths[basename(paths) == "GSE72509_SLE_RPKMs.txt.gz"]
stopifnot(length(chosen) == 1L)
supp_table <- read.delim(gzfile(chosen), check.names = FALSE)


SRA (Sequence Read Archive). Raw sequencing resources use identifiers such as SRR (run), SRX (experiment), and SRP (study). Reprocessing can be useful when available summaries do not match the needed feature definition or pipeline. Several runs can come from one specimen; preserve that mapping instead of treating runs as biological replicates.
recount3 and ARCHS4 provide large reprocessed expression resources. A common processing pipeline can reduce one source of heterogeneity, but studies can still differ in collection, assay design, population, and metadata. Inspect each resource’s actual units and construction before substituting it for a deposited matrix.
ArrayExpress / BioStudies (EMBL-EBI). The European counterpart to GEO; many GEO array studies are mirrored there (E-GEOD-xxxxx), and some European studies are only there.
ImmPort. NIH’s immunology data repository: clinical trials and cohort studies in immunology with expression, cytometry, and clinical data, including lupus studies. Registration required; worth it for immunology and autoimmune disease.
GTEx is a multi-tissue donor resource. Tissue and donor selection matter when using it as a reference; it is not a universally exchangeable healthy-control group for another study. Several tissues from the same donor also retain a shared donor identity.
TCGA, through the GDC portal, provides cancer molecular and clinical data. Tumor, adjacent tissue, and external control samples define different comparisons. Check specimen types, person IDs, and processing compatibility before combining them.
Single-cell resources, including CELLxGENE and the Human Cell Atlas, provide cell-level data and annotations. Millions of cells can still come from a modest number of independently sampled donors. For a donor-population contrast, preserve donor and specimen IDs; a cell-type label alone is not enough. The Perez et al. lupus study below illustrates that distinction.
Access conditions. Some molecular and clinical records require controlled access through resources such as dbGaP or the European Genome-phenome Archive. A public study record does not mean every raw file or covariate is openly downloadable. Establish which files and identifiers are available before choosing a research question around them.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
8 Lupus cohorts you will meet
These examples illustrate different observation units and deposited scales. Counts below describe the cited study/deposit, not a promise about the analysis-ready subset. Reconstruct people, visits, and technical repeats from the actual imported metadata before fitting a model.

GSE65391. Banchereau et al. (2016, Cell), longitudinal pediatric whole-blood arrays. GEO lists 996 arrays: 924 SLE measurements from 158 patients and 72 control measurements, including 24 technical control replicates. The deposited total is therefore neither the number of people nor the number of distinct biological specimens. The linked clinical metadata make repeated visits, disease activity, and blood composition useful audit questions.
GSE49454. Chiche et al. (2014, Arthritis and Rheumatology), adult whole-blood arrays. The study reports 157 SLE samples from 62 patients, alongside 20 controls. Compare the publication’s patient count with the deposit’s sample count; visit labels need explicit parsing and validation before person-level inference.
GSE88884. Baseline arrays from the ILLUMINATE-1 and ILLUMINATE-2 tabalumab trials, with 1,760 SLE patients and 60 controls. The parent study includes later visits, but this accession’s stated comparison is baseline. Two trial sources plus separately obtained controls require careful technical and population comparisons; a trial label is not automatically a pure batch variable.
GSE72509. Hung et al. (2015, Science), whole-blood RNA-seq with 117 sample records. The named supplementary matrix contains RPKM, not raw counts. Verify group labels, available covariates, and person identifiers from the deposit; a count-based likelihood cannot be applied merely because the original assay was sequencing.
GSE174188. Perez et al. (2022, Science), more than 1.2 million PBMCs from 162 cases and 99 controls. GEO lists 88 multiplexed pool records and directs users to controlled-access data. Neither 88 pools nor 1.2 million cells equals the 261 donor units. Identify an accessible data product with the necessary donor, specimen, and cell-type mappings before defining a donor-level analysis.

Record whatever you find on first contact in the project README for the next person.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
9 A first-contact checklist
When you open a new dataset, before anything else:

Technology and scale. Array or RNA-seq; counts, CPM, log, or intensities; which log base.
Dimensions. Genes by samples; how many genes survive filtering.
Metadata. Group labels, subject identifiers, batch, sex, age, time point. How many samples per group, per subject, per batch. Some deposits, such as GSE72509, have almost none of these.
Sample distributions and PCA. Compare technical and biological labels, remembering that a pattern is a diagnostic clue, not proof of its cause.
Identity checks. Compare available metadata, replicate relationships, and informative expression patterns; investigate discrepancies using the source records.
Biological context. Inspect relevant gene programs, including interferon-related transcripts in suitable lupus blood cohorts. Unexpected patterns prompt investigation of tissue, treatment, assay, labels, and heterogeneity; they do not by themselves prove the data are wrong.
Write everything in steps 1 to 6 into a script that produces a short report, and save the cleaned matrix and metadata together with the script that made them.

title: Gene expression data, for people who have never seen any
text:
10 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · OM-01 — Identify measurements and biological replication
Task type: Interpretation.
A raw RNA-seq matrix has 15,000 genes and 30 specimen columns. Ten people each contributed three visits; five people are controls and five are patients. A metadata table gives person ID, visit, group, sequencing run, and library size.
Identify the feature, specimen, and independent biological unit under an independent-person sampling model. Explain why 30 columns are not 30 independent people, why counts require a scale/preprocessing decision before comparison, and what identifiers must be checked before joining the matrix to metadata.
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish measurement units from replication and describe the information needed to interpret the matrix.
Transfer: What changes if the three columns are technical repeats of the same specimen rather than three visits?


Hint

One matrix column records one specimen; independence is a statement about the sampling design.



Solution outline — open after trying

The features are measured genes, the columns are visit specimens, and the independent biological units in this design are ten people. The three visits within each person can be dependent. Library sizes and other measurement differences affect raw counts, so the target scale and normalization assumptions must be specified. Match each specimen column to one metadata record using specimen IDs; retain person IDs for clustering and check visit/group consistency, duplicated IDs, missing joins, and run–group confounding.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Pull GSE72509 with GEOquery and inspect which components contain measurements. Find the named supplementary file, establish its scale, identify controls in the metadata, and list the checklist items the available record does not support. Do not generalize one deposit’s file layout to all RNA-seq series.
Using the simulated count matrix above or any RNA-seq count matrix, compute log-CPM with offsets of 0.1, 1, and 5 CPM and plot the per-gene SD against the mean for each. Describe what the offset does to low-count genes and to correlations among them.
Simulate a two-cell-type mixture: 200 genes specific to type A, 200 to type B, mixing proportions varying across 100 samples. Compute the gene-gene correlation matrix and describe its block structure. Nothing in this simulation involves gene regulation; where did the network come from?
In GSE65391, identify the subject identifier and tabulate visits per subject. How unequal is it? This is the design the permutation guide is about. Repeat for GSE49454, where you must build the subject identifier from the sample title.

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
text: Before reading: Understanding an omics dataset, means, logarithms, and basic regression.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
section: 1 The output of preprocessing is part of the analysis
text:
1 The output of preprocessing is part of the analysis
An analysis of log-normalized expression estimates a quantity involving log-normalized expression. It does not automatically estimate a difference in absolute molecules per cell. Writing the target after choosing a pipeline can hide this change of question.
Distinguish three operations. A fixed transformation, such as a prespecified logarithm with a fixed offset, defines a new measured variable. A normalization learned from the dataset uses estimated reference quantities and brings additional sampling dependence. An adjustment for biological covariates specifies which population association or contrast is being isolated. The operations can coexist, but they require different justifications.
For each operation, finish the sentence “After this step, one value represents …”. Dividing a signal by specimen volume gives a different unit from dividing by a sum of feature signals. Taking a log changes the summary being averaged. Regressing out a biological covariate changes the comparison. A clean-looking matrix is not a sufficient description of any of these choices.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
section: 2 Relative measurements cannot answer every absolute question
text:
2 Relative measurements cannot answer every absolute question
The toy example has two molecular features. Feature A has the same absolute abundance in both specimens; B increases ninefold. Both specimens receive the same sequencing budget. Predict what happens to the expected reads for A.


Code
abundance <- rbind(A = c(100, 100), B = c(100, 900))
colnames(abundance) <- c("Specimen 1", "Specimen 2")
shares <- sweep(abundance, 2, colSums(abundance), "/")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
barplot(abundance, col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00"),
        ylab = "Absolute molecules", main = "Biological quantities")
barplot(1000 * shares, col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00"),
        ylab = "Expected reads out of 1,000", main = "Relative measurement",
        legend.text = rownames(abundance))








Figure 1: A synthetic fixed read budget: A stays at 100 molecules but falls from half to one tenth of the expected reads as B rises.





In specimen 1, A’s share is 100/(100+100)=1/2, giving 500 expected reads out of 1,000. In specimen 2, it is 100/(100+900)=1/10, giving 100 expected reads. Its expected measured count falls fivefold while its absolute amount stays fixed. The denominator changed because B increased.
More generally, a composition p_g=x_g/\sum_hx_h is unchanged when every x_g is multiplied by the same positive constant. Consequently relative observations alone cannot distinguish all absolute-abundance worlds, even with arbitrarily many reads. Equal library sizes do not supply the missing scale.
Normalization can recover useful comparisons under a stated reference or stability assumption. For example, estimating a specimen’s multiplicative factor from reference features assumes their joint behavior can anchor that factor. An increase shared by every feature can be absorbed into the estimated reference. External calibration tied to specimen amount, cell number, or another defined unit may be needed for an absolute target. The two-feature toy illustrates an identification issue; it does not evaluate a particular normalization algorithm under its own assumptions.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
text:
3 Transformation changes the target
Let L=\log_2(Y+c) with a prespecified offset c>0 and Y+c>0. Define the group contrast \Delta_L=E[L\mid A=1]-E[L\mid A=0]. Then

2^{\Delta_L}
=\frac{2^{E[\log_2(Y+c)\mid A=1]}}
       {2^{E[\log_2(Y+c)\mid A=0]}}.

Each term is the population geometric mean of Y+c. This is generally different from E[Y\mid A=1]/E[Y\mid A=0], the arithmetic-mean ratio. The log is nonlinear, so transforming and averaging do not commute. The offset also forms part of the variable being summarized, particularly near zero.
The following positive-valued example needs no offset. Predict both mean ratios before running it.


Code
a <- c(1, 1, 1, 17)
b <- c(5, 5, 5, 5)
c(arithmetic_ratio = mean(b) / mean(a),
  geometric_ratio = 2^(mean(log2(b)) - mean(log2(a))))


arithmetic_ratio  geometric_ratio 
        1.000000         2.462395 


Both arithmetic means are 5, so their ratio is 1. Group A’s geometric mean is 17^{1/4}\approx2.03, whereas group B’s is 5, giving ratio about 2.46. The contrast is sensitive to distributional shape as well as the largest values. Select the summary that answers the biological question, and report its scale.
An offset has units too. Adding one to a read count differs from adding one CPM after depth normalization. At small values the offset can determine much of the transformed difference. Report where it was added, its numerical value, and the logarithm base; another offset defines another observed-scale target.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
section: 4 Filtering changes the family and sometimes the population
text:
4 Filtering changes the family and sometimes the population
Feature filtering defines which features are analyzed. Removing 5,000 low-count genes leaves conclusions about the retained family; it does not establish no change in the excluded genes. With a relative representation, removing features and recomputing its reference can also change the remaining features’ values. Keep the filtering and reference rules explicit.
Sample exclusion can change the target population, especially if failed measurements are related to disease severity or the outcome. If only specimens passing QC are averaged, the immediate target is a mean among included specimens. Extending it to everyone eligible needs an argument about the observation process or an adjusted estimator. This is different from reducing the number of tested genes. Keep both feature-flow and person/specimen-flow records.
A filter used before testing still needs an inferential justification. Being applied “before” the test in code is not the same as being independent of the null test statistic. Filtering on a group contrast and then testing that same contrast generally changes calibration. See Multiple testing when the tests are not independent.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
section: 5 Batch and cell composition are not interchangeable nuisances
text:
5 Batch and cell composition are not interchangeable nuisances
A batch variable records a technical process. Cell composition may represent biological differences as well as variation one wants to adjust for. Removing a composition-associated signal can change the scientific question rather than simply clean the data. Define whether the desired target is a bulk-tissue contrast, a contrast at common composition, or a cell-type-specific quantity.
For example, if Y=\alpha+\tau A+\gamma B+\varepsilon describes a measured outcome, A is group and B is batch. When every case is in batch 1 and every control in batch 0, B=A and the mean becomes \alpha+(\tau+\gamma)A. The data identify only the combined coefficient, not its biological and technical parts separately. Including both columns in software does not fix the missing within-batch comparison.
When groups overlap across batches, adjustment can use those comparisons under the chosen model. Inspect how much overlap exists: a formally estimable coefficient can still depend heavily on a small subset of the data. Independent technical controls may supply additional calibration information, but their applicability needs a measurement model. Adjusting for a covariate also does not establish causality; that requires its own identification argument.
For composition, the bulk group difference includes whatever mixture changes occurred in that population. A standardized target instead averages conditional group means over one chosen composition distribution. Adding estimated composition to a regression does not automatically identify expression within a particular cell type; that requires a model and information separating the cell-type contributions.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
section: 6 Learned preprocessing belongs in the fitting argument
text:
6 Learned preprocessing belongs in the fitting argument
For held-out prediction or cross-fitted nuisance estimation, fit outcome-dependent selection, imputation, tuning, and other learned operations on training units, then apply the fitted operations to validation units. Keep all records from one independent unit in the same fold. Fixed, independently specified transformations can be applied consistently throughout.
Some unsupervised normalization procedures use the whole cohort by design. If changing another person’s specimen changes my normalized value, the derived observations share an estimated reference. An inference argument that treats the resulting values as independent, fixed outcomes must account for that construction. A deterministic transform using only one person’s recorded measurements is a different case.
Whether cohort-wide fitting is appropriate depends on the target and analysis, not on the word “unsupervised.” For prospective prediction, an incoming specimen must be processed using the reference available at deployment. For cross-fitted nuisance estimation, a learned preprocessing step belongs in the fold-specific procedure unless another argument justifies the dependency. Validate the complete fitting procedure, including its reference and tuning.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
text:
7 Make preprocessing auditable
For every operation, record the input version, parameters, reference set, fitting data, output scale, and reason. Inspect before/after distributions, missingness, and group–batch tables. Evaluate the operation against the target rather than choosing it because it maximizes apparent group separation.
In edgeR, normalization factors modify effective library sizes. This illustrates a model-based correction, rather than a requirement to overwrite the raw count matrix. Preserve raw measurements and document the derived representation used by each analysis.
The Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions page gives a framework for labeling preprocessing changes, estimator changes, and identification departures.
crumbs: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated

title: Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated
text:
8 Exercises
The checkpoint is this page’s completion target. Additional practice is optional. Try the checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · PRE-01 — Name the target after each processing decision
Task type: Interpretation and diagnosis.
A workflow logs counts with an offset, selects genes by the case–control contrast, adjusts for cell composition, and compares the resulting group means. For each step, identify the target or inferential issue. Explain what must be justified before calling the result a disease effect on absolute expression.
Ready to continue when: you can separate a scale definition, selection, biological adjustment, and causal/measurement assumptions.
Transfer: If the target is the total bulk-tissue disease-associated difference, could removing all composition-associated variation remove part of that target?


Hint

Ask what random variable is being averaged, which family was selected, and what comparison remains after adjustment.



Solution outline — open after trying

Logging defines a mean log-scale target involving the offset. Selecting by the same contrast being tested can invalidate ordinary null calibration. Composition adjustment changes a bulk comparison to a composition-adjusted one under the chosen model. Neither the transform nor adjustment establishes an absolute-abundance or causal interpretation; those need calibration and identification assumptions. A defensible analysis specifies the target first, uses justified selection/inference, documents the fitting pipeline, and reports the scale and adjustment.




Additional practice (optional)

Repeat the log-scale example with offsets 0.1, 1, and 5 and explain the resulting targets.
Design a group–batch table that is perfectly confounded and one that supports a within-batch group comparison.
List which steps in your own pipeline learn information from outcomes or from validation units.

9 Reading

edgeR workflow: filtering, normalization factors, and weighted comparisons.
Love, Huber, and Anders (2014), DESeq2: a count-model framework with explicit normalization assumptions.

title: Omics data and measurement
text:
An omics matrix is the output of an assay and a processing history. A count, a fluorescence intensity, a normalized peak, and a methylation proportion are different observations. Their independent units, scale, identity, and observation process determine what a statistical contrast can mean.
The shared introduction and preprocessing pages develop these decisions through worked examples: a join error can reverse a comparison, normalization can hide an absolute change, and transformation can change the population summary. The assay primers then explain how these issues arise through capture, calibration, detection, composition, and coverage. They are parallel specializations; the one relevant to your measurements is the completion branch for your work.

title: Omics data and measurement
text:
What you’ll learn

Reconstruct the observation: identify the biological and technical units, feature evidence, scale, metadata alignment, and missing-value conventions.
Defend the biological interpretation: explain what normalization, transformation, selection, calibration, composition, and detection permit or prevent you from claiming.

Completion means auditing a dataset and stating the population quantity that its chosen representation supports. OM-02 and PRE-01 assess the common tasks; the assay checkpoints assess the corresponding specialization. Additional practice and other assay branches are optional.

title: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand
text: Before reading: The Understanding an omics dataset page, means and logarithms; read Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated alongside this page.
crumbs: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand

title: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand
section: 1 Start with the feature, not the column heading
text:
1 Start with the feature, not the column heading
Proteomics measures proteins or evidence about proteins. In bottom-up mass spectrometry, proteins are digested into shorter amino-acid sequences called peptides. The instrument measures ions from those peptides, and a pipeline assigns identities and quantities. A protein table is therefore a derived summary, rather than a direct count of intact protein molecules.
A peptide sequence can occur in more than one protein. If the detected evidence cannot distinguish the candidates, the pipeline can report a protein group. A gene symbol used as its display label does not resolve that ambiguity. A proteoform is a particular molecular form, for example one affected by sequence processing or modification; a shared-peptide summary may not distinguish such forms. Affinity assays instead measure reagent binding, with their own specificity and calibration requirements. A change in binding signal needs a platform-specific interpretation.
Before analysis, reconstruct the chain from specimen to run to quantified feature. Record the platform, acquisition and processing versions, feature definition, mapping rules, measurement units, normalization, missing-value codes, and identification confidence. QFeatures keeps peptide and protein assay levels connected. Identification FDR addresses incorrect identifications among accepted identifications; differential-abundance FDR addresses false group-comparison discoveries. Controlling the first does not automatically control the second.


Which object does the comparison concern?



Independent people and specimensAliquots, runs, and peptide measurements retain their person and specimen IDs.


Measured evidencePeptide signals or reagent-binding measurements have platform-specific units.


Defined feature summaryMapping and aggregation produce a protein, protein group, or assay target.


Population contrastSpecify the scale, population, covariates, and observation process before inference.



More peptides can improve measurement of one specimen. They do not create more independently sampled people. Technical replicates are useful for studying assay error; their role differs from biological replication.
crumbs: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand

title: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand
section: 2 Aggregation makes an assumption about a shared signal
text:
2 Aggregation makes an assumption about a shared signal
Suppose the idealized log2 intensity for peptide p in person i is

L_{ip}=a_p+Q_i+\epsilon_{ip}.

Here a_p is a peptide-specific response and Q_i a common protein-level component. Let A_i denote group and assume errors have mean zero within each group. If a_p is stable across groups, subtraction gives

E[L_{ip}\mid A_i=1]-E[L_{ip}\mid A_i=0]=E[Q_i\mid A_i=1]-E[Q_i\mid A_i=0].

The peptide’s baseline response cancels even if one peptide is systematically much brighter than another. Averaging a fixed set of peptides then estimates the shared contrast. It does not make raw intensities directly comparable or calibrate Q_i to concentration.
If specimens contribute different subsets of peptides, the average offset can change: the mean of a_p among observed peptides need not stay fixed. Missingness can therefore affect aggregation before a group test. Shared peptides, modifications, interference, or changing proteoform mixtures can also break the model. A discordant peptide warrants investigation; it does not identify a particular mechanism by itself.
Let \mathcal S_i be the peptides observed in specimen i. The naïve average of their log2 intensities is

\begin{aligned}
\overline L_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
&=Q_i+\overline a_{\mathcal S_i}
       +\overline\epsilon_{i,\mathcal S_i}.
\end{aligned}

The bars denote averages over the retained peptides. Even with unchanged protein signal Q_i, this summary can change when the mean peptide response \overline a_{\mathcal S_i} changes.
The following noiseless synthetic example holds Q_i=12 in every specimen. Five peptides have fixed response offsets -2,-1,0,1,2, giving intensities 10 through 14. All five are observed in group 0. In group 1, progressively more of the lower-response peptides are unobserved. The missingness pattern is imposed for this illustration; the measured values that remain do not change. Follow each matrix column down to its average before reading the result.








Figure 1: An imposed missingness pattern changes the peptide mix used in each average. Every specimen has protein signal 12, zero errors, and fixed peptide responses. Gray crosses mean unobserved, not zero. The naïve group contrast is +1.25 despite a true contrast of zero.





The apparent contrast comes entirely from changing which peptide offsets enter the average. For example, S8 contributes only peptide E, whose response is high in both groups. The group-1 summaries rise without a change in any retained peptide’s intensity. A protein-summary method needs a justified way to handle peptide responses and observation patterns; treating each specimen’s available-peptide average as the same quantity can fail.
A separate example: discordant peptide changes. For peptide contrasts 1, 1, and 0, the unweighted average is 2/3, while the concordant pair averages to 1. These log2 contrasts imply factors 2^{2/3}\approx1.59 and 2 for the defined geometric-mean summaries. The discrepancy shows the role of aggregation; it does not identify which summary is the true molecular change.
Selecting concordant peptides after looking at group effects can bias the downstream comparison. Prespecify mapping/aggregation or account for selection. Keep the original peptide evidence so a protein-level claim can be checked. ProteomeXchange’s reporting guidance distinguishes identification results, quantification outputs, and reconstruction files.
crumbs: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand

title: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand
section: 3 Missing signals do not have a single explanation
text:
3 Missing signals do not have a single explanation
An entry can be missing because the analyte was not detected, a peptide was not selected or confidently identified, quality control removed a value, or a sample failed. Some mechanisms depend on abundance; others need a different model. Do not interpret every missing entry as zero concentration or every positive entry as a calibrated molecule count.
Consider a threshold mechanism: latent log2 intensity L is observed only if L>c. The observed-data mean is E[L\mid L>c], not E[L]. Detection depends directly on the outcome, so the MAR argument for a missing mean cannot be imported without further assumptions.
The figure uses L=\mu+U, with U\sim N(0,1). Detection is the event U>c-\mu. The standard-normal tail identity gives

E[L\mid L>c]
=\mu+\frac{\varphi(c-\mu)}{1-\Phi(c-\mu)},

where \varphi and \Phi are the normal density and CDF. The added term is positive: only an upper tail is observed. At c=10, full group means 9 and 10 become detected means about 10.53 and 10.80. Their contrast falls from 1 to about 0.27 because selection differs between groups. This is what DetectedMean() calculates.
Knowing a threshold tells us that a non-detected value lies below it, but not where it lies. A parametric censored-data model can extrapolate under assumptions; the unseen distribution is not identified nonparametrically from the inequality alone.


Code
cutoff <- seq(6, 12, length.out = 150)
DetectedMean <- function(mu, cutoff) {
  a <- cutoff - mu
  mu + dnorm(a) / pnorm(a, lower.tail = FALSE)
}
observed_difference <- DetectedMean(10, cutoff) - DetectedMean(9, cutoff)
plot(cutoff, observed_difference, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00",
     xlab = "Detection threshold on latent log2 scale", ylab = "Group 1 minus group 0 mean",
     ylim = c(0, 1.15))
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "#2F80C8")
legend("bottomleft", c("Detected-value contrast", "Full-population contrast"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "#2F80C8"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")








Figure 2: A teaching censoring model with unit normal errors. Raising the threshold increasingly separates the mean of detected values from the full mean. This is a population calculation, not a universal proteomics detection model.





Filling every missing value with a low constant replaces an uncertain outcome by an assumed value. If detection fractions differ, the number of inserted constants also differs, changing the group contrast. Treating filled values as observed can understate uncertainty. Imputation needs an observation/outcome model and an uncertainty argument; a complete matrix alone supplies neither.
A detection-frequency target can be legitimate if explicitly defined, but it concerns the assay and detection rule as well as biology. Start with missingness by feature, group, run order, batch, and specimen quality; do not choose imputation by which method yields more discoveries.
crumbs: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand

title: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand
section: 4 Write the estimand on the available scale
text:
4 Write the estimand on the available scale
For a prespecified, fully observed log2 feature summary Y, an unadjusted between-group contrast is E[Y\mid A=1]-E[Y\mid A=0]. An adjusted population-standardized contrast can instead be

\begin{aligned}
\psi&=E_{Z\sim P_*}\{m_1(Z)-m_0(Z)\},\\
m_a(z)&=E[Y\mid A=a,Z=z].
\end{aligned}

Z contains the chosen covariates and P_* defines one covariate population used for both groups. Compare groups at the same z, then average using the same weights. For two equally weighted strata with conditional contrasts 1 and 0, the standardized contrast is 1/2, irrespective of their different frequencies in the observed groups. Both groups need outcome support at the target covariate values; otherwise modeling requires extrapolation. This remains associational unless additional causal assumptions justify more.
Outcome regression and, when needed, group/observation probabilities are nuisance functions. The From an influence function to an estimator page explains augmentation and remainder conditions; an assay-specific missingness mechanism must be identified first. Cross-fitting does not supply concentration calibration or a model for unseen outcomes.
Exponentiating a mean log2 contrast concerns geometric means of the defined positive measurement. Calling it a concentration ratio requires a calibration argument. Equal loading, reference samples, and internal standards address different sources of variation; record which quantity each normalization anchors. Global shifts can be absorbed by an assumed stable reference. Affinity-assay units likewise require their platform’s interpretation rather than an automatic absolute-abundance claim.
crumbs: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand

title: Proteomics: from measured evidence to an estimand
text:
5 Before differential abundance analysis
Check sample IDs and technical replicates; inspect peptide counts/mapping ambiguity, quality measures, missingness patterns, and reference behavior. Check group–batch overlap and the estimability of the chosen contrast. Freeze the feature family, aggregation, scale, and inclusion rules before testing. Report pointwise uncertainty and the multiplicity procedure separately. The Differential expression and abundance page supplies a design/contrast framework; reuse it only after defending the proteomics measurement and variance assumptions.

Checkpoint · PROT-01 — Reconstruct a protein-level claim
Task type: Interpretation and diagnosis.
A protein group has three peptides, contrasts 1, 1, and 0 on the log2 scale, and 30% missing values concentrated in controls. There are 20 people per group, each run twice. State the independent replication count, calculate the unweighted peptide-average contrast, and identify what is still needed for a claim about absolute protein abundance.
Ready to continue when: you can separate biological replication, aggregation, observation, and calibration assumptions.
Transfer: Would adding ten technical runs per person identify the concentrations below a detection threshold?


Hint

Follow the specimen–peptide–protein chain; a technical run is not a new person.



Solution outline — open after trying

There are 40 independent people under independent sampling, not 80. The average peptide contrast is 2/3. Its protein interpretation needs an aggregation model and mapping evidence. Differential missingness can change the detected-value target; a full-data contrast needs an observation model or sensitivity analysis. Absolute abundance additionally needs calibration. Selecting the two increasing peptides after seeing the contrasts introduces selection.




Additional practice (optional)

Vary the peptide offsets in the missingness figure while holding every protein signal at 12. Which observed-peptide averages change? What happens if all peptide offsets are zero? Explain which two ingredients create the apparent group difference.
In the threshold example, calculate the detected fraction in each group at threshold 10 and describe a sensitivity analysis for the unseen values.
Audit a protein table: distinguish accession, protein group, gene symbol, peptide count, and quantitative unit.

title: Survival models and efficiency (optional)
text: Before reading: Model restrictions and efficiency, likelihood scores, and basic survival concepts. This extension introduces risk-set and counting-process notation; it is not required for the missing-outcome mean construction.

title: Survival models and efficiency (optional)
text:
1 The Cox model
Let T be an event time, C a censoring time, and X a baseline covariate. One observed record is W=(U,\Delta,X), where U=\min(T,C) and \Delta=1\{T\le C\}. We observe an event when \Delta=1; otherwise we know only that the event had not occurred by U. Assume independent people, continuous times, and conditionally independent censoring, T\perp C\mid X. The censoring law has nuisance parameters distinct from the event-model parameters. This permits censoring to depend on X, but excludes unrecorded dependence between T and C after conditioning on X.
The Cox model specifies the event hazard

\lambda(t\mid X)=\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta X}.

The hazard is an instantaneous event rate among people who have survived to time t. It is not the probability of an event at an exact time. The unknown baseline hazard \lambda_0 is unrestricted; e^\beta is the hazard ratio for a one-unit increase in X. The target is the common log hazard ratio \beta under this model.

1.1 Express the score as observed events minus predicted events
Define the at-risk indicator R(t)=1\{U\ge t\} and event-counting process N(t)=1\{U\le t,\Delta=1\}. For a single person, N jumps from zero to one if an observed event occurs. The notation dN(t) denotes that jump. Write

dM(t)=dN(t)-R(t)e^{\beta X}\lambda_0(t)\,dt.

The second term is the event count predicted over a small time interval by the model and observed history. Their difference is a martingale innovation: its conditional expectation given the past is zero. The integral \int f\,dM adds weighted event jumps and subtracts the corresponding integrated predictions. We use a stated covariance identity below; developing stochastic integration is beyond this optional extension.
To see where the score comes from, put \Lambda_0(u)=\int_0^u\lambda_0(t)\,dt. Under the censoring assumption, the event-model part of one person’s log likelihood is

\ell=\Delta\{\log\lambda_0(U)+\beta X\}
      -e^{\beta X}\Lambda_0(U).

The remaining factors describe censoring and the covariate law. Differentiating the displayed expression with respect to \beta gives

\begin{aligned}
S_\beta&=X\Delta-Xe^{\beta X}\Lambda_0(U)\\
       &=\int X\,dM(t).
\end{aligned}

A bounded baseline direction a(t) gives the path \lambda_{0,u}(t)=\lambda_0(t)\{1+u a(t)\}, positive for sufficiently small |u| wherever the original hazard is positive. Differentiating its log likelihood gives the nuisance score S_a=\int a(t)\,dM(t). Unlike S_\beta, its integrand depends only on time.


1.2 Project away the baseline-hazard directions
For suitable predictable, square-integrable integrands f and a, the martingale covariance identity is

E\left[\left(\int f\,dM\right)\left(\int a\,dM\right)\right]=E\int f(t)a(t)R(t)e^{\beta X}\lambda_0(t)\,dt.

Here “predictable” means that the integrand uses information available just before the time in question. The identity replaces the ordinary product calculation used in the partially linear model. At each time with a nonempty population risk set, the best time-only predictor of X minimizes E[R(t)e^{\beta X}\{X-a(t)\}^2]. Setting its derivative to zero gives E[R(t)e^{\beta X}\{X-a(t)\}]=0, hence

\bar x(t) = \frac{E\big[X\,e^{\beta X}R(t)\big]}{E\big[e^{\beta X}R(t)\big]},

This is a hazard-weighted risk-set mean: people with larger e^{\beta X} receive more weight. It is an ordinary mean among people at risk only when those weights are constant. Subtracting it makes the score orthogonal to every baseline-hazard direction. Under the stated censoring model, event-martingale scores are also orthogonal to the censoring and covariate-law nuisance scores. The efficient score, information per person, and EIF are therefore

\begin{aligned}
S_{\text{eff}}&=\int\{X-\bar x(t)\}\,dM(t),\\
I_{\text{eff}}&=E\int\{X-\bar x(t)\}^2 \times R(t)e^{\beta X}\lambda_0(t)\,dt,\\
\phi_{\text{eff}}&=I_{\text{eff}}^{-1}S_{\text{eff}}.
\end{aligned}

Assume 0<I_{\text{eff}}<\infty. The influence-variance bound is I_{\text{eff}}^{-1}, the estimator-variance bound is 1/(NI_{\text{eff}}), and the corresponding SE bound is 1/\sqrt{NI_{\text{eff}}}. Risk-set covariate variation and observed events supply information; severe censoring can reduce both.


1.3 Connect the projection to partial likelihood
The sample counterpart of the weighted mean is

\bar X_N(\beta,t)=
\frac{\sum_iR_i(t)e^{\beta X_i}X_i}
     {\sum_iR_i(t)e^{\beta X_i}}.

By construction, \sum_iR_i(t)e^{\beta X_i}\{X_i-\bar X_N(\beta,t)\}=0. Consequently the integrated prediction terms cancel when the individual residual scores are summed. What remains is

U_N(\beta)=\sum_{i:\Delta_i=1}
\{X_i-\bar X_N(\beta,U_i)\}.

At each event, compare that person’s covariate with the hazard-weighted mean among those still at risk, then add the differences. This is Cox’s partial-likelihood score for untied event times. The cancellation explains why the score can be computed without estimating \lambda_0. Under the relevant identification, integrability, and large-sample conditions, its root attains the EIF and is efficient. Deriving the population projection suggests the estimator; the counting-process asymptotic argument establishes attainment.
Compare this with the partially linear example in Model restrictions and efficiency. Both remove the component explained by the nuisance directions, although their scores and inner-product weights differ. In the Cox model the projection is onto functions of time under risk-set weights. What remains supplies information about \beta that changing the baseline hazard cannot reproduce.

title: Survival models and efficiency (optional)
text:
2 Checking the Cox model
The simulated Cox model has a covariate X\sim N(0,1), a Weibull baseline hazard \lambda_0(t)=1.5t^{0.5}, \beta=0.5, and independent censoring uniform on (0,2), which censors about 42% of observations. The continuous draws avoid ties. Four estimators are compared: coxph; a score with each event weighted by w(t)=e^{-2t}; Weibull regression; and exponential regression.
The time-weighted score still has population expectation zero at the true coefficient. With a unique root and appropriate regularity, it can consistently estimate \beta, but its nonconstant weighting generally loses efficiency. Weibull regression makes an additional, correct restriction on the baseline family while estimating its parameters. Exponential regression imposes a constant baseline hazard, incorrect in this experiment.


Code
library(survival)
beta <- 0.5
SimCox <- function(n) {
  x <- rnorm(n); u <- runif(n)
  t <- (-log(u) / exp(beta * x))^(1 / 1.5)        # hazard 1.5 * t^0.5 * exp(beta * x)
  cens <- runif(n, 0, 2)
  data.frame(time = pmin(t, cens), status = as.numeric(t <= cens), x = x)
}

# At each event time: the covariate of the person who fails minus the average covariate of the
# risk set, multiplied by a weight w(t). With w = 1 this is Cox's partial likelihood score.
WeightedCox <- function(d, w = function(t) rep(1, length(t))) {
  d <- d[order(d$time), ]; wt <- w(d$time)
  Score <- function(b) {
    r <- exp(b * d$x)
    s0 <- rev(cumsum(rev(r))); s1 <- rev(cumsum(rev(d$x * r)))   # sums over the risk set at each time
    sum(wt * d$status * (d$x - s1 / s0))
  }
  uniroot(Score, c(-5, 5))$root
}

set.seed(2027)
d <- SimCox(400)
c(censored = 1 - mean(d$status), coxph = unname(coef(coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x, d))),
  unit_weight_score = WeightedCox(d))


         censored             coxph unit_weight_score 
        0.4175000         0.6932629         0.6932629 


With every weight equal to 1, the custom score agrees numerically with coxph on this sample. This is a useful implementation check for the untied-time example. It does not itself establish efficiency; that follows from the model-specific argument. Now compare repeated samples.


Code
EstCox <- function(d) {
  cf <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x, d)
  wb <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ x, d, dist = "weibull")
  ex <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ x, d, dist = "exponential")
  # survreg uses an accelerated failure time scale; dividing by the Weibull scale gives the hazard-ratio coefficient
  c(coxph = unname(coef(cf)), coxph_se = sqrt(vcov(cf)[1, 1]),
    weighted = WeightedCox(d, function(t) exp(-2 * t)),
    weibull = -unname(coef(wb)["x"]) / wb$scale,
    exponential = -unname(coef(ex)["x"]))
}
set.seed(2028)
R <- 1000; n <- 400
res <- t(replicate(R, EstCox(SimCox(n))))
est <- setdiff(colnames(res), "coxph_se")
data.frame(estimator = est, mean = round(colMeans(res[, est]), 3),
           sd = round(apply(res[, est], 2, sd), 4), row.names = NULL)


    estimator  mean     sd
1       coxph 0.501 0.0729
2    weighted 0.503 0.0828
3     weibull 0.503 0.0724
4 exponential 0.408 0.0574


Code
round(mean(res[, "coxph_se"]), 4)    # the average model-based standard error of coxph


[1] 0.072


Compare each mean with the true value 0.5 and the standard deviations with one another. The Monte Carlo standard error is about 0.002 for each mean and 0.0016 for each standard deviation.

Cox’s estimator is approximately centered at the target in this simulation, and its standard deviation, 0.073, is close to its average model-based SE, 0.072. Its squared SE estimates 1/(NI_{\text{eff}}), the estimator-variance bound; the SE itself estimates the square root of that bound.
The weighted estimator is also approximately centered in this simulation. Its standard deviation, 0.083, is about 14% above Cox’s, which is a variance about 29% higher.
Weibull regression uses the correct baseline family. Its standard deviation, 0.072, is close to Cox’s within Monte Carlo error. This experiment detects little precision gain from that additional restriction; it does not prove equal efficiency bounds for the two models. The cost of nuisance freedom depends on the model, the population law, and which restrictions are compared.
The exponential regression has a smaller standard deviation, 0.057, and the wrong center, 0.41. It assumes a constant hazard, which is a working model in the sense of What is your estimator actually estimating?, and when the hazard is not constant its limit differs from \beta.

title: Statistical models, targets, and paths
text: Before reading: Large-sample reasoning for methods research, Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity, elementary expectations and derivatives, and the target/model distinction in What is your estimator actually estimating?. The advanced resampling and cluster branches can be revisited after influence functions.

title: Statistical models, targets, and paths
section: 1 Keep the distribution, model, and target separate
text:
1 Keep the distribution, model, and target separate
Let W be one observation record and P its population distribution. A model \mathcal M is a set of distributions we allow for that record. The actual population law is one member of this set, although we do not know which member. A scalar target is a map \psi:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R: it assigns a population quantity to every allowed law. The map defines the question; \psi(P) is its value at the actual population.
For complete observations of a feature Y, write the mean target as \mu(P)=E_P[Y]. This is the same mean \mu used in the previous guide, now displaying which distribution supplies the expectation. Choosing a sample-mean algorithm does not decide which populations are allowed.
For example, both a normal model and an unrestricted finite-variance model contain the mean as a target. The normal model allows only normal distribution shapes; the larger model permits many other shapes. A partially linear model instead restricts a conditional mean to \beta X+g(Z) while leaving g unspecified. These are restrictions on population laws, rather than names of software routines.
The term nuisance depends on the question. When the mean is the target in a normal model, the variance may be a nuisance parameter. If the variance itself is the question, its role changes. Nuisance quantities can be scientifically important; they are simply not the final quantity being estimated in the current argument.
A low-dimensional target can be studied in a fully nonparametric model. Semiparametric estimation is therefore not limited to partially linear or proportional-hazards regression. The missing-outcome mean later uses a broadly unrestricted observed-data model for W=(Z,R,RY), after identification assumptions connect its functional to the full-population question.

title: Statistical models, targets, and paths
section: 2 Move through the model along a valid path
text:
2 Move through the model along a valid path
A path P_t is a one-parameter family in the model with P_0=P. Think of t as a small hypothetical population perturbation, not a sample size or an observation’s value. Different paths change different aspects of the distribution. The path must remain inside the model for sufficiently small t.
If the path has densities p_t relative to a common reference measure and the derivative is justified, its score at zero is

s(W)=\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\log p_t(W)\right|_{t=0}.

The score describes a relative density change: \partial_t p_t|_0=p\,s. Positive values of s increase probability locally and negative values decrease it. Differentiating the total probability \int p_t=1, with a justified interchange, gives E_P[s]=0. Probability added in some places must be removed elsewhere.
A concrete construction begins with a bounded, mean-zero function s and sets

dP_t=(1+ts)dP.

This means reweighting the original law by 1+ts. Its total mass is E_P[1+ts]=1. If |s|\le K<\infty, choosing |t|K<1 keeps every weight positive. Finally,

\begin{aligned}
\left.\partial_t\log p_t(W)\right|_0&=\left.\frac{s(W)}{1+ts(W)}\right|_0\\
&=s(W).
\end{aligned}

Thus we have checked normalization, nonnegativity, and the score itself. In an unrestricted model this gives a valid path. A normal-shape or symmetry restriction imposes further requirements; a normalized density need not preserve them.
For three equally likely feature values, the construction is concrete:



Y
Original probability
Score s(Y)
Path probability




0
1/3
-1
(1-t)/3


2
1/3
0

4
