For |t|<1, the probabilities are positive and sum to one. At t=0.3, they are approximately 0.233, 0.333, and 0.433: probability moves from 0 to 4 while the middle probability stays fixed. Direct averaging gives

\begin{aligned}
\mu(P_t)&=\frac{2+4(1+t)}3\\
&=2+\frac43t.
\end{aligned}

The target’s derivative at zero is therefore 4/3. It is a rate of population-mean change per unit perturbation, not the standard error of an estimate.

title: Statistical models, targets, and paths
text:
3 Represent the target’s derivative
Instead of computing the target derivative separately for every path, we seek one function that represents all the permitted directional derivatives. A square-integrable, mean-zero gradient \phi satisfies, for every regular score path under consideration,

\left.\frac{d}{dt}\psi(P_t)\right|_{0}=E_P[\phi(W)s(W)].

The right side is an L_2(P) inner product: multiply the gradient by the path’s score and take a population expectation. The score specifies which change we are making; the gradient describes the target’s sensitivity to that change. A representation must work for all allowed directions, not just one convenient path.
For the mean and the bounded-score construction, ordinary expectation algebra gives

\begin{aligned}
\mu(P_t)&=E_P[Y(1+ts)],\\
\left.\frac{d}{dt}\mu(P_t)\right|_0&=E_P[Ys]\\
&=E_P[(Y-\mu)s].
\end{aligned}

The last equality uses E_P[s]=0. Thus \phi(Y)=Y-\mu represents the mean derivative. In the three-point example, E[(Y-2)s(Y)]=(2+0+2)/3=4/3, agreeing with the direct calculation. Integrability of Y suffices for this bounded-direction derivative; finite variance makes Y-\mu a square-integrable gradient suitable for the usual CLT argument.
The sample mean has the separate identity \bar Y-\mu=P_n(Y-\mu). This is why the same centered function appears both in a population derivative and in a sampling expansion. For a general target, the derivative calculation alone does not supply an estimator expansion, its negligible remainder, or a feasible SE. Those require their own arguments.
A point-contamination path (1-\varepsilon)P+\varepsilon\delta_y instead places a little mass at a chosen value y. For a continuous law it introduces an atom where P assigns zero mass, so it is generally not a smooth dominated score path through P. It can also leave a restricted model. Influence functions uses this convenient derivative for elementary unrestricted functionals, then relates it to the score-path representation above.

title: Statistical models, targets, and paths
text:
4 What a tangent space records
The tangent space \mathcal T\subseteq L_2^0(P) records the model’s permitted first-order directions. The notation L_2^0(P) means functions with finite second moment and expectation zero; its inner product is E_P[fg] and its norm is \|f\|_2=\sqrt{E_P[f^2]}.
To form \mathcal T, take linear combinations of regular path scores and include their L_2 limits. This is the closed linear span. “Closed” matters because approximating a direction increasingly well should not exclude its limiting direction. In the unrestricted model, bounded mean-zero scores are dense in L_2^0(P), giving \mathcal T=L_2^0(P). Restrictions can remove directions and leave a smaller space.
For example, if the population probability of a binary stratum Z is known and fixed by the model, a path can alter outcomes within strata but cannot change their probability weights. The conditional-expectation restriction on its score is then E[s\mid Z]=0. Model restrictions and efficiency will use this example to show how an excluded direction changes the efficient gradient.
Under the appropriate linearity and continuity assumptions, the target derivative has a unique representing element inside the closed tangent space. This is its canonical gradient, or efficient influence function. A representation outside that space may contain an extra component orthogonal to every permitted score, contributing zero to every derivative inner product. Model restrictions and efficiency explains why such a component can add sampling variance.
The general Hilbert-space representation theorem is useful mathematical background. Proving its existence statement is an optional extension; the completion task here is to construct and differentiate an actual valid path.

title: Statistical models, targets, and paths
text:
5 Exercises
The checkpoint is a completion target. Additional practice is optional.


Checkpoint · SP-03 — Build a valid path and calculate its score
Task type: Proof and interpretation.
In an unrestricted model, let s(W) be bounded, with E[s]=0, and define dP_t=(1+ts)dP. Assume E[|Y|]<\infty for the mean target.
Check normalization and nonnegativity for sufficiently small t, calculate the log-density score at zero, and derive the path derivative of E_t[Y]. Explain why an arbitrary path of this form may not stay in a restricted statistical model.
Ready to continue when: you can verify that a proposed perturbation is a probability distribution and relate its score to the target derivative.
Transfer: For a symmetric location model, can an arbitrary mean-zero s change the nuisance density while preserving symmetry? What restriction would its direction need?


Hint

Bound |t|\|s\|_\infty by a number below one, then use E[s]=0.



Solution outline — open after trying

The total mass is E[1+ts]=1 and 1+ts>0 if |t|\|s\|_\infty<1 (a zero score gives a constant path). The log-density derivative is s/(1+ts), equal to s at zero. Since s is bounded and Y integrable, E_t[Y]=E[Y]+tE[Ys], so the mean derivative is E[(Y-\mu)s]. A restricted model only permits paths preserving its restrictions; normalization alone does not establish membership.




Additional practice (optional)

Verify the three-point table’s normalization, nonnegativity, score, and mean derivative.
Give a bounded mean-zero direction that changes the probabilities of a symmetric three-point distribution asymmetrically. Why does that path leave a symmetric model?
Compare a distributional derivative with the sample-mean expansion. Which extra argument supplies a sampling distribution?

title: Quantiles and local expansions
text:
Before reading: Statistical models, targets, and paths, Influence functions, and the LLN/CLT and stochastic orders from Large-sample reasoning for methods research.
This transfer page keeps the same goal: connect a population derivative to a sample expansion and a justified standard error. A stated empirical-CDF lemma supplies the extra probability step; proving its general empirical-process version is additional theory.
For i.i.d. observations, P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(Y_i) and Pf=E[f(Y)].

title: Quantiles and local expansions
section: 1 A quantile has a nonsmooth sample equation
text:
1 A quantile has a nonsmooth sample equation
Let F(u)=\Pr(Y\le u) be the population CDF and fix 0<\tau<1. The target is the quantile q=\inf\{u:F(u)\ge\tau\}. The median uses \tau=1/2. Assume i.i.d. observations, a continuous distribution with a unique interior quantile, and a density f continuous and positive near q. These conditions give F(q)=\tau and a nonzero population slope f(q).
The empirical CDF is F_n(u)=n^{-1}\sum_i1\{Y_i\le u\}. Use the order-statistic quantile \hat q=Y_{(k)} with k=\lceil n\tau\rceil, corresponding to R’s type = 1. With no ties, F_n(\hat q)=k/n, so

\begin{aligned}
0&\le F_n(\hat q)-\tau\\
&<1/n.
\end{aligned}

For five ordered values (1,2,4,6,9), the median is 4 and the empirical CDF there is 3/5. The sample equation misses 1/2 by 1/10. This small root error is acceptable because 1/n is negligible on the root-n scale.
The sample CDF is a step function: between observations its derivative is zero, and at jumps an ordinary derivative is unavailable. We cannot Taylor-expand that random step function as if its derivative were the population density. Instead, write E_n(u)=F_n(u)-F(u) for the empirical CDF error and \Delta_n=E_n(\hat q)-E_n(q). The exact decomposition is

F_n(\hat q)-\tau=F_n(q)-\tau +\{F(\hat q)-F(q)\}+\Delta_n.

The three right-hand terms have different jobs: sampling fluctuation at the fixed q, a smooth population-CDF change, and an empirical increment caused by evaluating at a random argument.

1.1 Establish consistency and the local rate
Use the uniform CDF consistency result \sup_u|F_n(u)-F(u)|\xrightarrow{p}0. For any sufficiently small fixed \delta>0, positive density gives F(q-\delta)<\tau<F(q+\delta). Once the empirical CDF is uniformly close enough, its crossing of \tau lies between these two endpoints. This proves \hat q\xrightarrow{p}q.
To obtain a rate, examine the deterministic thresholds q\pm C/\sqrt n for fixed C. Their population CDF values differ from \tau by approximately \pm Cf(q)/\sqrt n. The count of observations below either threshold is binomial. Its CLT shows that crossing beyond the threshold requires a fluctuation in a corresponding normal tail. Choosing C large makes both tail probabilities small, giving \hat q-q=O_p(n^{-1/2}). This rate argument uses binomial fluctuations, rather than a derivative of the sample indicator.


1.2 Use the stated empirical-CDF lemma
We supply the additional probability result needed for the random argument. For every fixed C<\infty,

\sqrt n\sup_{|u-q|\le C/\sqrt n}
|E_n(u)-E_n(q)|\xrightarrow{p}0.

This is stochastic equicontinuity over shrinking neighborhoods: on that local scale, changing the evaluation point changes the empirical error by less than root-n fluctuation. The rate established above places \hat q in such a neighborhood with arbitrarily high probability after choosing C large. Consequently \Delta_n=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
The full empirical-process proof of this lemma is additional theory. The completion task uses it as a stated result, with its role and required neighborhood made explicit.


1.3 Invert the population slope
Taylor-expand only the population CDF. Its differentiability and the local rate give

F(\hat q)-F(q)=f(q)(\hat q-q) +o_p(n^{-1/2}).

In the exact decomposition, the sample-root error is O(1/n) and the empirical increment is negligible. Move the fixed-point fluctuation to the other side and divide by the nonzero f(q):

\begin{aligned}
\hat q-q&=P_n\phi_q+o_p(n^{-1/2}),\\
\phi_q(Y)&=\frac{\tau-1\{Y\le q\}}{f(q)}.
\end{aligned}

An observation below q has negative influence, pulling the quantile downward; one above it has positive influence. The factor 1/f(q) translates CDF noise into outcome units. A flat population CDF near the quantile makes its location harder to determine precisely.

title: Quantiles and local expansions
section: 4 Check the approximation in a simulation
text:
4 Check the approximation in a simulation
For a standard-normal median, f(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}, giving limiting variance \pi/2 for \sqrt n\hat q. The code uses known density only to assess the theory in a known simulation, not as an available input in a real cohort.


Code
set.seed(21)
ns <- c(40, 160, 640); R <- 500
z <- lapply(ns, function(n) {
  replicate(R, sqrt(n) * quantile(rnorm(n), 0.5, type = 1) / sqrt(pi / 2))
})
plot(density(z[[1]]), xlim = c(-4, 4), ylim = c(0, 0.5),
     xlab = "Scaled median error", main = "Quantile normal approximation", col = "#2F80C8")
lines(density(z[[2]]), col = "#D55E00")
lines(density(z[[3]]), col = "#009E73")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c(paste("n =", ns), "N(0,1)"),
       col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "black"), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), bty = "n")
data.frame(n = ns, variance = sapply(z, var),
           coverage = sapply(z, function(a) mean(abs(a) <= 1.96)))


    n  variance coverage
1  40 1.0349580    0.952
2 160 1.0011091    0.940
3 640 0.8686863    0.966








Figure 1: Synthetic normal medians, scaled by their theoretical asymptotic standard deviation. Increasing sample size is compared on a common N(0,1) scale.





The reported variances concern the standardized errors and should approach 1; they are not variances of the unscaled medians. The coverage calculation uses the known density to assess an idealized normal interval in this simulation. A real-data procedure would need to estimate the required uncertainty or use another justified method.
Across 500 replications, coverage near 0.95 has Monte Carlo SE about 0.01. Both the numerical variances and coverages fluctuate. A familiar-looking density is evidence about this experiment, not a substitute for the assumptions and proof.

title: Quantiles and local expansions
text:
5 Exercises
The checkpoint is this page’s completion target. Additional practice is optional.


Checkpoint · SP-06 — Derive the quantile expansion and influence function
Task type: Derivation using a stated stochastic lemma.
Under the quantile conditions in this page, derive the expansion using the displayed CDF decomposition and stated stochastic-equicontinuity fact. Identify the influence function, its variance, and the additional requirement for a feasible standard error. Independently derive the path derivative by differentiating F_t(q_t)=\tau along a valid bounded-score path. Explain why a pointwise derivative of the sample indicator cannot replace the argument.
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish the population derivative from the stochastic increment and obtain both the expansion and pathwise representation.
Transfer: For the standard-normal median, compute the variance. Which step fails when the density is zero at the target?


Hint

The approximate sample root has an error of order 1/n. Along a path, differentiating the CDF changes both its distribution and its endpoint.



Solution outline — open after trying

The approximate-root error and empirical-CDF increment are o_p(n^{-1/2}). The population change is f(q)(\hat q-q) plus a negligible remainder, so inversion gives \hat q-q=(\tau-F_n(q))/f(q)+o_p(n^{-1/2}). The influence function is (\tau-1\{Y\le q\})/f(q) with variance \tau(1-\tau)/f(q)^2. For a score s, differentiation gives 0=E[1\{Y\le q\}s]+f(q)\dot q; using E[s]=0 recovers \dot q=E[\phi_qs]. A feasible variance estimate needs density consistency at q or another justified method. The sample CDF is discontinuous, so its pointwise derivative does not supply the population density. For a standard-normal median the influence variance is \pi/2, giving first-order estimator variance \pi/(2n); a zero density prevents the displayed derivative inversion.




Additional practice (optional)

Compare R quantile types 1 and 7 and explain why their first-order limits can agree.
Identify the derivative step that fails when the density vanishes at the target.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text: Before reading: Estimating equations and the projection identity from Conditional expectation and L2 geometry.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
1 The one idea
Likelihood theory gives the simplest version of a semiparametric problem. A parameter of interest changes the distribution in one direction; a nuisance parameter changes it in another. The score measures each direction. To estimate the parameter of interest efficiently, keep the part of its score that the nuisance cannot imitate.
In a finite-dimensional model this is ordinary projection of one vector of scores on another. In a semiparametric model, the nuisance has infinitely many directions, but the calculation is the same. This page develops the finite-dimensional version first.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
2 Likelihood and score
Suppose one observation record W has density or probability mass function p_\theta(w), indexed by a scalar parameter \theta. Lowercase w denotes a possible value of that record. The log likelihood for a sample is

\ell_n(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(W_i).

The i.i.d. model makes the joint density a product, and taking logarithms turns it into this sum. For observed data, likelihood is a function of candidate parameter values: it compares how the model describes the same dataset as \theta varies. It is not a probability density over \theta.
The score is the derivative of the log density,

S_\theta(W) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_\theta(W).

For one observation, S_\theta(W) is a random variable. Its value tells us the local slope of the log density at a candidate parameter. The total sample score is \ell_n'(\theta)=\sum_iS_\theta(W_i); dividing by n gives the average score. An interior, differentiable maximum likelihood estimate satisfies

P_n S_{\hat\theta}(W)=0.

So maximum likelihood is a special case of the estimating-equation framework in the Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity page. Its special feature is that the same derivative that defines the equation also encodes how the distribution changes when \theta changes.
This zero condition need not hold at a boundary or identify the global maximum. For the regular model calculation below, assume the needed differentiability and integrability, a common support, and valid interchanges of derivatives and integrals. Then the population score has mean zero at the truth:

E_\theta[S_\theta(W)] = 0.

To see why, differentiate \int p_\theta(w)\,dw=1:

\begin{aligned}
0&=\int\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}p_\theta(w)\,dw\\
&=\int p_\theta(w)\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_\theta(w)\,dw.
\end{aligned}

The score is therefore a mean-zero random variable, just like the estimating functions in Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity.
The expectation here is under the same model value at which the score is evaluated. It is not a statement that an observed sample score vanishes at every candidate value. Parameter-dependent supports can invalidate this calculation: the uniform-endpoint example in Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference has boundary behavior that these regular score identities do not capture.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
3 Normal mean: the complete calculation
Let Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), with \sigma^2 known. Then

\log p_\mu(Y)=-\frac12\log(2\pi\sigma^2) -\frac{(Y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2},

so the score is

S_\mu(Y) = \frac{Y-\mu}{\sigma^2}.

The derivative of the quadratic term contributes (Y-\mu)/\sigma^2. Summing the scores and setting them to zero gives \sum_i(Y_i-\hat\mu)=0, hence \hat\mu=\bar Y. The score is a centered observation scaled by the known variance.
The Fisher information is the score’s second moment:

\begin{aligned}
I(\mu)&= E[S_\mu(Y)^2]\\
&= \frac{1}{\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}

Equivalently, under the same regularity conditions,

I(\mu)=-E\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\mu^2}\log p_\mu(Y)\right].

This is information per observation. The score variance calculation is \sigma^2/\sigma^4=1/\sigma^2. For n independent observations, total information is nI(\mu), and expected sample curvature is -nI(\mu). Larger information produces a more concentrated sampling distribution for an efficient estimator under this model.
The curvature identity follows by differentiating E_\theta[S_\theta]=0, including the change in the density as well as the change in the score:

0=E_\theta[\partial_\theta S_\theta]+E_\theta[S_\theta^2].

Thus the score equation has derivative expectation A=-I and contribution variance B=I. Substituting into the estimating-equation formula -A^{-1}S gives

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{IF}(Y)&=I(\mu)^{-1}S_\mu(Y)\\
&=Y-\mu,
\end{aligned}

and the mean’s first-order variance is I(\mu)^{-1}/n=\sigma^2/n, exact for this sample mean. The score and influence function are different objects: multiplying the score by inverse information supplies the normalization needed for an estimation contribution. If Y=7, \mu=5, and \sigma^2=4, the score is 1/2, the information is 1/4, and the influence contribution is 2. The mean estimator’s SE in a study of n people is 2/\sqrt n.




The score tells you which way the likelihood increasesA normal log likelihood parabola peaks at the sample mean; its derivative crosses zero at the same point, positive on the left and negative on the right.

The score tells you which way the likelihood increasesNormal mean example with n = 4 and known σ² = 1.
-101-4-20μ − ȲLog likelihood relative to maximum-101-606μ − ȲTotal scoreLeft of the maximum: positive score. At the maximum: zero. Right: negative.


Figure 1: The sample log likelihood is \ell_n(\mu)-\ell_n(\bar Y)=-n(\mu-\bar Y)^2/(2\sigma^2). Its derivative is the total score \sum_iS_\mu(Y_i)=-n(\mu-\bar Y)/\sigma^2. The maximum and score zero coincide. The curvature is -n/\sigma^2=-4, while information per observation is I=1/\sigma^2=1.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
4 The information bound
Why does information set a variance bound? Assume 0<I(\theta)<\infty. For the regular asymptotically linear estimators studied here, a centered, square-integrable influence function \phi must represent a unit change in the target coordinate: E[\phi S_\theta]=1. Cauchy–Schwarz then gives

\begin{aligned}
1&=(E[\phi S_\theta])^2\\
&\le E[\phi^2]E[S_\theta^2],\\
E[\phi^2]&\ge I(\theta)^{-1}.
\end{aligned}

The influence variance is the limiting variance of the scaled estimation error; dividing it by n gives the estimator’s first-order variance. The bound is therefore 1/(nI), and equality requires \phi=I^{-1}S_\theta. An estimator attaining it is efficient within this model. A regular maximum likelihood estimator attains it under the conditions supporting its expansion and variance calculation.
The finite-sample Cramér–Rao inequality is related but has a different statement: under its differentiability and unbiasedness conditions, an unbiased estimator has variance at least 1/(nI). The asymptotic result above concerns first-order contributions of regular estimators and allows finite-sample bias. It does not give an exact variance formula for every estimator or every sample size. Model restrictions and efficiency explains the role of regularity along nearby distributions.




Sharper likelihood, more concentrated estimatesTwo likelihood shapes and two normal sampling densities. Sigma one half yields information four and standard error one quarter; sigma one yields information one and standard error one half.

Sharper likelihood, more concentrated estimatesSame n = 4; less observation noise gives more information.

Figure 2: The left curves hold \bar Y fixed to compare likelihood shape; they are not probability densities for \mu. The right curves are the exact sampling distributions of the normal sample mean centered at the true mean. In this example \operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)=1/(nI)=\sigma^2/n, so the mean reaches the information bound. Efficiency compares regular estimators within the same model; it does not assert that every estimator has this variance.







Efficiency compares estimators in the same modelTwo centered normal error densities in the same model. The full mean has variance one quarter, attaining the information bound. A mean using only half the available observations has variance one half.

These exact normal calculations illustrate the bound without changing the model or the available data. More generally, the guide’s efficiency statement concerns first-order variance among regular estimators.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
5 Add a nuisance parameter
Now consider a normal linear model,

Y \mid X \sim N(\alpha+\beta X,\sigma^2),

where \beta is the target and \alpha is an unknown nuisance intercept. Take \sigma^2>0 as known for this derivation and assume the required covariate moments exist, with \operatorname{Var}(X)>0. We treat X as random with a law not indexed by (\alpha,\beta), and use the conditional likelihood of Y given X. Expectations average over the population covariates as well as outcomes.
The intercept is a nuisance because our current question concerns the slope; it need not be scientifically unimportant. Write \varepsilon=Y-\alpha-\beta X. Differentiating the conditional normal log density gives

\begin{aligned}
S_\beta&= \frac{X\varepsilon}{\sigma^2},\\
S_\alpha&= \frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}

Since E[\varepsilon^2\mid X]=\sigma^2, their cross moment is

E[S_\beta S_\alpha] = \frac{E[X]}{\sigma^2}.

If E[X]\ne0, the two scores are correlated: part of a slope change can be imitated by moving the intercept. Seek a coefficient c making S_\beta-cS_\alpha orthogonal to S_\alpha. Solving E[(S_\beta-cS_\alpha)S_\alpha]=0 gives c=E[S_\beta S_\alpha]/E[S_\alpha^2]=E[X]. Subtracting that projection yields

\begin{aligned}
S_{\text{eff}}
&= S_\beta - \frac{E[S_\beta S_\alpha]}{E[S_\alpha^2]}S_\alpha \\
&= \frac{\{X-E[X]\}\varepsilon}{\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}

This is the efficient score for \beta after accounting for the nuisance intercept. The information for \beta is its squared length,

\begin{aligned}
I_{\text{eff}}&= E[S_{\text{eff}}^2]\\
&= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}

If the intercept were known, slope information would instead be E[X^2]/\sigma^2. Estimating the intercept removes the part (E[X])^2/\sigma^2 that it can imitate. When E[X]=0, the scores are already orthogonal and the information bound is unchanged. An unknown nuisance need not cause a strict first-order information loss in every model.
The remaining slope information depends on variation around the covariate mean. If X were constant, a slope change could be completely absorbed into the intercept and I_{\mathrm{eff}} would be zero. Re-expressing the covariate as X-E[X] makes the separation visible; it does not create additional information or change the fitted slope when an intercept is included.




Letting the nuisance adapt makes the likelihood flatterA fixed-intercept likelihood is sharply curved with information 13; the profile likelihood after re-fitting the intercept is flatter with information 4.

Letting the nuisance adapt makes the likelihood flatterFixed design: mean(X) = 3, mean((X − 3)²) = 4; σ² = 1.
-0.800.8-2-10β − β̂Relative log likelihood per observationIntercept fixed at α̂Curvature = −13Intercept re-fittedCurvature = −4Best response:α − α̂ = −3(β − β̂)Changing the intercept can partly offset a change in slope.


Figure 4: For a fixed design with sample mean 3 and sample second central moment 4, these are exact log-likelihood differences from the joint maximum (\hat\alpha,\hat\beta). Holding the intercept fixed gives a drop -13(\beta-\hat\beta)^2/2 per observation. Re-fitting it gives \alpha-\hat\alpha=-3(\beta-\hat\beta) and a smaller drop -4(\beta-\hat\beta)^2/2. This explains the information loss in terms of indistinguishable changes in fitted means.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
section: 6 Information matrices and the Schur complement
text:
6 Information matrices and the Schur complement
With parameter (\beta,\eta), where \eta is a nuisance vector, partition the Fisher information matrix as

I =
\begin{pmatrix}
I_{\beta\beta} & I_{\beta\eta} \\
I_{\eta\beta} & I_{\eta\eta}
\end{pmatrix}.

The efficient score is

S_{\text{eff}} = S_\beta - I_{\beta\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}S_\eta,

and its information is

I_{\text{eff}}
= I_{\beta\beta}-I_{\beta\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\beta}.

To obtain the projection coefficient, solve the moment equation

\begin{aligned}
E[(S_\beta-cS_\eta)S_\eta^\top]&=I_{\beta\eta}-cI_{\eta\eta}\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

Assuming I_{\eta\eta} is invertible gives c=I_{\beta\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}. Expanding the second moment of the residual score gives the displayed Schur complement. It is the amount of information left after nuisance-score projection.
When I_{\mathrm{eff}}>0, the efficient influence function and first-order variance bound are

\begin{aligned}
\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}&=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}S_{\mathrm{eff}},\\
\text{variance bound}&=\frac1{nI_{\mathrm{eff}}}.
\end{aligned}

The normalization ensures E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}S_\beta]=1 while E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}S_\eta]=0. Removing nuisance overlap makes the score shorter, so information decreases or stays the same. Taking its reciprocal then increases or preserves the estimator variance bound. This is why a smaller efficient score is compatible with less precision.
This formula is worth recognizing because the semiparametric version changes only one thing: instead of projecting onto the span of finitely many nuisance scores, project onto a whole nuisance tangent space.




Remove the score component that the nuisance can imitateA quantitatively scaled right triangle has horizontal length 3, vertical length 2 and hypotenuse square root 13. Information bars have values 13, 9 and 4.

Remove the score component that the nuisance can imitateLengths use the score inner product E[UV]; information is squared length.
3Sα: length 3S_efflength 2Sβ: length √13The Schur complement is PythagorasRaw information: 13Removed: 9Remaining: 4I_eff = 13 − 3 × 1⁻¹ × 3 = 4; efficient variance bound = 1/(4n).


Figure 5: For the preceding regression, I_{\alpha\alpha}=1, I_{\beta\alpha}=3 and I_{\beta\beta}=13. The projection is 3S_\alpha and the orthogonal remainder is S_{\mathrm{eff}}=(X-3)\varepsilon. The triangle is drawn with side lengths in the ratio 3:2:\sqrt{13}; the bars show their squares. Thus the Schur complement measures the information remaining after nuisance projection.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
section: 7 Check the projection in a regression
text:
7 Check the projection in a regression
Here the covariate has nonzero mean, so the slope and intercept scores are correlated. Centering X removes that correlation.


Code
set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
x <- rnorm(n, mean = 3, sd = 2)
y <- 1 + 0.7 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)
fit <- lm(y ~ x)
e <- residuals(fit)

# Scores are scaled by sigma^2; the common scale does not change correlations.
slope_score <- x * e
intercept_score <- e
centered_slope_score <- (x - mean(x)) * e

c(raw_score_correlation = cor(slope_score, intercept_score),
  centered_score_correlation = cor(centered_slope_score, intercept_score),
  slope = coef(fit)["x"])


     raw_score_correlation centered_score_correlation 
                0.81481782                 0.01754632 
                   slope.x 
                0.70482441 


These are fitted score contributions in one dataset. Their empirical correlation involves products such as (X_i-\bar X)e_i^2, whereas the OLS normal equations balance X_i e_i. Exact OLS residual balance therefore does not force these score correlations to vanish. Under this correctly specified homoscedastic generator, the population score orthogonality explains the approximate finite-sample pattern as the sample grows.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
section: 8 From a nuisance vector to a nuisance function
text:
8 From a nuisance vector to a nuisance function
In the partially linear model,

Y = \beta X + g(Z) + \varepsilon,

retain the homoscedastic Gaussian outcome-error assumption, \varepsilon\mid X,Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2), for this score derivation. The nuisance is the unknown function g, rather than only an intercept. The conditional-mean model alone needs additional work and may have a different efficiency calculation under heteroscedasticity. Moving g in a direction k(Z) gives a nuisance score proportional to k(Z)\varepsilon. The efficient score for \beta is obtained by projecting X\varepsilon onto all such directions. The answer is

S_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\{X-E[X\mid Z]\}\varepsilon}{\sigma^2}.

Compare this to the intercept example. The constant E[X] has become the conditional expectation E[X\mid Z]. The finite-dimensional span of nuisance scores has become the infinite-dimensional space of functions of Z. The geometry has not changed.
The Conditional expectation and L2 geometry page supplies the residualization identity. The Model restrictions and efficiency page derives the full efficient influence function and explains the efficiency bound.




What remains after nuisance adjustment?After subtracting the overall mean one, a sinusoidal residual conditional mean remains. After subtracting the full conditional mean, the residual conditional mean is zero, though residual variance can still depend on Z.

What remains after nuisance adjustment?Z uniform on [−1, 1], X = 1 + sin(πZ) + U and E[U | Z] = 0.
After removing only the mean-101-101ZConditional mean of residualResidual: sin(πZ) + UAfter removing E[X | Z]-101-101ZConditional mean of residualResidual: UNo remaining conditional mean does not imply independence from Z.


Figure 6: The marginal mean is E[X]=1. Removing it leaves X-1=\sin(\pi Z)+U, whose conditional mean still follows the orange curve. Removing E[X\mid Z]=1+\sin(\pi Z) leaves U, whose conditional mean is the green zero line. This removes the predictable mean, not necessarily all dependence on Z: the conditional variance of U can still vary with Z. Under the homoscedastic Gaussian outcome-error model used for the score derivation, the efficient score changes from (X-1)\varepsilon/\sigma^2 with an intercept nuisance to U\varepsilon/\sigma^2 with a nuisance function.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
9 What likelihood assumes
Likelihood is powerful because it makes a detailed probability model do a great deal of work. It also means that its conclusions are tied to that model.

The score equation targets the parameter of the specified model. Under misspecification, it generally converges to a pseudo-true value rather than the scientific target. See the What is your estimator actually estimating? page.
The usual information-matrix standard error uses the equality between score variance and expected curvature. Under misspecification, these differ; the sandwich variance from the Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity page is the appropriate first-order calculation.
A semiparametric model keeps the pieces of the likelihood that define the target while declining to specify a nuisance distribution or function fully. The price is that the nuisance must be projected out rather than simply estimated with a few coefficients.

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
10 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · SP-07 — Remove a nuisance score and compute the bound
Task type: Derivation and interpretation.
Let Y\mid X,Z\sim N(\beta X+\alpha+\gamma Z,\sigma^2) with known positive \sigma^2. Write C=(1,Z)^\top and assume E[CC^\top] is nonsingular. Assume the required second moments exist and X has positive residual variance after its linear projection onto C.
Derive the target and nuisance scores, remove the nuisance-score projection, and obtain the efficient score, efficient information, EIF, and variance bound. Explain why the residualization here is linear in C rather than automatically X-E[X\mid Z].
Ready to continue when: you can carry the same nuisance projection through to information and estimator variance, with its model assumptions stated.
Transfer: If the nuisance is an unrestricted function g(Z) instead, identify the larger nuisance space and the prediction that replaces aC.


Hint

Let a=E[XC^\top]E[CC^\top]^{-1} and R_X=X-aC. Use E[\varepsilon^2\mid X,Z]=\sigma^2.



Solution outline — open after trying

The scores are S_\beta=X\varepsilon/\sigma^2 and S_\eta=C\varepsilon/\sigma^2. The score projection is aC\varepsilon/\sigma^2, leaving S_{\mathrm{eff}}=R_X\varepsilon/\sigma^2. Its second moment is I_{\mathrm{eff}}=E[R_X^2]/\sigma^2. Therefore the EIF is R_X\varepsilon/E[R_X^2] and the variance bound is \sigma^2/\{nE[R_X^2]\}. The nuisance span here contains the intercept and linear Z score. It does not contain every function of Z, so linear projection need not equal conditional expectation.





Checkpoint · SP-09 — Compare information with known and unknown variance
Task type: Derivation.
For Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), first take \sigma^2>0 as known. Derive the score, information per observation, and variance bound for \mu. Then treat (\mu,\sigma^2) as unknown, derive both scores and their information matrix, and determine whether the efficient bound for \mu changes.
Ready to continue when: you can show why adding a nuisance parameter may leave the target information unchanged, rather than assuming information always decreases strictly.
Transfer: Compare this with the slope/intercept example in the guide, where the scores are generally correlated.


Hint

Use the centered normal third and fourth moments: E[(Y-\mu)^3]=0 and E[(Y-\mu)^4]=3v^2.



Solution outline — open after trying

The scores, differentiating with respect to \mu and \sigma^2, are

\begin{aligned}
S_\mu&=\frac{Y-\mu}{\sigma^2},\\
S_{\sigma^2}&=\frac{(Y-\mu)^2-\sigma^2}{2\sigma^4}.
\end{aligned}

Their cross moment is zero and the information matrix is diagonal, with entries 1/\sigma^2 and 1/(2\sigma^4). Thus projecting the mean score off the variance score leaves it unchanged. The bound for the mean is \sigma^2/n in either model and its EIF is Y-\mu. Estimating \sigma^2 still affects how finite-sample intervals are constructed; orthogonal scores do not make the variance known.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Simulate the regression example with E[X]=0, then with E[X]=5. Compare the correlation between the raw slope and intercept scores. Does the slope estimate change when you center X?
Show algebraically that the (\beta,\beta) entry of I^{-1} equals I_{\text{eff}}^{-1} for a scalar target and vector nuisance. This is the matrix form of “removing what the nuisance can imitate.”

title: Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency
text:
11 Reading

Cox, D. R. and Hinkley, D. V. (1974). Theoretical Statistics. Chapman and Hall. Chapters 2 and 9 for likelihood and nuisance parameters.
van der Vaart, A. W. (1998). Asymptotic Statistics. Cambridge. Chapter 7 for maximum likelihood and information bounds.
Bickel, P. J., Klaassen, C. A. J., Ritov, Y., and Wellner, J. A. (1993). Efficient and Adaptive Estimation for Semiparametric Models. Johns Hopkins University Press. Chapters 1 and 2 for the parametric geometry that leads into the semiparametric version.
Tsiatis, A. A. (2006). Semiparametric Theory and Missing Data. Springer. Chapter 3 for efficient scores, information, and their semiparametric extension.

title: Research practice and reproducibility
text:
A statistical result is useful only if its inputs, analysis decisions, and interpretation can be understood and checked. Reproducibility links the scientific question to the data history, implementation, computational environment, and reported evidence.
Successful execution is one part of that record. It does not establish that a metadata join is correct, an exclusion is ignorable, or an inferential assumption holds. Good research practice makes those decisions visible so that collaborators and readers can assess them.
Two habits organize this guide. First, make the analysis a chain that another researcher can rebuild and audit, including the decisions that change its data and population. Second, make every written claim traceable to a result with a defined target, assumptions, and uncertainty. A reproducible mistake is still a mistake; a persuasive paragraph without recoverable evidence cannot be checked.

title: Research practice and reproducibility
text:
What you’ll learn

Build an inspectable research record: connect data versions, identifiers, transformations, exclusions, code, configuration, environment, and retained outputs; then test the documented execution route in a fresh session.
Report what the evidence supports: state the target and assumptions, distinguish estimates from performance summaries, label uncertainty, and link each claim to the analysis that produced it.

The checkpoints are completion targets. Additional practice is optional. The group’s published manuscripts supply research case studies; these pages use small synthetic examples to make the workflow and reporting arguments explicit.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
text: Before reading: Basic estimates, standard errors, and intervals. Evaluating a statistical method supports the performance discussion. The executable teaching example reuses the estimator from From an influence function to an estimator; you can read the reporting principles before completing that derivation.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
text:
1 Make the claim traceable
A methods report connects a scientific or methodological claim to a target, assumptions, procedure, and evidence. A reader should be able to reconstruct why the reported number supports the sentence written about it.
Start with the problem: what quantity matters, in which population and on what scale, and why an existing procedure may be inadequate. Define the independent observation and the observed data. Distinguish assumptions identifying the target from assumptions supporting an estimator or uncertainty calculation. A causal claim requires a causal identification argument; a descriptive association does not become causal through adjustment alone.
Then describe the estimator precisely enough to reproduce: estimating equation or objective, nuisance models and tuning, fold construction, preprocessing, fitting failures/retries, and confidence-interval calculation. State whether the result is an estimate of the scientific target, a model projection, or an approximation to another procedure.
A claim has several components that can be checked separately. “We estimated an adjusted difference” needs a definition of adjustment and the population over which it is averaged. “With 95% confidence intervals” needs an interval construction and its conditions. “More accurate” needs a target, a loss or performance measure, a comparator, and an evaluation setting. Start from those concrete statements rather than describing a method as universally robust or superior.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
text:
2 Match evidence to the claim








Claim
Evidence to report
What it does not establish alone




The target is identified
Observed-data functional and explicit assumptions
That assumptions hold in the application


An estimator has a stated limit
Argument and conditions, including remainder control
Finite-sample accuracy everywhere


Intervals attain nominal coverage in a scenario
Repeated-sampling coverage, MCSE, failures, scenario definition
Coverage in all populations


A method is efficient in a model
Relevant efficiency bound and an attainment argument
A small SE in one dataset


An omics analysis is scientifically informative
Effect scale, uncertainty, design, diagnostics, biological context
Ground-truth validation of every feature


A result is reproducible
Inputs, environment, configuration, code, execution record
Scientific correctness



Use Evaluating a statistical method to define performance measures before writing a comparison. In a real-data example, truth is usually unknown; call it an application or illustration unless a validation target is actually available.

2.1 State a theorem at the scope it supports
For an influence-function estimator, a useful theoretical statement identifies the target, statistical model, sampling assumptions, nuisance controls, and conclusion. For example, a first-order expansion has the form

\hat\mu-\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_P(W_i)+o_p(n^{-1/2}),

where W_i is one person’s complete observed record and the contribution is mean zero with finite positive variance. For i.i.d. people, together with variance consistency, it supports asymptotic normal inference. It does not assert exact unbiasedness or 95% coverage at every finite n. If efficiency is claimed, specify the model’s canonical gradient and explain why the estimator attains its variance bound. A small reported SE alone is not that argument.
For the missing-outcome example below, identification needs an outcome-observation assumption and support. The estimator additionally needs suitable nuisance consistency, a negligible product remainder, moment control, and a variance argument. Cross-fitting addresses a particular empirical term, not every source of error. Put the precise theorem or a clear reference near the claim; do not make a reader infer its conditions from an algorithm’s name.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
text:
3 A worked synthetic reporting example
Reuse the estimator from From an influence function to an estimator so that the report and estimator share one implementation. Its downloadable R functions generate independent synthetic people; the true full-population mean is 7/3. Covariates are available for everyone. Outcomes are missing at random given Z in this generator, with observation probabilities bounded away from zero. These are known features of a teaching simulation, not verified assumptions about a clinical dataset.


Code
source("../examples/missing-mean.R")
example <- SimulateMissingMean(n = 800, seed = 51)
fit <- CrossFitMissingMean(example$data, K = 5, seed = 52)
s <- fit$summary
s


  estimate         se    lower    upper observed   n probability_clipped
1 2.354531 0.04003445 2.276063 2.432998      329 800                   0
  mean_clipped
1            0


The next paragraph is generated from that result. It names the target, units, method, uncertainty, and observation count. It does not claim that a single covering interval establishes 95% coverage.

Code
cat(sprintf(paste0(
  "Among %d independently generated people, %d had observed outcomes. ",
  "For the full-population mean outcome in the synthetic measurement units, ",
  "the five-fold cross-fitted augmented estimator was %.3f ",
  "(estimated SE %.3f; approximate 95%% Wald interval %.3f to %.3f). ",
  "Inference uses the MAR/overlap and nuisance-rate conditions in the capstone; ",
  "the generator and fitted model classes satisfy its teaching setup. ",
  "Fitted probabilities were clipped for %.1f%% of people and fitted means for %.1f%%.\n\n"),
  s$n, s$observed, s$estimate, s$se, s$lower, s$upper,
  100 * s$probability_clipped, 100 * s$mean_clipped))

Among 800 independently generated people, 329 had observed outcomes. For the full-population mean outcome in the synthetic measurement units, the five-fold cross-fitted augmented estimator was 2.355 (estimated SE 0.040; approximate 95% Wald interval 2.276 to 2.433). Inference uses the MAR/overlap and nuisance-rate conditions in the capstone; the generator and fitted model classes satisfy its teaching setup. Fitted probabilities were clipped for 0.0% of people and fitted means for 0.0%.
A real-data paragraph would name the assay scale, actual sampling design, population, acquisition and exclusion rules, and justification for MAR and overlap; it would not have access to the unobserved population truth. If the target were a log-scale contrast, interpret it on that scale or explicitly state the transformation used for a ratio interpretation.


3.1 Walk from the result to the sentence
The person and observation counts come from s$n and s$observed. The point estimate, SE, and endpoints come from the same fit$summary. The five-fold choice comes from the call to the estimator. The MAR and nuisance-rate assertions come from the generator and theorem, not from the numeric result table. Keep that distinction when auditing a paragraph: some words are computed facts, while others state the assumptions under which those facts are interpreted.
Because this is synthetic, we can also inspect its realized estimation error:

Code
error <- s$estimate - example$truth
cat(sprintf(paste0(
  "The generator's true mean is %.3f. This estimate differs from it by %.3f, ",
  "or %.2f estimated SEs. This is one realized error; ",
  "it is not an estimate of the procedure's bias or coverage.\n\n"),
  example$truth, error, error/s$se))

The generator’s true mean is 2.333. This estimate differs from it by 0.021, or 0.53 estimated SEs. This is one realized error; it is not an estimate of the procedure’s bias or coverage.
Bias averages signed error across repeated datasets. Coverage averages whether the target is included by their intervals. A single interval contributes one zero-or-one coverage outcome, not evidence that its construction achieves 95%. The stated 95% level describes a repeated-sampling property under the relevant conditions; it is not a probability assigned to the fixed mean after seeing this interval.
For a real analysis, retain the output object or table and generate the paragraph’s numbers from it when rendering the manuscript. If an exclusion changes the analysis population, regenerate the estimate, denominator, diagnostics, and associated text together. Updating the displayed number while leaving the old population description is a substantive reporting error even if the number itself is correct.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
section: 4 Report an evaluation with its uncertainty
text:
4 Report an evaluation with its uncertainty
A simulation table should identify scenarios, target values, attempted replicate counts, successful counts, bias, empirical SD, mean SE, interval coverage, and MCSEs for the summaries. Retain method pairing and report runtime or resource requirements if they are part of the claim. Explain whether a failure is counted as an unusable interval or omitted from a conditional summary. Avoid declaring one method superior from a difference smaller than its simulation uncertainty.
Separate absolute calibration from relative performance. “Coverage was near 95%” requires its estimate and MCSE, sample size, scenario, and failure denominator. “Coverage improved” additionally needs a paired difference and its uncertainty when methods used the same datasets. A difference of 0.01 with MCSE 0.012 is an imprecise estimate of improvement, not strong evidence of a gain. Conversely, lack of a clear difference does not establish equivalence; a practical equivalence claim needs its own criterion and precision.
Report the regimes in which the theory is being checked, those near a boundary, and deliberate failure cases. A good working-model scenario shows that an implementation can behave as predicted there. It does not establish robustness to every misspecification. If a method fails on difficult datasets, report those attempts alongside any summaries conditional on success.
A figure caption should be understandable without reconstructing the entire analysis: state what is plotted, units and target, independent-unit and replicate counts as relevant, what points/lines/bands mean, and whether a reference line is known truth, a null, or an estimate. Standard error bars, confidence intervals, empirical SDs, and MCSE bars need different labels.
For feature-wise omics results, name the hypothesis family and multiplicity procedure, effect scale, adjustment variables, and selection/filtering decisions. A small adjusted p-value does not imply a large effect, a causal effect, or independent biological replication.
More discoveries can reflect stronger effects, a different family, a changed target, a more liberal test, or better power. State which comparison is intended and how error control was assessed. A pointwise interval displayed for a selected feature does not become simultaneous or selection-adjusted because the p-values received an FDR adjustment. A comparison of network significance labels likewise does not replace a direct test of an edge contrast.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
text:
6 Keep a compact reporting contract
A complete first draft can follow this sequence:

Question and target: population, measurement scale, independent unit, estimand.
Identification and design: observed data, missingness/selection, assumptions, support and confounding limitations.
Procedure and uncertainty: exact algorithm, nuisance fitting/folds/tuning, variance/interval formula, failure policy.
Evaluation: scenarios and truth where known, comparisons, replicate counts, metrics and MCSE.
Application and interpretation: data provenance, effect estimates, diagnostics, limits of real-data evidence.
Reproduction: code revision, input manifest, configuration, environment, run instructions, and retained outputs.

Separate prespecified choices from exploratory revisions and discuss where conclusions are sensitive to them. Link each displayed result to the code or retained output that produced it. Use A reproducible research project and Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset to make this contract executable.
Before sharing a draft, choose one central sentence and follow it backwards: the displayed value, retained result, run configuration, data version and exclusions, then the target and assumptions. If a link is missing, repair that evidence chain. Then read forwards: does the sentence claim only what that chain supports? This small audit is more useful than checking that every methods section contains the same fashionable technique names.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
text:
7 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · WRITE-01 — Rewrite a claim to match its evidence
Task type: Interpretation and reporting.
A draft says: “Our new method is unbiased and efficient because its confidence interval contains the true effect in one simulated dataset. In the omics application it discovers more significant genes, proving better accuracy.” Rewrite this as a defensible description and list the evidence still needed for the stronger claims. Include the distinction between an estimate’s SE and a simulation summary’s MCSE.
For the generated paragraph in this page, identify which statements come from result fields, which come from configuration, and which depend on assumptions or theory. State what needs to be regenerated if an exclusion changes the target population.
Ready to continue when: you can state what the reported evidence supports and identify the missing target, assumptions, uncertainty, or validation needed for each stronger claim.
Transfer: How would the caption change if the dashed reference line were a full-data estimate rather than known simulation truth?


Hint

One interval is one random outcome; discovery counts mix signal, calibration, filtering, and power.



Solution outline — open after trying

Report the one estimate, its stated target/scale, SE, interval, and the known synthetic truth as an illustration. Assess bias and coverage over independent replicates with MCSE and failures; efficiency needs a relevant bound and an attainment argument. In the application report effect sizes, uncertainty, multiplicity family/procedure, and assumptions. More discoveries alone do not establish accuracy when truth is unknown. SE concerns estimator variation across samples; MCSE concerns uncertainty in a simulation summary from finitely many replicates.
The counts and estimates are result fields; K=5 is a fitting choice; MAR, support, and nuisance-rate controls belong to the identification and inferential argument. A changed exclusion can alter the population, weights, fitted nuisances, estimates, diagnostics, and report text. Trace and rebuild their dependencies together.




Additional practice (optional)

Write a self-contained caption for an empirical omics contrast without an oracle truth line.
Draft a methods paragraph and a reproducibility appendix for one checkpoint analysis; have a reader identify the target and independent unit.

title: What is your estimator actually estimating?
text: Before reading: Means, conditional means, covariance, and basic regression. The population and observation record are introduced in From a research question to an identified estimand.
crumbs: What is your estimator actually estimating?

title: What is your estimator actually estimating?
section: 1 Write the target before choosing the procedure
text:
1 Write the target before choosing the procedure
An estimand is a quantity we intend to learn about a stated population. An estimator is a rule applied to a random sample; an estimate is its numerical output. The probability limit of an estimator describes what that rule approaches as the sample grows. The target and the limit need not be the same quantity.
Keep one example in view. We want the mean measured feature level \mu=E[Y] among eligible people. Covariates Z are recorded for everyone, and R indicates whether the feature is observed. The record is W=(Z,R,RY); when R=0, the product is an encoding of a missing contribution, not an observed zero. The observed-outcome mean targets E[Y\mid R=1], which can differ from E[Y].
The estimand is fixed by the population and question, not by which estimator is convenient. An estimator is random before a sample is drawn; after observing the data, its output is one estimate. Its probability limit is another population quantity, determined by the rule and sampling process. Consistency for a target means that this limit equals that target under the stated conditions.
crumbs: What is your estimator actually estimating?

title: What is your estimator actually estimating?
section: 2 A model is a set of possible distributions
text:
2 A model is a set of possible distributions
A model specifies which data-generating distributions are allowed. It is separate from the fitting algorithm. A parametric model uses finitely many coordinates, such as a normal mean and variance. A nonparametric model leaves the distribution broadly unrestricted, subject to stated conditions. Semiparametric work combines a low-dimensional target with distributional features that are not described by a finite parameter vector.
For the missing mean, the unknown regression m(z)=E[Y\mid Z=z,R=1] and observation probability \pi(z)=P(R=1\mid Z=z) will be nuisance functions: population objects needed to estimate the target, rather than the final quantity reported. Naming a regression learner does not define these objects or establish their identifying assumptions.
A parameter can also be an estimand. For example, a mean is a functional on distributions, and a linear projection coefficient can be defined outside a linear conditional-mean model. What matters is the domain on which the quantity is defined and the interpretation claimed for it. A causal interpretation needs a separate identifying argument.
crumbs: What is your estimator actually estimating?

title: What is your estimator actually estimating?
section: 3 A precise answer to a different question
text:
3 A precise answer to a different question
Suppose half the eligible people have Z=0 and half have Z=1. Their feature means are 0 and 4. Outcomes are observed with probabilities 0.8 and 0.2, respectively, independently of the outcome within each stratum.
The observed fraction is 0.5(0.8)+0.5(0.2)=0.5. Among observed people, the probability of Z=1 is 0.5(0.2)/0.5=0.2 by Bayes’ rule; the other stratum has weight 0.8. Selection has changed the averaging weights, without changing either stratum’s mean.



Quantity
Population weights on the strata
Value




Eligible-population mean
1/2,1/2
2


Mean among observed outcomes
0.8,0.2
0.8



The unweighted observed-outcome mean can consistently estimate 0.8. If our target is the eligible-population mean, the procedure has asymptotic discrepancy 0.8-2=-1.2. More independent people can make its standard error smaller without removing that discrepancy. If the scientific question instead concerns the observed subset, 0.8 may be the intended target.
This is a target mismatch. It should be distinguished from finite-sample bias, which concerns the expectation of an estimator at a particular sample size. It should also be distinguished from nonidentification: two full populations can sometimes generate the same observed record while having different target means.

3.1 Why that is the procedure’s limit
The complete-case mean is a ratio,

T_n=\frac{n^{-1}\sum_iR_iY_i}{n^{-1}\sum_iR_i}.

For independent identically distributed records, finite required expectations, and P(R=1)>0, the law of large numbers makes the numerator and denominator approach their population averages. Their ratio approaches

\begin{aligned}
\mu^\star&=\frac{E[RY]}{P(R=1)}\\
&=E[Y\mid R=1].
\end{aligned}

The denominator is nonzero with probability approaching one. This explains the limit rather than assuming that a familiar sample mean must estimate the desired mean. Large-sample reasoning for methods research later develops the convergence argument formally.
Now separate the error around the limit from the mismatch:

T_n-\mu=(T_n-\mu^\star)+(\mu^\star-\mu).

The first term gets smaller as the estimator learns its own target. The second stays at −1.2 in this example. Even a perfectly estimated SE for the first term cannot remove the second. Whether we can instead identify and estimate the full mean depends on the observation assumptions, addressed on the next missingness page.
crumbs: What is your estimator actually estimating?

title: What is your estimator actually estimating?
section: 4 A working regression has a population meaning
text:
4 A working regression has a population meaning
For a nonconstant scalar X with suitable moments, the least-squares slope with an intercept targets

\beta^*=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.

This is a legitimate projection functional even if the conditional mean is curved. Under a stated model Y=\beta X+\gamma Z+\varepsilon with E[\varepsilon\mid X,Z]=0,

\beta^*=\beta+\gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.

The coefficient at fixed Z and the marginal projection slope answer different questions. Calling the second “biased” requires naming the first as the intended target. Neither is automatically a causal effect. The detailed pooling and imperfect-adjustment calculations appear in Association targets, pooling, and imperfect adjustment, where they serve a network-analysis question.
To see where the projection formula comes from, minimize the population squared error E[(Y-a-bX)^2]. The intercept condition gives a=E[Y]-bE[X]. The slope condition then gives \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)-b\operatorname{Var}(X)=0. These conditions define the best linear approximation, whether or not the true conditional mean is linear. Under the displayed richer mean model, expanding \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) gives the stated omitted-variable term.
There are therefore two separate possibilities. The reduced regression can describe the observed X–Y relation adequately but its coefficient answers a different question from the slope at fixed Z. Or its conditional-mean model can be wrong and its fitted coefficient still approach a well-defined projection. In either case, first specify which interpretation is wanted; then assess uncertainty for that quantity.
crumbs: What is your estimator actually estimating?

title: What is your estimator actually estimating?
section: 5 Definition, identification, and estimation have different jobs
text:
5 Definition, identification, and estimation have different jobs
Definition states what is wanted. Identification connects that quantity to the observable distribution under assumptions. Estimation supplies a sample procedure for the identified functional. Inference studies its uncertainty and approximation errors.
For the running mean, missing at random, positive observation probabilities over the target support, and covariates recorded for everyone identify E[Y] as E[m(Z)]. Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target works through that claim. Later guides construct an estimator and show when its uncertainty can be justified.
A formula for a discrepancy can suggest a diagnostic only when its relevant ingredients are observable or identified. A test on the observed data cannot generally verify missing at random or rule out unmeasured confounding. Non-rejection does not certify that a working assumption is true.
crumbs: What is your estimator actually estimating?

title: What is your estimator actually estimating?
text:
6 Exercises
The checkpoint is a completion target. Additional practice is optional.


Checkpoint · DES-03 — Separate a target from a procedure’s limit
Task type: Interpretation and calculation.
Use the two-stratum example to calculate the eligible-population and observed-outcome means. Name the estimand and probability limit when the observed-outcome mean is used to answer the full-population question. Explain what increasing the sample size changes. Then define a question for which the observed-outcome mean is the intended target.
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish target mismatch, sampling uncertainty, finite-sample bias, and nonidentification.
Transfer: If the conditional mean is nonlinear, can a linear projection coefficient still be a well-defined estimand?


Hint

First calculate the distribution of Z among observed outcomes; then keep the scientific question fixed while evaluating the procedure.



Solution outline — open after trying

The eligible mean is 2. Selection changes the stratum weights to 0.8 and 0.2, giving an observed-outcome mean 0.8. The procedure converges to 0.8 under the stated sampling conditions, so its asymptotic discrepancy for the target 2 is -1.2. More independent people reduce sampling variation around that limit. A question explicitly about the observed subset can instead target 0.8. Whether the full mean is identified requires assumptions about the unobserved outcomes. A linear projection is meaningful outside a linear conditional-mean model when its moments and denominator are defined.




Additional practice (optional)

Change the observation probabilities while keeping the eligible population fixed. Which target stays the same?
Derive the least-squares slope limit under the displayed two-variable conditional-mean model.
Specify a standardized group contrast and explain why its target distribution must be named.

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
text: Before reading: Elementary means, conditional means, and basic regression. The observation and sampling unit are introduced here; no assay-specific biology is assumed.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
section: 1 Write the question in population language
text:
1 Write the question in population language
“Compare the patients and controls” does not specify a unique estimand. You still need a feature scale, population, time, contrast, adjustment, and weighting rule. A coefficient returned by software is a candidate answer only after those choices are connected to its population meaning.
A useful first statement is: among the eligible people in this cohort, compare the mean log-expression of feature g between groups, standardized to a specified covariate distribution. A different question might concern prediction for a new person, a within-person trajectory, or an intervention effect. Those questions can use related data and algorithms while requiring different assumptions and evaluation criteria.
Make the statement operational. “Eligible” needs inclusion criteria and a time window. “Mean expression” needs the measured scale and a rule for repeated specimens. “Adjusted” needs both the covariates and the population over which comparisons are averaged. These are parts of the question, not details to leave to the software defaults.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
text:
2 A running population mean
For a first example, Y is one measured feature level per eligible person on a stated scale. Z is recorded for everyone, and R says whether Y was observed. The target is the eligible-population mean \mu=E[Y], and the observed record is W=(Z,R,RY). Retain R so that an unrecorded outcome is not confused with an observed zero.
Here the eligibility rule defines the population from which people are sampled. The expectation is over that population’s distribution, not just an average of the outcomes that happened to be observed. A mean for a fixed finite enrolled cohort is another possible target, but it needs that finite-population interpretation and its sampling/observation argument stated explicitly.
A study can contain repeated specimens from a person. The independent sampling unit for a person-level question is the person, not automatically the specimen, cell, or matrix column. Units of analysis, replication, and study design develops the weighting and replication choices. An assay’s detailed interpretation comes later in Omics data and measurement.
A difference between two population means is a subsequent extension. Standardization then asks which covariate distribution should be used for each mean; the binary-stratum example below keeps those weights visible.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
text:
3 Four kinds of question
A descriptive target summarizes a specified population. An associational target relates variables within that population, possibly after adjustment. A predictive target concerns a loss or accuracy measure in a stated deployment population, for a learning rule with a defined training procedure. A causal target concerns outcomes under interventions and needs assumptions linking those potential outcomes to observations.
The categories describe the interpretation being claimed, not whether a method is sophisticated. Flexible regression can estimate an associational target. A simple mean can identify a causal contrast in an appropriately randomized design.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
section: 4 Definition and identification are different steps
text:
4 Definition and identification are different steps
For a target \psi, definition says what quantity is wanted. Identification expresses it as a unique functional of the observable distribution under assumptions. Estimation constructs a finite-sample procedure for that functional. Inference studies uncertainty and approximation errors.
For the missing mean, definition names all eligible people’s Y values as the quantity of interest, even though some are unobserved. Identification must explain how those missing outcomes relate to what was recorded. Estimation then replaces the identified population averages or regressions by sample quantities. Inference asks how much that estimate varies and which approximation errors remain. A precise estimate at the last step cannot supply an assumption missing at the second.
For example, E[Y\mid A=1]-E[Y\mid A=0] is an observed-data group contrast if both groups occur and the means exist. A standardized contrast

\begin{aligned}
\psi_Q&=\int\{m_1(z)-m_0(z)\}\,dQ(z),\\
m_a(z)&=E[Y\mid A=a,Z=z],
\end{aligned}

also specifies a covariate distribution Q. Identifying it from the observed data requires that the needed group–covariate combinations are supported, or additional extrapolation restrictions. Choosing Q as the overall cohort covariate distribution differs from choosing the control or patient distribution.
This displayed contrast initially assumes fully observed outcomes and group conditional means defined on the support used by Q. With missing outcomes, the full-group means additionally need an observation-process argument. If a group never occurs in a target stratum, its conditional mean there is not uniquely defined by that observed joint law. An extrapolated response model or a potential-outcome formulation must define what is intended there before asking how to identify it.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
section: 5 A contrast can change after standardization
text:
5 A contrast can change after standardization
This separate numerical example concerns a group contrast. Consider a binary covariate Z with population probability P(Z=1)=1/2. Group membership is associated with Z: P(A=1\mid Z=0)=0.2 and P(A=1\mid Z=1)=0.8. The conditional means are m_0(z)=1+2z and m_1(z)=2+3z.
The within-Z contrasts are 1 and 2. Predict the contrast averaged equally over Z, and compare it with the crude group difference.


Code
pz <- c(0.5, 0.5); pa <- c(0.2, 0.8)
m0 <- c(1, 3); m1 <- c(2, 5)
pz_a1 <- pz * pa / sum(pz * pa)
pz_a0 <- pz * (1 - pa) / sum(pz * (1 - pa))
c(crude = sum(pz_a1 * m1) - sum(pz_a0 * m0),
  standardized = sum(pz * (m1 - m0)),
  at_Z0 = m1[1] - m0[1], at_Z1 = m1[2] - m0[2])


       crude standardized        at_Z0        at_Z1 
         3.0          1.5          1.0          2.0 


The answers are 3, 1.5, 1, and 2. Work through the weights: group 1 has stratum probabilities 0.2 and 0.8, so its mean is 0.2(2)+0.8(5)=4.4. Group 0 has probabilities 0.8 and 0.2, so its mean is 0.8(1)+0.2(3)=1.4. Subtracting gives 3.
Equal-Z standardization instead compares the means within each stratum, then uses the same weights: 0.5(2-1)+0.5(5-3)=1.5. Using the patient covariate distribution gives 0.2(1)+0.8(2)=1.8; using the control distribution gives 1.2. None of these answers is intrinsically wrong. They summarize different comparisons. Calling one “corrected” is insufficient without explaining why its adjustment and target population answer the question.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
section: 6 A causal interpretation needs an additional argument
text:
6 A causal interpretation needs an additional argument
If the target is E[Y^1-Y^0], a common identification argument uses consistency, conditional exchangeability Y^a\perp A\mid Z, and treatment positivity over the target covariate support. These are distinct from choosing a flexible regression learner. Under them, standardization to the target population’s Z distribution identifies the causal mean contrast.
Here consistency means Y=Y^A: the observed outcome agrees with the specified intervention received. This causal linking assumption is different from statistical consistency, which later describes an estimator approaching its target. Conditional exchangeability lets us replace an intervention-specific conditional mean by an observed group mean at the same Z. Positivity supplies observations for each intervention comparison required by the target population. These are separate roles; fitting an accurate prediction model addresses none of them by itself.
The assumptions must match the intervention and study. A group label such as disease status may not define a sufficiently specified intervention. Adjusting for a variable affected by the exposure can change the causal question. Unmeasured common causes are not removed by a good prediction score. This collection introduces the identification distinction; deeper causal designs are a separate branch.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
section: 7 The partially linear coefficient is another target
text:
7 The partially linear coefficient is another target
In Y=\beta X+g(Z)+\varepsilon with E[\varepsilon\mid X,Z]=0, residualizing X and Y identifies \beta when residual exposure variation is positive. That coefficient has a model-based interpretation. A causal effect interpretation additionally needs an intervention and identifying assumptions. Outside the model, the same sample equation may approach a projection-like functional rather than the original scientific contrast.
Use the What is your estimator actually estimating? page to study that limit. Do not use model flexibility as a substitute for identifying the quantity in the first place.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
text:
9 Write an estimand specification
Record the eligible population and sampling frame; independent unit; assay feature and measurement scale; time or visit summary; contrast and weighting; covariate distribution; missingness assumptions; and interpretation. Then write the observable functional and list the support needed to evaluate it. If a required combination is absent, state whether the analysis changes population, introduces extrapolation, or cannot identify the target.
A short specification should allow another analyst to disagree about the assumptions while still knowing exactly which quantity you intend to estimate. This is more useful than choosing an algorithm name as the analysis plan.
When identification depends on an untestable restriction, use Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions to distinguish a changed assumption from a changed target.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
text:
10 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · ID-01 — Separate definition, identification, and estimation
Task type: Interpretation and derivation.
Use the binary-Z example to define the equal-Z standardized contrast and derive 1.5. Suppose both groups still occur in both strata, but P(R=1\mid A=0,Z=1)=0 in the population, while outcomes are observed in the other cells and the target gives Z=1 weight 1/2. Which conditional mean is unsupported? Describe two observed-data-compatible choices for it that give different targets. Would a flexible learner or a sandwich standard error resolve this?
Ready to continue when: you can show nonidentification by constructing different compatible targets, rather than describing it only as a software difficulty.
Transfer: If you restrict the target to Z=0, what is gained and what population claim is lost?


Hint

The target still needs m_0(1) even when that conditional mean cannot be observed.



Solution outline — open after trying

The contrast is \{m_1(0)-m_0(0)+m_1(1)-m_0(1)\}/2. With all means supplied it is (1+2)/2=1.5. If group 0 still occurs at Z=1 but none of its outcomes are observed, changing its full-group conditional mean from 3 to 7 leaves the law of (Z,A,R,RY) unchanged but changes the contrast from 1.5 to -0.5. Additional restrictions, a new population target, or new observations are needed. Learning and variance estimation cannot identify an unrestricted mean in an unsupported stratum.




Additional practice (optional)

Replace the overall covariate distribution by the patient distribution and compute the standardized contrast.
Write separate estimand specifications for a bulk-expression contrast and a composition-adjusted contrast.
For a prediction study, specify deployment population, loss, training procedure, and validation unit.
