title: From a research question to an identified estimand
text:
11 Reading

Kennedy, Semiparametric theory, for an estimation framework with explicitly defined target functionals.
crumbs: From a research question to an identified estimand

title: Research questions, study design, and estimands
text:
A research question needs a population, an independent unit, a measurement scale, and a quantity to estimate. Study design and observation determine which comparisons are supported. A regression formula alone does not specify those choices.
The running example asks for the mean measured feature level among eligible people when some outcomes are missing. It separates that population from the observed subset, then uses simple strata to show what identifying assumptions supply and what absent support leaves unknown.
crumbs: Research questions, study design, and estimands

title: Research questions, study design, and estimands
text:
What you’ll learn

Specify the scientific target: name the population, unit, time, scale, contrast and weighting, and distinguish it from a procedure’s limit.
Establish identification: express the target using the observed distribution under explicit assumptions, or construct compatible populations with different answers.

Completion means being able to write an estimand and identification specification for a research question, including an unsupported claim or missing piece of information. The page checkpoints exercise this through replication, target mismatch, standardization, and missingness; additional practice is optional.
crumbs: Research questions, study design, and estimands

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text: Before reading: Basic calculus, expectations, and Large-sample reasoning for methods research. Its sample-mean identity motivates the general equation here. The later residualization example uses Conditional expectation and L2 geometry and can be revisited after that page.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
1 The one idea
An estimator is often introduced as a formula: a mean, a regression coefficient, a maximum likelihood estimate. For theory, a more useful description is the equation it solves.
Let W_1,\ldots,W_n be i.i.d. observation records: one record might contain a person’s outcome and covariates. Here W denotes the whole record, while Y denotes an outcome within it. Let \theta be a candidate parameter value and \psi(W;\theta) its estimating function, with the same dimension as \theta. Here \psi names an equation contribution, rather than the population mean. Write P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(W_i) for a sample average and Pf=E[f(W)] for its population expectation.
An estimating equation chooses a value \hat\theta that balances the average contribution at zero:

\begin{aligned}
P_n\psi(W;\hat\theta)&= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \psi(W_i;\hat\theta)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

The population version is

\begin{aligned}
P\psi(W;\theta_0)&=E[\psi(W;\theta_0)]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

The population equation defines the value \theta_0 that this procedure aims to estimate. To connect the two equations, we need consistency: the selected sample root must approach that population root in probability. An LLN is part of this argument, but convergence of the equation at each fixed parameter value is not automatically convergence of a root selected from the data. The root must be identified and the equation controlled near it.
Once consistency is established, a local Taylor expansion explains how random equation noise moves the estimated root. This gives the recurring sequence: identify the population root, show the sample root approaches it, linearize, and justify uncertainty. Means, ordinary least squares, likelihood estimators, and many other procedures fit this pattern.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
2 Familiar estimators as equations
Use \mu=E[Y] for the population mean. If a is a candidate mean, its sample equation is

\begin{aligned}
P_n(Y-a)&=\bar Y-a\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

The solution is \hat\mu=\bar Y. The population equation is E[Y-a]=\mu-a=0, with unique root a=\mu. The LLN gives \bar Y\xrightarrow{p}\mu, directly proving consistency in this example. Positive and negative deviations balance at the mean because they sum to zero there.
The least-squares coefficient in a regression of Y on a covariate vector X solves the normal equations below. Include a constant component in X when fitting an intercept.

P_n\left[X\{Y-X^\top\beta\}\right]=0.

With suitable finite moments, the population equation is E[XY]-E[XX^\top]\beta=0. If E[XX^\top] is nonsingular, its solution is the projection coefficient \beta^*=E[XX^\top]^{-1}E[XY]. This remains a population functional when the conditional mean is nonlinear. An LLN for the sample moments and continuous mapping through the matrix inverse establish consistency for that coefficient. Whether it answers the scientific question is a separate issue, developed in What is your estimator actually estimating?.
An estimator defined by a minimization problem is often an estimating-equation estimator too. If

\hat\theta = \mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_\theta P_n\ell(W;\theta),

and \ell is differentiable, an interior, unconstrained minimizer satisfies

P_n\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ell(W;\hat\theta)=0.

These optimization-based procedures are called M-estimators. Estimators defined directly by a zero of P_n\psi are often called Z-estimators. A zero derivative is a necessary condition for the stated interior minimum; it need not distinguish a minimum from another stationary point. Boundary constraints and nonsmooth losses require the corresponding optimization conditions.




A familiar estimator is a zero of an averageTwo plots for observations 1 through 5. Average residual decreases linearly through zero at 3. Mean squared loss is a parabola minimized at 3.

A familiar estimator is a zero of an averageMove μ: positive and negative observation residuals balance at the mean.
02346-303candidate mean μAverage residual023460510candidate mean μMean squared lossSolve an equationMinimize the matching lossSame data: Y = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; both calculations give μ̂ = 3.


Figure 1: For these five observations, P_n(Y-\mu)=3-\mu. Its zero is also the minimum of P_n(Y-\mu)^2=(\mu-3)^2+2. The derivative of that loss is -2P_n(Y-\mu): minimization and zero-solving describe the same estimator.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
section: 3 From the sample equation to a linear approximation
text:
3 From the sample equation to a linear approximation
First consider a scalar parameter and a consistent sample root. At the population root, P\psi(W;\theta_0)=0, but the sample average P_n\psi(W;\theta_0) usually is not zero. This discrepancy is equation noise: a new sample produces a different discrepancy even though \theta_0 stays fixed.
Changing the candidate parameter changes the average contribution. A first-order expansion gives

\begin{aligned}
0&=P_n\psi(W;\hat\theta)\\
&\approx P_n\psi(W;\theta_0)+A(\hat\theta-\theta_0),
\end{aligned}

where

A = E\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\psi(W;\theta_0)\right].

Rearranging gives

\hat\theta-\theta_0
\approx -A^{-1}P_n\psi(W;\theta_0).

The multiplier -A^{-1} translates a vertical equation error into a horizontal parameter error. A shallow population equation has small |A|, so the same equation noise can move its root farther. The minus sign moves the candidate in the direction that offsets the noise.
To make this an asymptotic linear expansion, the approximation must have a controlled remainder:

\begin{aligned}
\hat\theta-\theta_0&=P_nD_0+R_n,\\
D_0(W)&=-A^{-1}\psi(W;\theta_0),\\
R_n&=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{aligned}

The leading term is an average of fixed, mean-zero observation contributions, since PD_0=-A^{-1}P\psi(\theta_0)=0. The remainder becomes negligible after root-n scaling. Under the conditions proved below, the estimator’s influence function is

\operatorname{IF}(W)=-A^{-1}\psi(W;\theta_0).

The Influence functions page develops influence functions for arbitrary smooth functionals. Here we see one of the main ways they arise from an estimator.
For the sample mean, \psi(Y;a)=Y-a and A=-1. Therefore

\begin{aligned}
\hat\mu-\mu&=P_n(Y-\mu),\\
\operatorname{IF}(Y)&=Y-\mu.
\end{aligned}

The remainder is exactly zero because the sample equation is already linear in the candidate mean. Nonlinear equations need the additional remainder argument.

A tangent gives an approximate root, not an exact oneExample: ψ(Y; θ) = Y − θ², θ > 0; E[Y] = 4 and the observed mean is 4.6.

Figure 2: The population equation is 4-\theta^2 and has root \theta_0=2. The sample equation is 4.6-\theta^2 and has exact root \sqrt{4.6}\approx2.145. Its tangent at 2 is 0.6-4(\theta-2), giving the approximate root 2.15. The magnified panel makes the small Taylor remainder visible. More generally, the vertical fluctuation P_n\psi(\theta_0) becomes a horizontal shift through multiplication by -A^{-1}; applying this multiplier to each observation’s estimating function gives its influence contribution.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
section: 4 Standard errors and the sandwich formula
text:
4 Standard errors and the sandwich formula
Assume i.i.d. observations and finite, positive equation variance B. Because the population contribution has mean zero, its second moment equals its variance. The CLT gives

\begin{aligned}
\sqrt n\,P_n\psi(W;\theta_0)&\xrightarrow{d}N(0,B),\\
B&=E[\psi(W;\theta_0)^2].
\end{aligned}

Combining this with the linear expansion gives

\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)
\mathrel{\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}}
N\left(0,\frac{B}{A^2}\right).

Here B/A^2 is the limiting variance of the scaled error \sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0). The estimator’s first-order variance is B/(nA^2), so its SE is approximately \sqrt{B/n}/|A|. This division by n distinguishes the limiting contribution variance from the uncertainty of an estimate based on n people.
For a vector parameter, the first-order estimator variance becomes

\frac{1}{n}A^{-1}B(A^{-1})^\top,

where A=E[\partial\psi/\partial\theta^\top] is the Jacobian and B=E[\psi\psi^\top] is the covariance matrix of contributions at \theta_0. The transpose on the right is needed because, for a fixed matrix L, covariance transforms as \operatorname{Var}(LX)=L\operatorname{Var}(X)L^\top. This is the sandwich variance: the equation covariance lies between two derivative-inverse factors.
For a scalar equation, compute

\begin{aligned}
\widehat A&=P_n\dot\psi(W;\hat\theta),\\
\widehat B&=P_n\{\psi(W;\hat\theta)^2\},\\
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)
&=\frac{\sqrt{\widehat B}}{\sqrt n\,|\widehat A|}.
\end{aligned}

The dot denotes a derivative with respect to the parameter. Consistency of \widehat A and \widehat B and A\ne0 let continuous mapping and Slutsky justify these substitutions. Because the evaluation point \hat\theta is random, the required LLN/continuity controls must hold locally, not only at a fixed parameter. For the mean, \widehat A=-1 and \widehat B=n^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y)^2; the resulting SE is asymptotically equivalent to s_Y/\sqrt n, with the familiar finite-sample divisor difference.
The sandwich is the general variance calculation for a justified smooth equation. Its use still depends on the sampling unit, moments, root consistency, and remainder conditions.




Two ingredients determine sandwich uncertaintyA shared-axis normal density comparison. Baseline B one A magnitude one gives SE 0.10. Either B four or A magnitude one half gives SE 0.20 and the same wider density.

Two ingredients determine sandwich uncertaintyB measures equation noise; |A| measures how strongly the equation responds to θ.
-0.500.5024estimation error θ̂ − θ₀Approximate sampling densityn = 100 in every caseB = 1, |A| = 1SE = 0.10B = 4, |A| = 1SE = 0.20B = 1, |A| = 0.5SE = 0.20 (same orange curve)More equation noise or less sensitivity can produce the same wider error distribution.


Figure 3: For a scalar equation, \operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)\approx\sqrt{B/n}/|A|. Relative to the blue case, either quadrupling B or halving |A| doubles the standard error and gives the orange curve. The areas under both densities are one: the lower peak reflects a wider distribution, not less total probability. This comparison changes A or B separately; merely rescaling \psi changes both and leaves B/A^2 unchanged.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
section: 5 Example: a regression slope under heteroscedasticity
text:
5 Example: a regression slope under heteroscedasticity
Suppose Y=\alpha+\beta X+\varepsilon with E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0, while the variance of \varepsilon depends on X. This is heteroscedasticity. Under suitable moment and rank conditions, ordinary least squares is consistent for the intercept and slope, but the usual constant-variance SE can misdescribe its uncertainty.
For the covariate vector C=(1,X)^\top, the estimating function is C(Y-C^\top\gamma), where \gamma=(\alpha,\beta)^\top. Thus A=-E[CC^\top] and B=E[CC^\top\varepsilon^2]. The dependence of squared errors on X belongs inside this expectation. The code fits \alpha=1 and \beta=0.8, with error SD 0.3+|X|.


Code
set.seed(1)
n <- 250
x <- rnorm(n)
eps <- rnorm(n, sd = 0.3 + abs(x))
y <- 1 + 0.8 * x + eps
fit <- lm(y ~ x)

# Manual HC0 sandwich standard error for the slope.
X <- model.matrix(fit)
u <- residuals(fit)
bread <- solve(crossprod(X))
meat <- t(X) %*% diag(u^2) %*% X
vcov_hc0 <- bread %*% meat %*% bread

c(estimate = coef(fit)["x"],
  usual_SE = summary(fit)$coef["x", "Std. Error"],
  sandwich_SE = sqrt(vcov_hc0["x", "x"]))


 estimate.x    usual_SE sandwich_SE 
 0.90177237  0.08591487  0.13819053 


Both SE calculations aim to describe uncertainty in the same fitted slope. They use different assumptions about B: the usual calculation replaces the individual squared residuals with one common variance, while the sandwich retains their joint variation with the covariates. In the code, X is the design matrix with rows C_i^\top, bread is (X^\top X)^{-1}, and meat is \sum_i C_iC_i^\top\hat\varepsilon_i^2. These use sums rather than averages; their factors already include the required sample-size scaling.
This HC0 example assumes independent observations and the stated conditional mean. More generally, a sandwich can support inference for a projection coefficient under misspecification when its own moment and expansion conditions hold. It does not change that coefficient into another scientific target. Clustered data require contributions and variance calculations at the independent-unit level.




Why one common residual variance can understate uncertaintyA fan shaped residual scatter and a contribution plot. True squared slope contributions rise faster in the tails than a common variance approximation.

Why one common residual variance can understate uncertaintyLarge |X| brings both greater leverage and larger errors in this example.
-202-606XRegression error ε-20203060XExpected squared slope contributionOrange: X² Var(ε | X)Dashed: X² × one common variance


Figure 4: Left: a simulated sample from the guide’s error model. Right: population squared slope-score contributions E[(X\varepsilon)^2\mid X]=X^2(0.3+|X|)^2, compared with the homoscedastic substitution X^2E[\varepsilon^2] for standard-normal X. The sandwich “meat” retains the joint variation of leverage and error size through X_i^2\hat\varepsilon_i^2. The next simulation checks the resulting confidence-interval coverage.




5.1 Check repeated samples
The following experiment repeats that data-generating process. A nominal 95% confidence interval built with the sandwich standard error should cover more reliably than the homoscedastic interval.


Code
OneRep <- function(n = 250) {
  x <- rnorm(n)
  y <- 1 + 0.8 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3 + abs(x))
  fit <- lm(y ~ x)
  X <- model.matrix(fit); u <- residuals(fit)
  V <- solve(crossprod(X)) %*% (t(X) %*% diag(u^2) %*% X) %*% solve(crossprod(X))
  b <- coef(fit)["x"]
  c(usual = abs(b - 0.8) <= 1.96 * summary(fit)$coef["x", "Std. Error"],
    sandwich = abs(b - 0.8) <= 1.96 * sqrt(V["x", "x"]))
}
colMeans(t(replicate(1000, OneRep())))


   usual.x sandwich.x 
     0.784      0.946 


Each replication generates a new study of 250 independent people, refits the slope, and checks whether each interval contains the fixed truth 0.8. Averaging the indicators estimates repeated-sampling coverage. With 1,000 replications and coverage near 0.95, its Monte Carlo SE is about \sqrt{0.95(0.05)/1000}\approx0.007. A single simulated proportion therefore has its own numerical uncertainty.
The simulation evaluates this generator. A proof additionally verifies the expansion, CLT, and variance consistency for the estimator under stated conditions. Simulation studies for methods research explains how to build a fuller evaluation.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
6 Identification comes before asymptotics
The expansion only helps when the population equation has a meaningful, unique solution in the stated parameter space. For example, E[Y-\theta^2]=\mu-\theta^2 has two roots when \mu>0 if both signs of \theta are allowed. Restricting the target to the positive square root gives a unique root. A numerical solver must respect that choice.
For the mean, the proposed target is not defined as a finite quantity if E[Y] does not exist. A distinct identification failure occurs when different parameter values give the same observable distribution or population equation. For a regression slope, it fails if X has no variation. For the partially linear model from the Conditional expectation and L2 geometry page,

\begin{aligned}
\beta&= \frac{E[\widetilde X\widetilde Y]}{E[\widetilde X^2]},\\
\widetilde X&=X-E[X\mid Z],
\end{aligned}

identification requires E[\widetilde X^2]>0. If X is almost fully predicted by Z, the denominator is small: the coefficient may be identified in theory but estimated with large uncertainty. This is the semiparametric version of weak information.
It is useful to separate three claims:

The population equation defines the scientific target or a clearly named approximation target.
The target is identified by the observed data distribution.
The sample solution is sufficiently close to the population solution for the linear expansion to hold.

These claims are often bundled together in a theorem. Read them separately.




Less residual variation means less information about βPopulation and illustrative sample equations with residual variances one, 0.04 and zero. Sampling noise and slopes both decrease; root uncertainty increases from 0.1 to 0.5. With zero variation every coefficient is a root.

Less residual variation means less information about βPartialling out: X̃ = √v U, ε independent of U; E[U²] = Var(ε) = 1.
Residual variance = 1-101-101β − β₀Estimating equationSE ≈ 0.10Residual variance = 0.04-101-101β − β₀Estimating equationSE ≈ 0.50Residual variance = 0-101-101β − β₀Estimating equationEvery β solves itBlue: population equation     Dashed orange: one illustrative sample equation


Figure 5: For \psi=\widetilde X(\widetilde Y-\beta\widetilde X), the population slope is A=-v and the equation variance at the truth is B=v. Hence \operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta)\approx1/\sqrt{nv}: 0.10 and 0.50 at n=100. The orange equations use the population derivative and illustrative intercept perturbations of one negative standard deviation, -\sqrt{v/n}; they show a local sample approximation rather than simulated data. Noise shrinks as v falls, but sensitivity shrinks faster. At v=0, both equations are identically zero and no unique \beta is identified.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
7 A smooth estimating-equation proof
Here is the argument behind the earlier approximation. Allow an approximate numerical root, with residual r_n=P_n\psi(W;\hat\theta)=o_p(n^{-1/2}). An exact root has r_n=0; for an approximate root, the numerical error must be smaller than sampling fluctuation on this scale.
Assume P\psi(W;\theta_0)=0 and \hat\theta\xrightarrow{p}\theta_0. For a scalar target, suppose the equation is differentiable near \theta_0, its population derivative is continuous there, and

\begin{aligned}
A&=P\dot\psi(W;\theta_0)\\
&\ne0,\\
0&<B\\
&=P\psi(W;\theta_0)^2\\
&<\infty.
\end{aligned}

Also require a uniform derivative LLN on a neighborhood \mathcal N of \theta_0:

\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal N}
|(P_n-P)\dot\psi(W;\theta)|\xrightarrow{p}0.

“Uniform” means the sample and population derivatives are close throughout that neighborhood, including at a random intermediate value selected using the data. A fixed-parameter LLN alone does not establish this.
These are conditions to verify for the problem. Consistency itself can follow from a uniform LLN for the equation and a separated unique population root, with an appropriate parameter set and root-selection rule. Separation means values outside any fixed neighborhood of \theta_0 cannot have population equation values arbitrarily close to zero. The LLN then prevents a well-chosen approximate sample root from remaining outside that neighborhood.
A Taylor expansion uses an intermediate value \tilde\theta between the consistent estimate and target:

\begin{aligned}
P_n\psi(\hat\theta)&=P_n\psi(\theta_0)+\widetilde A_n(\hat\theta-\theta_0),\\
\widetilde A_n&=P_n\dot\psi(\tilde\theta)\\
&\xrightarrow{p}A.
\end{aligned}

Consistency keeps \tilde\theta near \theta_0 with probability tending to one. Uniform derivative control and population continuity therefore give \widetilde A_n\xrightarrow{p}A\ne0. Rearranging the equality shows both sources of error:

\hat\theta-\theta_0=-\widetilde A_n^{-1}P_n\psi(\theta_0) +\widetilde A_n^{-1}r_n.

The CLT makes P_n\psi(\theta_0)=O_p(n^{-1/2}). Continuous mapping gives \widetilde A_n^{-1}-A^{-1}=o_p(1), so replacing the intermediate inverse by A^{-1} changes the expression by o_p(n^{-1/2}). The numerical-root term has that same negligible order because r_n=o_p(n^{-1/2}) and the inverse is O_p(1). Hence

\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0)=\sqrt nP_nD_0+o_p(1).

The fixed-function CLT handles the leading average; Slutsky removes the negligible remainder. Thus the influence function is -A^{-1}\psi(W;\theta_0) and the limiting variance is B/A^2.
The intermediate \widetilde A_n establishes the proof and need not be observable. For computation, use \widehat A=P_n\dot\psi(W;\hat\theta) and \widehat B=P_n\psi(W;\hat\theta)^2 from the sandwich section. Their consistency needs the corresponding local LLN and continuity arguments. These complete the inference proof after root consistency and linearization.
For a vector equation, use the Jacobian integrated along the segment from target to estimate, with convergence to a nonsingular matrix A. A single intermediate point for every component is not generally a valid multivariate mean-value argument.
The smooth-root checkpoint SP-01 supplies a concrete example with \hat\theta=\sqrt{\bar Y}. Its exact factorization makes the negligible-remainder argument especially transparent. Quantiles and local expansions is a later transfer that handles a nonsmooth sample equation with a different local argument.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
8 What the theorem hides
The Taylor expansion uses conditions that can fail.

The observations must have enough independence for an average to obey a central limit theorem. Repeated observations, time series, and related samples need a different variance calculation or a different estimating equation.
A must be nonzero in one dimension, or invertible in several dimensions. Low equation sensitivity relative to its random fluctuation can produce unstable estimates. Interpret the derivative together with B: multiplying the whole equation by a constant changes both without changing the estimator or its variance.
The estimating function must be smooth enough near the truth. Quantiles, thresholds, and selection procedures need extra work because they are not ordinary differentiable equations.
The remainder in the Taylor expansion must be smaller than n^{-1/2}. In semiparametric work that remainder includes error from estimating nuisance functions.

The point is not to memorize a list of technical assumptions. It is to know what a theorem is buying: a valid first-order approximation, and therefore a standard error and confidence interval.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
9 Where this connects

The Conditional expectation and L2 geometry page gives a population residualization identity. Its sample analogue becomes an estimating equation.
The Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency page is an important special case: a maximum likelihood estimator solves the score equation.
The Influence functions page generalizes the linear expansion from a chosen estimating equation to smooth functionals of a distribution.
The Orthogonality and cross-fitting page studies the remainder when \psi contains estimated nuisance functions.

Use the core theorems and stochastic-order definitions in Large-sample reasoning for methods research to identify each step of the proof above.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
10 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · SP-01 — Complete a smooth estimating-equation argument
Task type: Derivation and asymptotic reasoning.
Let Y_i>0 be i.i.d., with E[Y]=\mu>0 and 0<\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2<\infty. The target is \theta_0=\sqrt\mu, and \hat\theta=\sqrt{\bar Y} solves P_n(Y-\theta^2)=0.

Prove consistency using the law of large numbers.
Use the identity (\hat\theta-\theta_0)(\hat\theta+\theta_0)=\bar Y-\mu to derive an expansion with an o_p(n^{-1/2}) remainder.
Identify A, the influence function, and the limiting distribution of \sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta_0).
Give a consistent standard-error estimate. Explain which steps use independence, finite variance, and \mu>0.

Ready to continue when: you can connect the population root to consistency, a negligible remainder, a CLT, and an estimated standard error.
Transfer: Apply the same reasoning to a smooth function g(\bar Y). What derivative multiplies Y-\mu, and what would require rechecking if \mu approached a boundary?


Hint

The denominator \hat\theta+\theta_0 converges to 2\theta_0>0. Combine that with \bar Y-\mu=O_p(n^{-1/2}).



Solution outline — open after trying

The LLN and continuity give \hat\theta\to_p\theta_0. Then

\begin{aligned}
\hat\theta-\theta_0&=\frac{\bar Y-\mu}{2\theta_0}+R_n,\\
R_n&=(\bar Y-\mu)D_n,\\
D_n&=\frac1{\hat\theta+\theta_0}-\frac1{2\theta_0}.
\end{aligned}

Here D_n=o_p(1) and \bar Y-\mu=O_p(n^{-1/2}) by the CLT. Their product R_n is o_p(n^{-1/2}). Here A=-2\theta_0, so \phi(Y)=(Y-\mu)/(2\theta_0) and the limiting variance is \sigma^2/(4\mu). A standard error is s_Y/(2\hat\theta\sqrt n). The i.i.d. assumption and finite variance support the LLN, CLT, and variance consistency; positivity keeps the root away from the derivative-zero boundary. Slutsky’s theorem justifies replacing unknown quantities with consistent estimates.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Write the estimating equation for the sample variance with divisor n, treating both the mean and variance as unknown parameters. Derive its sandwich variance.
Show that the least-squares normal equation identifies the coefficient \beta^\ast = E[XX^\top]^{-1}E[XY] when E[XX^\top] is invertible. What does it target if the conditional mean of Y is nonlinear?
Repeat the coverage simulation with n=50, 250, and 1000. Report the Monte Carlo standard error for each estimated coverage probability.
In the partially linear model, let X=Z exactly. Which step in the identification argument fails? Simulate X=Z+\sigma U for several small values of \sigma and describe what happens to the standard error of \hat\beta.

title: Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity
text:
11 Reading

van der Vaart, A. W. (1998). Asymptotic Statistics. Cambridge. Chapters 5 and 7 give the general Z-estimation argument and M-estimation examples.
Huber, P. J. (1967). The behavior of maximum likelihood estimates under nonstandard conditions. In Proceedings of the Fifth Berkeley Symposium. An early source for the general sandwich result.
White, H. (1982). Maximum likelihood estimation of misspecified models. Econometrica, 50(1), 1 to 25. The classic treatment of pseudo-true targets and robust variance under misspecification.
Stefanski, L. A. and Boos, D. D. (2002). The calculus of M-estimation. The American Statistician, 56(1), 29 to 38. A compact and practical introduction.

title: Estimation and uncertainty
text:
An estimator is a random rule applied to a sample. Its probability limit names the quantity it approaches as information grows; its sampling distribution describes variation across repeated studies. A small standard error does not establish that the limit equals the scientific target.
For a completely observed population mean, the estimation error is exactly an average of centered observations. Linearization extends this idea to sample equations and smooth transformations. A negligible remainder, a suitable central limit theorem, and consistent estimation of the contribution variance then support uncertainty statements. The worked arguments connect each theorem to the step it justifies.

title: Estimation and uncertainty
text:
What you’ll learn

Connect sample and population: use laws of large numbers and a population equation to understand what an estimator approaches.
Justify and interpret uncertainty: derive a first-order contribution, control the remainder, estimate its variance, and interpret confidence intervals and tests.

The core completion targets begin with LS-01–LS-04: interpret convergence, expand expectation notation, distinguish SD from SE, and combine the working theorems. SP-01 then develops the smooth-root argument, and INF-01 checks uncertainty interpretation. Cluster inference and bootstrap apply the same reasoning to particular designs and procedures; their checkpoints are completion targets when you work through those extensions. The bridge and full checkpoint catalog are references, rather than prerequisites at the start.

title: Completion checkpoints
text:
This catalog is a reference across the guides. It is not an assignment to finish every topic before continuing. Each page labels its completion checkpoint, gives a readiness standard, and separates Additional practice (optional). A checkpoint in a specialized extension assesses that topic when you study it.
Try the task before opening the hint or solution. Explain the objects, assumptions, and reasoning, then attempt its transfer question. The guide overview states the one or two outcomes that these tasks build toward.

title: Completion checkpoints
section: Research questions, study design, and estimands
text:
Research questions, study design, and estimands

ID-01 — Separate definition, identification, and estimation. Ready when you can show nonidentification by constructing different compatible targets, rather than describing it only as a software difficulty.
DES-02 — Choose a unit, weighting, and resampling design. Ready when you can connect target weights and independent records to estimation, derive the grand-mean variance, and choose an uncertainty and validation unit.
DES-03 — Separate a target from a procedure’s limit. Ready when you can distinguish target mismatch, sampling uncertainty, finite-sample bias, and nonidentification.
MIS-01 — Identify the target under an observation process. Ready when you can distinguish a complete-case target, an identified full-population target, and a genuinely unidentified component.

title: Completion checkpoints
text:
Estimation and uncertainty

LS-01 — Interpret consistency and a limiting law. Ready when you can distinguish concentration near a target, a limiting law for scaled errors, and convergence along almost every sample path.
LS-02 — Expand empirical and population expectations. Ready when you can expand the expectation shorthand, identify its distribution, and distinguish averaging transformed observations from transforming an average.
LS-03 — Separate measurement spread from mean uncertainty. Ready when you can calculate the variance and SE of a sample mean and explain why averaging reduces estimation uncertainty without reducing population heterogeneity.
LS-04 — Combine theorems and check a remainder. Ready when you can justify studentization with the core theorems and distinguish a negligible root-n remainder from an error that changes the limiting law.
SP-01 — Complete a smooth estimating-equation argument. Ready when you can connect the population root to consistency, a negligible remainder, a CLT, and an estimated standard error.
INF-01 — Interpret a standard error, interval, and test. Ready when you can connect a sampling approximation to an interval and test without confusing measurement variability, coverage, null probability, and target alignment.
CL-01 — Derive the cluster contribution for the chosen target. Ready when you can derive both cluster-level contributions and connect target weighting to the independent-unit variance.
CL-02 — Construct a valid fold and variance argument. Ready when you can account for the shared component and preserve the independent unit in training, uncertainty, and resampling.
BOOT-01 — Derive what the bootstrap mean approximates. Ready when you can connect the empirical resampling law, the target error distribution, and the independent unit without confusing sampling error with Monte Carlo error.
BOOT-02 — Prove an ordinary bootstrap failure. Ready when you can diagnose a failure of the resampling approximation separately from limited replicate precision and an incorrect sampling unit.

title: Completion checkpoints
section: Statistical models, influence functions, and efficiency
text:
Statistical models, influence functions, and efficiency

SP-03 — Build a valid path and calculate its score. Ready when you can verify that a proposed perturbation is a probability distribution and relate its score to the target derivative.
SP-02 — Prove the projection property. Ready when you can derive the decomposition, justify the vanishing cross term, and state uniqueness up to almost-sure equality.
SP-04 — Derive mean and variance influence functions. Ready when you can differentiate both functionals, center their contributions, and explain the moment assumptions.
SP-05 — Differentiate a ratio of means. Ready when you can combine the two mean contributions, state the denominator condition, and interpret the correct population target.
SP-07 — Remove a nuisance score and compute the bound. Ready when you can carry the same nuisance projection through to information and estimator variance, with its model assumptions stated.
SP-09 — Compare information with known and unknown variance. Ready when you can show why adding a nuisance parameter may leave the target information unchanged, rather than assuming information always decreases strictly.
SP-08 — Prove the efficient-gradient variance comparison. Ready when you can identify both the object and the projection space, prove the variance comparison, and state what remains to show for an estimator to attain it.
SP-06 — Derive the quantile expansion and influence function. Ready when you can distinguish the population derivative from the stochastic increment and obtain both the expansion and pathwise representation.

title: Completion checkpoints
section: Semiparametric estimation with learned nuisance functions
text:
Semiparametric estimation with learned nuisance functions

SP-11 — Bound the nuisance-bias remainder. Ready when you can derive the exact product remainder, distinguish big-O from little-o, and identify the additional empirical and variance arguments needed for inference.
SP-10 — Derive a nuisance rate and assess its dimension requirement. Ready when you can distinguish squared error from its square root and translate a smoothness/dimension assumption into a sufficient inferential condition.
SP-12 — Control the cross-fitted empirical-process term. Ready when you can show exactly which random term cross-fitting controls and what it does not control.
SP-13 — Complete the missing-outcome mean capstone. Ready when you can reproduce the chain from target and assumptions through estimator, proof, uncertainty, and interpretation.
SP-14 — Distinguish identification, variance, and remainder failures. Ready when you can name the failed condition or term instead of treating every problem as insufficient sample size.

title: Completion checkpoints
text:
Omics data and measurement

OM-02 — Reconstruct the statistical observation. Ready when you can reconstruct the sampling unit and identify a scale/measurement gap before fitting a model.
PRE-01 — Name the target after each processing decision. Ready when you can separate a scale definition, selection, biological adjustment, and causal/measurement assumptions.
OM-01 — Identify measurements and biological replication. Ready when you can distinguish measurement units from replication and describe the information needed to interpret the matrix.
PROT-01 — Reconstruct a protein-level claim. Ready when you can separate biological replication, aggregation, observation, and calibration assumptions.
MET-01 — Separate a molecular quantity from its assay response. Ready when you can connect response correction, identification resolution, and acquisition design to the scope of a group contrast.
MIC-01 — Demonstrate scale nonidentification and name the reference. Ready when you can exhibit observationally equivalent absolute communities and distinguish reference-specific relative changes from absolute changes.
METH-01 — Distinguish scale and mixture effects. Ready when you can calculate scale and composition effects and state the extra information needed for a stronger biological interpretation.

title: Completion checkpoints
text:
Omics analysis problems

DE-01 — Write an estimable contrast. Ready when you can connect a design/contrast calculation to its population interpretation and check rank and confounding.
DE-02 — Explain what variance moderation changes. Ready when you can separate the target contrast, variance borrowing, hierarchical calibration, and the independent-unit/weighting assumptions.
MT-01 — Specify the family and error guarantee. Ready when you can state the family, distinguish an expectation from a realized fraction, execute the BH step-up rule, and identify the p-value and dependence assumptions.
MT-02 — Separate permutation resolution from validity and precision. Ready when you can distinguish a valid Monte Carlo p-value, its resolution, tail precision, and the error-rate summary being estimated.
NET-01 — Identify the association represented by an edge. Ready when you can distinguish marginal and residual targets and describe what the edge does and does not establish.
DES-01 — Separate the scientific target from a pooled association. Ready when you can name the population target and derive the procedure’s limit without treating a pooled quantity as intrinsically wrong.
PV-01 — Verify the linear pseudo-value case. Ready when you can derive the identity and explain why it does not make every pseudo-value a raw biological measurement.
COV-01 — Separate nuisance bias from held-out fluctuation. Ready when you can derive the covariance nuisance-bias remainder and distinguish its rate requirement from cross-fitting and variance consistency.
MV-01 — Match the permutation to the design and null. Ready when you can identify the randomization unit, preserve its dependent measurements, and limit the interpretation of an omnibus result.
CASE-01 — Specify and identify the expression contrast. Ready when you can distinguish the standardized target from a complete-case crude contrast, a constant regression coefficient, and a causal effect.
CASE-02 — Reconstruct the estimator and its remainder. Ready when you can connect every correction and condition to an observed-data quantity and explain what double-robust consistency does and does not establish.
CASE-03 — Interpret discoveries and uncertainty correctly. Ready when you can label each uncertainty quantity and error criterion, including the conditions multiplicity adjustment cannot repair.
CASE-04 — Reproduce and challenge the complete analysis. Ready when you can rebuild the result, trace a claim to its inputs and assumptions, and diagnose a failed condition without silently discarding failures.
NETCASE-01 — Derive the residual-edge contrast and its contribution. Ready when you can connect the edge definition, centering, nuisance cancellation, and remainder to the estimator actually implemented.
NETCASE-02 — Audit uncertainty and reproduce a failure case. Ready when you can trace each conclusion to its target, inputs, conditions, and evaluation record rather than relying on a plot of discoveries.

title: Completion checkpoints
text:
Developing and evaluating methods

EVAL-01 — Separate target bias from uncertainty calibration. Ready when you can distinguish the target, the procedure’s limit, sampling uncertainty, and Monte Carlo uncertainty, and compute a paired performance difference.
SENS-01 — Separate unidentified variation from sampling uncertainty. Ready when you can construct compatible missing-data worlds, calculate a sensitivity curve, and label the identification and sampling uncertainties separately.
SENS-02 — Name what each robustness check changes. Ready when you can keep the estimand explicit while distinguishing an estimator choice, an assumption departure, and a changed population or measurement.
SIM-01 — Write a target-based simulation protocol. Ready when another reader could implement your protocol and distinguish the scientific null, the procedure’s target, and simulation uncertainty.

title: Completion checkpoints
text:
Research practice and reproducibility

REP-01 — Specify a complete rerun contract. Ready when another reader can identify the inputs, configuration, environment, entry point, and expected outputs, and you can verify a rerun without your interactive workspace.
PROV-01 — Audit a join and its population consequences. Ready when you can reconstruct the joins and exclusions and distinguish the retained-data target from the original eligible-population target.
WRITE-01 — Rewrite a claim to match its evidence. Ready when you can state what the reported evidence supports and identify the missing target, assumptions, uncertainty, or validation needed for each stronger claim.

Additional practice is optional
Variations, extra simulations, and optional research extensions do not silently become extra completion requirements. The quantile page supplies its empirical-CDF lemma; a full general proof is additional theory. The survival extension is relevant to projects using that model.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
text: Before reading: Means, variance, elementary calculus, and independent sampling. Use A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference as a notation reference when needed.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
section: 1 Start with a random sample and a fixed target
text:
1 Start with a random sample and a fixed target
Suppose independent people have complete measurements Y_1,\ldots,Y_n from the same population. We assume these observations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), with population mean \mu=E[Y] and finite, positive variance \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y). The population SD is \sigma>0; this notation does not assume normally distributed measurements. The target \mu stays fixed as we repeat sampling. The sample mean \bar Y=n^{-1}\sum_iY_i is an estimator: its value changes from one random sample to another.
The first question is whether this procedure learns the intended population quantity as the sample grows. An estimator is consistent for a target if its probability of missing that target by more than any fixed positive tolerance tends to zero. For the sample mean, the law of large numbers (LLN) supplies precisely this result. It connects an average of observations to the expectation under the population that produced them.
To see the connection, write the estimation error as an average of centered measurements:

\bar Y-\mu=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\mu).

Each centered measurement has expectation zero. The LLN says their average approaches zero in probability, establishing consistency of \bar Y for \mu. Thus, for a sufficiently large sample, a fixed-size estimation error becomes unlikely. This does not require each new observation to move the estimate closer to \mu, and it does not make the estimate equal to \mu in a finite sample.
Consistency is a statement about the procedure and the population actually sampled. If we average only observed outcomes from a selected subset, the LLN may establish consistency for E[Y\mid R=1]. It does not turn that quantity into the eligible-population mean E[Y]. The target distinction from the previous guide still matters.
After consistency comes a second question: how much does the estimator fluctuate around its limit, and how can we describe that uncertainty? The central limit theorem (CLT) supplies a scale and a distributional approximation under additional conditions. Consistency alone supplies neither.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
section: 2 The probability tools and what they do
text:
2 The probability tools and what they do
The notation below separates three tasks: establishing a limit, describing a sampling distribution, and comparing the sizes of random errors. Throughout, probabilities refer to repeated sampling under the stated population law.

2.1 Convergence in probability
We write

X_n\xrightarrow{p}c.

This reads “X_n converges in probability to c.” For a fixed number c, the definition requires, for every fixed \varepsilon>0,

\Pr(|X_n-c|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.

Convergence in probability controls departures from a fixed quantity. For example, \bar Y\xrightarrow{p}\mu means that the chance of a sample mean more than 0.1 units from \mu tends to zero; the same must hold for every other fixed positive tolerance. The distribution of \bar Y concentrates increasingly near \mu. The definition does not prescribe how quickly this happens.


2.2 Almost sure convergence: a stronger, pathwise property
You will also encounter

X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}c.

This reads “X_n converges almost surely to c.” With the whole sequence defined on a common probability space, it means

\Pr\!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n=c\right)=1.

Think of drawing one infinite sequence of observations and computing an estimate from its first n entries as n grows. Each realization produces a numerical sequence of estimates: a sample path. Almost sure convergence says that, except on a set of paths with probability zero, this numerical sequence converges in the ordinary sense. For each fixed positive tolerance, all estimates after some path-dependent sample size stay within that tolerance. The estimates can still fluctuate along the way.
This is stronger than convergence in probability. The latter controls the chance of a departure at sample size n; it does not by itself guarantee that a single path makes only finitely many fixed-size departures. Almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability, but the converse need not hold.
The stronger property is useful when the claim concerns an entire sequence:

Strong consistency. The strong LLN shows that the sample mean converges almost surely to \mu for i.i.d. observations with E[|Y|]<\infty. This describes what happens along almost every growing dataset, rather than only giving a probability bound at each sample size.
Eventual control of errors. The first Borel–Cantelli lemma says that if \sum_n\Pr(E_n)<\infty, then the failure events E_n occur only finitely often with probability one. Applying this to errors exceeding each tolerance 1,1/2,1/3,\ldots is one way to prove almost sure convergence. This summable bound is stronger than merely having \Pr(E_n)\to0.
Long-run behavior of random algorithms. Some stochastic-approximation and martingale-convergence proofs establish that an iterative procedure converges along almost every random trajectory. Those results require their own stability and integrability conditions.

For the inference arguments in these guides, we will use consistency in probability, negligible remainders expressed through o_p, and CLTs in distribution. We will not need almost sure convergence as a proof step. It is a useful stronger conclusion when available, but even almost sure consistency alone supplies neither a root-n rate nor a normal sampling approximation.


2.3 Convergence in distribution, or law
We write

X_n\xrightarrow{d}X.

This reads “X_n converges in distribution (or in law) to X.” Let F_X(t)=\Pr(X\le t) be the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of X. The definition requires, at every continuity point t of F_X,

\Pr(X_n\le t)\longrightarrow F_X(t).

In words, at each such threshold t, the probability of a repeated-sample outcome below that threshold approaches the probability specified by the limiting law.
Convergence in distribution describes a limiting law. It need not concentrate at one number. For example, \sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2) says that the scaled estimation errors have a distribution approaching a normal law with variance \sigma^2. Their unscaled errors shrink, but multiplying by \sqrt n reveals fluctuations that remain visible.
Convergence in law also does not mean that two random variables take nearly equal values. If X_n and X are independent standard normals, their distributions already agree for every n, yet X_n-X has the same N(0,2) distribution for every n. Its probability of exceeding a fixed positive tolerance in absolute value stays positive, so there is no convergence in probability of X_n to that particular X. Convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution; the reverse implication holds when the limiting law is a point mass at a constant, but not in general.


2.4 Big-O and little-o for random errors
Let a_n>0 be a deterministic scale, such as n^{-1/2}. The statement X_n=O_p(a_n) means that X_n/a_n is bounded in probability. For every tail-probability tolerance \varepsilon>0, there are a finite M>0 and an n_0 such that

\sup_{n\ge n_0}\Pr\!\left(\frac{|X_n|}{a_n}>M\right)
<\varepsilon.

After rescaling, sufficiently large values remain uniformly unlikely for large n. The bound M can depend on \varepsilon, but not on n. This is a probability bound, not a claim that every possible realization is bounded by M.
The stronger statement X_n=o_p(a_n) means X_n/a_n\xrightarrow{p}0. Equivalently, for every fixed \delta>0,

\Pr\!\left(\frac{|X_n|}{a_n}>\delta\right)\longrightarrow0.

For example, n^{-1/2} is O_p(n^{-1/2}) but not o_p(n^{-1/2}): dividing by that scale gives 1. In contrast, n^{-1} is o_p(n^{-1/2}), because the ratio is n^{-1/2}\to0. Random errors obey the same scale comparison, with convergence understood in probability.
Useful product rules are

\begin{aligned}
O_p(a_n)O_p(b_n)&=O_p(a_nb_n),\\
O_p(a_n)o_p(b_n)&=o_p(a_nb_n).
\end{aligned}

These rules do not require independence. In particular, a remainder that is merely O_p(n^{-1/2}) need not disappear after multiplication by \sqrt n. To remove it from a first-order limit, we generally need o_p(n^{-1/2}).


2.5 Population error for a fitted function
Later we will measure a regression fit by \|\hat m-m\|_2^2=E[(\hat m(Z)-m(Z))^2]. Here the expectation averages over a fresh population covariate Z, holding the fitted function fixed. The norm is still random across training samples. Thus \|\hat m-m\|_2\xrightarrow{p}0 describes consistency in population prediction error; it is not a statement that training error is small. This distinction matters when a proof contains functions learned from data.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
section: 3 Two statements about the same sample mean
text:
3 Two statements about the same sample mean
Return to the i.i.d. measurements with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2. The LLN and CLT answer different questions about the same estimator:

\begin{gathered}
\bar Y\xrightarrow{p}\mu,\\
\sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2).
\end{gathered}

The first establishes consistency: where the estimator settles as information grows. The second describes its fluctuations on the root-n scale. For sufficiently large n, the sampling distribution of \bar Y is approximately N(\mu,\sigma^2/n). This approximation concerns the sample mean; the individual measurements can have a nonnormal distribution.

3.1 Measurement variability and estimation uncertainty
The population standard deviation \sigma describes differences between individual measurements. The standard error of \bar Y describes differences between sample means obtained in repeated studies of size n. These are different random objects: one measurement Y versus an average \bar Y.
Independence explains why averaging reduces the second kind of variation:

\begin{aligned}
E[\bar Y]&=\mu,\\
\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)&=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)\\
&=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\\
\operatorname{SE}(\bar Y)&=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)}\\
&=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}

The covariance terms vanish because the observations are independent. These mean and variance identities are exact under our assumptions; the CLT supplies the approximate normal shape of the sampling distribution.
For example, suppose a feature has population mean 50 and population SD 10, in the feature’s measurement units:








Number of independent people
SD of an individual measurement
SE of the sample mean




25
10
2


100
10
1


400
10
0.5



In a study of 100 people, individual measurements still vary with SD 10. Across repeated studies of 100 people, the means vary around 50 with SD 1. Collecting more people makes the population mean easier to estimate; it does not make the people themselves more alike. Quadrupling the sample size halves the SE, while the population SD stays the same.


3.2 Replace the unknown population variance
In an actual study, \sigma^2 is usually unknown. For n\ge2, estimate it using the sample variance:

\begin{aligned}
s_Y^2&=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y)^2,\\
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar Y)&=\frac{s_Y}{\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}

The sample SD s_Y estimates the spread of individual measurements. Dividing by \sqrt n turns it into an estimated SE for their mean. Reporting s_Y as an SE would confuse population heterogeneity with uncertainty about \mu.
There is a consistency argument behind this substitution. Write

s_Y^2=\frac{n}{n-1}
\left\{\frac1n\sum_iY_i^2-\bar Y^2\right\}.

The LLN gives n^{-1}\sum_iY_i^2\xrightarrow{p}E[Y^2] and \bar Y\xrightarrow{p}\mu. Continuous mapping and n/(n-1)\to1 then give s_Y^2\xrightarrow{p}E[Y^2]-\mu^2=\sigma^2. Thus the estimated contribution variance approaches the population variance.
Finally, combine the CLT with this consistency result:

\begin{aligned}
\frac{\bar Y-\mu}{s_Y/\sqrt n}&=\frac{\sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu)}{s_Y}\\
&\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).
\end{aligned}

This last step uses Slutsky’s theorem, stated below. It justifies using an estimated standard error in a large-sample interval or test. Merely knowing that the mean is consistent would not justify that step.
A finite population mean without finite variance can still support an LLN while defeating this particular CLT and variance calculation. Clustered measurements require the independent sampling unit and its contribution to be reconsidered. The theorem must match the problem, not just the formula used by software.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
section: 4 The delta method is the same first-order idea
text:
4 The delta method is the same first-order idea
If \sqrt n(\hat\eta-\eta_0)\to_d N(0,\Sigma) and g is differentiable at \eta_0, then

\sqrt n\{g(\hat\eta)-g(\eta_0)\}
\to_d N(0,\nabla g^\top\Sigma\nabla g).

It propagates the joint covariance, not only separate standard errors. For a ratio or correlation, dropping the covariance between components can give the wrong uncertainty. If the gradient vanishes, the ordinary first-order limit may be degenerate and a higher-order analysis may be needed.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
section: 5 The first-order pattern for a more complicated estimator
text:
5 The first-order pattern for a more complicated estimator
Now move from the particular mean \mu to a general scalar target \psi_0. The central goal is an expansion

\begin{aligned}
\widehat\psi-\psi_0&=(P_n-P)D_0+R_n,\\
PD_0&=0,\\
R_n&=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{aligned}

The sample mean fits this pattern with D_0(Y)=Y-\mu and remainder exactly zero. For a more complicated estimator, the remainder needs its own argument. When 0<PD_0^2<\infty, a fixed-function CLT handles the average. The condition R_n=o_p(n^{-1/2}) makes \sqrt nR_n=o_p(1), so Slutsky leaves the same normal limit after adding the remainder.
A feasible standard error additionally needs consistent estimation of the contribution variance. This follows the sample-mean walkthrough: establish the population limit, isolate the leading random average, control what remains, and justify the estimated variance. Calling a function an influence function or fitting a flexible regression does not establish these steps.
Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity derives this pattern by linearizing a sample equation. Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests explains what the resulting approximation lets us claim.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
text:
6 Check your understanding
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. These four checkpoints check the fundamental interpretations and calculations used throughout the later theory. Try each before opening its hint or solution outline. The longer smooth-root derivation is SP-01 on the next page.


Checkpoint · LS-01 — Interpret consistency and a limiting law
Task type: Interpretation and probability notation.
Let Y_1,\ldots,Y_n be i.i.d., with mean \mu and finite, positive variance \sigma^2.

Write the probability statement that defines \bar Y\xrightarrow{p}\mu. Explain what a fixed tolerance \varepsilon>0 means in this statement.
Explain how this differs from \sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2). Why can the unscaled error approach zero while the scaled error has a nondegenerate limiting distribution? Does either statement say that individual measurements are normally distributed?
What would almost sure convergence add to the consistency statement? Is that stronger conclusion required for the CLT and feasible standard-error argument on this page?

Ready to continue when: you can distinguish concentration near a target, a limiting law for scaled errors, and convergence along almost every sample path.
Transfer: Suppose an estimator converges in probability to \mu+b for a fixed b\ne0. Is it consistent for \mu? Would collecting more observations remove that target mismatch?


Hint

For consistency, start with the event |\bar Y-\mu|>\varepsilon. For the CLT, identify which random quantity has a limiting normal law. For almost sure convergence, think about one growing dataset rather than a separate probability at each sample size.



Solution outline — open after trying

Consistency means that, for every fixed \varepsilon>0,

\Pr(|\bar Y-\mu|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.

The tolerance stays fixed as n grows. The probability of exceeding it tends to zero; this does not say that each additional observation brings the estimate closer to \mu.
The CLT instead describes the repeated-sample distribution of \sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu). The error shrinks on the n^{-1/2} scale, so multiplying by \sqrt n reveals fluctuations that remain visible. Neither statement requires normally distributed individual measurements, and the CLT is a limiting statement rather than an exact finite-sample normality claim.
Almost sure convergence says that along almost every infinite sample path, the estimates eventually stay within each fixed positive tolerance. We do not need that stronger conclusion for the inference argument here. It would not, by itself, supply a root-n rate or a normal limit.
In the transfer question, the estimator is consistent for \mu+b, not \mu. For example, its probability of lying within |b|/2 of \mu tends to zero. More observations concentrate it near the wrong target.





Checkpoint · LS-02 — Expand empirical and population expectations
Task type: Calculation and notation.
The observed values are Y_1=1, Y_2=1, and Y_3=4. Take f(y)=y^2. No population distribution P is supplied.

What probabilities does the empirical distribution P_n assign to the distinct values 1 and 4?
Write P_nf as both E_{P_n}(f(Y)) and an explicit average, and calculate its value. Write Pf as a population expectation. Can you calculate that population quantity from the three observations alone?
Expand (P_n-P)f in this example. Which part is known from the sample?
Take g(u)=u^2. Calculate g(\bar Y) and compare it with P_nf. Explain the difference between these operations.

Ready to continue when: you can expand the expectation shorthand, identify its distribution, and distinguish averaging transformed observations from transforming an average.
Transfer: Now take f(y)=\mathbf{1}\{y>2\}, the indicator that equals 1 when y>2 and 0 otherwise. What are P_nf and the population quantity Pf?


Hint

Drawing from P_n means selecting one of the three observed records with equal probability. The value 1 occurs twice. Keep the factor 1/3 when averaging squares; for g(\bar Y), average first and then square.



Solution outline — open after trying

The empirical distribution gives probability 2/3 to 1 and 1/3 to 4. Thus

\begin{aligned}
P_nf&=E_{P_n}(Y^2)\\
&=\frac{1^2+1^2+4^2}{3}\\
&=6.
\end{aligned}

The population quantity is Pf=E_P(Y^2). The sample provides an estimate of that expectation, not its exact value. Without specifying P, its value is unknown. Therefore (P_n-P)f=6-E_P(Y^2); only the first term is known.
Here \bar Y=2, so g(\bar Y)=\bar Y^2=4, whereas P_nf=6. Squaring each observation and then averaging differs from squaring their average.
For the indicator in the transfer question, P_nf=1/3 is the observed fraction exceeding 2. Its population counterpart is Pf=E_P(\mathbf{1}\{Y>2\})=\Pr_P(Y>2), which is not known exactly from these observations.





Checkpoint · LS-03 — Separate measurement spread from mean uncertainty
Task type: Calculation and interpretation.
Suppose independent measurements from one population have SD \sigma=12.

Calculate the exact variance and SE of the sample mean for n=36 and n=144. What happens to the SD of individual measurements?
In practice, \sigma is unknown. If a study of 36 people gives sample SD s_Y=15, what estimated SE should be reported for \bar Y? Explain why 15 is not that estimated SE.
A colleague says, “With enough people, the measurements themselves become less variable and normally distributed.” Explain what is wrong with both parts of this statement.

Ready to continue when: you can calculate the variance and SE of a sample mean and explain why averaging reduces estimation uncertainty without reducing population heterogeneity.
Transfer: Keeping the population and independent sampling design fixed, how must n change to halve the SE?


Hint

Use \operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)=\sigma^2/n and \operatorname{SE}(\bar Y)=\sigma/\sqrt n. Label the random object whose spread each number describes.



Solution outline — open after trying

For n=36, the variance is 144/36=4 and the SE is 2. For n=144, the variance is 144/144=1 and the SE is 1. The population SD of individual measurements remains 12 in both cases.
The estimated SE from the observed sample is 15/\sqrt{36}=2.5. The sample SD 15 estimates the spread of individual measurements; dividing by \sqrt n estimates the spread of sample means across repeated studies. That estimated SE need not equal the true SE in one sample.
Increasing n changes the uncertainty of the average, not the population distribution of individual measurements. The CLT concerns the limiting distribution of scaled errors in the average. It does not make individual measurements normal. The variance and SE identities here are exact under independent, identically distributed sampling with finite variance; a normal approximation is a separate step.
Since SE is proportional to 1/\sqrt n, halving it requires quadrupling n under the same assumptions.





Checkpoint · LS-04 — Combine theorems and check a remainder
Task type: Theorem selection and rate reasoning.
Continue with i.i.d. measurements of mean \mu and finite, positive variance \sigma^2, and the sample SD s_Y.

Explain what the LLN, CLT, continuous mapping, and Slutsky’s theorem each contribute to

\frac{\sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu)}{s_Y}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).

Include why s_Y^2 consistently estimates \sigma^2. Must \bar Y and s_Y be independent?
Consider \tilde\mu_n=\bar Y+R_n. For each deterministic remainder R_n=n^{-1} and R_n=n^{-1/2}, calculate \sqrt nR_n. Which remainder is o_p(n^{-1/2})? Which is O_p(n^{-1/2})?
For which remainder can you retain the standard normal limit after replacing \bar Y with \tilde\mu_n in the display? Does merely proving R_n\to0 settle this question?

Ready to continue when: you can justify studentization with the core theorems and distinguish a negligible root-n remainder from an error that changes the limiting law.
Transfer: If \mu>0, what derivative does the delta method use for \sqrt{\bar Y}, and what large-sample SE estimate follows on the event \bar Y>0?


Hint

Write s_Y^2 in terms of the average of Y_i^2 and \bar Y^2. For the remainders, divide by n^{-1/2} before deciding whether the ratio tends to zero or stays bounded.



Solution outline — open after trying

The LLN gives \bar Y\xrightarrow{p}\mu and n^{-1}\sum_iY_i^2\xrightarrow{p}E_P(Y^2). The second use needs a finite second moment, which our finite-variance assumption supplies. Continuous mapping and n/(n-1)\to1 give

\begin{aligned}
s_Y^2&=\frac{n}{n-1}
\left\{\frac1n\sum_iY_i^2-\bar Y^2\right\}\\
&\xrightarrow{p}\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}

Continuity of the square root gives s_Y\xrightarrow{p}\sigma>0. The CLT gives \sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2), and Slutsky justifies division by s_Y to obtain N(0,1). Independence of \bar Y and s_Y is not required. As in the theorem discussion, define the ratio arbitrarily if s_Y=0; that event has probability tending to zero.
For R_n=n^{-1}, \sqrt nR_n=n^{-1/2}\to0, so R_n=o_p(n^{-1/2}) and also O_p(n^{-1/2}). For R_n=n^{-1/2}, \sqrt nR_n=1, so it is O_p(n^{-1/2}) but not o_p(n^{-1/2}).
The first remainder vanishes in the scaled limit. The second adds 1/s_Y\to_p1/\sigma to the studentized statistic, shifting its limit to N(1/\sigma,1). Both remainders tend to zero and preserve consistency for \mu, but only the first preserves the centered standard normal limit.
For the transfer, g'(\mu)=1/(2\sqrt\mu). The delta-method SE is estimated by s_Y/(2\sqrt{\bar Y}\sqrt n) when \bar Y>0. Consistency and \mu>0 make that event have probability tending to one.




Additional practice (optional)

Apply the delta method to \log\bar Y for a positive population mean. Derive the limiting variance and an estimated SE, and state the domain condition.
Explain why a consistent estimator need not have a root-n rate. Construct an example by adding a deterministic shrinking error to \bar Y.
For the numerical example in section 3, calculate how many independent people would be needed to reduce the SE from 1 to 0.25. What happens to the population SD?
State what changes in the argument if the contribution is fitted using the same observations.

title: How to write a research paper
text: This note outlines how to write an applied statistics research paper. At this stage, you have already performed a literature review for a research topic, you drafted an analysis plan, you carried out that analysis (possibly adding to/modifying what was planned), and you have your results prepared in a set of tables and figures. Now, it’s time to write.1

title: How to write a research paper
text:
2.1 Templates
These skeletons give you something to fill in. Replace every bracket with specific content from your own paper.
Abstract (four sentences):

[Problem: what is unknown or unresolved, and why it matters]. [What we did: design, data, and main method]. [Main result, with at least one number]. [Conclusion: what the result means for the problem].

Introduction (one paragraph per step; typically three to five paragraphs):

Establish the topic and why it matters. “[Topic] affects [who or what], [with supporting fact] (cite).”
Summarize what is known. “Previous studies found [finding] (cite) and [finding] (cite).”
Build tension. “However, [gap, inconsistency, or overlooked issue]. As a result, [consequence for the reader].”
Resolve it. “In this paper, we [what you did] to [address the gap]. We found [headline result].”

Methods (subsection headings you can reuse): Data source, Data processing, Statistical analysis, Software.
Results (for each table or figure): “[Table/Figure reference] shows [what it displays]. [Key numbers, with units and uncertainty].”
Discussion (in order): Recap of the problem, Key findings, Comparison with the literature, Implications, Limitations, Future directions.

title: How to write a research paper
text:
5.1 Abstract

Before: Alertness is important for students. We did a study on walking and alertness. Walking was found to be somewhat helpful. This could be useful for many people.
After: Afternoon drowsiness is common among students, but few randomized studies have tested whether a short walk reduces it. We randomly assigned 60 students to a 10-minute walk or 10 minutes of quiet sitting after lunch and compared self-rated alertness (1–10 scale) at 2:00 pm. The walking group’s mean alertness was 0.8 points higher (95% CI 0.05 to 1.55; p = 0.037). A short post-lunch walk was associated with higher self-rated alertness in this sample, which supports testing it in a larger and more varied population.

Why the “after” is better: it states the problem, the design, a number with its uncertainty, and a conclusion that doesn’t go further than the data.

title: How to write a research paper
text:
5.2 Introduction

Before: Everyone knows that exercise is good for you, and many studies have shown it is important for the brain. Students are often tired in the afternoon, which can be a problem. It would be interesting to see whether walking could help. In this paper we investigate this.
After: Afternoon drowsiness reduces attention during classes held after lunch (Author A, Year). Observational studies report that people who walk more also report higher alertness (Author B, Year; Author C, Year). However, these studies could not separate walking from other differences between active and inactive people, and the few randomized trials used walks of 30 minutes or longer (Author D, Year), which do not fit in a typical lunch break. It is therefore unknown whether a 10-minute walk is enough to raise alertness. In this paper, we randomly assigned students to a 10-minute walk or to quiet sitting after lunch, and measured self-rated alertness at 2:00 pm.

What changed: “Everyone knows” and “important” are replaced by cited facts. The words “however” and “unknown” build tension, and the last sentence resolves it by stating what the paper did.

title: How to write a research paper
text:
5.3 Methods

Before: We looked at students and compared walking to not walking. The walking group did better, so we used a t-test.
After: We recruited 60 students from an introductory statistics course in Fall 2026. Students were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to a walking group or a sitting group using a random number generator. After lunch, the walking group walked at a self-selected pace for 10 minutes on a marked campus loop, and the sitting group sat quietly for 10 minutes. At 2:00 pm, each student rated their alertness from 1 (very drowsy) to 10 (very alert) on a paper form. Mean ratings were compared between groups using a two-sample t-test with equal variances, with a two-sided significance level of 0.05. All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.0) (R Core Team, Year).

What changed: the “before” contains a result (“did better”), which does not belong in Methods. The “after” is in past tense and gives enough detail that another student could repeat the study.

title: How to write a research paper
text:
5.4 Results

Before: Walking clearly worked and made students much more alert, which is probably because exercise wakes up the brain.
After: The walking group (n = 30) had a mean alertness rating of 6.9 (SD 1.4) and the sitting group (n = 30) had a mean rating of 6.1 (SD 1.5) (Table 1). The difference in means was 0.8 points (95% CI 0.05 to 1.55; p = 0.037).
