title: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference
text:
4 Interval recipes make different transformations
Let q^*_{a} be an a-quantile of the bootstrap estimates. At nominal 95% coverage:









Construction
Interval
What must be justified




Normal approximation
\widehat\theta\pm1.96\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_*
A centered normal approximation and a consistent variance


Percentile
[q^*_{.025},q^*_{.975}]
An appropriate bootstrap approximation; this does not automatically correct bias


Basic
[2\widehat\theta-q^*_{.975},2\widehat\theta-q^*_{.025}]
Approximation of the centered error distribution


Studentized
Invert quantiles of (\widehat\theta^*-\widehat\theta)/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}^*
A justified SE within each replicate and a valid studentized approximation




The basic interval follows by approximating the estimation-error distribution. The bootstrap error quantiles are q^*_{.025}-\widehat\theta and q^*_{.975}-\widehat\theta. If those bracket \widehat\theta-\theta_0, solving the two inequalities for \theta_0 reverses and reflects the endpoints:

\left[2\widehat\theta-q^*_{.975},\;
2\widehat\theta-q^*_{.025}\right].

For example, with observed estimate 10 and bootstrap estimate quantiles 8 and 13, the percentile interval is [8,13] and the basic interval is [7,12]. Their difference comes from the transformation, not from more data or a different replicate count. With a symmetric, centered normal approximation they can agree at first order; skewness and bias make the distinction more visible.
For studentization, calculate an SE in each resample and form T^*=(\widehat\theta^*-\widehat\theta)/\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}^*. If t^*_{.025} and t^*_{.975} are its quantiles, inversion gives

\left[\widehat\theta-t^*_{.975}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}},\;
\widehat\theta-t^*_{.025}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}\right].

The final SE here comes from the original study; each starred SE was needed to construct the resampled standardized errors. The procedure requires both the estimator and its variance calculation to behave appropriately under resampling.
The boot.ci documentation also describes BCa intervals. Their corrections and extra accuracy require additional conditions; choosing a sophisticated interval label does not remove those conditions.


Code
q <- quantile(boot_mean, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
rbind(normal = mean_hat + c(-1, 1)*qnorm(0.975)*sd(boot_mean),
      percentile = q, basic = 2*mean_hat-rev(q))


               [,1]     [,2]
normal     2.046090 2.710119
percentile 2.042315 2.715710
basic      2.040499 2.713894


In this particular simulated sample, all three intervals lie above the known mean 2. That is one random noncoverage event; it does not estimate a method’s coverage probability. Assess coverage across independent datasets under stated conditions.
These are pointwise intervals for one target. They do not automatically provide simultaneous or post-selection coverage for thousands of features. See Multiple testing when the tests are not independent.
crumbs: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference

title: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference
section: 5 Preserve the independent unit and the target weights
text:
5 Preserve the independent unit and the target weights
For independent people with repeated records, draw people with replacement and carry all of each sampled person’s records together. The resampled object should reproduce the sampling design. A bootstrap for a stratified design may need resampling within the original sampling strata; a complex survey or dependence across clusters needs its own scheme.
Resampling rows independently would break the pattern of shared person effects in the data. Holding people together preserves their joint records. This choice addresses dependence; the statistic recomputed on those records still determines whether the target weights people or records equally.
If the target is the mean of a person’s recorded-visit average, first form one summary per person. If it is a record-weighted ratio, retain each person’s total and record count and recompute the ratio after resampling. The following invented records demonstrate both, using the same resampled people.


Code
set.seed(3102)
G <- 80; size <- sample(c(2, 5), G, replace = TRUE)
id <- rep(seq_len(G), size)
values <- rep(rnorm(G), size) + rnorm(sum(size), sd = 0.5)
total <- as.numeric(rowsum(values, id))
bootstrap <- replicate(1999, {
  selected <- sample.int(G, G, replace = TRUE)
  c(person = mean(total[selected]/size[selected]),
    record = sum(total[selected])/sum(size[selected]))
})
apply(bootstrap, 1, sd)


   person    record 
0.1259339 0.1324401 


Duplicating a person in a bootstrap sample is intentional. If rebuilding a raw-record analysis, give the duplicate cluster copies distinct bootstrap cluster IDs where needed. Do not replace person weighting with row weighting by accident. The Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference page derives the corresponding influence functions and few-cluster limitations.
crumbs: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference

title: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference
text:
6 Decide what must be refitted
A full bootstrap statistic repeats the estimator’s learned preprocessing, model fitting, selection, tuning, and uncertainty calculation according to its declared algorithm. Holding fitted parts fixed changes what is being approximated; it needs an argument. Repeating the full algorithm is also not sufficient for bootstrap consistency when the target or selection is nonregular.
Cross-fitting requires particular care. Copies of an original person’s outcomes can leak between training and evaluation if bootstrap duplicates are randomly sent to different folds. Specify a bootstrap weighting/identity and fold scheme whose theory applies to the estimator. Grouping duplicates can prevent that leakage, but does not itself prove conditional remainder control. There is no universal instruction to bootstrap every machine-learning pipeline in the same way.

6.1 Later extension: multiplier resampling (optional)
Return to this extension after learning influence functions. A multiplier approximation can avoid nuisance refitting when a valid asymptotically linear representation is already available. If the estimated centered contributions are \widehat D_i, independent multipliers \xi_i with mean zero and variance one, also independent of the data, generate

Z^*=\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_i\xi_i\widehat D_i.

With a valid negligible estimator remainder, consistent contribution/variance estimation, and conditional CLT/non-dominance conditions, this approximates the first-order error law. For Gaussian multipliers and a scalar target it is conditionally normal with variance n^{-1}\sum_i\widehat D_i^2; that variance match alone does not prove the estimator’s expansion. With independent clusters, use cluster contributions and the cluster count. This construction approximates the first-order fluctuation; it does not measure persistent nuisance bias.
Conditional on the data, the \widehat D_i are fixed, and independent mean-zero multipliers make the covariance terms vanish. This explains the displayed variance. Z^* is on the scaled-error scale of \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta_0); divide it by \sqrt n to approximate an unscaled estimation error. Inference still depends on having correctly derived the original estimator’s expansion.
crumbs: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference

title: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference
section: 7 A concrete failure: estimating a support endpoint
text:
7 A concrete failure: estimating a support endpoint
Let Y_i be i.i.d. uniform on [0,\theta] and estimate \theta by the sample maximum M_n. Here we study the positive gap \theta-M_n and its bootstrap counterpart M_n-M_n^*; both reverse the sign of the earlier estimate-minus-target convention. The scaling is n, rather than the usual square root. Define the scaled gap’s CDF as F_n(t)=\Pr\{n(\theta-M_n)/\theta\le t\}. For 0\le t\le n,

\begin{aligned}
F_n(t)&=1-(1-t/n)^n\\
&\longrightarrow1-e^{-t}.
\end{aligned}

To obtain this, note that M_n\le x requires all n independent observations to be at most x, giving probability (x/\theta)^n for 0\le x\le\theta. The scaled-error event instead asks whether M_n is at least \theta(1-t/n), so taking the complement gives the formula. Its limiting law is exponential, not the mean’s normal limit.
With a unique sample maximum, the ordinary bootstrap maximum equals M_n whenever that observed maximum is selected at least once:

\begin{aligned}
\Pr_*(M_n^*=M_n)&=1-(1-1/n)^n\\
&\longrightarrow1-e^{-1}.
\end{aligned}

Each draw misses that particular record with probability 1-1/n; all n draws miss it with probability (1-1/n)^n. The bootstrap cannot generate a larger value than the observed maximum. Thus it retains positive probability of exactly zero centered error even as the dataset grows.
The centered bootstrap error consequently retains an atom at zero, whereas the sampling limit is continuous. Increasing the number of bootstrap replicates estimates the wrong approximation more precisely. An ordinary percentile interval is particularly revealing: both endpoints are at most M_n<\theta almost surely, so it cannot cover the true endpoint. Specialized endpoint procedures require another argument; the failure does not say every resampling procedure fails for every endpoint problem.


Code
set.seed(3103)
x <- runif(80); n_endpoint <- length(x); maximum <- max(x)
boot_max <- replicate(3999, max(x[sample.int(n_endpoint, n_endpoint, replace = TRUE)]))
endpoint_error <- n_endpoint*(maximum-boot_max)/maximum
plot(ecdf(endpoint_error), xlim = c(-0.2, 5), verticals = TRUE,
     do.points = FALSE, col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2, main = "",
     xlab = "Endpoint error on the n scale", ylab = "CDF")
t_grid <- seq(0, 5, length.out = 300)
lines(t_grid, 1-(1-t_grid/n_endpoint)^n_endpoint, col = "#2F80C8", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("Conditional bootstrap", "Exact sampling law"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "#2F80C8"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
c(empirical_atom = mean(boot_max == maximum),
  exact_atom = 1-(1-1/n_endpoint)^n_endpoint)


empirical_atom     exact_atom 
     0.6256564      0.6344319 








Figure 2: One uniform(0,1) teaching sample (n=80), with 3,999 ordinary bootstrap maxima. The conditional bootstrap CDF has a large jump at zero; the exact sampling CDF is continuous. This compares endpoint errors on their n scale, not sqrt(n).





Bickel and Freedman give foundational consistency results and counterexamples. Nonsmooth sample equations are not automatically failures: Quantiles and local expansions develops the regular positive-density case. Boundary behavior, unstable selection, weak identification, infinite moments, and the bootstrap’s own remainder conditions require examination.
crumbs: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference

title: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference
section: 8 Separate sampling uncertainty from resampling Monte Carlo error
text:
8 Separate sampling uncertainty from resampling Monte Carlo error
The dataset size controls information about the population. The replicate count B controls simulation accuracy conditional on that dataset. At a fixed threshold, a bootstrap tail probability estimated from independent replicates has MCSE approximately \sqrt{p_*(1-p_*)/B}. An interval endpoint is a quantile; its Monte Carlo error also depends on local density and cannot be read directly from this probability-scale formula.
For example, if a conditional tail probability is 0.025, 1,999 resamples supply about 50 observations in that tail on average. Increasing B to 19,999 reduces probability-scale Monte Carlo error by about \sqrt{10} while leaving the original study unchanged. It does not divide the study’s SE by \sqrt{10}. For a cluster bootstrap, the population information is governed by the number and structure of independent clusters, rather than simply the row count.
Check endpoint stability with independent resampling seeds or a justified quantile-uncertainty calculation. Report the scheme, resampling unit, statistic, refitting/fold rules, replicate count, seed, interval construction, and failed or degenerate replicates. A failed replicate is an outcome to diagnose, not a row to silently discard.
crumbs: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference

title: Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference
text:
9 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · BOOT-01 — Derive what the bootstrap mean approximates
Task type: Derivation and interpretation.
For i.i.d. scalar observations with finite nonzero variance, derive the conditional mean and variance of the ordinary bootstrap sample mean. Explain the center and scaling of the bootstrap root, construct percentile and basic intervals from bootstrap quantiles, and distinguish n from the replicate count B. State what changes for a mean of person-level visit averages.
Ready to continue when: you can connect the empirical resampling law, the target error distribution, and the independent unit without confusing sampling error with Monte Carlo error.
Transfer: Would holding every fitted nuisance fixed approximate the same finite-sample algorithm as refitting it? When could a first-order multiplier approximation still be justified?


Hint

A bootstrap draw is uniform over the n observed values. Conditional on the dataset, the n draws are independent.



Solution outline — open after trying

The conditional mean is the observed mean and the variance is (n−1)s²/n². The bootstrap root sqrt(n)(mean*−mean) approximates sqrt(n)(mean−μ) under the mean CLT and bootstrap conditions. Percentile endpoints are the estimate quantiles; basic endpoints reverse and reflect them about the observed estimate. Increasing B reduces conditional simulation error, while increasing n adds population information. For equally person-weighted visit averages, resample whole people or their defined summaries and use the person count.





Checkpoint · BOOT-02 — Prove an ordinary bootstrap failure
Task type: Derivation and diagnosis.
For a continuous uniform sample with a unique maximum, derive the probability that an ordinary bootstrap sample contains that maximum. Compare its limiting atom with the sampling limit of n(θ−M_n)/θ. Explain why an ordinary percentile interval cannot cover θ, and whether increasing B or resampling rows instead of people could repair the respective validity problems.
Ready to continue when: you can diagnose a failure of the resampling approximation separately from limited replicate precision and an incorrect sampling unit.
Transfer: Why does a positive-density sample median require a different diagnosis from a support maximum?


Hint

Compute the probability of never drawing the maximum in n draws. Both percentile endpoints must be observed-sample-supported maxima.



Solution outline — open after trying

The probability is 1−(1−1/n)^n, tending to 1−exp(−1). The bootstrap centered error therefore has a nonvanishing atom at zero, while the sampling endpoint error converges to a continuous exponential law. Percentile endpoints are at most M_n, below θ almost surely, so coverage is zero. More replicates sharpen this invalid approximation; an independent-row bootstrap also cannot reproduce within-person dependence. Each problem requires a different justified procedure.




Additional practice (optional)

Use three independent bootstrap seeds with B=199 and B=1999. Compare interval endpoint stability without changing the dataset.
Derive the conditional variance of the Gaussian multiplier root and explain why matching it is not a proof of target consistency.
Write the full refitting and identity rules for bootstrapping one of your own estimators; identify which step still needs a bootstrap-validity argument.

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
text: Before reading: Units of analysis, replication, and study design, means, and variances. Start with the person-summary examples; Influence functions and Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity support the contribution and sandwich derivations when you return to those sections.

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
section: 1 Count the independent draws before counting rows
text:
1 Count the independent draws before counting rows
Repeated specimens, cells nested within people, technical replicates, and samples grouped by collection site can be correlated. A sandwich formula using one row at a time only addresses dependence if those rows are the independent units required by its argument.
This page uses independently sampled clusters, typically people. Within a cluster, observations may be dependent. Let G be the number of clusters and M_i the number of records in cluster i. Large-cluster-count asymptotics send G to infinity, with moment and non-dominance conditions; merely collecting many records from a fixed small number of people does not invoke that theorem. Dependence across people, such as family or site effects, may require a larger cluster unit or another framework.
Think of one statistical observation as the whole record C_i=(M_i,Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{iM_i}). In the basic setup, these cluster records are i.i.d. The total row count N=\sum_iM_i may be much larger than G, but the LLN and CLT are applied to averages of functions of the G independent cluster records. Within-person correlation is preserved inside each function.
Read Units of analysis, replication, and study design first for target weighting. This page supplies the uncertainty calculation and its connection to influence functions. Cameron and Miller discuss practical cluster-inference limitations, including few clusters and multiple clustering dimensions.

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
text:
2 Two means, two cluster contributions
Let T_i=\sum_{j=1}^{M_i}Y_{ij} and \bar Y_i=T_i/M_i, with M_i\geq1. A randomly sampled person’s mean record outcome has target

\begin{aligned}
\mu_P&=E[\bar Y_i],\\
\widehat\mu_P&=G^{-1}\sum_i\bar Y_i.
\end{aligned}

A record-weighted target is instead a ratio over the same cluster population:

\begin{aligned}
\mu_R&=\frac{E[T_i]}{E[M_i]},\\
\widehat\mu_R&=\frac{\sum_i T_i}{\sum_i M_i}.
\end{aligned}

Their cluster-level influence functions are

\begin{aligned}
D_{P,i}&=\bar Y_i-\mu_P,\\
D_{R,i}&=\frac{T_i-\mu_R M_i}{E[M_i]}.
\end{aligned}

The weighting difference can be seen at the row level. In \widehat\mu_P, each row from person i has weight 1/(GM_i): the person’s total weight is 1/G. In \widehat\mu_R, every row has weight 1/N, so people with more records contribute more weight. The two targets can therefore differ when record count and outcomes are associated.

For a concrete population, suppose half the people have one record with outcome 0 and half have five records, each with outcome 3. Then E[\bar Y_i]=(0+3)/2=1.5, while E[T_i]=7.5 and E[M_i]=3, giving \mu_R=2.5. Both targets concern the same population of people; they answer different averaging questions.
To derive the contributions, first apply the cluster LLN to \bar Y_i, T_i, and M_i, under the required integrability conditions. The person estimator is an ordinary mean of person summaries. For the record estimator, write \bar M=G^{-1}\sum_iM_i and use the exact identity

\widehat\mu_R-\mu_R
=\frac{G^{-1}\sum_i(T_i-\mu_RM_i)}{\bar M}.

The numerator is an average of mean-zero cluster quantities. If E[M_i]<\infty, the LLN gives \bar M\xrightarrow{p}E[M_i]>0. With finite variance for T_i-\mu_RM_i, the CLT and Slutsky allow replacement of \bar M by E[M_i] at first order, giving D_{R,i} above. This is the ratio rule from Checkpoint SP-05, now applied to a person’s totals and counts.
Each contribution is one random cluster, even for the record-weighted target. Correcting an SE changes uncertainty about the selected target; it does not change the target weights.
Neither is intrinsically correct for every study. Irregular visits can be informative, and an observed-record mean is not automatically an outcome at a fixed scheduled time. Dropout and measurement timing may require identification assumptions before either target answers the intended longitudinal question.

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
text:
3 Estimate variance across cluster contributions
For an estimator with expansion

\widehat\theta-\theta_0
=G^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^G D_i+o_p(G^{-1/2}),

a cluster CLT gives \sqrt G(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,V_C) when E[D_i]=0 and 0<V_C=\operatorname{Var}(D_i)<\infty. The estimator’s first-order variance is V_C/G.
Estimate V_C by the variance of the estimated cluster contributions:

\begin{aligned}
s_D^2&=\frac1{G-1}\sum_{i=1}^G(\widehat D_i-\overline{\widehat D})^2,\\
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\theta)&=\frac{s_D}{\sqrt G}.
\end{aligned}

This is the same logic as the sample-mean SE, with the random object changed from a row to a cluster. Consistency of the estimated contribution variance and a negligible remainder justify studentization. When cluster sizes grow with the study, extra moment and non-dominance conditions are needed so one large cluster cannot supply most of the fluctuation. A normal interval remains an asymptotic statement about increasing independent cluster counts.


Code
ClusterMean <- function(y, id, target = c("person", "record")) {
  target <- match.arg(target)
  stopifnot(is.numeric(y), length(y) == length(id),
            all(is.finite(y)), !anyNA(id))
  totals <- rowsum(cbind(total = y, size = rep(1, length(y))), id, reorder = FALSE)
  G <- nrow(totals); stopifnot(G >= 2)
  T <- totals[, "total"]; M <- totals[, "size"]
  estimate <- if (target == "person") mean(T/M) else sum(T)/sum(M)
  D <- if (target == "person") T/M - estimate else (T - estimate*M)/mean(M)
  c(estimate = estimate, SE = sd(D)/sqrt(G), clusters = G, records = length(y))
}
y <- c(0, rep(3, 5)); id <- c("short", rep("long", 5))
rbind(person = ClusterMean(y, id, "person"), record = ClusterMean(y, id, "record"))


       estimate        SE clusters records
person      1.5 1.5000000        2       6
record      2.5 0.8333333        2       6


The two-cluster output demonstrates the formulas, not trustworthy normal inference from two people. For the person mean, the SE is simply the SE of the person summaries. For the record target, the varying denominator enters the influence function. Using the row SD divided by the square root of the row count ignores within-person covariance.

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
section: 4 Why extra records do not supply extra independent people
text:
4 Why extra records do not supply extra independent people
Take a balanced random-intercept model Y_{ij}=\mu+B_i+\epsilon_{ij}, with independent zero-mean components, \operatorname{Var}(B_i)=\tau^2, and \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{ij})=\sigma^2. There are m records per person. Write the grand mean’s error as

\widehat\mu-\mu
=\frac1G\sum_iB_i
+\frac1{Gm}\sum_i\sum_j\epsilon_{ij}.

The shared person component B_i appears once in every record from that person, so averaging their records does not remove it. Its variance contribution is \tau^2/G. The independent record noise contributes \sigma^2/(Gm). Adding them gives

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu)
&=\frac{\tau^2+\sigma^2/m}{G},\\
\text{design effect}
&=1+(m-1)\rho,\\
\rho&=\frac{\tau^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2}.
\end{aligned}

Two records from the same person have covariance \tau^2, so \rho is their intraclass correlation. Treating all Gm rows as independent would use variance (\tau^2+\sigma^2)/(Gm). Dividing the correct variance by that calculation gives the displayed design effect. Its square root is the corresponding SE inflation.
For G=100, m=4, \tau^2=0.8, and \sigma^2=0.2, the correct variance is 0.0085 and SE about 0.0922. The independent-row calculation gives variance 0.0025 and SE 0.05. The variance ratio is 3.4; the SE ratio is \sqrt{3.4}\approx1.84.
With G fixed, increasing m leaves a variance floor \tau^2/G when \tau^2>0. Additional records reduce measurement noise, but estimating the population mean consistently in this model requires more independent people. This design-effect formula belongs to the stated balanced model; other weighting schemes or cluster structures need their own variance calculation.


Code
m_grid <- 1:20; G <- 100
correct <- sqrt((0.8 + 0.2/m_grid)/G)
naive <- sqrt(1/(G*m_grid))
plot(m_grid, correct, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#2F80C8", ylim = c(0, 0.11),
     xlab = "Records per person", ylab = "SE of the grand mean")
lines(m_grid, naive, lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00", lty = 2)
abline(h = sqrt(0.8/G), lty = 3)
legend("right", c("Cluster model", "Independent-row calculation", "Person-variance floor"),
       col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00", "black"), lty = c(1, 2, 3), bty = "n")








Figure 1: Exact SEs in a balanced random-intercept model with 100 people, person variance 0.8, and record-noise variance 0.2. Additional records reduce noise but do not remove the person component.





Now check coverage under this explicitly Gaussian, balanced generator. There are 500 independent simulated datasets, each with 100 people and four records. Both estimators have the same point estimate; the SE calculation differs. Monte Carlo SE describes uncertainty in the estimated coverage, not uncertainty in one study’s mean.


Code
set.seed(2701)
coverage <- replicate(500, {
  id <- rep(seq_len(100), each = 4)
  y <- rep(rnorm(100, sd = sqrt(0.8)), each = 4) + rnorm(400, sd = sqrt(0.2))
  fit <- ClusterMean(y, id)
  se <- c(row = sd(y)/sqrt(length(y)), cluster = unname(fit['SE']))
  abs(mean(y)) <= qnorm(0.975) * se
})
coverage_rate <- rowMeans(coverage)
data.frame(method = names(coverage_rate), coverage = coverage_rate,
           MCSE = sqrt(coverage_rate * (1-coverage_rate)/ncol(coverage)))


         method coverage       MCSE
row         row    0.750 0.01936492
cluster cluster    0.948 0.00992935

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
section: 5 The cluster sandwich is the same linearization at a different unit
text:
5 The cluster sandwich is the same linearization at a different unit
Suppose \widehat\theta solves G^{-1}\sum_i S_i(\theta)=0, where S_i is the whole-cluster score. If A=E[\partial S_i(\theta_0)/\partial\theta^T] is nonsingular and consistency, a CLT, differentiability, and remainder control hold, then

\begin{aligned}
D_i&=-A^{-1}S_i(\theta_0),\\
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\theta)
&=G^{-1}\widehat A^{-1}
  \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(S_i)
  \widehat A^{-T}.
\end{aligned}

Here A^{-T}=(A^{-1})^\top. Evaluate the cluster scores and their derivatives at \widehat\theta to estimate the covariance and A, with consistency justified by the corresponding LLNs. For OLS, S_i=\sum_j X_{ij}(Y_{ij}-X_{ij}^\top\beta). Writing each row contribution as \psi_{ij} shows what changes in the variance calculation:

S_iS_i^\top=\sum_j\sum_\ell\psi_{ij}\psi_{i\ell}^\top.

The terms with j\ne\ell retain covariance between records from the same person. A rowwise sandwich uses only the same-record terms and therefore can miss the shared variation. The derivative and variance factors must both use the same whole-cluster normalization.
The point estimate still targets the selected regression equation. If each row enters equally, people with more rows contribute more to that equation. A cluster variance correction preserves those weights and the target they define. Omitted confounding and a rank-deficient design require separate arguments.

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
section: 6 Cross-fitting and resampling must preserve clusters
text:
6 Cross-fitting and resampling must preserve clusters
Place every record from a person in the same fold when people are independent. Train preprocessing, tuning, feature selection, and nuisance fits within training clusters. Otherwise the held-out record can still share a person’s outcome information with its training records. With fixed K folds, condition on training clusters and apply the same held-out empirical-term argument as in SP-12, now to whole-cluster contributions. Appropriate cluster-level L2/product-remainder and variance conditions remain necessary.
In the random-intercept example, a learner trained on one record can gain information about that person’s B_i. Another record from the same person is consequently not a fresh independent validation draw conditional on the training data. Holding out the whole person restores the intended separation under independent-person sampling. It does not by itself make the fitted nuisance functions accurate enough for inference.
For a cluster bootstrap, resample people with replacement and carry all their records together. Give repeated copies distinct bootstrap cluster IDs if refitting. Whether nuisance fits should be recomputed depends on the inferential procedure; a shortcut must be justified rather than assumed. A valid permutation scheme instead follows the assignment or exchangeability design, which may differ from a bootstrap. See the Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests page.
With few clusters, highly unequal leverage, one dominant person/site, cross-cluster dependence, or few clusters per treatment group, the normal approximation may fail. Small-sample corrections and specialized bootstrap/randomization methods require their own assumptions; no single cluster-count threshold validates them all. Report the cluster definition, count and size distribution, target weights, fold/resampling scheme, and variance method.

title: Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference
text:
7 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · CL-01 — Derive the cluster contribution for the chosen target
Task type: Derivation and interpretation.
Let T be a person’s outcome sum and M≥1 their record count. Derive influence functions for E[T/M] and E[T]/E[M] under independent person sampling. For equally common types (M,Y)=(1,0) and (5,3), calculate both targets and explain why replacing only the SE does not change the point target.
Ready to continue when: you can derive both cluster-level contributions and connect target weighting to the independent-unit variance.
Transfer: If visit frequency depends on disease severity, which target would a scheduled-time scientific question require?


Hint

Use the mean derivative for the first target and the ratio rule for the second.



Solution outline — open after trying

The contributions are T/M−μ_P and (T−μ_R M)/E[M]. The targets are 1.5 and 2.5. Their variance is calculated across independent people, but they average different quantities. A covariance correction changes uncertainty, not the equation defining the point estimate.





Checkpoint · CL-02 — Construct a valid fold and variance argument
Task type: Derivation and diagnosis.
In the balanced random-intercept model, derive Var(grand mean) and the design effect. Use G=100, m=4, τ²=0.8, σ²=0.2. Then explain why random row folds and a row bootstrap are inappropriate for an estimator trained on repeated person outcomes.
Ready to continue when: you can account for the shared component and preserve the independent unit in training, uncertainty, and resampling.
Transfer: If people are nested in a small number of sites with shared errors, is person-level independence still defensible?


Hint

Average the person intercept once per person and the record noise over all records.



Solution outline — open after trying

The variance is (0.8+0.2/4)/100=0.0085 and SE≈0.0922. The independent-row variance would be 1/400=0.0025; the design effect is 3.4. Row folds can put one person in both training and validation; row resampling breaks their joint record distribution. Use person folds and person contributions/resampling under independent-person sampling, with the requisite asymptotic and nuisance conditions.




Additional practice (optional)

Vary the cluster size distribution in the two-type example and compare person and record targets.
Repeat the coverage simulation with larger G and with larger m; separate Monte Carlo variation from the predicted SE behavior.
Write whole-cluster scores for a prespecified covariate-adjusted regression and identify its weighting and rank conditions.

title: Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests
text: Before reading: Large-sample reasoning for methods research and Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity.

title: Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests
text:
1 What a standard error describes
Continue with a completely observed feature mean \mu=E[Y], estimated by \hat\mu=\bar Y from n independent people. Let \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y). The population SD \sigma describes variation between people. The standard error \sigma/\sqrt n describes the spread of sample means across repeated studies of this size. Estimate it by s_Y/\sqrt n, where s_Y is the sample SD.
For example, a study of 100 people might have mean 2.5 and SD 2. Its estimated SE is 2/\sqrt{100}=0.2. The measurements vary on the scale of 2 units; the estimated mean’s sampling uncertainty is on the scale of 0.2 units. A confidence interval for the population mean will use the latter. Predicting a new person’s measurement requires a different calculation that includes individual variability.
The inferential starting point is the standardized error

\frac{\hat\mu-\mu}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\mu)}
\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).

The numerator measures estimation error in outcome units; dividing by the estimated SE expresses it in units of sampling uncertainty. This is called studentization. The CLT, variance consistency, and Slutsky’s theorem justify it for the i.i.d. finite-variance mean.
The same construction applies to a more general scalar target \theta_0 when \hat\theta-\theta_0=P_nD_0+o_p(n^{-1/2}), PD_0=0, and 0<PD_0^2<\infty, with a consistently estimated contribution variance. The sampling unit, target, centering, and remainder conditions remain part of the argument.

title: Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests
section: 2 A confidence interval is a random procedure
text:
2 A confidence interval is a random procedure
For a standard normal variable Z, \Pr(-1.96\le Z\le1.96)\approx0.95. Apply this reference to the standardized estimation error:

\Pr\!\left(
\frac{|\hat\mu-\mu|}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\mu)}
\le1.96\right)\approx0.95.

Rearranging the inequality for the unknown \mu produces the approximate 95% Wald interval:

\left[\hat\mu-1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}},\;
\hat\mu+1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}\right].

For the example above, its margin is 1.96(0.2)=0.392, giving [2.108,2.892]. The point estimate and both endpoints would change if we collected another sample. The population mean would remain fixed.
Coverage is the probability that this random interval procedure includes the fixed population mean. Under the approximation’s conditions, about 95% of intervals from repeated studies cover it. In 1,000 simulated studies, the number covering need not be exactly 950. Once a particular dataset is observed, its endpoints are fixed; the frequentist coverage statement does not assign a 95% posterior probability to that realized interval containing \mu.
For independent normal measurements, replacing 1.96 by the appropriate t_{n-1} quantile gives an exact t interval. For more general asymptotically linear estimators, normal calibration is a large-sample approximation whose accuracy must be assessed for the setting.
A narrow interval can be centered at the wrong population quantity. If the observed-outcome mean targets 0.8 while the eligible-population mean is 2, a correct SE around 0.8 does not turn it into inference about 2. As the SE shrinks around the wrong limit, coverage for the intended target can deteriorate. Identification and target alignment precede interval calibration.

title: Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests
section: 3 A test asks about a stated null
text:
3 A test asks about a stated null
Specify the null before calculating a p-value. For the mean, take the point null H_0:\mu=\mu_\star. Under that null, the standardized statistic has an approximately standard normal distribution:

Z_n=\frac{\hat\mu-\mu_\star}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}}.

Let z_{\mathrm{obs}} be the statistic’s observed value. A two-sided p-value is the probability, under the null reference law, of a statistic at least this far from zero in either direction:

\begin{aligned}
p&\approx\Pr(|Z|\ge|z_{\mathrm{obs}}|)\\
&=2\{1-\Phi(|z_{\mathrm{obs}}|)\},\\
Z&\sim N(0,1).
\end{aligned}

Here \Phi(t)=\Pr(Z\le t) is the standard normal CDF. In the numerical example, testing \mu_\star=2 gives z_{\mathrm{obs}}=(2.5-2)/0.2=2.5 and p\approx0.0124. The observed mean is 2.5 estimated SEs above the null value. About 1.24% of a standard normal reference distribution lies at least that far from zero in absolute value.
With valid calibration, rejecting when p<0.05 gives a rejection probability of approximately 0.05 when the null is true. This is a repeated-sampling Type I error statement. It is not the probability that this particular null is true or that this particular finding is a false positive. The estimated difference, 0.5 outcome units here, describes magnitude; its practical importance requires scientific context.
For the same two-sided Wald procedure, a 95% interval excludes a null value exactly when its p-value is below 0.05, apart from rounding. Both decisions compare the distance from the estimate to the null with 1.96\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}. The example’s interval excludes 2, agreeing with its p-value. This agreement requires matched procedures; an arbitrary interval and test need not agree.
A non-rejection can reflect limited precision even when a scientifically relevant difference exists. To assess which differences the data support, inspect the estimate and interval. Establishing equivalence requires a specified equivalence margin and a corresponding inferential procedure.

title: Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests
text:
4 See coverage across repeated samples
This synthetic experiment draws complete normal measurements with mean 2 and SD 1. It uses the approximate Wald rule with an estimated SE. It evaluates one prespecified mean, rather than a family of selected features.
Each replication draws a fresh group of 40 people, calculates its own mean and SE, and builds its own interval. The indicator covered records whether that interval contains the known \mu=2. In this matched example, noncoverage is also rejection of the true point null; it is not a power calculation under an alternative.


Code
set.seed(812)
n <- 40
replicates <- 500
means <- ses <- numeric(replicates)
for (b in seq_len(replicates)) {
  y <- rnorm(n, mean = 2, sd = 1)
  means[b] <- mean(y)
  ses[b] <- sd(y) / sqrt(n)
}
covered <- abs(means - 2) <= 1.96 * ses
c(coverage = mean(covered),
  rejection_under_null = mean(!covered),
  coverage_MCSE = sqrt(mean(covered) * (1 - mean(covered)) / replicates))


            coverage rejection_under_null        coverage_MCSE 
         0.950000000          0.050000000          0.009746794 


Code
shown <- seq_len(80)
plot(means[shown], shown, xlim = range(means[shown] + 1.96 * ses[shown],
     means[shown] - 1.96 * ses[shown]), xlab = "Feature mean", ylab = "Independent sample",
     pch = 16, col = ifelse(covered[shown], "#2F80C8", "#D55E00"))
segments(means[shown] - 1.96 * ses[shown], shown,
         means[shown] + 1.96 * ses[shown], shown,
         col = ifelse(covered[shown], "#2F80C8", "#D55E00"))
abline(v = 2, lty = 2)








Figure 1: Eighty intervals from a synthetic repeated-sampling experiment. The vertical line is the known population mean. Intervals missing that target are highlighted. The simulation also reports coverage over all 500 samples.





Coverage in a finite simulation fluctuates. With 500 replications and coverage near 0.95, the Monte Carlo SE is about \sqrt{0.95(0.05)/500}\approx0.01, or one percentage point. More simulated datasets improve the precision of this evaluation; increasing the number of people in each dataset changes the inferential problem itself. The plot shows 80 intervals for readability, while the numerical summary uses all 500.
One interval containing the truth is not evidence that a procedure has 95% coverage, and one miss is not evidence that it fails. Repeated-sampling evaluation studies the procedure. Its assumptions and asymptotic argument explain when we expect that evaluation to transfer beyond this generator.

title: Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests
section: 5 Individual uncertainty and a family of claims
text:
5 Individual uncertainty and a family of claims
A pointwise interval concerns one prespecified target. Searching many genes, selecting the smallest p-values, and reporting those intervals is a different procedure. A collection of pointwise 95% intervals is not automatically a simultaneous confidence statement or a false-discovery guarantee. Multiple testing when the tests are not independent handles the family-level question after the individual inferential argument has been established.

title: Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests
text:
6 Exercises
The checkpoint is a completion target. Additional practice is optional.


Checkpoint · INF-01 — Interpret a standard error, interval, and test
Task type: Calculation and interpretation.
For 100 independent people, a prespecified feature has sample mean 2.4 and sample SD 2. Calculate the mean’s SE, an approximate 95% Wald interval, and the two-sided Wald p-value for a population mean of 2. Explain the coverage claim, what the p-value does not mean, and why these calculations would not repair a mismatch between the scientific target and the estimator’s limit.
Ready to continue when: you can connect a sampling approximation to an interval and test without confusing measurement variability, coverage, null probability, and target alignment.
Transfer: Would the same SE apply if the 100 rows were five visits from each of 20 people?


Hint

The SD of the observations is 2. Divide by the square root of the independent sample size to estimate the mean’s SE.



Solution outline — open after trying

The SE is 0.2; the Wald interval is approximately [2.008, 2.792]. The null statistic is 2, giving p approximately 0.0455. The matched interval excludes 2. Under the procedure’s conditions, its coverage concerns repeated samples of intervals around a fixed target. The p-value is a null-tail probability, not a posterior null probability. Neither calculation establishes identification or centers an estimator at a different scientific quantity. Repeated rows need a variance calculation based on the independent people and their within-person dependence.




Additional practice (optional)

Compare the Wald and exact t procedures in the normal simulation.
Simulate a biased estimator whose SE shrinks with n and inspect coverage for the intended target.
Explain which additional question arises when 15,000 features are examined.

title: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference
text:
You may recognize projections and derivatives before you recognize an estimand, or recognize regression and confidence intervals before you recognize a Hilbert space. Both are useful starting points. This reference connects the language; read the substantive pages first when the terminology is new. It is not a gate requiring all later theory before beginning the guide.
The same concepts can be familiar in one language and unfamiliar in the other. The examples below connect the algebra, population quantities, and uncertainty arguments.
crumbs: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference

title: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference
text:
One example connects the languages
Suppose Y_1,\ldots,Y_n are independent observations from the same population, E[Y]=\mu, and 0<\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2<\infty.
The estimand is \mu: a number describing the population. The estimator is \bar Y: a function of a random sample. The estimate is its numerical value for the sample you collected. Repeating the sampling would usually change the estimate while leaving the population target fixed.
The estimating equation P_n(Y-a)=0, where a is a candidate mean and P_n means a sample average, has solution \hat\mu=\bar Y. Evaluating its error around the population mean gives the exact identity

\hat\mu-\mu=P_n(Y-\mu).

The centered contribution Y-\mu has expectation zero and variance \sigma^2. It will also be the influence function for the population mean in the unrestricted model. For now, follow the three statistical steps supplied by this identity.
First, the LLN makes the average contribution approach zero in probability, so \hat\mu is consistent for \mu. Second, the CLT gives a distribution for its fluctuations:

\sqrt n(\hat\mu-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2).

The limiting variance \sigma^2 belongs to the scaled error. The estimator itself has variance \sigma^2/n and SE \sigma/\sqrt n. Thus observation variability and mean-estimation uncertainty use the same population variance but different scales.
Third, \sigma^2 is unknown, so we estimate the SE by s_Y/\sqrt n. Variance consistency and Slutsky justify the standardized error

\frac{\hat\mu-\mu}{s_Y/\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).

A first-order algebraic identity, a population-limit argument, and a feasible uncertainty calculation are connected pieces. Each contributes something the others do not establish alone. Large-sample reasoning for methods research walks through the theorem statements and substitutions; Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests translates the standardized limit into a confidence procedure. Clustered observations, infinite variance, or a different target require rechecking the argument.
Transfer question: if your target is \sqrt\mu for positive Y, how does the influence contribution change? Work through Checkpoint SP-01.
crumbs: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference

text:

title: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference
text:
Functions as vectors
For square-integrable functions, \langle f,g\rangle=E[fg] and \|f\|_2=\sqrt{E[f^2]}. Expected products play the role of dot products. “Square-integrable” means the expected square is finite, so this length is defined.
For the centered measurement f=Y-\mu, the squared length is E[(Y-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2. Its inner product with the constant function 1 is zero because E[Y-\mu]=0. This is the geometric statement that the residual after subtracting the population mean is orthogonal to constants.
The same point follows from an optimization calculation. For a fixed candidate constant c,

E[(Y-c)^2]=\sigma^2+(\mu-c)^2.

Expand Y-c=(Y-\mu)+(\mu-c); the cross term vanishes after taking expectation. The best constant squared-error prediction is therefore \mu. Replacing population expectations by sample averages makes the best constant the sample mean. Conditional expectation and L2 geometry extends this idea from constants to functions of covariates.
crumbs: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference

title: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference
section: Derivatives with respect to a distribution
text:
Derivatives with respect to a distribution
A target can change when the data-generating distribution changes. For the mean, mix the population law P with a small mass \varepsilon at a value y. The new law P_\varepsilon=(1-\varepsilon)P+\varepsilon\delta_y has mean

\mu(P_\varepsilon)=(1-\varepsilon)\mu+\varepsilon y.

Its derivative at zero is y-\mu: the same centered contribution that appears in the sample-mean expansion. This connects a mathematical sensitivity calculation to the statistical variability of an estimator. One calculation changes a population distribution; the other studies a random sample from a fixed population. Establishing that they agree for a general target takes additional work.
Statistical models, targets, and paths explains which paths stay inside a specified model and introduces their scores. Influence functions develops the derivative-to-estimator connection with its assumptions. These concrete examples precede general representation-theorem language.
crumbs: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference

title: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference
text:
Read a large-sample statement

X_n\to_p x means that the probability of a fixed-size departure from x tends to zero. It does not say X_n=x in a finite sample.
X_n\to_d X describes convergence of distributions; it is the kind of approximation used in a CLT.
X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}x means convergence along almost every sample path. It is stronger than convergence in probability; our inference arguments use the weaker probability limits. The detailed comparison is in Large-sample reasoning for methods research.
\|\hat f-f\|_2\to_p0 describes consistency of an estimated function in population root-mean-square error, holding the fitted function fixed when taking the norm. It is not the same as a small training error.
X_n=O_p(a_n) means X_n/a_n is bounded in probability. X_n=o_p(a_n) means that ratio tends to zero in probability. Thus O_p(1) does not imply convergence to zero.

A typical inference argument establishes

\begin{aligned}
\hat\theta-\theta_0&=(P_n-P)\phi_0+R_n,\\
R_n&=o_p(n^{-1/2}),
\end{aligned}

where P\phi_0=0 and 0<P\phi_0^2<\infty. Scaling by \sqrt n makes the remainder o_p(1); a CLT handles the first term, and Slutsky’s theorem allows a consistent estimated variance in the final standardized statistic.
The rate notation locates an error relative to the scale of the inference. A term n^{-1/2} becomes 1 after root-n scaling and can affect the limit. A term n^{-1} becomes n^{-1/2} and disappears. In a proof, o_p(n^{-1/2}) makes that latter comparison for a random remainder. The probability definitions and product rules are developed in Large-sample reasoning for methods research.
You must show why the remainder is negligible. When \phi is learned from the same observations, treating it as a fixed function is generally unjustified. Cross-fitting helps separate estimation and evaluation, while population bias can remain. The From an influence function to an estimator page derives the decomposition and proves the fold-wise conditional bound (SP-12) before completing inference for the missing-outcome mean (SP-13).
Finite moments and permitted interchanges of derivatives and integrals are assumptions to verify. For bounded-score paths and elementary integrable targets, the calculations can often be checked directly. More general arguments need an appropriate domination or differentiability result.

title: A bridge between mathematics and statistical inference
section: Decide whether you are ready to continue
text:
Decide whether you are ready to continue
A checkpoint is a completion exercise for its page. Work through it with your notes, then explain the assumptions and reasoning in your own words. After checking the solution outline, return to the transfer question without copying the solution. You are ready to continue when you can do the task, interpret the result, and recognize an important boundary of the argument.
Additional practice is optional. Choose it for further examples and computation. Research extensions are optional deeper investigations. A checkpoint in an optional application branch is relevant when you choose that branch; it is not a prerequisite for every reader.
Use Completion checkpoints as a reference for locating tasks. In this guide, LS-01–LS-04 check the probability, notation, and uncertainty foundations in Large-sample reasoning for methods research. The next core endpoints are the complete smooth-root argument in Checkpoint SP-01 and the uncertainty interpretation in Checkpoint INF-01. The cluster and resampling pages have their own completion tasks when those extensions are relevant to your work.
Two further transfer routes are Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference, which changes the independent unit in the expansion, and An end-to-end residual-network analysis, which derives and tests a covariance contrast.

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text: Before reading: From a research question to an identified estimand, the independent unit, and elementary conditional means. For discrete Z, the law of total expectation simply averages the stratum means using population stratum probabilities; the geometric projection theory is introduced later.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
section: 1 A missing outcome is an observation process
text:
1 A missing outcome is an observation process
Let Y be one outcome or feature measurement on a specified scale, Z covariates available for every eligible unit, and R an indicator that Y is observed. The observed record is often written W=(Z,R,RY). The indicator is essential: RY=0 when R=0 encodes an unrecorded outcome, not evidence that the outcome equals zero. In R, keep unobserved outcomes as NA and form contributions only for observed rows.
The target here is \mu=E[Y] in the full eligible population. The mean among complete cases is E[Y\mid R=1], a different target. Whether the latter answers the scientific question is not determined by how few values are missing.
Missing outcomes, missing covariates, assay non-detection, and selection of whole people create different observed-data problems. A method developed for one pattern should not be transferred solely because both datasets contain NA.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text:
2 A simple selection calculation
Suppose half the eligible people have Z=0 and half Z=1. The outcome means are 0 and 4. Observation probabilities are 0.8 and 0.2. Selection on Z changes the mix of complete cases even if observation is independent of the outcome within each stratum.


Code
pz <- c(0.5, 0.5); pi_z <- c(0.8, 0.2); m <- c(0, 4)
pz_observed <- pz * pi_z / sum(pz * pi_z)
c(full_mean = sum(pz * m), complete_case_mean = sum(pz_observed * m))


         full_mean complete_case_mean 
               2.0                0.8 


The full mean is 2 and the complete-case mean is 0.8. No within-stratum outcome-dependent missingness was needed to create the discrepancy.

This reuses the example from What is your estimator actually estimating?. That page establishes the naive procedure’s limit. Here the next question is what lets us learn the full mean from incomplete observations.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text:
3 Identification under missing at random
Assume E[|Y|]<\infty, R\perp Y\mid Z (missing at random for this outcome), and \pi(Z)=P(R=1\mid Z)>0 almost surely over the target population. Also assume Z is recorded for that population. Then

\begin{aligned}
m(Z)&=E[Y\mid Z,R=1]\\
&=E[Y\mid Z],\\
\mu&=E[m(Z)]\\
&=E\left[\frac{RY}{\pi(Z)}\right].
\end{aligned}

The first equality is the identifying restriction. The outer expectation must use the target covariate distribution, not only the complete cases. Positive observation probability supplies outcome information in each needed stratum. For simple variance and remainder arguments, stronger conditions such as \pi\ge c>0 and suitable moments are often imposed; mere positivity for identification is weaker.
Work through the weighted identity by conditioning on Z:

\begin{aligned}
E\left[\frac{RY}{\pi(Z)}\,\middle|\,Z\right]&=\frac{P(R=1\mid Z)}{\pi(Z)}E[Y\mid Z,R=1]\\
&=m(Z).
\end{aligned}

The denominator cancels the chance of observing that stratum’s outcome. Averaging m(Z) over all eligible people’s covariates then gives the full mean. For this mean target, equality of the relevant conditional means is sufficient; the usual MAR assumption equates the full conditional outcome distributions and is stronger. It is still an assumption about outcomes we do not observe.
Small positive observation probability and zero probability cause different problems. If \pi(z)=0.01, the stratum is represented in the population observed-data law, but a finite study may contain very few outcomes and unstable large weights. If \pi(z)=0 for a positive-mass target stratum, unrestricted identification fails. Truncating weights can trade bias against variation, but cannot create outcomes in that absent stratum. An empty finite-sample cell also does not by itself prove a population structural zero.
Neither MAR nor an unobserved outcome distribution can generally be verified from the observed data alone. Compare mechanisms scientifically, inspect patterns, and assess sensitivity. A model that predicts R well does not prove MAR.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text:
4 A self-contained weighted example
The next example uses known observation probabilities because the simulation supplies them. It should move the weighted mean toward 2, while the complete-case mean remains near 0.8. In a real study the observation probabilities often have to be estimated and their errors accounted for.


Code
set.seed(41)
n <- 2000
z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5); prob <- 0.8 - 0.6 * z
full_y <- 4 * z + rnorm(n)
r <- rbinom(n, 1, prob)
y <- ifelse(r == 1, full_y, NA_real_)
contribution <- numeric(n)
contribution[r == 1] <- y[r == 1] / prob[r == 1]
weight <- numeric(n)
weight[r == 1] <- 1 / prob[r == 1]
c(complete_case = mean(y[r == 1]),
  known_weight_mean = mean(contribution),
  normalized_weight_mean = sum(contribution) / sum(weight), truth = 2)


         complete_case      known_weight_mean normalized_weight_mean 
             0.7912569              1.9026191              1.9678026 
                 truth 
             2.0000000 


The Z=0 outcomes receive weight 1/0.8=1.25; the less frequently observed Z=1 outcomes receive weight 1/0.2=5. The weights restore the target’s representation in expectation. The contribution average divides by all n eligible people, including those with an unrecorded outcome.
Dividing that weighted sum by the observed count would instead approach \mu/P(R=1)=4 here. It is not the same normalization. The normalized weighted ratio divides by the sum of the observation weights; that denominator divided by n approaches E[R/\pi(Z)]=1, so the ratio also consistently targets \mu. It need not equal the contribution average in a finite sample and has its own variance calculation. Identification supplies the population identity; it does not make every sample implementation equivalent.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text:
5 Non-detection is not automatically MAR
If a feature is observed only when its concentration exceeds a detection limit, R depends on the missing Y even after conditioning on routinely measured covariates. MAR is then generally unsupported. A recorded zero may mean a real zero, an unobserved value below a threshold, or a processing convention; inspect the assay record.
A censoring or measurement model can exploit a known limit under additional assumptions. Multiple imputation also requires a model and appropriate uncertainty propagation; generating several completed tables does not by itself resolve nonidentification. A deterministic fill value is a scientific/modeling choice, not the observed truth.
When an outcome is known to lie in [L,U], a simple assumption-light bound is

\begin{aligned}
E[Y]&\ge E[RY]+L P(R=0),\\
E[Y]&\le E[RY]+U P(R=0).
\end{aligned}

Here RY is the observed contribution with zero assigned only to that algebraic contribution when missing. The bounds do not assert that the missing outcomes are zero. Better measurement information can tighten them; an observed-data point estimate outside its identifying assumptions should not be presented as more certain than the information supports.
When a population stratum has no observed outcomes, keep its missing mean explicit. With eligible weights one half each, mean zero at Z=0, and no observed outcomes at Z=1, the latter stratum could have mean 4 or 8. Both full populations generate the same observed record, but their full means are 2 and 4. We know the stratum’s weight because Z is recorded for everyone; its outcome mean remains unknown.
If the assay establishes that every missing value lies in [L,d], with d<U, replace U by d in the upper bound. This uses actual measurement information. It is unavailable for records missing for unrelated technical or selection reasons. These are population identification bounds; estimating their endpoints adds sampling uncertainty, as developed in Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
section: 6 Selection and covariate missingness need separate targets
text:
6 Selection and covariate missingness need separate targets
Let S indicate enrollment or inclusion in the dataset, and reserve R for outcome observation within it. Correcting missing outcomes among S=1 people does not by itself generalize to S=0 people. If only included people have Z recorded, the full eligible covariate distribution may itself be unknown. Generalizing to that population can require external information, sampling weights, or selection assumptions. MAR for outcomes among included people does not solve that separate problem.
Missing covariates change which nuisance functions can be evaluated. Either define an observed-data pattern-specific analysis with a justified target, or supply assumptions and methods for the joint missing-data process. Dropping every row with any missing feature can dramatically change the population and the analysis family in high-dimensional omics.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text:
7 Connect identification to construction
The From an influence function to an estimator page continues the same full-population mean question with a richer continuous covariate example. It combines regression and observation models, derives the influence function, and states the stronger conditions needed for normal inference. “Either model correct” is a consistency property for that construction, not a substitute for MAR and positivity.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text:
8 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · MIS-01 — Identify the target under an observation process
Task type: Derivation and diagnosis.
The two-stratum example has eligible-population mean 2 and complete-case mean 0.8, as calculated in What is your estimator actually estimating?. Derive why E[RY/\pi(Z)]=2 under the stated MAR and positivity assumptions, and explain how the inverse probabilities restore the eligible-population weights. Then set the observation probability at Z=1 to zero. Show why two different missing-stratum means give the same observed distribution but different population means. Explain what happens if missing outcomes are silently filled with zero and then treated as observed.
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish a complete-case target, an identified full-population target, and a genuinely unidentified component.
Transfer: Which extra information would let you tighten bounds for outcomes below a known detection limit?


Hint

Condition on Z to calculate E[RY/\pi(Z)\mid Z]. Separate the observation indicator from the outcome value, and identify the step that requires a positive observation probability.



Solution outline — open after trying

MAR gives E[RY\mid Z]=\pi(Z)E[Y\mid Z]. With \pi(Z)>0, division and the law of total expectation give E[RY/\pi(Z)]=E[Y]=2. Numerically, the stratum contributions are 0.5(0.8)(0)/0.8=0 and 0.5(0.2)(4)/0.2=2. Inverse weighting cancels the unequal observation probabilities rather than preserving the complete-case stratum mix.
If \pi(1)=0, that division is unavailable in the second stratum. Choosing its unobserved mean as 4 or 8 leaves the observed distribution unchanged but changes the full mean from 2 to 4. Filling missing outcomes with zero and treating them as observed targets E[RY] rather than E[Y]; in the original positive-probability example this is 0.5(0.2)(4)=0.4. It hides the missing component rather than identifying it.




Additional practice (optional)

Simulate an observation probability that also depends on the unobserved outcome and assess the MAR-weighted estimator.
Compute the bounds when 30% of outcomes are missing and all outcomes lie in [0,5]. State what observed quantity is still needed.
List separately the assumptions for selection into your cohort and missing outcomes within it.
crumbs: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target

title: Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target
text:
9 Reading

Kennedy, review of efficient functional estimation, includes the missing-outcome mean as an observed-data functional.
Rubin (1976), Inference and missing data, for foundational distinctions about missing-data mechanisms.

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
text: Before reading: The population and observation record in From a research question to an identified estimand, elementary means, variance, and basic regression.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
section: 1 Count the units that support the claim
text:
1 Count the units that support the claim
A study can contain thousands of features, hundreds of specimens, and only a few independently sampled people. Those counts answer different questions. More technical measurements can improve the precision of a person’s measurement without providing more independent evidence about variation between people.
A biological replicate is defined relative to the scientific comparison. A person may be the replicate for a patient–control question; a culture or independently randomized animal may be the replicate in another experiment. A specimen is collected material. An aliquot or assay run is a technical measurement. A cell is nested in a specimen and person unless the design supports another independence argument.
Write the sampling and treatment-assignment units separately. Randomization establishes a known assignment mechanism; independent sampling supports population generalization under the sampling model. Neither follows from having one row per measurement.
For example, a donor may supply two tissues, several assay runs, and thousands of cells. The cells describe within-donor variation; the independently sampled donors supply between-donor evidence. In a trial randomized by clinic, people can also share a clinic-level assignment and dependence. State the largest relevant shared unit instead of assuming that “person” is always sufficient. The target’s averaging unit, assignment unit, and independent sampling unit can differ, and the analysis must connect them.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
text:
2 Weighting visits changes the target
Suppose one person has one visit with mean outcome 0 and another has four visits with mean outcome 4. A pooled visit mean weights the second person four times as heavily. A mean of person means weights the people equally.


Code
d <- data.frame(person = c("p1", rep("p2", 4)), y = c(0, 4, 4, 4, 4))
person_mean <- tapply(d$y, d$person, mean)
answers <- c(visit_weighted = mean(d$y), person_weighted = mean(person_mean))
answers


 visit_weighted person_weighted 
            3.2             2.0 



The pooled calculation is (0+4+4+4+4)/5=3.2. The person calculation is (0+4)/2=2. Both use the same measurements, but answer different averaging questions. These two people illustrate weighting; they do not provide a reliable population SE by themselves.
For a population of independent person records, these correspond to E[\sum_tY_{it}]/E[M_i] and E[M_i^{-1}\sum_tY_{it}], respectively, when every person has at least one visit and the relevant expectations exist. They need not coincide if visit count M_i is related to outcomes. A balanced schedule removes this particular weighting difference, but not dependence within a person.
Write each person’s recorded-visit average as \bar Y_i. The difference between the population visit-weighted and person-weighted means is

\begin{aligned}
\mu_{\rm visit}&=\frac{E[M_i\bar Y_i]}{E[M_i]},\\
\mu_{\rm person}&=E[\bar Y_i],\\
\mu_{\rm visit}-\mu_{\rm person}
&=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(M_i,\bar Y_i)}{E[M_i]}.
\end{aligned}

This identifies the mechanism: people with more measurements receive more weight, and the summaries differ when measurement count co-varies with their recorded average. Even a person-weighted recorded-visit mean is not automatically a fixed-time trajectory if visits are triggered by disease activity. Equal person weights address weighting, not informative observation times.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
section: 3 Why pseudoreplication makes uncertainty too small
text:
3 Why pseudoreplication makes uncertainty too small
For a balanced model with J independent people, m measurements per person, marginal variance \sigma^2, and common within-person correlation \rho, the grand mean has variance

\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)=\frac{\sigma^2}{Jm}\{1+(m-1)\rho\}.

To derive it, one person’s sum has m variance terms and m(m-1) covariance terms. There are J independent such sums, and the grand mean divides their total by Jm:

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^mY_{it}\right)&=m\sigma^2+m(m-1)\rho\sigma^2,\\
\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)&=\frac{J\{m\sigma^2+m(m-1)\rho\sigma^2\}}{(Jm)^2}.
\end{aligned}

For positive \rho, treating rows as independent omits a factor greater than one. The often-used effective sample size Jm/\{1+(m-1)\rho\} follows from this particular balanced model; it is not a universal formula for longitudinal or single-cell data.


Code
set.seed(12)
J <- 30; m <- 4
person <- rep(seq_len(J), each = m)
y <- rnorm(J)[person] + rnorm(J * m)  # theoretical ICC = 1/2
c(naive_SE = sd(y) / sqrt(length(y)),
  person_level_SE = sd(tapply(y, person, mean)) / sqrt(J),
  theoretical_inflation = sqrt(1 + (m - 1) * 0.5))


             naive_SE       person_level_SE theoretical_inflation 
            0.1165274             0.1770482             1.5811388 


The sample ratio varies. The model calculation predicts an inflation factor of \sqrt{2.5} relative to independent measurement sampling. This is a statement about the grand mean; other contrasts and unbalanced designs require their own variance calculation.

3.1 What more measurements can and cannot buy
The simulation uses a random intercept: Y_{it}=\mu+U_i+\varepsilon_{it}, with independent person terms of variance \tau^2 and independent measurement errors of variance \sigma_e^2. Then

\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y)=\frac{\tau^2}{J}+\frac{\sigma_e^2}{Jm}.

More measurements reduce the second term. With J fixed, they do not remove the first, which reflects variation between sampled people. More independent people reduce both terms. This is why reducing assay noise and increasing biological replication are different design decisions.








Figure 1: Exact model SEs as measurements per person increase, holding the number of independent people at 30. Between-person and measurement-error variances are both one. Correct uncertainty approaches a between-person floor; treating every row as independent incorrectly predicts continued reduction toward zero. These are model calculations, not estimated SEs from a simulated dataset.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
section: 4 Match the design to the contrast
text:
4 Match the design to the contrast
For a paired before/after question, define D_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i0} and analyze the independent person-level differences. Its mean has variance \operatorname{Var}(D_i)/J, incorporating the within-person covariance. An unpaired analysis discards that structure.
Here positive within-person correlation can improve precision: \operatorname{Var}(D_i)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i1})+\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i0})-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{i1},Y_{i0}). Shared person-level variation cancels in the difference. Thus “dependence always inflates every SE” is the wrong lesson. The lesson is to derive uncertainty for the chosen contrast using the actual independent records.
For a subject-level treatment randomized to people, keep each person’s records together in a randomization test. For an observational group comparison, whole-person relabeling additionally needs a justified null exchangeability argument. Merely preserving clusters does not make the labels exchangeable.
For a within-person factor, the allowed relabeling depends on the assignment or symmetry assumptions within that person; an arbitrary shuffle of visit times can destroy a time trend. Use the Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests page to connect these distinctions to permutation tests.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
section: 5 Design and adjustment have different jobs
text:
5 Design and adjustment have different jobs
A design matrix describes the modeled mean; a covariance model or cluster-robust variance handles residual dependence. Including a person fixed effect can support within-person comparisons, but cannot separately estimate a group effect constant within person when the indicators are collinear. A mixed model can use between-person information under its assumptions; it does not create independent subjects.
If every patient is measured in one batch and every control in another, a mean model cannot separate the group and batch contributions without additional restrictions or data. Adding both variable names to a formula does not create the missing comparison. Conversely, a full-rank mean design does not establish independence of repeated specimens. Check what the design identifies and how sampling uncertainty is calculated as separate tasks.
Similarly, technical batch correction is not a substitute for modeling within-person sampling. The single-cell pseudoreplication study by Zimmerman and colleagues documents the practical importance of distinguishing cells from independent individuals. Model choice still depends on the target, design, and measurement distribution.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
section: 6 Resampling and prediction use the same unit decision
text:
6 Resampling and prediction use the same unit decision
If the goal is generalization to a new person, keep all visits or cells from that person in one validation fold. Otherwise the fitting procedure can see the person’s other measurements. Bootstrap independent person records, not arbitrary rows, when that is the sampling model. For a visit-specific target conditional on an existing person, a different validation question may be appropriate; name it explicitly.
Before collecting or analyzing data, record the population, assignment unit, sampling unit, nesting, pairing, timing, planned weights, and which contrasts are identifiable. Inspect whether group varies within each technical batch and whether follow-up counts differ by group. These checks connect replication to the estimand rather than to a universal preferred model.
For the corresponding contribution and SE calculations, continue to Dependent observations and cluster-aware inference.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design

title: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
text:
7 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · DES-02 — Choose a unit, weighting, and resampling design
Task type: Derivation and design.
A study enrolls 20 controls and 20 patients. Each control has two visits and each patient has six. The target is the equally person-weighted mean of each person’s recorded-visit average, contrasted between groups. Describe a matching estimator, variance/resampling unit, and fold allocation. In this fixed-count-per-group design, do pooled and person-summary group means differ? Which part of an independent-row analysis is still wrong, and what can change if visit counts vary within groups? Explain why whole-person label permutation is not automatically valid in this observational setting.
For the balanced random-intercept model, derive the grand-mean variance and its limit as measurements per person increase with the number of people fixed.
Ready to continue when: you can connect target weights and independent records to estimation, derive the grand-mean variance, and choose an uncertainty and validation unit.
Transfer: If follow-up is triggered by worsening disease within each group, does averaging recorded visits identify a fixed-time disease trajectory?


Hint

Start by forming one defined summary per person; then ask which labels were randomized or exchangeable.



Solution outline — open after trying

Average the recorded outcomes within each person, then compare the 20 independent summaries per group, with a variance model appropriate for their heterogeneity. Bootstrap whole people within the appropriate sampling strata and assign whole people to validation folds. A row-level mean weights records according to visit count; in this particular fixed-count-per-group design the within-group means coincide with averages of person means, but a row-level independent-error standard error is still wrong. With variable counts within groups the point-estimate weights can differ as well. The random-intercept variance is \tau^2/J+\sigma_e^2/(Jm) and approaches \tau^2/J as m increases with J fixed. Observational group labels and unequal follow-up structures need their own exchangeability justification; keeping a cluster intact is necessary for some schemes but not sufficient for validity.




Additional practice (optional)

Derive the balanced-cluster variance formula by summing variances and covariances.
Simulate paired measurements with increasing correlation and compare paired and unpaired interval widths.
Draw the nesting structure for a single-cell experiment with donors, tissues, technical runs, and cells.
crumbs: Units of analysis, replication, and study design
