title: A reproducible research project
text: Before reading: Basic R functions and file paths; no prior workflow system is required.

title: A reproducible research project
section: 1 A result should have an executable route back to its inputs
text:
1 A result should have an executable route back to its inputs
A reproducible project records what another researcher needs to regenerate a stated result: inputs, acquisition and inclusion rules, code, configuration, software environment, and a documented execution command. This makes an argument inspectable. It does not establish that its target is meaningful or its assumptions are true.
For a first project, use a small structure whose responsibilities are clear:
project/
  README.md             # question, inputs, environment, execution instructions
  data/raw/             # original inputs, or documented controlled acquisition
  data/metadata/        # manifests, identifiers, acquisition and decision logs
  R/                    # functions with explicit inputs and return values
  config/               # analysis settings and simulation scenarios
  results/              # derived tables, figures, and replicate-level records
  reports/              # Quarto sources connecting results to claims
  renv.lock             # R package environment, if using renv
Sensitive or restricted inputs need not be committed to a repository. Record how an authorized collaborator obtains the correct version, and provide synthetic data for exercising the pipeline where appropriate. Keep raw inputs unchanged; regenerate derived objects through code. Follow Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset for identifiers and transformation records.

title: A reproducible research project
section: 2 Separate a function from an analysis run
text:
2 Separate a function from an analysis run
A function should expose its statistical inputs. Avoid an estimator that silently reads a variable from an interactive workspace, changes its target according to a filename, or reuses a previously fitted model. An analysis run supplies the data and settings, calls functions, and saves labeled results.
A function is the statistical recipe; a run is a particular application of that recipe. For example, SummarizePeople(y, confidence) computes a mean interval from supplied values. GeneratePeople(config) creates synthetic inputs. The runner reads settings, calls those functions, and writes outputs. The estimator does not receive the generator’s true population mean.
The downloadable teaching project contains four files: R/analysis.R, config/config.csv, run.R, and README.md. It uses only standard R packages and invented people. The example below unpacks that actual archive into a temporary directory, reads its configuration, and computes the result. Students should keep an unpacked project in a persistent location when working through it.


Code
work_dir <- tempfile("teaching project-"); dir.create(work_dir)
unzip("../examples/research-project.zip", exdir = work_dir)
project_root <- normalizePath(file.path(work_dir, "research-project"))
source(file.path(project_root, "R", "analysis.R"))
config <- ReadConfig(file.path(project_root, "config", "config.csv"))
people <- GeneratePeople(config)
result <- SummarizePeople(people$outcome, config$confidence)
result


  n_people estimate        se confidence    lower    upper
1       80 2.021953 0.1162457       0.95 1.790572 2.253335


The configuration specifies 80 independent normal outcomes, population mean 2, seed 71, and confidence level 0.95. The interval is a normal-population t interval for the mean, in synthetic measurement units. Its assumptions come from this generator; running the code on dependent cells would require a different uncertainty argument.

2.1 Rebuild in a fresh R process
From the unpacked project directory, the documented entry point is:
Rscript --vanilla run.R . results/run-01
Rscript --vanilla run.R . results/run-02
The dot names the project root, and the final argument names a new output directory relative to it. Each command starts a separate R process. The runner finds its functions and configuration from the explicit root, so it can also be called from elsewhere using the appropriate script and root paths. It refuses an existing output directory, keeping the two attempts separate.
This page performs those fresh-process runs rather than merely repeating a function in its existing workspace:


Code
FreshRun <- function(root, output_relative) {
  command_output <- system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript"),
    args = c("--vanilla", shQuote(file.path(root, "run.R")),
             shQuote(root), shQuote(output_relative)),
    stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE)
  dir.create(file.path(root, "logs"), showWarnings = FALSE)
  writeLines(command_output,
    file.path(root, "logs", paste0(basename(output_relative), ".txt")))
  status <- attr(command_output, "status")
  if (!is.null(status) && status != 0L) stop(paste(command_output, collapse = "\n"))
  out <- file.path(root, output_relative)
  stopifnot(file.exists(file.path(out, "COMPLETE")))
  readRDS(file.path(out, "summary.rds"))
}
run_01 <- FreshRun(project_root, "results/run-01")
run_02 <- FreshRun(project_root, "results/run-02")
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(result, run_01, tolerance = 1e-12)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(run_01, run_02, tolerance = 1e-12)))
data.frame(run = c("Current process", "Fresh process 1", "Fresh process 2"),
           estimate = c(result$estimate, run_01$estimate, run_02$estimate),
           SE = c(result$se, run_01$se, run_02$se))


              run estimate        SE
1 Current process 2.021953 0.1162457
2 Fresh process 1 2.021953 0.1162457
3 Fresh process 2 2.021953 0.1162457


Agreement shows that these inputs and code reproduce the numeric result without relying on a fitted object left in the first process. It does not establish correctness of the statistical question or guarantee identical file bytes on every platform. State which outputs must agree and at what tolerance. Exact ID sets, row counts, and categorical decisions often deserve exact checks; floating-point estimates may need a justified numeric tolerance. “The conclusions looked similar” is too vague to serve as an output check.
 


2.2 Inspect what the run retained
Each completed run saves the synthetic people, summary table and R object, configuration used, input/code manifest, output checksums, R session details, and RNG setup. Its final COMPLETE file is written after the listed outputs. An interrupted directory without that marker is retained as an incomplete attempt, rather than mistaken for a successful analysis. The marker describes execution status, not statistical validity.



Code
input_manifest <- read.csv(file.path(project_root, "results", "run-01",
                                      "input-manifest.csv"))
knitr::kable(input_manifest, row.names = FALSE)





path
role
checksum




config/config.csv
configuration
e8784c6e9aeafd8d014d28ceb7386a17


R/analysis.R
functions
fa68c28933b1a691f6cbf27e9b48c61f


run.R
entry point
90a574b941d9a1fbba17f627cc9f9460






Read the manifest as a statement of dependencies. Changing config/config.csv changes the requested run even when the functions are identical. Changing R/analysis.R changes the procedure even when the settings are identical. The checksum identifies each saved file’s contents; the role column says why it matters. A real omics project additionally needs acquired data versions, annotation references, preprocessing, and exclusion rules. An analysis notebook’s filename alone does not identify those dependencies.

title: A reproducible research project
text:
3 Record the environment and randomness
A seed controls a random-number stream under a given setup; it does not identify the software, input data, or entire parallel execution schedule. Retain R and package versions, operating-system details when relevant, code revision, configuration, and seeds or per-replicate streams. Use stable replicate IDs when splitting simulation work across workers. Two jobs that each reset the same seed can accidentally generate duplicate replicates.
For projects using renv, its documented workflow includes initialization, recording package versions with a snapshot, and restoration from the lockfile. These are commands for a deliberately configured project, not commands automatically executed by this page:


Code
renv::init()
renv::snapshot()
# In a checkout that already contains the intended lockfile:
renv::restore()


A lockfile covers an important part of the R environment, not every external system dependency or input dataset. Document those separately. Check the restored project in a fresh environment before describing it as reproducible.
The base-R example uses --vanilla to skip startup files and saved workspaces, as described in R’s startup documentation. In a project using renv, however, the normal automatic activation is in .Rprofile, which that flag also skips. Activate the documented project environment explicitly, for example by sourcing renv/activate.R, or use the project’s documented startup route. A fresh session must still use the intended environment.
Keep randomness tied to the unit being reproduced. An analysis with learned nuisances may need fold assignments and tuning seeds; a simulation may need one recorded stream per replicate. Saving only the first seed can leave results dependent on method order or worker scheduling. The run record should let a collaborator recover the same dataset and fitting choices for a particular replicate, not merely obtain a similar overall rejection rate.

title: A reproducible research project
text:
4 Keep code changes reviewable
Use version control for code, configuration, report sources, and documentation. Make focused commits with messages explaining the analysis decision, and record the code revision used for a run. If results were generated with uncommitted changes, retain the corresponding changes as well; a commit identifier alone does not describe that state. Review a change together with its affected results and assumptions.
Keep credentials and restricted data outside the repository, with documented acquisition paths and appropriate ignore rules. Large derived outputs can be stored separately when they remain linked to the run manifest and can be regenerated. Collaborators should agree on which files are authoritative inputs and which are rebuildable outputs.
A protocol and a run manifest answer different questions. The protocol records the planned target, methods, exclusions, and comparisons, with reasons for amendments. A run manifest records the actual inputs, code, settings, and outputs of one attempt. Retain both: reproducing an exploratory revision does not make it prespecified. New outputs should receive a new run ID, rather than silently replacing the evidence for an earlier draft.

title: A reproducible research project
text:
5 Use caching deliberately
Quarto’s freeze feature can reuse prior computation during project renders; it makes repeated builds faster. A rendered page is therefore not evidence that its code was executed in that build. A data file or helper function may change without the report source itself changing.
Record a clean execution procedure that recomputes the analysis when inputs, settings, functions, or dependencies change. Check the run log and output timestamps or run identifiers. Treat cached/frozen results as outputs with provenance, and review Quarto’s execution and caching documentation when defining that procedure.
For example, exclusions.csv changes while the report source is untouched. A global project render using freeze: auto may reuse the old computation. Knitr caching is another layer: unchanged chunk text does not automatically detect every changed external input. For an executable R report, explicitly rendering the file bypasses project-level freeze, and --cache-refresh refreshes chunk caches:
quarto render reports/analysis.qmd --cache-refresh
Run the project’s analysis entry point first if the report reads previously saved results rather than fitting the model itself. Refreshing a report cache cannot regenerate a result file that no report chunk creates. Confirm that the displayed result belongs to the new input manifest and run ID; a recent HTML timestamp alone only establishes that a page was written.

title: A reproducible research project
text:
6 Decide what to retain
For a simple analysis, keep the result table, diagnostics, input manifest, configuration, session information, code revision, and report source. For a simulation, keep one record per attempted replicate and method, including failures and seeds. Avoid relying on a manually edited spreadsheet as the only record of a result.
A useful README answers: What scientific target is studied? What files or access permissions are required? Which environment is supported? What command runs the project? Which outputs should appear? What is intentionally excluded from a public release? A collaborator should not need your interactive command history to discover these answers.






NoteProcedure: audit a collaborator’s rerun




Start from the documented code revision and acquire the recorded input versions through the permitted route.
Establish the stated environment and a fresh analysis process, with project activation made explicit.
Execute the documented entry point into a new run directory, retaining its status and logs.
Check expected files, identifiers, dimensions, diagnostics, and numeric results against the stated comparison criteria.
Resolve any discrepancy by tracing changed inputs, settings, code, software, or randomness. Record the resolution and any remaining limitation.

Completion means: the declared result is recoverable through the documented route. Its scientific assumptions remain part of the research argument.

title: A reproducible research project
text:
7 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · REP-01 — Specify a complete rerun contract
Task type: Construction and diagnosis.
A report renders successfully on its author’s laptop but fails in a fresh R session because fit is absent. Its frozen output also predates a changed sample-exclusion file. Write a minimal project structure and rerun procedure that resolves both problems. Identify what a seed and a package lockfile each fail to record.
Use the downloadable teaching project to perform two fresh-process runs. State which inputs and outputs you compare, how you distinguish an incomplete run, and whether each comparison needs byte identity, exact records, or numeric agreement.
Ready to continue when: another reader can identify the inputs, configuration, environment, entry point, and expected outputs, and you can verify a rerun without your interactive workspace.
Transfer: How would you preserve reproducibility if raw data could only be accessed inside a controlled computing environment?


Hint

Follow the dependencies of fit and the exclusion decision all the way to the reported table.



Solution outline — open after trying

Create fit from explicit data and settings in a function called by the entry script or report. Record the exclusion file/version in an input manifest, regenerate the analysis after it changes, and rebuild the report with recomputation verified. Document acquisition, environment restoration, execution, and output checks. A seed does not specify inputs or package versions; a package lockfile does not specify biological inclusion rules, all system dependencies, or acquired data. Test the instructions in a fresh session.
For the teaching project, run the same configuration into two new directories, inspect their input manifests and completion markers, and compare the numeric summaries at the stated tolerance. A completion marker without matching inputs is insufficient. A renamed output directory need not make every recorded path identical; the comparison should concern the scientific output and the dependencies that produced it.




Additional practice (optional)

Apply the README questions to a small existing project and ask a collaborator to perform the rerun.
Split a toy simulation into two batches with distinct replicate IDs and verify that the combined record has no duplicate replicates.

title: A reproducible research project
text:
8 Reading

Wilson et al., Good enough practices in scientific computing.
Official renv introduction and Quarto project execution.

title: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset
text: Before reading: Read Understanding an omics dataset; the examples use base R.
crumbs: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset

title: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset
section: 1 An analysis matrix needs a history
text:
1 An analysis matrix needs a history
A numerical matrix alone does not tell you where measurements came from, which people they represent, or why some samples disappeared. Provenance connects an acquired object to its analysis version and makes those choices inspectable.
For each input, record its source and accession or institutional identifier, release/version, acquisition date, access conditions, file identity/checksum, assay and units, reference genome or feature-annotation version where relevant, and the code that reads it. Use actual identifiers from the source; a synthetic example should explicitly say its identifiers are invented.
For each derived object, record its parent inputs, transformation code and version, settings, inclusion/exclusion decisions, and output identity. Preserve the distinction between a person, specimen, aliquot, assay run, and matrix column. Their relations may be one-to-many. The Understanding an omics dataset page explains these objects.
Provenance has two parts. File identity tells us which objects were used. Data meaning tells us what their rows, columns, labels, and values represent, and why those objects answer the question. An unchanged file can have misinterpreted group labels. A correctly labeled assay can belong to an earlier preprocessing release. The research record needs both kinds of information.
crumbs: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset

title: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset
section: 2 Align by identifiers and check cardinality
text:
2 Align by identifiers and check cardinality
The following toy data have invented specimen and person identifiers, and arbitrary synthetic measurement units. Matrix columns are specimens; two specimens belong to the same person. The contract is one metadata record per matrix column, keyed by specimen. Person ID is a grouping variable, not a unique specimen key.


Code
assay <- matrix(c(2, 4, 3, 5, 8, 9), nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(c("feature_A", "feature_B"), c("S1", "S2", "S3")))
metadata <- data.frame(specimen = c("S3", "S1", "S2"),
                       person = c("P2", "P1", "P1"),
                       usable = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE),
                       reason = c("retained", "retained", "prespecified assay QC"))
AlignSpecimens <- function(assay, metadata) {
  stopifnot(is.matrix(assay), is.numeric(assay),
            all(c("specimen", "person", "usable", "reason") %in% names(metadata)),
            !is.null(colnames(assay)), !anyNA(colnames(assay)),
            all(nzchar(trimws(colnames(assay)))), !anyDuplicated(colnames(assay)),
            !anyNA(metadata$specimen), !anyDuplicated(metadata$specimen),
            all(nzchar(trimws(metadata$specimen))),
            !anyNA(metadata$person), all(nzchar(trimws(metadata$person))),
            is.logical(metadata$usable), !anyNA(metadata$usable),
            setequal(colnames(assay), metadata$specimen))
  aligned <- metadata[match(colnames(assay), metadata$specimen), , drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(assay), aligned$specimen))
  aligned
}
aligned <- AlignSpecimens(assay, metadata)
aligned


  specimen person usable                reason
2       S1     P1   TRUE              retained
3       S2     P1  FALSE prespecified assay QC
1       S3     P2   TRUE              retained


Code
# An intentional error is caught before a join can multiply observations.
bad_metadata <- rbind(metadata, metadata[1, ])
tryCatch(AlignSpecimens(assay, bad_metadata),
         error = function(e) "Rejected: duplicate specimen key")


[1] "Rejected: duplicate specimen key"


setequal deliberately requires the same specimen set in this teaching contract. If unmatched records are expected, use an explicit policy and output both unmatched sets before continuing. An inner join that silently drops unmatched records conceals an exclusion decision. A duplicated feature-to-symbol map can similarly multiply rows: retain stable feature identifiers and define how one-to-many annotations will be handled rather than silently summing or deduplicating them.

2.1 Work through the matching operation
The assay order is S1, S2, S3; the metadata order is S3, S1, S2. Matching produces indices 2, 3, 1 and reorders the metadata to the assay. Comparing only row counts would miss a positional assignment error:


Code
data.frame(matrix_specimen = colnames(assay),
  positional_metadata_key = metadata$specimen,
  positional_person = metadata$person, matched_person = aligned$person)


  matrix_specimen positional_metadata_key positional_person matched_person
1              S1                      S3                P2             P1
2              S2                      S1                P1             P1
3              S3                      S2                P1             P2


There are no missing values in the wrong positional assignment. The mistake is that S1 is attributed to P2 and S3 to P1. A numerical fit could succeed while relating measurements to the wrong people. The final identical() assertion checks ordering after key matching.


2.2 State the relationship before joining
For a key k with a_k rows in one table and b_k in the other, an ordinary match-based join can produce a_kb_k rows. Duplicated specimen annotations can therefore duplicate measurements. Joining two visit tables by person alone can pair every visit with every other visit for that person. Those extra rows are not additional independent observations.
Use specimen IDs for specimen metadata, run IDs for assay runs, or a person–visit key only when the protocol guarantees one record per combination. Multiple aliquots at a visit need another identifier. Represent valid one-to-many relationships explicitly, with an aggregation or analysis rule; keeping the first match silently chooses a record.
For a planned assay intersection, report setdiff(first_keys, second_keys) and setdiff(second_keys, first_keys) before applying the inclusion rule. If the assays use different identifiers, first establish a documented crosswalk at the intended person, visit, or specimen level. Equal-looking strings alone do not establish that relationship.

title: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset
text:
3 Retain exclusions and denominators


Code
decision_log <- aligned[c("specimen", "person", "usable", "reason")]
keep <- aligned$usable
analysis_assay <- assay[, keep, drop = FALSE]
analysis_metadata <- aligned[keep, , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(colnames(analysis_assay), analysis_metadata$specimen))
attrition <- data.frame(
  stage = c("Acquired", "Retained after QC"),
  specimens = c(ncol(assay), ncol(analysis_assay)),
  people = c(length(unique(aligned$person)),
             length(unique(analysis_metadata$person))))
attrition


              stage specimens people
1          Acquired         3      2
2 Retained after QC         2      2


Code
decision_log


  specimen person usable                reason
2       S1     P1   TRUE              retained
3       S2     P1  FALSE prespecified assay QC
1       S3     P2   TRUE              retained


Removing a specimen does not always remove a person; losing every specimen from a person does. Here specimens fall from three to two while people remain two. Keep both denominators. In a real study, define whether a person must have both visits, a particular assay, or complete covariates to enter the final analysis. A complete-case multi-omics intersection can select a different population from any individual assay cohort.
QC exclusions can also depend on biology. Explain whether the estimand concerns all eligible people or the retained subset, and what assumptions would connect the two. An audit trail makes selection visible; it does not make selection ignorable. See Missingness, selection, and the observed-data target.
Retain separate reason flags if a specimen fails several criteria. If a table assigns one primary reason so that removed counts add up, state the assignment rule. Otherwise overlapping reasons can be double-counted. Record exclusions at each actual stage, rather than reconstructing the flow from the retained sample alone.
 

3.1 Counts and weighting answer different questions
Before exclusions, averaging matrix columns weights people by their specimen counts. P1 contributes two specimens and P2 one. For feature A:


Code
c(specimen_average = mean(assay["feature_A", ]),
  person_average = mean(tapply(assay["feature_A", ], aligned$person, mean)),
  retained_specimen_average = mean(analysis_assay["feature_A", ]))


         specimen_average            person_average retained_specimen_average 
                 4.333333                  5.250000                  5.000000 


The acquired specimen average is 13/3\approx4.33. Averaging within each person first gives (2.5+8)/2=5.25. After QC the retained values are 2 and 8, giving 5. These summaries answer different questions. Define whether the analysis averages people, visits, specimens, or scheduled-time contrasts. QC can change both who remains and the weights among people who remain. An unchanged person count does not imply an unchanged target or weighting.

title: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset
section: 4 Use file checks alongside semantic checks
text:
4 Use file checks alongside semantic checks
A checksum helps determine whether a stored file changed. It does not tell you that the matrix uses the right units, that labels are correct, or that the scientific target is identified. The example uses tools::md5sum only for local change detection, not as a security guarantee.


Code
record_dir <- tempfile("provenance-"); dir.create(record_dir)
input_files <- file.path(record_dir, c("synthetic-assay.csv", "synthetic-metadata.csv"))
write.csv(assay, input_files[1])
write.csv(metadata, input_files[2], row.names = FALSE)
manifest <- data.frame(file = basename(input_files),
  role = c("acquired assay", "specimen metadata"),
  source = "synthetic teaching example", version = "1",
  checksum = unname(tools::md5sum(input_files)))
manifest


                    file              role                     source version
1    synthetic-assay.csv    acquired assay synthetic teaching example       1
2 synthetic-metadata.csv specimen metadata synthetic teaching example       1
                          checksum
1 0404810db3b07a81d095a3b5863a1b22
2 080659f5cb9e674dda9ba75467718dc7


Code
stopifnot(identical(unname(tools::md5sum(input_files)), manifest$checksum))


Semantic checks should encode the intended data contract: unique keys at the stated unit; expected feature and specimen sets; allowed missingness; measurement scales; valid visit order; group/batch cross-tabulations; and appropriate ranges. Choose checks that would expose plausible mistakes. A count matrix might require nonnegative integer entries, while normalized log expression generally should not be tested as counts.
For a derived assay, also record the parent objects, code revision, filtering settings, and output identity. Its checksum cannot explain why S2 disappeared; the decision log can. A decision log without exact parent versions cannot establish which values were filtered. Preserve acquired versions when releases change and generate a new derived version rather than relabeling the old one.

title: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset
section: 5 Deliver an analysis-ready object with context
text:
5 Deliver an analysis-ready object with context
Retain the assay, aligned metadata, feature annotations, processing settings, decision log, and manifest together or with explicit cross-references. State the independent sampling unit and any clustering identifiers. Document which objects contain outcomes only on observed units and which covariates are available for the whole eligible population.
A useful handoff lets the next analyst answer: Which population do these columns represent? Which scale is measured? How did this feature label arise? Why is an eligible participant absent? Which code produced this version? If these cannot be answered, the object is numerically convenient but not yet ready for a defensible analysis.
The teaching object can keep its aligned components together:


Code
analysis_object <- list(
  assay = analysis_assay, specimens = analysis_metadata,
  decisions = decision_log, input_manifest = manifest,
  description = list(scale = "arbitrary synthetic measurement units",
    matrix_column = "specimen", independent_unit = "person",
    inclusion = "usable specimens; both original people retain a specimen"))
stopifnot(identical(colnames(analysis_object$assay),
                    analysis_object$specimens$specimen))
names(analysis_object)


[1] "assay"          "specimens"      "decisions"      "input_manifest"
[5] "description"   


That packaging helps maintain alignment, but does not choose the weighting rule. Record that rule with the analysis configuration. A matrix-aware container such as SummarizedExperiment coordinates subsetting of assays and metadata; it still depends on correctly constructed identifiers and annotations at entry.

title: Data provenance and an analysis-ready dataset
text:
6 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · PROV-01 — Audit a join and its population consequences
Task type: Data checking and interpretation.
A study acquires two visits per person. A metadata join duplicates some specimens, then an inner join to a second assay drops every specimen from 12 people. Specify the keys and cardinality checks, the two unmatched-record reports, an attrition table, and the decisions needed before calling the result analysis-ready. Explain whether checksums alone would reveal either problem.
Using the three-specimen example, also calculate the specimen-weighted average and the equally weighted person average. Explain why retaining the same number of people after QC does not by itself preserve the weights or target.
Ready to continue when: you can reconstruct the joins and exclusions and distinguish the retained-data target from the original eligible-population target.
Transfer: How would a many-to-one feature-annotation mapping alter your checks compared with a one-to-one specimen join?


Hint

Count records at specimen and person levels before and after each transformation.



Solution outline — open after trying

Require unique specimen keys where a one-to-one specimen join is intended; retain person/visit links separately. Report records present only in the first and only in the second assay. Stop on unexpected duplication, and log any intentional one-to-many relationship. Tabulate specimens and distinct people at acquisition, each assay, their intersection, and final analysis, with reasons. Decide whether the target is the intersection population or the full eligible population and state the selection assumptions for the latter. Checksums establish file identity/change, not valid join semantics or ignorability. In the toy data the specimen average is 13/3, the equally weighted person average is 5.25, and the retained average is 5. Changing specimen contributions can change weighting without removing a person.




Additional practice (optional)

Extend the example with a person who loses all specimens and show how both attrition columns change.
Write a data contract for a methylation proportion or metabolite-intensity matrix; explain why a raw-count assertion would be inappropriate.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text: Before reading: Expectations, covariance, and basic regression; see the What is your estimator actually estimating? page for the choice of adjustment.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text:
1 The one idea
Much of semiparametric theory is a carefully organized version of a familiar move: remove from a variable the part another variable can predict, then work with what remains. In ordinary linear regression that means subtracting a fitted line. In the settings that matter later, the fitted object is allowed to be any function.
Let X be a measurement and Z recorded covariates, and assume E[X^2]<\infty. The conditional expectation

m_X(Z)=E[X\mid Z]

is a random variable obtained by applying a population prediction function to Z. At a particular covariate value z, m_X(z) is the conditional mean of X. For continuous covariates, this is defined through a conditional distribution; it is not a literal average over observations with exactly the same covariate value in a finite dataset.
For a discrete example, suppose half the people have Z=0 and half have Z=1, with conditional means 1 and 3. Then m_X(Z)=1+2Z. Subtracting 1 in the first stratum and 3 in the second leaves a residual whose mean is zero in each stratum, not just after pooling them.
The residual X-m_X(Z) has the following population property:

E\left[\{X-m_X(Z)\}h(Z)\right]=0.

This holds for every square-integrable function h(Z). It says that the residual is perpendicular to every allowed direction depending only on Z. The meaning of “perpendicular” here comes from an expectation inner product, rather than angles in an observation-level scatterplot.





Conditional expectation is the closest predictionSchematic in L₂(P): lengths are root mean squared magnitudes.0m(Z) = E[X | Z]X − m(Z)Xh(Z)Choose another prediction h(Z)Its error has two perpendicular pieces:X − h = (X − m) + (m − h)E[(X − h)²]= E[(X − m)²] + E[(m − h)²]irreducible error + prediction errorThe horizontal line represents directions in the space of functions of Z.



Figure 1: Conditional expectation is an orthogonal projection. The horizontal line shows part of the space of functions of Z; the residual is perpendicular to the entire space. Any alternative h(Z) adds prediction error to the minimum possible mean squared error. The geometry is schematic, not a scatterplot of observations.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
section: 2 Expectations as averages and inner products
text:
2 Expectations as averages and inner products
For a random variable U, E[U] is its population average. We usually cannot compute it exactly, so we replace it with the sample average

P_n U = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n U_i.

The notation P_n says “take an average.” Under the appropriate LLN, this sample quantity approaches the population expectation for a fixed integrable function of i.i.d. observations. The distinction matters: a population identity involving E need not be an exact identity after replacing the unknown function by a fitted one.
If U and V have finite second moments, define

\langle U,V\rangle = E[UV].

This behaves like a dot product. Its associated squared length is \|U\|^2 = E[U^2]. The collection of random variables with finite second moments is called L_2(P). You do not need functional analysis to use the notation. Keep three translations in mind:

\langle U,V\rangle = 0 means that U and V are orthogonal.
Orthogonal random variables are uncorrelated if both have mean zero.
A projection is the closest element of a set under squared-error loss.

For centered variables, E[UV] is their covariance. An orthogonal residual is therefore uncorrelated with a function of the covariates under the stated moment conditions. Zero covariance is a statement about one expected product; independence is a stronger statement about an entire joint distribution.
Functions that agree with probability one have zero L_2 distance and are treated as the same element of this space. Thus a projection is unique up to equality almost surely. This concerns agreement on a population observation, rather than almost sure convergence of a sequence of estimates.
The sample version is ordinary linear algebra. If u and v are vectors of observed values, n^{-1}u^\top v estimates E[UV]. Exact perpendicularity of two fitted data vectors and population orthogonality of two random variables are related, but distinct, statements.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text:
3 Conditional expectation is a projection
The conditional expectation E[X\mid Z] is the best prediction of X that can use Z, where “best” means smallest population mean squared error. With E[X^2]<\infty, conditional Jensen’s inequality gives E[m_X(Z)^2]\le E[X^2], so the prediction itself is square-integrable. For every square-integrable candidate h(Z),

E\left[\{X-E[X\mid Z]\}^2\right]
\leq E\left[\{X-h(Z)\}^2\right].

It is not necessary for E[X\mid Z] to be linear, smooth, or easy to estimate. It is the population object that wins among all functions of Z.
The proof gives the fact we will use. Let m(Z)=E[X\mid Z]. For any h(Z),

\begin{aligned}
E[(X-h)^2]&=E[(X-m+m-h)^2]\\
&=E[(X-m)^2]+E[(m-h)^2]+2E[(X-m)(m-h)].
\end{aligned}

The final term is zero. First, conditioning on Z gives

\begin{aligned}
E[X-m\mid Z]&=E[X\mid Z]-m(Z)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

Next, (m-h) is fixed once Z is known, so it can be taken outside that conditional expectation. Finally, the law of total expectation averages the conditional result:

\begin{aligned}
E[(X-m)(m-h)]&=E[(m-h)E[X-m\mid Z]]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

Finite second moments make this product integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. The extra error from predicting with h is therefore exactly E[(m-h)^2]\ge0. Equality holds precisely when h(Z)=m(Z) with probability one. This is the Pythagorean theorem in L_2(P) and the uniqueness statement behind “best prediction.”

3.1 Check it with data
Here X has a nonlinear conditional mean. A straight line misses the curve; a spline gets closer. Neither fact changes the population definition of m_X.


Code
set.seed(1)
n <- 800
z <- runif(n, -1, 1)
x <- sin(2 * pi * z) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.45)

fit_line <- lm(x ~ z)
fit_spline <- smooth.spline(z, x, df = 10)
x_line <- fitted(fit_line)
x_spline <- predict(fit_spline, z)$y

c(linear_MSE = mean((x - x_line)^2),
  spline_MSE = mean((x - x_spline)^2),
  no_adjustment_MSE = mean((x - mean(x))^2))


       linear_MSE        spline_MSE no_adjustment_MSE 
        0.6541736         0.2248078         0.7259596 


Here the true conditional mean is \sin(2\pi Z) and the irreducible conditional noise variance is 0.45^2. The reported MSEs are training errors, evaluated on the data used to fit each predictor. They illustrate how the chosen fits follow this sample; they do not estimate fresh-population risk without further justification. A sufficiently flexible fit could reduce training error while predicting poorly on new people.
The population projection is defined before choosing an algorithm. To assess a learner’s approximation to it, evaluate prediction error on independent observations or use an appropriate validation scheme. The optional exercises include this comparison.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
section: 4 The residual is orthogonal to every function of Z
text:
4 The residual is orthogonal to every function of Z
Set \widetilde X = X-m_X(Z). For any h(Z),

\begin{aligned}
E[\widetilde X h(Z)]&=E\left[E\{\widetilde X h(Z)\mid Z\}\right]\\
&=E\left[h(Z)E\{X-m_X(Z)\mid Z\}\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

The first step is the law of total expectation; the second takes h(Z) outside the conditional expectation and uses the conditional mean-zero residual. This is the residualization identity. It contains several familiar special cases, whenever the displayed functions have the required moments.

Taking h(Z)=1 gives E[\widetilde X]=0.
Taking h(Z)=Z gives \operatorname{Cov}(\widetilde X,Z)=0.
Taking h(Z)=Z^2, \sin(Z), or an indicator of a subgroup gives the same result.

In a finite-sample OLS fit, the normal equations make the fitted residual vector orthogonal to the included design columns. At the population level, a best linear predictor satisfies the corresponding finite set of moment equations. The true conditional-expectation residual satisfies the larger collection of equations for every square-integrable function of Z. Estimating a flexible regression aims to approximate this population object; it does not grant all these identities automatically.
Orthogonality also need not remove dependence. Let Z be binary and U an independent, mean-zero, unit-variance variable. For X=Z+(1+Z)U, the conditional mean is Z and the residual is (1+Z)U. Its conditional mean is zero, yet its variance is 1 when Z=0 and 4 when Z=1. The residual’s distribution still depends on Z.


Code
# The residual from a flexible fit is nearly orthogonal to several functions of z.
r <- x - x_spline
c(mean = mean(r),
  z = mean(r * z),
  z_squared = mean(r * z^2),
  sine = mean(r * sin(2 * pi * z)))


         mean             z     z_squared          sine 
 5.027173e-14  1.068541e-13 -6.825678e-06  2.476831e-02 


These are sample products using an estimated function on its own training data. They are a numerical illustration, not a proof of population orthogonality. If a square-integrable fitted function \hat m_X is instead held fixed and evaluated on a fresh observation, conditioning on Z gives

E[(X-\hat m_X(Z))h(Z)]=E[(m_X(Z)-\hat m_X(Z))h(Z)].

Its remaining population moment depends on regression error. Orthogonality and cross-fitting explains how training/evaluation separation and nuisance accuracy enter inference.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text:
5 Conditional covariance and partialling out
For two variables X and Y with finite second moments, write

\psi_{XY}=E\big[\{X-m_X(Z)\} \times\{Y-m_Y(Z)\}\big].

Condition on Z and expand the product:

\begin{aligned}
E[(X-m_X)(Y-m_Y)\mid Z]&=E[XY\mid Z]-m_X(Z)m_Y(Z)\\
&=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid Z).
\end{aligned}

The outer expectation therefore averages conditional covariance over the population’s covariate distribution. The analogous residual variances are \psi_{XX}=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Z)] and \psi_{YY}=E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid Z)]. When both are finite and positive, their ratio gives a residual correlation:

\rho_{XY\cdot Z} =
\frac{\psi_{XY}}{\sqrt{\psi_{XX}\psi_{YY}}}.

The expression is useful in network work: a marginal correlation can be large merely because two genes both change with cell composition, batch, or disease severity. Residualizing against a measured Z asks about association left after that predictable structure is removed.
The order of operations matters: averaging covariances and then standardizing generally differs from averaging within-stratum correlations. Also, positive and negative conditional covariances can cancel in the population average. A zero value does not even force every stratum’s covariance to be zero, much less establish conditional independence.
These are associational targets. Whether adjusting for Z is scientifically appropriate, or supports a causal interpretation, requires the argument in What is your estimator actually estimating?.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text:
6 The partially linear model
A later efficiency calculation uses the partially linear model:

\begin{gathered}
Y=\beta X+g(Z)+\varepsilon,\\
E[\varepsilon\mid X,Z]=0.
\end{gathered}

Here \beta is the quantity of interest and g is an unknown nuisance function. Taking conditional expectations given Z gives

E[Y\mid Z] = \beta E[X\mid Z] + g(Z).

Subtract this equation from the original one:

Y-m_Y(Z) = \beta\{X-m_X(Z)\}+\varepsilon.

The error term has mean zero conditional on (X,Z), so

\begin{aligned}
E[(X-m_X(Z))\varepsilon]&=E[(X-m_X(Z))E[\varepsilon\mid X,Z]]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}

Multiplying the residualized outcome equation by X-m_X(Z) and taking expectations therefore gives the following ratio, provided its denominator is positive:

\beta =
\frac{E[\{X-m_X(Z)\}\{Y-m_Y(Z)\}]}
     {E[\{X-m_X(Z)\}^2]}.

This is Robinson’s partialling-out identity. The numerator is the residual cross moment and the denominator is residual exposure variation, just as in a regression slope. If X=m_X(Z) almost surely, that denominator is zero: changing \beta can be absorbed into the unrestricted function g(Z), so the coefficient cannot be separated from that nuisance. Positive residual variation is the identification condition. Efficiency and the cost of estimating the nuisance functions require the later model-specific arguments.


Code
set.seed(2)
n <- 1000
z <- runif(n)
x <- 1.5 * sin(2 * pi * z) + rnorm(n)
y <- 0.6 * x + sin(2 * pi * z) + rnorm(n)

mx <- predict(smooth.spline(z, x, df = 12), z)$y
my <- predict(smooth.spline(z, y, df = 12), z)$y
x_res <- x - mx; y_res <- y - my

c(true_beta = 0.6,
  naive_linear_adjustment = coef(lm(y ~ x + z))["x"],
  residual_slope = sum(x_res * y_res) / sum(x_res^2))


                true_beta naive_linear_adjustment.x            residual_slope 
                0.6000000                 0.8203026                 0.6245794 


Here the shared sine component remains after linear adjustment for Z, producing a population slope bias. Nonlinearity alone would not imply that bias: the omitted component must also be associated with the residual exposure. Spline residualization removes most of the shared nonlinear component in this example. In a real analysis we must still account for errors in \hat m_X and \hat m_Y; that is the later reason for orthogonal formulas and cross-fitting.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text:
7 Where this connects

The What is your estimator actually estimating? page asks whether adjustment for Z answers the scientific question. This page shows the population calculation once the adjustment is justified.
The Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity page treats the residual identity as an equation whose solution is an estimator.
The Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency page shows the same residualization as projection of a score away from a finite-dimensional nuisance.
The Model restrictions and efficiency page makes the nuisance space infinite-dimensional and derives the efficient influence function.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text:
8 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · SP-02 — Prove the projection property
Task type: Proof and interpretation.
Assume E[X^2]<\infty, let m(Z)=E[X\mid Z], and let h(Z) be square-integrable.

Prove E[(X-m(Z))h(Z)]=0 using conditional expectation.
Derive E[(X-h)^2]=E[(X-m)^2]+E[(m-h)^2].
Conclude that m minimizes mean squared error and state exactly when equality holds.
Explain why perpendicularity here refers to random variables in L_2(P), rather than a scatterplot of individual observations.

Ready to continue when: you can derive the decomposition, justify the vanishing cross term, and state uniqueness up to almost-sure equality.
Transfer: Use h(Z)=a+bZ with population coefficients. Under what condition can this linear predictor achieve the population minimum over all functions of Z? Distinguish that condition from estimating its coefficients in a finite sample.


Hint

Write X-h=(X-m)+(m-h) and condition the cross term on Z.



Solution outline — open after trying

Because h is a function of Z, E[(X-m)h]=E[hE[X-m\mid Z]]=0. The same argument applies to m-h. Squaring X-h=(X-m)+(m-h) and taking expectations therefore removes the cross term. The remaining extra term E[(m-h)^2] is nonnegative and is zero exactly when h=m almost surely. Finite second moments make the products integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. This is orthogonality under the inner product E[UV].




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

In the simulation above, replace 1.5\sin(2\pi Z) by a linear function of Z. Compare linear adjustment and spline residualization. When is the simpler adjustment enough?
Simulate X = Z + U and Y = Z + U + V, where Z,U,V are independent standard normals. Compare the marginal correlation of X and Y with their residual correlation after adjusting for Z. Explain both numbers.
Evaluate the fitted line and spline from the first example on a fresh sample from the same generator. Compare training MSE, validation MSE, and the population noise variance 0.45^2.

title: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry
text:
9 Reading

Tsiatis, A. A. (2006). Semiparametric Theory and Missing Data. Springer. Sections 3.1 to 3.3 for the geometry in full generality.
van der Vaart, A. W. (1998). Asymptotic Statistics. Cambridge. Sections 25.1 and 25.2 for Hilbert-space notation used in semiparametric theory.
Robinson, P. M. (1988). Root-N-consistent semiparametric regression. Econometrica, 56(4), 931 to 954. The partialling-out construction.
Buja, A., Brown, L., and Berk, R. (2019). Models as approximations, Part I. Statistical Science, 34(4), 523 to 544. A useful account of regression adjustment when a linear model is only an approximation.

title: Statistical models, influence functions, and efficiency
text:
A statistical model specifies which distributions and local changes are allowed. A target is a functional on that model. An influence function can represent how the target changes along permitted directions; a separate estimator argument connects that derivative to a sample expansion.
The complete-data mean provides the first example: its centered contribution is both a distributional derivative and the term controlling the sample mean’s uncertainty. Conditional-expectation geometry and likelihood scores then explain how model restrictions affect the possible representations and their variance. A mean with known population stratum weights makes the variance gain concrete before the partially linear regression example.
crumbs: Statistical models, influence functions, and efficiency

title: Statistical models, influence functions, and efficiency
text:
What you’ll learn

Represent local target changes: construct valid score paths and derive centered influence functions for means, variances, and ratios.
Understand model-relative information: distinguish score residualization from gradient projection, and explain which representation gives the regular-estimation variance bound.

Completion means deriving an elementary influence function with its path and moment assumptions, then explaining the projection and variance comparison in a stated model. SP-02–SP-05 and SP-07–SP-09 develop these core skills. SP-06 is the completion target for the quantile extension, which uses a stated probability lemma. The survival page and all additional practice are optional.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
text: Before reading: Conditional expectation and L2 geometry, Estimating equations and asymptotic linearity, Likelihood, scores, and parametric efficiency, and Influence functions.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
section: 1 Begin with a stated model and target
text:
1 Begin with a stated model and target
A model is a set of permitted distributions, and the target is a functional on that set. Statistical models, targets, and paths introduced these objects and valid score paths; Influence functions derived elementary gradient representations. Here the question is which representation gives the smallest regular-estimation variance.
The complete-data mean has influence function Y-\mu in the unrestricted model. The partially linear example below is a transfer to a restricted model with a scalar coefficient and an unknown regression function. Its extra assumptions must be stated before interpreting its efficiency bound.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
section: 2 What the extra freedom buys and costs
text:
2 What the extra freedom buys and costs
Allowing an unknown nuisance function avoids imposing an incorrect parametric shape. It does not automatically protect an estimator: identification, adequate nuisance estimation, and a controlled remainder are still required. The partially linear model also needs assumptions on the conditional error and residual exposure variation.
The estimator must support its inferential claim under the nuisance variations permitted by the model. A smaller model can exclude some of those variations and yield a smaller variance bound at a shared population law. The reduction need not be strict. The comparison is always between stated models and regular estimators, not between arbitrary algorithms with small empirical variances.
Work at a fixed population law P and scalar target \beta(P), with all expectations below taken under P. Let W denote one complete observation record and N the number of independent records. Assume the target has a square-integrable gradient on the model’s tangent space. We will distinguish its limiting influence variance from the estimator variance, which includes division by N.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
section: 3 Moving the truth: paths, scores, and the tangent space
text:
3 Moving the truth: paths, scores, and the tangent space
Recall from Statistical models, targets, and paths that valid paths have mean-zero scores and their closed linear span is the tangent space \mathcal T. Here we use that construction to compare the directions different models permit. A path may change \beta, change the nuisance, or change both.

In a parametric model there is one score per parameter, and \mathcal T is the span of those few functions.
In a nonparametric model, every bounded mean-zero function s is the score of a path, namely f_t = f\,(1 + t s). Taking limits fills out every mean-zero function with a finite variance, so \mathcal T is all of them.
In the semiparametric parameterizations used here, a path moving \beta while holding the nuisance fixed has score S_\beta. Paths changing only the nuisance generate the closed nuisance tangent space \mathcal T_\eta. The full tangent space is the closed linear span of S_\beta and \mathcal T_\eta. These spaces need not be orthogonal before projection.

The influence function from the Influence functions page is also a derivative along a path. It was defined with one particular path, which contaminates F with a point mass. Smooth paths give the same derivative in a more convenient form. In a nonparametric model, a path with score s gives

\left.\frac{d}{dt}\beta(P_t)\right|_0=E[\phi(W)s(W)].

For the bounded-score path f_t=f(1+ts) and the differentiable functionals studied earlier, this follows by differentiating along that path. A contamination derivative alone would not establish the representation for an arbitrary functional.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
section: 4 What an influence function has to satisfy
text:
4 What an influence function has to satisfy
An asymptotically linear estimator has expansion \hat\beta-\beta=N^{-1}\sum_i\phi(W_i)+o_p(N^{-1/2}), with E[\phi]=0 and finite variance. This describes its behavior at a fixed law. Regularity additionally requires stability under nearby laws in the model.
The working local comparison takes a regular path P_t and studies data from P_{h/\sqrt N} for each fixed h. A regular estimator’s centered, scaled error \sqrt N\{\hat\beta-\beta(P_{h/\sqrt N})\} has the same limiting law across these local shifts. Establishing this property uses the corresponding regular-submodel theory; a pointwise CLT alone is not enough.
For example, an estimator that always reports zero has zero variance and is correct at a population mean of zero. Along nearby populations with mean h/\sqrt N, its centered scaled error is -h, so its limiting behavior depends on the local shift. Such a procedure cannot bypass an efficiency bound by being correct at one special population.
For regular asymptotically linear estimators, stability gives the derivative constraint: the mean shift of the contribution must match the target’s path derivative. Thus, for every permitted score s,

E[\phi(W)s(W)]=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\beta(P_t)\right|_0.

For a path that moves only the nuisance, the right side is zero, because \beta has not changed. For the path that moves only \beta, at unit speed, it is one. So in a semiparametric model an influence function has to satisfy two conditions.

E[\operatorname{IF}\cdot s] = 0 for every score s in the nuisance tangent space \mathcal T_\eta.
E[\operatorname{IF}\cdot S_\beta] = 1.

These conditions describe first-order centering: a nuisance-only perturbation leaves the target fixed, while a unit-speed target perturbation changes it at rate one. They do not say that a finite-sample estimate or its variance stays unchanged whenever a nuisance changes.
In the unrestricted model, \mathcal T=L_2^0(P), and the derivative equations for every permitted score determine a unique mean-zero gradient. When restrictions give a proper smaller closed tangent space, adding a mean-zero component orthogonal to that space preserves the derivative equations. If that orthogonal complement is nontrivial, more than one gradient represents the same derivatives. A model restriction alone does not guarantee a smaller tangent space at every distribution. These representations are candidate first-order contributions. Constructing a regular estimator that attains a candidate influence function requires further conditions; the derivative equations alone do not construct one.
To see how they differ, suppose \operatorname{IF}_1 and \operatorname{IF}_2 both satisfy the two conditions. Their difference is orthogonal to S_\beta and to every score in \mathcal T_\eta, so it is orthogonal to the whole tangent space. Exactly one influence function lies inside \mathcal T itself, and it is called the efficient influence function (EIF). Every other influence function is the EIF plus a piece h that is orthogonal to \mathcal T. The two pieces are orthogonal to each other, so

\begin{aligned}
E[\operatorname{IF}^2]&=E[\operatorname{EIF}^2]+E[h^2]\\
&\ge E[\operatorname{EIF}^2].
\end{aligned}

The extra h is orthogonal to every permitted score, so it changes none of the target derivatives. It adds E[h^2] to the variance of a centered contribution. For an estimator attaining that influence function, the limiting variance of its scaled error is E[\operatorname{IF}^2], and its first-order estimator variance is E[\operatorname{IF}^2]/N. The canonical gradient has the smallest variance among gradient representations, giving a lower bound for regular asymptotically linear estimators. Attainment is a separate question; an estimator attaining it is semiparametrically efficient.

Figure 1: The geometry behind the efficiency bound. Left: the score for \beta splits into the part that a direction in the nuisance tangent space can imitate (its projection) and what is left, the efficient score, which is perpendicular to every nuisance direction. Right: the tangent space drawn as a plane. The efficient influence function (EIF) lies in it. Any other influence function is the EIF plus a piece h that sticks out of the plane, so its second moment is larger by E[h^2].




4.1 A mean with known stratum probabilities
Consider i.i.d. records W=(Z,Y) with binary Z. The model specifies P(Z=0)=P(Z=1)=1/2 as known, while allowing unrestricted conditional outcome laws with the needed finite second moments. The target is still the population mean \mu=E[Y]. Sampling produces random stratum counts; the known population probabilities are additional model information.
A permitted score must satisfy E[s\mid Z]=0, since paths cannot change the marginal stratum probabilities. Write m(Z)=E[Y\mid Z]. The unrestricted-model mean contribution decomposes as

Y-\mu=\{Y-m(Z)\}+\{m(Z)-\mu\}.

The first piece has conditional mean zero and lies in this model’s tangent space. The second is a function of Z, so its inner product with every allowed score is zero. Projection therefore gives the efficient gradient Y-m(Z), with influence variance E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid Z)]. The full sample mean remains a valid regular estimator, but carries the additional variance \operatorname{Var}(m(Z)).
At a population with stratum means 0 and 4 and within-stratum variances 1, \mu=2. The full mean has influence variance 1+4=5, while the efficient influence variance is 1. Their first-order estimator variances are 5/N and 1/N.
An estimator achieving the latter combines the two within-stratum means using the known weights: \hat\mu=(\bar Y_0+\bar Y_1)/2. To check its contribution, write p_z=P(Z=z) and m_z=E[Y\mid Z=z]. The stratum mean is a ratio,

\bar Y_z=\frac{P_N[1\{Z=z\}Y]}{P_N[1\{Z=z\}]}.

Its ratio-rule contribution is 1\{Z=z\}(Y-m_z)/p_z. Multiplying by the known p_z and summing over strata leaves Y-m(Z), the efficient gradient. Each stratum has positive population probability, so its count grows and empty-stratum events vanish asymptotically.
If the weights were instead the same dataset’s observed stratum frequencies, this weighted average would reduce to the full sample mean. The gain depends on the assumed known population weights; uncertainty in externally estimated weights would require another contribution.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
text:
5 Finding the efficient influence function
The left panel of Figure 1 is the recipe. Take the score for \beta and remove the part of it that the nuisance can imitate. That part is the projection of S_\beta onto \mathcal T_\eta, which is the best least-squares prediction of S_\beta from the functions in \mathcal T_\eta. What remains is the efficient score,

\begin{aligned}
S_{\text{eff}}&=S_\beta-\Pi(S_\beta\mid\mathcal T_\eta),\\
\operatorname{EIF}&=\frac{S_{\text{eff}}}{E[S_{\text{eff}}^2]}.
\end{aligned}

Both conditions hold. The efficient score is orthogonal to \mathcal T_\eta by construction, which is condition 1. The score S_\beta is the efficient score plus a piece in \mathcal T_\eta, and that piece is orthogonal to the efficient score, so E[S_{\text{eff}}\,S_\beta] = E[S_{\text{eff}}^2] and the division gives condition 2. The EIF is built from elements of \mathcal T, so it lies in \mathcal T. The efficiency bound is \{N\,E[S_{\text{eff}}^2]\}^{-1}. With no nuisance, S_{\text{eff}} = S_\beta and the bound is the inverse Fisher information. With a nuisance, E[S_{\text{eff}}^2] \le E[S_\beta^2], and the difference is the price of not knowing the nuisance.
Keep the two projections separate:

Project a gradient onto the full tangent space \mathcal T. This preserves its target derivatives and removes an unnecessary orthogonal component, reducing or preserving its influence variance. The known-stratum example does this.
Project a target score onto the nuisance space \mathcal T_\eta, then subtract. This isolates the efficient score. Its squared length is information; taking its inverse gives the variance bound after normalization. This is the score calculation from the likelihood page.

A smaller score norm means less information compared with knowing the nuisance. A smaller gradient norm means lower variance among derivative representations within the stated model. The objects and comparison spaces explain the different directions of these inequalities.

5.1 The partially linear model
Take Y=\beta X+g(Z)+\varepsilon with \varepsilon\mid X,Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2), where \sigma^2>0 is constant, g and the covariate law are unrestricted subject to the needed moments, and v_X=E[\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Z)]>0. This is a conditional Gaussian model, stronger than specifying a conditional mean alone. Write m_X(Z)=E[X\mid Z].
Treat \sigma^2 as known for the derivation. If it is unknown, its normal variance score is orthogonal to the mean scores because the centered normal third moment is zero. Estimating it therefore leaves this first-order bound for \beta unchanged, while a feasible SE still needs its estimation. The remaining scores are

Moving \beta gives S_\beta = X\varepsilon/\sigma^2.
Moving g to g+tk along an admissible square-integrable direction gives score k(Z)\varepsilon/\sigma^2.
Moving the covariate law generates mean-zero scores a(X,Z), with the tangent space including their appropriate limits.

These nuisance directions have zero cross inner product because E[\varepsilon\mid X,Z]=0. The target score is already orthogonal to the covariate-law scores by the same conditioning argument. For the remaining directions, seek h(Z) such that (X-h(Z))\varepsilon is orthogonal to every k(Z)\varepsilon. Conditioning on (X,Z) gives

E[(X-h(Z))k(Z)\varepsilon^2]=\sigma^2E[(X-h(Z))k(Z)].

This is zero for every k when h=m_X, by the conditional-expectation projection property. Thus the nuisance-score projection removes m_X(Z)\varepsilon/\sigma^2, leaving the residual-exposure score below. Its second moment is v_X/\sigma^2, giving

\begin{aligned}
S_{\text{eff}}&=\frac{(X-m_X(Z))\varepsilon}{\sigma^2},\\
\operatorname{EIF}&=\frac{(X-m_X(Z))\varepsilon}{v_X},\\
\text{variance bound}&=\frac{\sigma^2}{Nv_X}.
\end{aligned}

The nuisance g can absorb the part of X predictable from Z. The residual variation supplies the remaining information about \beta. The corresponding estimator form regresses residualized Y on residualized X (Robinson, 1988), using Y-E[Y\mid Z]=\beta(X-m_X(Z))+\varepsilon. Attaining the bound additionally requires sufficiently accurate nuisance fits and a justified estimator expansion. When v_X is small, the bound is large; when v_X=0, the target coefficient cannot be separated from g in this model.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
text:
6 Checking the partially linear model
The code below checks three claims for the partially linear model: the two conditions, the bound, and the price of the extra freedom. The simulated model has Z \sim U(0, 1), X = 1.5\sin(2\pi Z) + u with u \sim N(0, 1), \beta = 0.5, and \sigma = 1. Then E[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)] = 1, so the bound is a variance of 1/N.
Three candidate influence functions are compared. The first is the efficient one. The second is the same construction with a weight w(Z) = e^{2Z},

\operatorname{IF}_w = \frac{w(Z)\,(X - m_X(Z))\,\varepsilon}{E[w(Z)\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)]},

which satisfies both conditions for a positive weight with finite second moments and a finite, nonzero denominator (exercise 2). It is the candidate influence function for residual-on-residual regression with each observation weighted by w(Z), subject to the required nuisance-learning and remainder conditions.
The third candidate comes from ordinary least squares of Y on X and Z. At a law where g is linear, its influence function is (X-L(Z))\varepsilon/E[(X-L(Z))^2], where L(Z) is the best linear predictor of X from Z. This representation is valid for the smaller model restricting g to a line. We now ask whether it also satisfies the derivative constraints of the larger model, which permits curved changes to g. A large simulated sample stands in for expectations, and two nuisance directions k(Z)\varepsilon test condition 1.


Code
set.seed(5)
n <- 2e6
z <- runif(n); mX <- 1.5 * sin(2 * pi * z)      # E[X | Z]; Var(X | Z) = 1
x <- mX + rnorm(n); eps <- rnorm(n)             # beta = 0.5 and sigma = 1, so S_beta = x * eps
S_beta <- x * eps

w <- exp(2 * z)
r_lin <- resid(lm(x ~ z))                       # X minus its best linear predictor from Z
IF <- list(efficient = (x - mX) * eps / mean((x - mX)^2),
           weighted  = w * (x - mX) * eps / mean(w * (x - mX)^2),
           ols_line  = r_lin * eps / mean(r_lin^2))

k1 <- sin(2 * pi * z) * eps; k2 <- (z - 0.5)^3 * eps    # two nuisance directions
round(sapply(IF, function(f) c(`E[IF * S_beta]` = mean(f * S_beta),
                               `E[IF * k1]` = mean(f * k1), `E[IF * k2]` = mean(f * k2),
                               `E[IF^2]` = mean(f^2))), 2)


               efficient weighted ols_line
E[IF * S_beta]         1     1.00     1.00
E[IF * k1]             0     0.00     0.20
E[IF * k2]             0     0.00     0.01
E[IF^2]                1     1.31     0.69


The simulated moments approximately match the derivative constraints for the efficient and weighted candidates: E[\operatorname{IF}\cdot S_\beta]=1 and both nuisance moments are zero. Their validity for all admissible directions follows from the population calculation, not from testing only two directions. Their second moments differ: the efficient one has E[\operatorname{IF}^2]=1, the influence-variance bound, while the weighted one has 1.31. An estimator attaining the latter contribution has first-order variance 31% above the bound.
The least squares candidate has E[\operatorname{IF}\cdot S_\beta]=1 but fails condition 1, with an inner product of about 0.20 for the first nuisance direction. One failing direction is enough: even at a law with linear g, this estimator is not regular for \beta under the larger model’s curved local perturbations. Its second moment, 0.69, can lie below that model’s bound because it does not meet the bound’s requirements. A fixed curved g can produce a larger, persistent bias, illustrated next.
The difference between the weighted and the efficient influence functions is the piece h of the previous section, and the decomposition says its second moment accounts for the whole gap.


Code
c(extra_second_moment = mean(IF$weighted^2) - mean(IF$efficient^2),
  second_moment_of_h  = mean((IF$weighted - IF$efficient)^2))


extra_second_moment  second_moment_of_h 
          0.3092308           0.3121518 


Next, the estimators themselves. The efficient and weighted estimators regress the residuals of Y on the residuals of X, with both residualized on Z by a smoothing spline. The least squares estimator uses a line for g. The simulation runs two scenarios, one in which g is a line and one in which it is a curve.


Code
beta <- 0.5
SimPL <- function(n, g) {
  z <- runif(n); x <- 1.5 * sin(2 * pi * z) + rnorm(n)
  data.frame(z = z, x = x, y = beta * x + g(z) + rnorm(n))
}
EstPL <- function(d, df = 8) {
  rx <- d$x - predict(smooth.spline(d$z, d$x, df = df), d$z)$y   # X minus its smoothed mean given Z
  ry <- d$y - predict(smooth.spline(d$z, d$y, df = df), d$z)$y
  wz <- exp(2 * d$z)
  c(ols_line  = unname(coef(lm(y ~ x + z, d))["x"]),
    efficient = sum(rx * ry) / sum(rx^2),
    weighted  = sum(wz * rx * ry) / sum(wz * rx^2))
}
g_list <- list(line  = function(z) 2 * z,
               curve = function(z) 2 * sin(2 * pi * z))

set.seed(11)
n <- 500; R <- 2000
sims <- lapply(g_list, function(g) t(replicate(R, EstPL(SimPL(n, g)))))
do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sims), function(s)
  data.frame(g = s, estimator = colnames(sims[[s]]), mean = round(colMeans(sims[[s]]), 3),
             sd = round(apply(sims[[s]], 2, sd), 4), row.names = NULL)))


      g estimator  mean     sd
1  line  ols_line 0.501 0.0369
2  line efficient 0.501 0.0445
3  line  weighted 0.500 0.0511
4 curve  ols_line 0.906 0.0438
5 curve efficient 0.499 0.0444
6 curve  weighted 0.499 0.0512


Code
# the standard deviation each estimator should have, from its influence function: sqrt(E[IF^2] / N)
round(sqrt(sapply(IF, function(f) mean(f^2)) / n), 4)


efficient  weighted  ols_line 
   0.0447    0.0512    0.0372 


Compare each mean with the true value 0.5. The last line predicts standard deviations from the efficient and weighted contributions under either scenario, and from the least squares contribution when g is linear. The displayed least squares formula is not automatically its influence function around its misspecified limit when g is curved; assess that scenario’s center and spread directly. Monte Carlo uncertainty is roughly 0.001 for each mean and 0.0007 for each standard deviation, with the precise values depending on the estimator.

The efficient-form estimator is approximately centered in these simulations whether g is a line or a curve. Its standard deviations, 0.0445 and 0.0444, are close to the SE bound 1/\sqrt{500}=0.0447; the corresponding variance bound is 1/500.
The weighted estimator is also approximately centered in this simulation. Its standard deviation, about 0.051, matches the 0.0512 that its influence function predicts, which is about 15% above the efficient estimator’s.
Least squares shows both sides of the trade. When g is a line, it is approximately centered in this simulation and has the smallest standard deviation of the three, 0.037, because it uses the knowledge that g is a line. The efficient estimator, which does not use that knowledge, pays about 20% in standard deviation. When g is a curve, the knowledge is wrong, and least squares has a mean of 0.91 instead of 0.5, a bias of more than nine of its own standard deviations.

The size of the price depends on how much of X lies in curved functions of Z. Here E[X \mid Z] is a sine curve, which a line cannot follow. Had it been a line in Z, the least squares and efficient estimators would have had the same variance.
The estimator labels refer to their intended first-order contributions. These finite simulations do not prove efficiency or zero finite-sample bias. In particular, a smoother with a fixed nominal complexity need not make approximation error vanish for every regression function; the nuisance-learning guide supplies the conditions needed for an estimator theorem.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
text:
7 A recipe
For a model with a parameter of interest and a nuisance, an efficient estimator is built in this order.

State the model: which parameter you want, and what is left unrestricted.
Find the scores: the score S_\beta for the parameter, and the nuisance tangent space \mathcal T_\eta from the paths that move only the nuisance.
Project S_\beta onto \mathcal T_\eta and subtract. The remainder is the efficient score, and dividing by its second moment gives the EIF and the bound.
Build an estimator whose influence function is the EIF, which usually means solving the sample version of the efficient score equation.
Compare it with the simple alternatives, using the two conditions and the bound as the yardsticks.

Step 4 hides the hard part. The efficient score contains quantities that have to be estimated, such as m_X(Z) in the partially linear model. Their estimation errors enter the procedure. Orthogonality and cross-fitting develops the required bias and empirical-term controls for the missing-outcome mean. A partially linear estimator needs the corresponding argument for its own score.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
text:
8 Words you will meet

A regular asymptotically linear (RAL) estimator is one with an influence function that tracks the estimand along every path in the model. The efficiency bound applies to this class.
The pathwise derivative maps each score direction to the target’s rate of change. A gradient is a mean-zero, square-integrable function representing that map through an inner product. An influence function of a regular asymptotically linear estimator must be such a gradient. The unique gradient in the tangent space is the EIF, also called the canonical gradient.
The efficient score is S_{\text{eff}}, and the efficient information is E[S_{\text{eff}}^2]. The bound is the inverse of the efficient information, divided by N.
An estimator is semiparametrically efficient when its influence function is the EIF, so that it reaches the bound.

title: Model restrictions and efficiency
text:
9 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · SP-08 — Prove the efficient-gradient variance comparison
Task type: Proof and interpretation.
Let \mathcal T be a closed subspace of L_2^0(P) and let a square-integrable gradient \phi represent the target derivative on \mathcal T. Define \phi_{\mathrm{eff}}=\Pi(\phi\mid\mathcal T) and h=\phi-\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}.
Show that the projected gradient represents the same derivatives, prove the Pythagorean variance identity, and state the equality condition. Explain how this differs from projecting a target score away from the nuisance tangent space.
Ready to continue when: you can identify both the object and the projection space, prove the variance comparison, and state what remains to show for an estimator to attain it.
Transfer: Why can the variance inequality fail if you add a component that is not orthogonal to \mathcal T?


Hint

The projection residual has zero inner product with every element of \mathcal T. Scores are in that space.



Solution outline — open after trying

For any score s\in\mathcal T, E[hs]=0, so E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}s]=E[\phi s]. Also E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}h]=0. Both pieces are centered, giving E[\phi^2]=E[\phi_{\mathrm{eff}}^2]+E[h^2]. Equality holds iff h=0 almost surely. This compares valid gradients and, when attained by regular asymptotically linear estimators, their first-order variances. It does not construct an estimator or control its remainder. Score residualization instead subtracts \Pi(S_\beta\mid\mathcal T_\eta); the nuisance space and the object being projected are different.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Consider the regular location model X=\mu+\epsilon, where \epsilon has an unknown density f symmetric about zero. Assume finite positive variance and Fisher information, and the differentiation and boundary conditions needed for the score identities. Derivatives may hold almost everywhere, allowing the Laplace example. The nuisance is f. Show that nuisance scores are even functions of x-\mu and the location score S_\mu=-f'(x-\mu)/f(x-\mu) is odd. Conclude that S_{\text{eff}}=S_\mu. Show that the sample mean’s influence function x-\mu satisfies both derivative conditions, and that it differs from the EIF unless f is normal. For the Laplace density with scale b, compute both variances and check by simulation that the sample median has half the variance of the sample mean.
In the partially linear model, show that \operatorname{IF}_w satisfies both conditions for a positive weight w(Z) with 0<E[w\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Z)]<\infty and E[w^2\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Z)]<\infty. Show that its variance is \sigma^2 E[w^2 \operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)] / (E[w \operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)])^2 per observation, and that this is smallest when w is constant on the part of the population with positive conditional exposure variance (Cauchy–Schwarz). Check that w=e^{2Z} gives the 1.31 from the code.
Suppose the errors are heteroscedastic, \varepsilon \mid X, Z \sim N(0, \sigma^2(Z)), with \sigma^2(\cdot) known. Redo the derivation of the efficient score and show that the EIF is \operatorname{IF}_w with w(Z) = 1/\sigma^2(Z). Why is the estimator that was efficient in this page no longer efficient?

Bickel, P. J., Klaassen, C. A. J., Ritov, Y., and Wellner, J. A. (1993). Efficient and Adaptive Estimation for Semiparametric Models. Johns Hopkins University Press. The standard reference.
