title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
text: Before reading: Individual p-values and Type I error from Uncertainty, confidence intervals, and tests, and the null hypotheses for the analysis. This page moves from one prespecified test to a family of claims.
crumbs: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
text:
1 Define the family of claims
An omics paper often makes a list of claims: these genes differ, these edges change, or these pathways are associated with an outcome. Even when each individual test is well calibrated, inspecting many tests creates many opportunities for false claims. The aim is to control an explicitly chosen error rate for the whole reporting procedure.
List the hypotheses before choosing an adjustment: all measured genes, a prespecified pathway, all candidate network edges, or several contrasts per feature. These are different families. For example, H_{0g}:\psi_g=0 might concern a standardized expression contrast for gene g. Testing two contrasts for each of 1,000 genes creates 2,000 hypotheses if all belong to the same reported family. Separating them into families needs a scientific reporting rationale decided before looking at the results.
The starting point is a valid marginal null p-value. For every true null i, validity means

\begin{aligned}
\Pr(p_i\le t)&\le t,\\
0&\le t\\
&\le1.
\end{aligned}

In words, a null test rejects at threshold t no more than a fraction t of repeated datasets. Equality gives the familiar uniform null p-value; discrete tests can be conservative and still satisfy the inequality. “Marginal” refers to one test at a time. It does not mean that tests are independent, and it does not mean that the scientific target must be a marginal association.
Multiplicity adjustment starts after this calibration argument. It does not repair pseudoreplication, an invalid permutation scheme, or a test of the wrong estimand. Filtering or removing failed tests can also change the family. State which hypotheses were eligible and how uncomputable tests were handled; do not quietly redefine the family as the tests that produced attractive p-values.
crumbs: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
section: 2 The problem, sized for our work
text:
2 The problem, sized for our work
A differential expression analysis tests 15,000 genes. A differential network analysis on 1,000 genes tests 1000(999)/2=499{,}500 unordered edges. Under a global null with exactly uniform marginal p-values, unadjusted 0.05 testing gives expected false-positive counts of 750 and 24,975, respectively.
To see why dependence does not change those expectations, let \mathcal H_0 index the m_0 true nulls. At a common unadjusted threshold \alpha,

\begin{aligned}
V&=\sum_{i\in\mathcal H_0}1\{p_i\le\alpha\},\\
E[V]&=\sum_{i\in\mathcal H_0}\Pr(p_i\le\alpha)\\
&\le m_0\alpha.
\end{aligned}

Linearity of expectation does not require independence. Equality holds for exact uniform nulls. Dependence changes how the false positives occur together, and therefore can greatly change the variability of a discovery list. Shared genes, pathways, people, and preprocessing can all induce it.
crumbs: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
text:
4 FWER: Bonferroni and Holm
With m tests, Bonferroni rejects when p_i\le\alpha/m. The union bound explains its guarantee:

\begin{aligned}
\Pr(V\ge1)&\le\sum_{i\in\mathcal H_0}\Pr(p_i\le\alpha/m)\\
&\le m_0\alpha/m\\
&\le\alpha.
\end{aligned}

The probability of a union is at most the sum of its component probabilities, regardless of how the events overlap. That is why valid individual p-values suffice under any dependence. Holm also controls FWER under arbitrary dependence and can reject more hypotheses by progressively reducing the number still under consideration.






NoteAlgorithm: Holm’s step-down procedure



Inputs: the m p-values, their hypothesis IDs, and FWER level \alpha.

Sort the p-values as p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}, retaining their IDs.
Start at rank i=1. Compare p_{(i)} with \alpha/(m-i+1).
If it passes (\le), reject that hypothesis and advance to the next rank.
At the first failure, stop. Retain that hypothesis and every later one. If all comparisons pass, reject all m.
Return the decisions using the original hypothesis IDs.

Guarantee: FWER at most \alpha for valid marginal null p-values, with arbitrary dependence.




Code
set.seed(1)
m <- 1000
p <- c(runif(950), 2 * pnorm(-abs(rnorm(50, mean = 3.5))))     # 950 nulls, 50 non-nulls (z-tests, effect 3.5)
sum(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni") <= 0.05)


[1] 9


Code
sum(p.adjust(p, "holm") <= 0.05)


[1] 9


These FWER procedures remain valid with arbitrary dependence if the marginal null p-values are valid. They can be conservative when rejection events overlap, but positive correlations do not supply a universal effective-test count. With m=5\times10^5, the Bonferroni threshold is 10^{-7}; whether it has useful power depends on the effects and information available.
crumbs: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
text:
5 FDR: Benjamini-Hochberg
BH uses a rank-dependent threshold: a larger discovery set is allowed a larger raw-p-value cutoff. Its error criterion is FDR, so it generally rejects more than a procedure designed to protect against even one false claim.






NoteAlgorithm: Benjamini–Hochberg step-up procedure



Inputs: all m p-values in the stated family, their hypothesis IDs, and FDR target q.

Sort the p-values as p_{(1)}\le\cdots\le p_{(m)}, retaining their IDs.
At every rank i, compare p_{(i)} with iq/m.
Find the largest rank k whose comparison passes: p_{(k)}\le kq/m.
If no rank passes, reject nothing. Otherwise reject all hypotheses at ranks 1,\ldots,k, including any earlier rank whose own comparison failed.
Return the rejection list using the original IDs.

Guarantee: \mathrm{FDR}\le q\,m_0/m\le q under independence, or a suitable PRDS condition, with valid marginal null p-values. Arbitrary dependence requires a different justification or adjustment.


The difference from Holm is essential: BH does not stop at the first failed comparison. It looks for the last passing rank and then includes the entire prefix of the sorted list.

5.1 Walk through one list
Take m=6 and q=0.05. The p-values below are already sorted.

Rank 3 is the last passing rank, so BH rejects the first three hypotheses. Rank 2 is included because its p-value is below the selected cutoff 3q/6=0.025. Stopping at rank 2 would implement a different procedure.


Code
BH <- function(p, q = 0.05) {
  m <- length(p); o <- order(p)
  k <- max(c(0, which(p[o] <= q * seq_len(m) / m)))
  rej <- logical(m); if (k > 0) rej[o[seq_len(k)]] <- TRUE
  rej
}
sum(BH(p, 0.05)); sum(p.adjust(p, "BH") <= 0.05)     # the same decisions

[1] 28


The function implements the five steps for a complete vector of finite p-values. Package routines also offer conventions for missing p-values and a specified family size; choose those deliberately rather than letting dropped rows determine the scientific family.


5.2 What an adjusted p-value means
For a fixed family, the BH-adjusted p-value is the smallest target level q at which that hypothesis enters the BH list. In sorted order it is

\widetilde p_{(i)}
=\min\left\{1,\ \min_{j\ge i}\frac{m\,p_{(j)}}{j}\right\}.

Start from the largest rank, take a running minimum of the scaled values mp_{(j)}/j, and cap at one. The running minimum enforces the step-up rule: an earlier rank can enter because a later rank passes. In the six-test example the adjusted values are 0.024, 0.044, 0.044, 0.105, 0.360, and 0.800. Rank 2’s own scaled value is 0.054, but rank 3 brings it down to 0.044. Comparing these adjusted values with 0.05 reproduces the three rejections.
An adjusted p-value of 0.044 is not a 4.4% probability that this gene’s null is true. It indexes a decision rule for the family. It also does not quantify effect size or supply a confidence interval with automatic simultaneous or post-selection coverage.


5.3 The dependence assumption and the BY alternative
A convenient sufficient condition for BH is independence of the entire p-value vector. Benjamini and Yekutieli extended control to positive regression dependence on the subset of true nulls (PRDS). This is a joint monotonicity condition: conditioning on a larger value of a null coordinate must not reduce the probability of any coordinatewise increasing event in the full vector. It constrains more than pairwise correlations. Certain one-sided Gaussian tests satisfy it; replacing each signed statistic by its absolute value for a two-sided test does not automatically preserve it. Positive correlations among measured genes therefore do not, by themselves, justify BH for arbitrary two-sided gene or edge tests. The BY paper gives the precise condition and sufficient examples.
When that justification is unavailable, Benjamini–Yekutieli (BY) supplies a general dependence correction.






NoteAlgorithm: Benjamini–Yekutieli adjustment



Inputs: the same complete family and FDR target q.

Calculate the harmonic sum H_m=\sum_{j=1}^m1/j.
Run the BH step-up algorithm with target q/H_m. Equivalently, compare rank i with iq/(mH_m) and select the last passing rank.
Reject the entire prefix through that rank, or nothing if none passes. In R, compare p.adjust(p, "BY") with q.

Guarantee: FDR at most q under arbitrary dependence among valid marginal null p-values.


For 1,000 tests, H_m\approx7.49: a BY target of 0.10 uses BH thresholds at an effective level of about 0.0134. This can cost substantial power. It buys a dependence guarantee; it does not improve invalid individual tests.
Under BH’s stated conditions the bound is q m_0/m, although m_0 is unknown. Adaptive approaches such as Storey’s q-values estimate \pi_0=m_0/m using the p-value distribution. Their estimation and dependence assumptions need their own justification. They are not interchangeable with ordinary BH-adjusted p-values, and an estimated null fraction is not permission to rescale any dependent family arbitrarily.
crumbs: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
section: 6 Dependence: what it does to BH
text:
6 Dependence: what it does to BH
We will hold each test’s marginal distribution fixed and change only how the tests vary together. Each simulated dataset contains 1,000 test statistics. Tests 1–100 are nonnull with mean 3; tests 101–1,000 are null with mean zero. Every statistic has variance one. These are already-standardized test statistics, not expression measurements from 1,000 people.
In the independent world, every statistic gets its own independent standard-normal noise. In the dependent world, divide the tests into 20 blocks of 50: indices 1–50 form block 1, 51–100 block 2, and so on. The 100 signals occupy the first two complete blocks. A block is a set of related tests, such as tests sharing a source of variation; it is not a set of participants.
Write b(j) for the block containing test j. Generate

\begin{aligned}
Z_j^{\rm ind}&=\mu_j+\varepsilon_j,\\
Z_j^{\rm block}&=\mu_j+\sqrt{\rho}\,F_{b(j)}
                         +\sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_j,
\end{aligned}

where all block factors F_b and individual errors \varepsilon_j are independent standard normals. Each new dataset gets fresh factors and errors. Two tests in the same block share the same F_b, giving covariance \rho. Tests in different blocks share nothing, giving covariance zero. The total variance is \rho+(1-\rho)=1, so these covariances are also correlations. We use \rho=0.8.
Figure 1 shows the exact correlation structures used to generate the statistics. The signal locations and the dependence pattern are separate design choices.








Figure 1: Population correlations of the 1,000 test statistics, with the same test ordering in both panels. Left: only each statistic’s correlation with itself is nonzero. Right: 20 diagonal blocks, each containing 50 tests; distinct tests within a block have correlation 0.8, and tests in different blocks have correlation zero. Orange strips mark the 100 nonnull tests (the first two blocks); they do not encode correlation. These are specified model matrices, not sample correlation estimates.





In both worlds, a null statistic is exactly N(0,1), so 2\Phi(-|Z_j|) is a valid, uniform, two-sided null p-value. The nonnull marginal distributions also agree between worlds. In the block world a large positive or negative factor can make many null p-values small together. False discoveries can therefore arrive in clusters. This mechanism can change the spread of FDP even when its mean stays below q; a wide spread alone is not a failure of FDR control.


Code
set.seed(2)
m <- 1000; m1 <- 100; blocks <- 20; rho <- 0.8; n_sim <- 1000
mu <- c(rep(3, m1), rep(0, m - m1))
FDP <- function(z) { r <- BH(2 * pnorm(-abs(z)), q = 0.10); sum(r[-(1:m1)]) / max(sum(r), 1) }
fdp <- replicate(n_sim, {
  z_ind <- rnorm(m) + mu
  f <- rnorm(blocks)
  z_dep <- sqrt(rho) * rep(f, each = m / blocks) + sqrt(1 - rho) * rnorm(m) + mu
  c(independent = FDP(z_ind), block_dependent = FDP(z_dep))
})
rbind(mean_FDP = rowMeans(fdp), MCSE = apply(fdp, 1, sd) / sqrt(n_sim),
      SD_FDP = apply(fdp, 1, sd), q95_FDP = apply(fdp, 1, quantile, 0.95))


         independent block_dependent
mean_FDP 0.089981420     0.072636385
MCSE     0.001113368     0.004050366
SD_FDP   0.035207774     0.128083834
q95_FDP  0.149253731     0.341967495


For each dataset, the code applies BH at q=0.10, counts rejections among the 900 known nulls, and divides by the total discoveries (or one if there are none). It repeats that complete analysis 1,000 times under each world. These are independently generated datasets, not 1,000 permutations of one dataset.
The mean FDP estimates FDR. Its Monte Carlo SE is the sample SD of the dataset-level FDPs divided by \sqrt{n_{\rm sim}}. A general FDP is a fraction, not a Bernoulli outcome, so a binomial MCSE is inappropriate. The SD and 95th percentile describe how much individual lists vary; they answer a different question from the mean. In the independent world the theoretical FDR bound is 0.10(900/1000)=0.09.
This finite experiment concerns the two specified two-sided Gaussian constructions. The one-sided Gaussian PRDS result does not itself establish the needed condition for the two-sided block construction, and one simulation cannot prove a general dependence guarantee. Compare the estimated mean with its MCSE before interpreting small differences from a theoretical level.
In the seeded run, estimated FDR is about 0.090 under independence (MCSE 0.0011) and 0.073 under block dependence (MCSE 0.0041). Yet the 95th percentile of FDP rises from about 0.15 to 0.34. Thus this example does not demonstrate BH exceeding its target FDR: it demonstrates that a smaller mean false fraction can coexist with much more erratic individual lists. A paper should state which of those properties it evaluated.


Code
plot(ecdf(fdp[1, ]), xlim = c(0, 1), verticals = TRUE, do.points = FALSE,
     main = "FDP varies across discovery lists", xlab = "Realized FDP", ylab = "Fraction of datasets",
     col = "#2F80C8", lwd = 2)
lines(ecdf(fdp[2, ]), verticals = TRUE, do.points = FALSE, col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2)
abline(v = 0.10, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
legend("bottomright", c("Independent", "Block dependent"),
       col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00"), lty = 1, lwd = 2, bty = "n")








Figure 2: Realized FDP across 1,000 independent datasets under each synthetic dependence pattern. The vertical line is the FDR target q=0.10, not a cap on the FDP of every list. Estimated FDR is the mean FDP, not its 95th percentile.





To read the empirical CDF, choose an FDP value on the horizontal axis. The curve’s height is the fraction of datasets whose realized FDP was at most that value. At the dashed line, one minus the height estimates how often a list exceeded 10% false discoveries. FDR is the mean of all the FDP values; it is neither that height nor the 95th percentile. This is why controlling FDR does not promise that 95% of lists have FDP below q.
Shared-edge tests also need a distributional model before a covariance formula can be used. For jointly Gaussian standardized features, if \rho_{jk}=\rho_{j\ell}=0, the asymptotic Fisher-z statistics for edges (j,k) and (j,\ell) have correlation \rho_{k\ell}. Gaussian fourth-moment factorization supplies that simplification. General non-Gaussian data require their actual fourth moments, and nonzero shared-edge correlations require the fuller covariance formula. Dependence alone neither proves nor disproves PRDS.
An end-to-end expression analysis uses BY for a prespecified feature family, distinguishes pointwise intervals from FDR control, and estimates FDR with MCSE across independent datasets.

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
text:
7 Permutation calibration
When a valid permutation scheme reproduces the relevant joint null distribution, it can account for dependence without a parametric model for every pair of tests. The same relabeling must be applied to all features: it moves a person’s whole profile together and preserves the features’ relationship. Independently shuffling each gene destroys that relationship and supplies a different reference experiment.

7.1 Westfall–Young maxT for FWER
The question is now: how large could the largest absolute statistic in the family be under the null? Each permutation contributes one maximum, rather than m separate entries to a common marginal reference.






NoteAlgorithm: single-step permutation maxT



Inputs: the family of m statistics, an exchangeability scheme justified by the null/design, B independent uniform draws from the allowed permutations, and FWER level \alpha.

Compute every observed statistic T_i^{\rm obs}.
For each draw b=1,\ldots,B, relabel the exchangeable units using one shared permutation across all features. Recompute the whole analysis required by the statistic.
Save M_b=\max_i|T_i^{(b)}|, the maximum absolute statistic for that relabeling.
For each hypothesis, compute

p_i^{\rm maxT}
=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^B1\{M_b\ge|T_i^{\rm obs}|\}}{B+1}.

Reject hypotheses with p_i^{\rm maxT}\le\alpha.

Scope: a valid global-null permutation reference controls FWER under the global null (weak control). Strong control under every mixture of true and false nulls requires additional conditions or a separately justified construction.


The comparison in step 4 is with the maximum, so these are already multiplicity-adjusted p-values; do not apply Bonferroni to them again as if they were marginal p-values. The plus-one term includes the observed arrangement’s contribution. If all allowed arrangements are enumerated instead, use the exact fraction of arrangements, including the observed one, that meet the comparison.
Subset pivotality is a standard sufficient condition for extending the global-null argument: the joint distribution of statistics for any set of true nulls is unchanged by whether the other hypotheses are null or nonnull. This is a property to justify, not a consequence of running permutations. In particular, a global-null simulation alone cannot establish strong FWER control. The gene-expression permutation analysis by Rempala and Yang discusses the role and limitations of this condition.


Code
set.seed(3)
# Two groups, 200 genes in 4 correlated blocks, no true differences. Compare Bonferroni and maxT.
n1 <- 15; n2 <- 15; G <- 200; blocks <- 4
MakeData <- function() {
  f <- matrix(rnorm((n1 + n2) * blocks), ncol = blocks)
  f[, rep(1:blocks, each = G / blocks)] * sqrt(0.7) + matrix(rnorm((n1 + n2) * G), ncol = G) * sqrt(0.3)
}
Tstat <- function(Y, g) {
  a <- Y[g == 1, , drop = FALSE]; b <- Y[g == 2, , drop = FALSE]
  (colMeans(a) - colMeans(b)) / sqrt(apply(a, 2, var) / n1 + apply(b, 2, var) / n2)
}
g <- rep(1:2, c(n1, n2)); Y <- MakeData(); t_obs <- Tstat(Y, g)
B <- 499
max_perm <- replicate(B, max(abs(Tstat(Y, sample(g)))))
p_maxT <- vapply(abs(t_obs), function(t) (1 + sum(max_perm >= t)) / (B + 1), numeric(1))
c(maxT_rejections = sum(p_maxT <= 0.05),
  illustrative_maxT_cutoff = unname(quantile(max_perm, 0.95)),
  bonferroni_cutoff = qt(1 - 0.05 / (2 * G), df = n1 + n2 - 2))


         maxT_rejections illustrative_maxT_cutoff        bonferroni_cutoff 
                0.000000                 3.948490                 4.192911 


This is a global-null illustration with independent people and exchangeable group labels. The maxima retain the feature dependence. A lower observed cutoff than Bonferroni in this run is an illustration, not a fixed speed or power guarantee. Strong FWER claims under mixed nulls require conditions such as subset pivotality or another justified construction.


Code
hist(max_perm, breaks = 25, col = "#2F80C866", border = "white",
     main = "A joint null reference", xlab = "Maximum absolute t-statistic")
abline(v = quantile(max_perm, 0.95), lty = 2)








Figure 3: The maximum absolute statistic from each valid global-null relabeling. One permutation contributes one maximum, regardless of the number of features. The p-values use the Monte Carlo plus-one formula.







7.2 A pooled permutation null for FDR
Some procedures instead pool permuted statistics to estimate the number of null tail exceedances at a candidate cutoff. This supplies an estimated false count, which must be related to the observed discoveries through a specified procedure. A common null scale across tests, treatment of nonnull tests, an appropriate null-fraction estimate, and the rule choosing a cutoff all matter. Heterogeneous sample sizes or null distributions can defeat naive pooling. Dividing pooled counts by permutation count and calling the result an FDR estimate does not by itself give FDR control.
SAM (Tusher et al. 2001) is a specific method with its own modified statistic, cutoff rule, and false-discovery estimation. The paragraph above is a description of a family of ideas, not a complete implementation of SAM. Follow the actual procedure and its assumptions when using it.
Both tools inherit the requirements of the Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests page: permute the exchangeable units, and identify the null that justifies the actual relabeling. Equal means or correlations alone do not justify unrestricted label exchangeability.

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
text:
9 Some practical rules

Decide FWER or FDR before you look, and write it in the protocol.
Report the number of tests, the procedure, and the level. “Significant after adjustment” is not a method.
When the tests are edges, state the dependence justification. BH requires independence or a suitable positive-regression-dependence condition, not merely some positive correlations. Benjamini–Yekutieli (p.adjust(p, "BY")) controls FDR under arbitrary dependence with valid marginal p-values, at a possible power cost. Permutation methods need their own null and design justification.
Data-dependent filtering needs a null-independence argument or a procedure accounting for selection. Variance filtering is not automatically valid for every test and design; filtering on the same group contrast that is then tested generally changes the reference distribution.
Report effect estimates and their scale alongside adjusted p-values. Testing a zero contrast does not test whether a change exceeds a biologically relevant size; that requires its own null. Ordinary pointwise intervals also do not acquire simultaneous or post-selection coverage from an FDR adjustment.
Multiple testing is about false positives. Nothing here protects against the bias terms in the What is your estimator actually estimating? page: a procedure that is biased for every edge produces a list that is confidently, reproducibly wrong, and no adjustment catches it.

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
text:
10 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · MT-01 — Specify the family and error guarantee
Task type: Interpretation and computation.
You will report discoveries from 1,000 prespecified gene tests, each with a valid marginal null p-value. Define FWER, realized FDP, and FDR. Give the Bonferroni threshold for FWER 0.05. Explain why an FDR guarantee of 0.05 does not certify that at most 5% of your particular discovery list is false, and state what must be justified before choosing BH under dependence.
Then execute BH by hand on the six p-values in the worked table at q=0.05. Identify the selected rank, every rejection, and why the failed comparison at rank 2 does not stop the algorithm.
Ready to continue when: you can state the family, distinguish an expectation from a realized fraction, execute the BH step-up rule, and identify the p-value and dependence assumptions.
Transfer: If you test two contrasts for every gene, how must the family be specified before adjusting p-values?


Hint

FDR averages FDP over repeated datasets; Bonferroni uses a union bound. For BH, scan every rank and take the last passing comparison.



Solution outline — open after trying

FWER is the probability of one or more false rejections. FDP is the false discoveries divided by the number of discoveries, with denominator at least one; FDR is its expectation. The Bonferroni threshold is 0.05/1000=0.00005, requiring valid marginal p-values but no dependence restriction. A realized list can have FDP above 0.05 even under FDR control. Standard BH needs independence or an appropriate positive-regression-dependence condition; arbitrary positive pairwise correlations alone do not establish it.
In the worked list, ranks 1 and 3 pass their own comparisons; rank 3 is the last to pass. Therefore k=3 and BH rejects the hypotheses with p-values 0.004, 0.018, and 0.022. Rank 2 enters as part of that prefix. Stopping at its failed comparison would confuse BH’s step-up rule with a step-down procedure.





Checkpoint · MT-02 — Separate permutation resolution from validity and precision
Task type: Computation and interpretation.
You have 1,000 prespecified tests and 999 valid random permutations per test, using (b+1)/(B+1). At Bonferroni FWER 0.05, can any test reject? How many permutations are needed merely to reach that smallest threshold? Could BH at FDR 0.05 reject if 20 tests all attain p=0.001? Finally, state the MCSE for mean FDP over independent simulated datasets and explain why it is generally not a binomial MCSE.
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish a valid Monte Carlo p-value, its resolution, tail precision, and the error-rate summary being estimated.
Transfer: Does increasing the number of features rescue an invalid permutation scheme, even if it produces many tail values?


Hint

Compare the minimum p-value with the relevant step-specific cutoff, then use variation of entire replicate FDPs.



Solution outline — open after trying

The minimum p-value is 0.001, above the Bonferroni threshold 0.00005, so Bonferroni cannot reject. At least 19,999 permutations are needed for the minimum grid point to equal that threshold; this is a resolution requirement, not a precision guarantee. BH can reject at rank 20 because 20(0.05)/1000=0.001, assuming its p-value/dependence conditions hold. With M independent simulation replicates, MCSE of mean FDP is sample SD of replicate FDP divided by sqrt(M). A general FDP is a fraction, not a Bernoulli outcome; under a global null it reduces to the indicator of any rejection.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Rerun the dependence experiment with rho = 0.3 and rho = 0.95. Plot the distribution of realized FDP in each case. At what dependence does the 95th percentile of FDP exceed 2q?
The original experiment puts all 100 signals in the first two blocks. Redistribute them as five signals in each of the 20 blocks, keeping the total signal count, effect size, and within-block correlation fixed. Compare mean power, mean FDP with MCSE, and the FDP distribution. Why can signal placement matter even with the same marginal distributions?
Estimate pooled null tail counts in the MakeData() setting with 20 shifted genes. List the additional ingredients and assumptions required before calling the resulting cutoff a valid SAM or FDR procedure; contrast it with BH/BY using justified p-values.
Under the null, simulate expression for 30 genes in 40 samples with a block-correlation structure, compute all 435 Fisher z edge statistics, and estimate the correlation between the statistics for two edges that share a gene and two that do not. Relate what you see to the correlation structure you simulated.
Work through the six-test BH example by hand at q=0.04 and q=0.05, then recover the same decisions from the adjusted p-values. Explain why rank 2 can be rejected even when its own comparison fails. This extends MT-01’s guarantee calculation to execution of the algorithm.

title: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests
text: Before reading: Basic testing and the independent unit in the study design.
crumbs: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests

title: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests
text:
1 State the multivariate question
A profile contains many measured features, but “the groups differ” can mean different things: a mean-vector contrast on a chosen scale, a dispersion difference, or a broader distributional difference. A distance-based statistic is a summary chosen to detect some alternatives; it is not itself an effect-size estimand with a universal biological meaning.
Specify the population, features, preprocessing, distance, and sampling unit. A whole-profile test and thousands of feature-wise tests answer different questions. A significant omnibus result does not identify which features differ or establish that group centroids alone changed.
Write a person’s profile as \mathbf Y_i=(Y_{i1},\ldots,Y_{ip}). A mean-vector question compares E[\mathbf Y\mid A=1] with E[\mathbf Y\mid A=0]. A dispersion question compares spread around the group centers. Equality of the whole distributions is stronger than either: it excludes changes in means, spread, tails, and dependence among features. Keep that distinction visible when choosing the null that will justify a permutation reference.
crumbs: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests

title: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests
text:
2 The permutation idea
You have a statistic T that measures how different two groups look. If the null and design make the allowed label assignments equally likely, you can hold the observed profiles fixed and ask where the observed statistic falls among those assignments. This is a conditional reference distribution for this dataset. The exchangeability or randomization argument is what turns that conditional calculation into a test with a repeated-sampling error guarantee.






NoteAlgorithm: a Monte Carlo permutation test



Inputs: a prespecified statistic, its scientific null, and a justified set of equally likely label assignments.

Identify the exchangeable unit and the allowed assignments, including any blocking or pairing restrictions.
Compute the observed statistic T^{\rm obs}. Decide which direction is extreme; for a signed two-sided comparison use |T|.
Draw B independent uniform assignments from the allowed set. Move all features and required records from a unit together. Recompute the analysis under each assignment.
Count b, the assignments whose statistic is at least as extreme as observed, including ties.
Return (b+1)/(B+1) and compare it with the prespecified level.

Requirement: the null/design must justify these assignments. Increasing B refines a reference distribution; it cannot make an unjustified reference valid.




Code
set.seed(1)
x <- c(rnorm(15), rnorm(15, mean = 0.6))
g <- rep(c("a", "b"), each = 15)
T_obs <- diff(tapply(x, g, mean))
B <- 1999
T_perm <- replicate(B, diff(tapply(x, sample(g), mean)))
(sum(abs(T_perm) >= abs(T_obs)) + 1) / (B + 1)


[1] 0.106


Two things to get right from the start.
Exchangeability is the justification for the relabeling, not a synonym for every scientific null. The permutation argument requires that, under the null, the joint distribution of the data is unchanged by relabeling. That is true when the two groups have the same distribution. It is not true when they have the same mean but different variances, and a permutation test of a mean difference can then reject at well above its nominal rate (the Behrens-Fisher problem does not go away by permuting). For the simple unrestricted label-permutation test here, equal group distributions justify exchangeability. More general randomization, restricted, or suitably studentized permutation procedures can address other nulls under their own conditions; identify the justification for the procedure actually used.
The +1 in the p-value. With B random permutations, the p-value (b + 1)/(B + 1) includes the observed arrangement among the permutations and gives a valid, possibly conservative, Monte Carlo permutation p-value under the required exchangeability and sampling scheme (Phipson and Smyth 2010). Its smallest possible value is 1/(B + 1), so with 199 permutations you cannot see a p-value below 0.005, and a simulation study of level needs B large enough that the rejection threshold is well resolved. Reject when p \le \alpha, not p < \alpha: with B=99, the grid includes 0.05, whereas p<0.05 excludes it. Exact rejection probabilities depend on the valid randomization scheme, discreteness, and ties; the grid alone does not prove exact nominal size.
If all M allowed assignments are enumerated, including the observed one, the exact p-value is the number at least as extreme divided by M. The plus-one formula is for a random sample of assignments; do not add another observed arrangement to an already complete enumeration. With 12 people assigned six to each group, there are \binom{12}{6}=924 distinct label assignments. If each person has three visits, there are still 924 person-level assignments, rather than assignments of 36 independent visit labels.
crumbs: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests

title: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests
text:
3 What is being permuted
The permutation argument applies to units that are exchangeable under the null. Observations within the same subject are not exchangeable with observations from other subjects when subjects differ (an intraclass correlation above zero). If the factor you are testing is a subject-level factor, such as disease group, the exchangeable units are subjects, and the labels must be permuted across subjects, carrying each subject’s observations with them.
Permuting at the observation level treats N_{\text{obs}} correlated measurements as if they were N_{\text{obs}} independent ones. The test then rejects a true null far more often than it should.


Code
set.seed(2)
# Subjects nested in groups; `visits` observations per subject; intraclass correlation `icc`.
SimulateVisits <- function(n_subj = 20, visits = c(2, 6), icc = 0.5,
                           design = c("independent", "group-linked")) {
  design <- match.arg(design); J <- 2 * n_subj
  grp <- sample(rep(c("ctrl", "pat"), each = n_subj))
  if (length(visits) == 1) {
    M <- rep(visits, J)
  } else if (design == "independent") {
    M <- sample(rep(visits, length.out = J)) # schedule independent of assignment
  } else {
    M <- ifelse(grp == "ctrl", visits[1], visits[2]) # breaks record exchangeability
  }
  subj <- rep(seq_len(J), times = M)
  u <- rnorm(J, sd = sqrt(icc))
  y <- u[subj] + rnorm(length(subj), sd = sqrt(1 - icc))
  data.frame(subj = subj, group = grp[subj], y = y)
}

# One-way ANOVA F, written out so the permutation loop is fast
AnovaF <- function(y, g) {
  g <- as.integer(factor(g)); n <- length(y); k <- max(g)
  y <- y - mean(y)
  totals <- as.numeric(rowsum(y, g)); counts <- tabulate(g)
  ss_a <- sum(totals^2 / counts); ss_w <- sum(y^2) - ss_a
  (ss_a / (k - 1)) / (ss_w / (n - k))
}

PermTest <- function(d, B = 199, unit = c("observation", "subject")) {
  unit <- match.arg(unit)
  F_obs <- AnovaF(d$y, d$group)
  subj_group <- tapply(d$group, d$subj, `[`, 1)       # one label per subject, named by subject
  F_perm <- replicate(B, {
    g_perm <- if (unit == "observation") {
      sample(d$group)
    } else {
      perm <- setNames(sample(subj_group), names(subj_group))  # shuffle labels across subjects
      perm[as.character(d$subj)]                               # carry each subject's visits along
    }
    AnovaF(d$y, g_perm)
  })
  (sum(F_perm >= F_obs) + 1) / (B + 1)
}

# Prespecified rejection fractions; the group-linked case lacks the same null justification.
Level <- function(visits, unit, design = "independent", R = 200) {
  p <- replicate(R, PermTest(SimulateVisits(n_subj = 20, visits = visits,
                    icc = 0.5, design = design), B = 99, unit = unit))
  rate <- mean(p <= 0.05)
  c(rejection = rate, mcse = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / R))
}
designs <- list(`4 visits each` = list(visits = 4, design = "independent"),
  `2 or 6; assignment independent` = list(visits = c(2, 6), design = "independent"),
  `2 vs 6; group-linked records` = list(visits = c(2, 6), design = "group-linked"))
grid <- expand.grid(design = names(designs), unit = c("observation", "subject"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
res <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  cfg <- designs[[grid$design[i]]]
  Level(cfg$visits, grid$unit[i], cfg$design)
}, numeric(2)))
comparison <- cbind(grid, as.data.frame(res))
comparison


                          design        unit rejection       mcse
1                  4 visits each observation     0.215 0.02904953
2 2 or 6; assignment independent observation     0.245 0.03041176
3   2 vs 6; group-linked records observation     0.180 0.02716616
4                  4 visits each     subject     0.035 0.01299519
5 2 or 6; assignment independent     subject     0.040 0.01385641
6   2 vs 6; group-linked records     subject     0.030 0.01206234


For the first two designs, person assignment is independent of outcomes and visit schedules, and the generated outcomes have no treatment effect. Relabeling people reproduces the person-level randomization under its sharp null, even with unequal prespecified visit counts. Shuffling individual profiles does not reproduce that assignment and can yield a high rejection fraction under positive intraclass correlation.
The third design is deliberately different: record length depends on original group. Equal outcome means do not make those observed records exchangeable. Neither whole-person relabeling nor a conservative-looking empirical rejection fraction supplies the missing justification. The distinction is the assignment/observation process, not merely balance of the final row counts.
In the code, grp assigns one label per person and M gives that person’s record length. Under the independent schedule, a six-visit record could have received either group label. Under the group-linked schedule, a six-visit record identifies the original group. Relabeling it as a two-visit-group record while keeping all six visits does not recreate the observation process under a new assignment. This is why preserving clusters is necessary but does not, by itself, prove exchangeability.


Code
par(mar = c(5, 4, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.6, 3.4), ylim = c(0, max(0.35, comparison$rejection + 2*comparison$mcse)),
     xaxt = "n", xlab = "Visit schedule", ylab = "Rejection fraction at nominal 0.05")
axis(1, at = 1:3, labels = c("Balanced", "Unequal;\nindependent", "Group-linked\nrecords"), cex.axis = 0.8)
for (j in 1:2) {
  unit <- c("observation", "subject")[j]
  a <- comparison[comparison$unit == unit, ]
  x <- 1:3 + c(-0.07, 0.07)[j]
  color <- c("#D55E00", "#2F80C8")[j]
  points(x, a$rejection, pch = 15 + j, col = color)
  arrows(x, pmax(0, a$rejection - 2*a$mcse), x, a$rejection + 2*a$mcse,
         angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.04, col = color)
}
abline(h = 0.05, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Profile shuffle", "Person shuffle"), col = c("#D55E00", "#2F80C8"),
       pch = 16:17, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)








Figure 1: Rejection fractions and plus/minus two MCSEs across 200 independent synthetic datasets. The third design ties record length to group and lacks the first two designs’ randomization-null justification. The dashed line marks 0.05, not a guarantee for every relabeling scheme.





The accompanying table retains the numerical results; colors distinguish observation (orange) and person (blue) schemes. The Monte Carlo uncertainty is substantial at 200 replicates, so do not attach a universal numerical rejection rate to a design label.
For a within-person factor, within-person swaps need their own randomization or symmetry argument; chronological visits are not freely exchangeable merely because they belong to one person. Blocks can restrict a justified assignment scheme. The permute documentation distinguishes within-plot, whole-plot, and blocking controls. None substitutes for stating the scientific null.

title: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests
text:
4 Distance-based tests: PERMANOVA
Now suppose each observation is a high-dimensional vector (a gene expression profile, a microbiome composition) and you want to test whether groups differ. One route is to choose a distance between observations, compute the N \times N distance matrix, and ask whether within-group distances are smaller than between-group distances.
PERMANOVA (Anderson 2001) does this with an ANOVA-style decomposition that needs only distances. Here N is the number of profiles, G is the number of groups, and n_k is group k’s size; G does not denote the number of genes. With d_{ij} the distance between profiles i and j,

\begin{aligned}
SS_T&=N^{-1}\sum_{i<j}d_{ij}^2,\\
SS_W&=\sum_k n_k^{-1}\sum_{i<j:\,i,j\in k}d_{ij}^2,\\
SS_A&=SS_T-SS_W,
\end{aligned}

and the pseudo-F is F = \frac{SS_A/(G-1)}{SS_W/(N-G)}. For Euclidean distance, the coordinate-wise sums of squares add before the ratio is formed: this is not the sum of univariate F-statistics. Other dissimilarities define another geometry; negative principal-coordinate eigenvalues can complicate the centroid interpretation. Permutation calibration still needs a justified null and relabeling scheme, regardless of distance.
The Euclidean identity behind the calculation is

\frac1N\sum_{i<j}\|\mathbf Y_i-\mathbf Y_j\|^2
=\sum_i\|\mathbf Y_i-\bar{\mathbf Y}\|^2.

Thus SS_T measures total spread around the overall center, SS_W adds spread around each group’s center, and their difference SS_A measures the separation of group centers in this geometry. Dividing by G-1 and N-G gives an ANOVA-like ratio. The familiar shape of that ratio does not establish an ordinary parametric F reference; the example calibrates it by relabeling.


Code
PermanovaF <- function(D, g) {
  D <- as.matrix(D); N <- nrow(D); groups <- unique(g); G <- length(groups)
  ss <- function(idx) sum(D[idx, idx][lower.tri(D[idx, idx])]^2) / length(idx)
  SS_T <- ss(seq_len(N))
  SS_W <- sum(sapply(groups, function(k) ss(which(g == k))))
  ((SS_T - SS_W) / (G - 1)) / (SS_W / (N - G))
}

set.seed(3)
X <- matrix(rnorm(40 * 5), 40, 5); g <- rep(c("a", "b"), each = 20)
X[g == "b", ] <- X[g == "b", ] + 0.5
D <- dist(X)                                  # Euclidean
F_obs <- PermanovaF(D, g)
F_perm <- replicate(999, PermanovaF(D, sample(g)))
c(F = F_obs, p = (sum(F_perm >= F_obs) + 1) / 1000)


       F        p 
4.938003 0.001000 


The following executes the same one-factor analysis in vegan, using an explicit permutation matrix from permute. It also checks the coordinate sum-of-squares identity. These packages are required for this and the later package examples.


Code
meta <- data.frame(g = factor(g))
perms <- permute::shuffleSet(nrow(X), nset = 199)
ad <- vegan::adonis2(D ~ g, data = meta, permutations = perms)
ss_total <- sum(sweep(X, 2, colMeans(X))^2)
ss_within <- sum(vapply(split(seq_len(nrow(X)), g), function(i) {
  sum(sweep(X[i, , drop = FALSE], 2, colMeans(X[i, , drop = FALSE]))^2)
}, numeric(1)))
f_coordinates <- ((ss_total - ss_within)/(nlevels(meta$g)-1)) /
                 (ss_within/(nrow(X)-nlevels(meta$g)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(F_obs, f_coordinates)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(F_obs, as.numeric(ad[1, "F"]))))
ad


Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
Permutation: free
Number of permutations: 199

vegan::adonis2(formula = D ~ g, data = meta, permutations = perms)
         Df SumOfSqs    R2     F Pr(>F)   
Model     1   24.172 0.115 4.938  0.005 **
Residual 38  186.016 0.885                
Total    39  210.189 1.000                
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The F-statistics agree. The earlier hand-coded run used 999 random relabelings and this package call uses a fresh set of 199, so their Monte Carlo p-values need not match and have different minimum grid values. A p-value comparison must use the same justified reference and sampling scheme.
For models with several terms, by=NULL, sequential terms, and marginal tests answer different questions. Adding covariates does not make every raw-label permutation exact. Record both the model and the permutation method; see the official adonis2 documentation.

4.1 What PERMANOVA actually tests
Equality of group distributions is a sufficient exchangeability null for the simple independent-sample label test above. In a randomized experiment a relevant sharp no-effect null can instead justify the assignment reference. Neither should be silently replaced by the weaker assertion that population centroids are equal. The pseudo-F is sensitive to differences in location (the groups’ centroids differ) and also to differences in dispersion (one group is more spread out). A significant PERMANOVA does not tell you which. With unbalanced groups the problem is worse: Anderson and Walsh (2013) show that rejection relative to an equal-centroid scientific null can be distorted by unequal dispersions, especially with unequal group sizes. Those populations do not satisfy the equal-distribution null, so a rejection is not automatically a false positive for that stronger null. Warton, Wright, and Wang (2012) make the related point that distance-based methods confound location and dispersion because the mean-variance relationship in count data makes the more abundant group look more variable.
PERMDISP (Anderson 2006) assesses group dispersions through distances to group centers. In vegan::betadisper, the default center is a spatial median; centroid and bias-adjustment choices should be recorded. It is a useful companion diagnostic/test with its own conditions. A non-significant PERMDISP does not establish equal dispersion or prove that a PERMANOVA result is solely a location difference. Interpret both tests with their power, the distance, the balance of the design, and plots or estimates of the relevant quantities.


Code
dispersion <- vegan::betadisper(D, meta$g, type = "median", bias.adjust = TRUE)
vegan::permutest(dispersion, permutations = 199)$tab


          Df      Sum Sq    Mean Sq         F N.Perm Pr(>F)
Groups     1  0.06956812 0.06956812 0.1564657    199  0.705
Residuals 38 16.89563867 0.44462207        NA     NA     NA




Code
set.seed(7)
visual <- list(
  `Population location shift` = rbind(matrix(rnorm(60), 30, 2),
      sweep(matrix(rnorm(60), 30, 2), 2, c(1.5, 0), "+")),
  `Population dispersion change` = rbind(matrix(rnorm(60), 30, 2),
      matrix(rnorm(60, sd = 2), 30, 2)))
limits <- range(unlist(visual)); labels <- rep(0:1, each = 30)
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (name in names(visual)) {
  a <- visual[[name]]
  plot(a, pch = 16, cex = 0.6, col = c("#D55E0088", "#2F80C888")[labels+1],
       xlim = limits, ylim = limits, xlab = "Feature 1", ylab = "Feature 2", main = name, asp = 1)
  centers <- rbind(colMeans(a[labels == 0, ]), colMeans(a[labels == 1, ]))
  points(centers, pch = 4, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = c("#D55E00", "#2F80C8"))
}








Figure 2: Two synthetic geometries, each with 30 independent people per group. The first changes the population center; the second changes only population dispersion. Crosses mark sample centroids, which fluctuate even when population centers coincide. A significant distance test does not identify the mechanism by itself.







4.2 Choice of distance
The distance defines what “different” means, and the choice is part of the hypothesis.

Euclidean on log-transformed expression: differences in every gene count equally; dominated by high-variance genes unless scaled.
Bray-Curtis on compositions or counts: ignores joint absences, bounded in [0, 1], standard in microbiome work; it is not a metric (fails the triangle inequality), which matters for some downstream methods.
Correlation distance 1 - r between profiles: ignores overall level, sensitive to shape.
Aitchison (Euclidean after centered log-ratio): a compositional geometry for strictly positive components; zeros require an explicit measurement-aware treatment that can affect the analysis.

Any of these distances can be used within a permutation statistic, but validity still depends on the null and allowed relabelings. What differs is the alternative the test is powered against and how location and dispersion are confounded.
For example, two nonconstant profiles have correlation distance zero if one is a positive affine transformation of the other, even if their overall levels and magnitudes differ greatly. Euclidean distance retains such changes. Scaling each feature to unit variance before Euclidean analysis changes the relative contribution of features and therefore changes the comparison. Choose the geometry from the scientific question, rather than treating distance as an interchangeable software option.
If preprocessing uses group labels, such as selecting genes for a large observed group contrast, repeat that selection within every permutation when it is part of the tested procedure. Holding a label-selected feature set fixed gives the permuted analyses an advantage the observed analysis did not have to meet. A fixed, label-invariant transformation can have a different justification. Finally, an omnibus rejection followed by feature-wise claims creates a further testing family; one significant global test does not automatically validate every follow-up claim.

title: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests
text:
5 Repeated measures in distance-based tests
A person-level factor needs an assignment or exchangeability argument at the person level. strata=subject_id restricts row permutations within people; it does not move whole people between treatment groups. With a constant group label within person it is not the generic between-person test desired here.
For balanced records, Plots with free whole-plot permutations and Within(type="none") can preserve visit order while moving whole people. This executable example has 12 people, three visits each, and randomly assigned person-level groups. Under the appropriate sharp no-effect null, the whole-person reference reproduces the assignment.


Code
set.seed(8)
subject_id <- rep(seq_len(12), each = 3); visit <- rep(1:3, 12)
assigned <- sample(rep(0:1, each = 6))
repeated_meta <- data.frame(subject_id, visit, treatment = assigned[subject_id])
u <- matrix(rnorm(12*3), 12, 3)
profiles <- u[subject_id, ] + matrix(rnorm(36*3), 36, 3)
control <- permute::how(plots = permute::Plots(strata = factor(subject_id), type = "free"),
                       within = permute::Within(type = "none"))
whole_people <- permute::shuffleSet(36, nset = 199, control = control)
cbind(original_person = subject_id[1:9],
      permuted_person = subject_id[whole_people[1, 1:9]],
      original_visit = visit[1:9], permuted_visit = visit[whole_people[1, 1:9]])


      original_person permuted_person original_visit permuted_visit

 [4,]               2              10              1              1
 [5,]               2              10              2              2
 [6,]               2              10              3              3
 [7,]               3               9              1              1
 [8,]               3               9              2              2
 [9,]               3               9              3              3

Whole-plot row permutations require compatible record structures. With unequal visit counts, do not force these balanced row blocks onto the data. A custom reassignment of person-level labels with statistic recomputation, as in PermTest(), can reproduce a known assignment when visits were prespecified independently of treatment. Informative follow-up or an observational disease grouping needs additional assumptions or a different analysis. See Units of analysis, replication, and study design.

title: Multivariate comparisons: permutation and distance-based tests
text:
6 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · MV-01 — Match the permutation to the design and null
Task type: Diagnosis and interpretation.
Twelve people are independently enrolled in an experiment and randomly assigned, six per treatment. Each contributes three repeated multivariate profiles. You want a treatment comparison. Describe a design-valid reassignment of treatment labels, explain why arbitrary profile-level relabeling is inappropriate, and say whether a significant PERMANOVA plus non-significant PERMDISP proves a pure centroid difference.
Ready to continue when: you can identify the randomization unit, preserve its dependent measurements, and limit the interpretation of an omnibus result.
Transfer: Why would subject-level exchangeability require additional justification in an observational disease comparison?


Hint

Reproduce the treatment assignment at the person level. Failure to reject a dispersion test does not establish equal dispersion.



Solution outline — open after trying

Under the appropriate randomization null, reassign the six treatment labels among people and carry each person’s profiles together. Arbitrary relabeling of the 36 profiles does not reproduce the experiment and breaks the within-person structure. Define the statistic and null before calibrating it; exact randomization inference uses the relevant sharp null, while weaker nulls need their own justification. A non-significant PERMDISP may reflect low power and does not isolate a centroid-only effect. The distance, statistic, design, and distributional alternatives still matter.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Modify the first example so that the groups have equal means but standard deviations 1 and 3, and estimate the level of the permutation test of the mean difference over 1000 simulated datasets. Then repeat with unequal group sizes (10 and 40), both ways round. Relate what you see to exchangeability.
Run the clustered-data example with icc = 0 and with icc = 0.9. How does the inflation of the observation-level test depend on the intraclass correlation and on the number of visits?
Verify numerically that PermanovaF() with Euclidean distance equals the sum over variables of the univariate ANOVA sums of squares, decomposed the same way.
Simulate two groups with identical centroids and different dispersions (multiply one group’s deviations by 2), unbalanced 15 versus 45, and estimate PERMANOVA’s rejection rate both ways round. This is the Anderson and Walsh result; see it yourself.

title: Omics analysis problems
text:
An analysis result needs a population meaning before it becomes a biological claim. A feature contrast, a network edge, a pseudo-value summary, and an omnibus multivariate comparison are different targets. Their uncertainty arguments must match the observation, sampling design, and estimator.
These pages build two habits: define what a feature or edge estimate means in the population, then calibrate the evidence for the claims being reported. Regression contrasts, pooling, imperfect adjustment, and residual covariance show how a plausible analysis can answer a different question from the one intended. Multivariate tests add a whole-profile question whose null and resampling unit also need to be explicit.
Multiplicity connects all of these problems. A paper may report thousands of features or millions of edges, so a collection of individually calibrated tests still needs a justified reporting rule. The multiple-testing page develops the distinction between a realized false fraction and an expected error rate, works through the adjustment algorithms, and separates dependence among tests from invalidity of the individual tests.

title: Omics analysis problems
text:
What you’ll learn

Define the analysis target: distinguish feature contrasts, marginal and adjusted associations, observation-indexed summaries, and omnibus differences.
Assess the evidence for the stated family: match uncertainty, dependence, resampling and multiplicity to the target, and limit the biological interpretation to what is identified.

Use the pages relevant to your research problem. Their checkpoints are completion targets for that topic; additional practice is optional. The group’s published manuscripts supply research case studies, while the self-contained numerical examples make particular arguments reproducible.

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text: Before reading: Sample correlation and the What is your estimator actually estimating? page; Influence functions explains the first-order expansion.

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text:
1 What is the population quantity?
A jackknife pseudo-value is constructed from a cohort-level estimator; its observation-level appearance does not by itself make it a measurement of a person’s biological network. Before using pseudo-values as outcomes, define the population quantity their group means or regression coefficients should estimate. Because the values share the full cohort and leave-one-out fits, they are not independent raw observations. Inference needs a justification for that construction and the sampling design.
The examples below use correlation to expose the effect of pooled group composition. The construction is a useful optional application of resampling and Influence functions; the main semiparametric learning path can proceed without it.

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text:
2 The construction
Let \hat\theta be any statistic computed from N observations, typically an estimate of some feature \theta(F) of the population distribution F, and let \hat\theta_{(-i)} be the same statistic computed with observation i removed. The jackknife pseudo-value for observation i is

\theta_i = N\,\hat\theta - (N - 1)\,\hat\theta_{(-i)}.

Rearranged, \theta_i = \hat\theta + (N-1)(\hat\theta - \hat\theta_{(-i)}): the overall estimate, plus N - 1 times the amount observation i moved it. An observation that pulls the estimate up gets a high pseudo-value; one that pulls it down gets a low one; one with no influence gets \hat\theta itself.
“The same statistic” means rerunning its required estimation steps on the delete-one data. Holding part of a fitted pipeline fixed defines a different deletion calculation and needs its own argument. Here an observation is an independent person with their pair of gene values; deleting one gene is not the same operation. For clustered sampling, a person-level deletion can remove several records at once.
The picture below (Figure 1) shows three observations from one sample of 20.





Pulls the correlation up

gene A
gene B





















correlation, all 20 points:  0.565
correlation without this one:  0.426
pseudo-value:  3.2

Barely moves it

gene A
gene B





















correlation, all 20 points:  0.565
correlation without this one:  0.565
pseudo-value:  0.6

Pulls the correlation down

gene A
gene B





















correlation, all 20 points:  0.565
correlation without this one:  0.728
pseudo-value:  -2.5



Figure 1: How a pseudo-value is built, for one sample of 20 observations on two genes whose true correlation is 0.5. Each panel highlights one observation (vermilion). The correlation is computed with all 20 observations and again without the highlighted one, and the pseudo-value is the first number plus 19 times the difference. An observation far out along the diagonal pulls the correlation up and gets a high pseudo-value. An observation near the center barely moves the correlation and gets about the overall value. An observation far off the diagonal pulls the correlation down and gets a low one. Pseudo-values are not correlations, and they can leave the interval from -1 to 1.





Code
PseudoValues <- function(x, statistic, ...) {
  n <- length(x)
  theta_all <- statistic(x, ...)
  sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) n * theta_all - (n - 1) * statistic(x[-i], ...))
}


Quenouille (1949, 1956) introduced leave-one-out recomputation to reduce bias; Tukey (1958) named the jackknife and proposed the pseudo-values, suggesting they could be treated approximately as independent observations. That suggestion is why pseudo-values are used as data today, and why they can mislead.

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
section: 3 Three facts you can check in a few lines of code
text:
3 Three facts you can check in a few lines of code
If \hat\theta = \bar x, then \theta_i = x_i exactly, so for the mean the pseudo-values are the data. Try it.
Indeed, (N-1)\bar x_{(-i)}=N\bar x-x_i. Substituting that identity into the definition cancels the entire cohort sum and leaves x_i. The cancellation works because a mean is a sum of fixed observation-level contributions. A correlation has estimated means and SDs in its numerator and denominator; deleting one person changes those quantities for every retained person.


Code
set.seed(1)
x <- rnorm(8)
all.equal(PseudoValues(x, mean), x)


[1] TRUE


The average of the pseudo-values is the bias-corrected jackknife estimate, \bar\theta = N\hat\theta - (N-1)\overline{\hat\theta_{(\cdot)}}. For the mean it equals \bar x. For sufficiently smooth statistics such as the variance example below, its difference from \hat\theta is often of order 1/N under suitable moments. Nonlinearity by itself does not establish this rate. A classic example is the plug-in variance, which divides by N and is biased low by the factor (N-1)/N. Its jackknife estimate is exactly the sample variance with divisor N - 1.


Code
PlugInVar <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x))^2)     # divisor N
c(plug_in = PlugInVar(x), mean_pseudovalue = mean(PseudoValues(x, PlugInVar)), var_N_minus_1 = var(x))


         plug_in mean_pseudovalue    var_N_minus_1 
       0.6369472        0.7279396        0.7279396 


For this divisor-N plug-in variance, the pseudo-value has the exact form

\theta_i=\frac{N}{N-1}(x_i-\bar x)^2.

Its average is the divisor-(N-1) sample variance. It still uses the pooled mean \bar x, so a person’s large value can reflect displacement of their group from that pooled center, rather than large within-group variation. This simple example foreshadows the correlation artifact below. If the starting statistic is instead R’s var() with divisor N-1, the exact pseudo-value formula changes; optional exercise 3 asks for it.
The sample variance of the pseudo-values gives the familiar jackknife variance formula. Let \bar\theta be their mean and \bar\theta_{(-\cdot)} the mean of the delete-one estimates. Centering the definition gives

\begin{aligned}
\theta_i-\bar\theta
&=-(N-1)(\hat\theta_{(-i)}-\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)}),\\
\frac{s_\theta^2}{N}
&=\frac{N-1}{N}\sum_i
    (\hat\theta_{(-i)}-\bar\theta_{(-\cdot)})^2.
\end{aligned}

Thus computing the usual s_\theta/\sqrt N from the pseudo-values reproduces the jackknife SE exactly. This is an algebraic identity between two formulas. Whether either consistently estimates sampling uncertainty still depends on the estimator’s smoothness, moments, and sampling design; the identity does not make the pseudo-values independent or justify an arbitrary regression SE.


Code
pv <- PseudoValues(x, var)
loo <- sapply(seq_along(x), function(i) var(x[-i]))     # leave-one-out estimates
n <- length(x)
c(jackknife_se = sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((loo - mean(loo))^2)),
  se_of_pseudovalue_mean = sd(pv) / sqrt(n))


          jackknife_se se_of_pseudovalue_mean 
              0.334519               0.334519

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text:
4 Pseudo-values as data
Two literatures took Tukey’s suggestion further and use pseudo-values as a response variable.
In survival analysis, a subject’s survival status at time t is unobserved if they were censored before t. Andersen, Klein, and Rosthøj (2003) compute the Kaplan-Meier estimate of S(t) with and without each subject, form the pseudo-value, and regress the pseudo-values on covariates with generalized estimating equations. The pseudo-value stands in for the unobservable indicator 1\{T_i > t\}. The same idea extends to cumulative incidence and restricted mean survival time. The theory (Graw, Gerds, and Schumacher 2009; Overgaard, Parner, and Pedersen 2017) establishes when this works, meaning when a regression of the pseudo-values on covariates estimates how the probability of surviving past t depends on the covariates. The estimand is an average of a per-subject quantity, and, under independent-subject sampling and suitable censoring/support conditions, the pseudo-value can have, to first order,1 the same conditional mean given the covariates as that per-subject quantity. A regression on the pseudo-values then estimates the regression of the indicator 1\{T_i > t\} on the covariates, which is what the analysis is after.
In sample-specific network estimation, LIONESS (Kuijjer et al. 2019) estimates a co-expression network for every sample, starting from a method that estimates one network from all N samples. With Pearson correlation as that method, \hat\theta is the correlation between two genes across all N samples, \hat\theta_{(-i)} is the same with sample i removed, and LIONESS defines sample i’s edge as

e_i = N\,\hat\theta - (N - 1)\,\hat\theta_{(-i)},

which is the pseudo-value of the correlation. The resulting per-sample edges are then compared between groups, for example with t-tests or limma, regressed on phenotypes, or clustered. Other single-sample network methods use related ideas. SSN (Liu et al. 2016) measures how the correlation changes when a sample is added to a reference set, and BONOBO (Saha et al. 2024) builds each sample’s coexpression from a Bayesian model whose prior is formed from all the other samples.


Code
# LIONESS edge for one gene pair = pseudo-value of the correlation
set.seed(2)
n <- 60
g1 <- rnorm(n); g2 <- 0.5 * g1 + sqrt(0.75) * rnorm(n)
r_all <- cor(g1, g2)
edge <- sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) n * r_all - (n - 1) * cor(g1[-i], g2[-i]))
c(mean_edge = mean(edge), r_all = r_all)


mean_edge     r_all 
0.5168562 0.5153655 


The mean edge, 0.517, is close to the pooled correlation, 0.515, as the second fact says.

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text:
5 What a pseudo-value measures
The trap is in how the number is read.
In both literatures the pseudo-value \theta_i is read as a noisy measurement of the quantity of interest for people like subject i (their survival probability, or their correlation). For survival, that reading holds to first order under stated conditions,2 because S(t) is an average of individual indicators, and the average pseudo-value among people like subject i estimates their survival probability. For a correlation, the reading fails in a way that can be written down: the average pseudo-value among people like subject i need not estimate their correlation.
A pseudo-value measures the influence of observation i on the statistic computed from the whole pooled sample. It is anchored at \hat\theta, the pooled estimate. If the sample is a mixture of two groups with different means, an observation from the smaller group sits far from the pooled center, has a large influence on the pooled correlation, and gets a pseudo-value that reflects its group membership. That pseudo-value says little about the correlation within its group.
The calculation below connects a pseudo-value to the pooled estimate plus the observation’s influence function, to first order. The practical version is this simulation: two groups with identical within-group correlation, different means, and a mean difference in their LIONESS edges that is entirely an artifact.


Code
set.seed(3)
n_ctrl <- 200; n_pat <- 800; rho <- 0.5; shift <- 2
group <- rep(c("control", "patient"), c(n_ctrl, n_pat))
n <- n_ctrl + n_pat
z1 <- rnorm(n); z2 <- rho * z1 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)
a <- z1 + shift * (group == "patient"); b <- z2 + shift * (group == "patient")
LionessEdge <- function(x, y) {
  n <- length(x); r <- cor(x, y)
  sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) n * r - (n - 1) * cor(x[-i], y[-i]))
}
e <- LionessEdge(a, b)
tapply(e, group, mean)                               # groups differ...


 control  patient 
1.078159 0.595102 


Code
c(control = cor(a[group == "control"], b[group == "control"]),
  patient = cor(a[group == "patient"], b[group == "patient"]))   # ...but the correlations do not


  control   patient 
0.5094897 0.4758453 


In this sample the smaller group, the controls, has a mean edge of 1.08 and the patients 0.60, while both groups’ correlations are about 0.5 (0.51 and 0.48, which differ only by sampling variation). In the vocabulary of the What is your estimator actually estimating? page, the estimand for a group’s edge is that group’s own correlation, and the group’s average edge converges to a different limit.
The direction is systematic: the smaller group gets the higher edges. The gap changes sign when the two sample sizes are swapped and vanishes at balance, although at balance each group’s mean edge is still far above the true correlation (about 0.75 against 0.5 in a large sample with a shift of 2). The picture below (Figure 2) shows the mechanism and the size of the effect.

Figure 2: Why the smaller group gets the higher edges. Left: the sample of 20 controls (open circles) and 80 patients (filled circles) from Association targets, pooling, and imperfect adjustment, with the patients shifted by 2 in both genes, so that the correlation within each group is 0.5. The pooled center, which averages over everyone, lies close to the patients and far from the controls, so a control has a larger influence on the pooled correlation. Right: what each group’s average edge converges to as the fraction of controls changes, with the shift fixed at 2. The dotted line marks the 20% controls of the simulation above. In this equal-variance mixture, the asymptotic gap vanishes if each gene is centered within its group before the edges are computed: the relevant pooled and group moments then agree. A variance difference can create an additional artifact that centering does not remove. Group standardization can align the required moments in this common-correlation example. These are repairs for the stated target mismatch, not a general proof of pseudo-value independence or regression coverage. Optional exercise 2 explores the mean and variance changes.

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
section: 6 When the average pseudo-value estimates what you want
text:
6 When the average pseudo-value estimates what you want
Earlier we described how pseudo-values are used: regress them on covariates, or compare their averages between groups. Behind that use is a claim that the average pseudo-value among people with covariates x estimates the quantity of interest for people like them. In the vocabulary of the What is your estimator actually estimating? page, that quantity is the estimand \theta(F_x), the same feature \theta (a correlation, a survival probability) evaluated on F_x, the distribution of the subpopulation with covariates x. The average pseudo-value is computed from data, so it is an estimator, and it converges to a limit. Pseudo-value regression works as intended when the limit equals the estimand, because then the coefficients describe how the quantity of interest changes with the covariates. This is a claim about what the regression estimates. Standard errors and p-values are a separate question.
The limit equals the estimand when the estimand is linear in the distribution, meaning that \theta(F) is an average \int h\,dF of something computed on each observation. Then the pseudo-value is exactly h(x_i), as the mean’s pseudo-values are the data, and the average pseudo-value among people with covariates x is the average of h in their subpopulation, which is \theta(F_x). Survival probabilities, cumulative incidences, and restricted means are of this kind for complete data. Their observed-data pseudo-value regressions additionally need the censoring and estimation conditions above. (With censoring, the Kaplan-Meier pseudo-value approximates that quantity to first order.)
Correlations, variances, and regression coefficients are nonlinear in F, so this exact linear-functional argument is unavailable. Their pseudo-values can carry the pooled sample’s composition into subgroup averages (see Figure 2). Whether a discrepancy occurs depends on the subgroup distributions and functional; nonlinearity alone does not prove a nonzero bias in every configuration. The relevant limit and remainder must be checked, as developed in Association targets, pooling, and imperfect adjustment.

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text:
7 Check the influence approximation (optional)
This numerical check uses a fresh bivariate-normal sample, separately from the earlier cohort example.


Code
set.seed(1)
n <- 500
x <- rnorm(n); y <- 0.6 * x + 0.8 * rnorm(n)

# Weighted correlation of (x, y) with weights w
WCor <- function(x, y, w) {
  cv <- cov.wt(cbind(x, y), wt = w, method = "ML")$cov
  cv[1, 2] / sqrt(cv[1, 1] * cv[2, 2])
}

# Numerical IF of the correlation at the empirical distribution, evaluated at a new point
NumericIF <- function(x0, y0, eps = 1e-4) {
  w <- c(rep((1 - eps) / n, n), eps)
  (WCor(c(x, x0), c(y, y0), w) - cor(x, y)) / eps
}

# Analytic IF, standardized with divisor N (the scaling of the functional at the empirical distribution)
SdN <- function(v) sqrt(mean((v - mean(v))^2))
AnalyticIF <- function(x0, y0) {
  r <- cor(x, y)
  xt <- (x0 - mean(x)) / SdN(x); yt <- (y0 - mean(y)) / SdN(y)
  xt * yt - r / 2 * (xt^2 + yt^2)
}

pts <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(2, 2), c(2, -2), c(-1, 3))
cbind(pts, numeric = apply(pts, 1, function(p) NumericIF(p[1], p[2])),
      analytic = apply(pts, 1, function(p) AnalyticIF(p[1], p[2])))


                 numeric      analytic
[1,]  0  0 -0.0007942872 -0.0007942872
[2,]  2  2  1.7040853368  1.7047466919
[3,]  2 -2 -5.9163710249 -5.9186147672
[4,] -1  3 -5.7475178557 -5.7507604588




Code
if_vals <- AnalyticIF(x, y)
c(if_based_se = sd(if_vals) / sqrt(n),
  fisher_se   = sqrt((1 - cor(x, y)^2)^2 / n))   # textbook SE of r under normality


if_based_se   fisher_se 
 0.02941070  0.03066164 


The two standard errors agree to within sampling noise (0.029 and 0.031 here). The influence-function version does not assume normal data, and the textbook formula does.
The second use is the link to pseudo-values. Removing observation i from F_N gives F_{N,-i} = F_N + \frac{1}{N-1}(F_N - \delta_{X_i}). Write \phi_N(x)=\operatorname{IF}(x;T,F_N) for the empirical influence function. Apply the expansion with G=F_{N,-i} and F=F_N, using \int\phi_N\,dF_N=0:

T(F_{N,-i})-T(F_N)\approx-\frac{\phi_N(X_i)}{N-1}.

Substitute into the pseudo-value \theta_i = T(F_N) + (N-1)\big(T(F_N) - T(F_{N,-i})\big):

\theta_i\approx T(F_N)+\phi_N(X_i).

For a sufficiently smooth plug-in functional, this deletion expansion can give the estimate plus its empirical influence value, with an O_p(1/N) error for a typical observation under suitable moment and local-curvature control.3 A generic root-N asymptotic expansion alone does not imply this deletion rate: the leave-one-out remainder is multiplied by N-1. This is the precise content of Tukey’s heuristic, and it is exact when T is linear (for the mean, \bar x + (x_i - \bar x) = x_i).


Code
r <- cor(x, y)
pv <- sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) n * r - (n - 1) * cor(x[-i], y[-i]))
summary(pv - (r + AnalyticIF(x, y)))   # differences are O(1/N)


      Min.    1st Qu.     Median       Mean    3rd Qu.       Max. 
-1.690e-02 -4.204e-04 -1.185e-05  3.534e-04  2.229e-04  5.668e-02

title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text:
8 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · PV-01 — Verify the linear pseudo-value case
Task type: Derivation and interpretation.
Let \hat\theta=N^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i), where h is a fixed function and the required expectation exists. Derive the delete-one estimate and show that N\hat\theta-(N-1)\hat\theta_{(-i)}=h(X_i). Explain which step need not hold for a nonlinear functional such as correlation.
Ready to continue when: you can derive the identity and explain why it does not make every pseudo-value a raw biological measurement.
Transfer: For h(x)=x^2, what does the average pseudo-value target, and how does that differ from the variance?


Hint

Write (N-1)\hat\theta_{(-i)} as the full sum with term i removed.



Solution outline — open after trying

Multiplying the full estimate by N gives \sum_jh(X_j). Multiplying the delete-one estimate by N-1 gives \sum_jh(X_j)-h(X_i). Subtraction leaves h(X_i). For a nonlinear statistic, multiplication by sample size does not turn the estimator into a sum of fixed observation contributions; the cohort and leave-one-out fits remain part of each pseudo-value.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Reproduce the two-group simulation above with 500 controls and 500 patients. What happens to the edge difference, and how do the two mean edges compare with the true correlation of 0.5? Then try 800 controls and 200 patients. What is the sign of the difference now?
Center each gene within its group (a - ave(a, group)) and recompute the edges. Then give the patients a larger within-group variance in gene a only (multiply their centered a values by 2) and check whether centering alone still fixes the problem. Use large groups (thousands) so that the bias is large compared with the noise.
Compute pseudo-values for the sample variance of a normal sample and plot them against (x_i - \bar x)^2. They are nearly, but not exactly, equal. Why “nearly”? In fact the relationship is an exact straight line, so find its slope and intercept as functions of N and s^2.

text:

Tukey, J. W. (1958). Bias and confidence in not-quite large samples (abstract). Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 29, 614.

The theory behind pseudo-value regression, including the conditions under which it estimates what it should.
