title: Jackknife pseudo-values
text:
Footnotes


“To first order” is a phrase from calculus. It means keeping the largest term of an approximation and dropping the smaller ones. The standard picture is a curve near one point: the tangent line follows the curve closely there, and the gap between them grows like the square of the distance from the point. For example, \sqrt{1 + x} \approx 1 + x/2 for small x, and the dropped terms are of order x^2. A second-order approximation keeps the next term as well.
Here the point is the pooled sample and the line is the influence function, a derivative defined in the Influence functions page. A pseudo-value is treated as the estimate computed from everyone plus one correction term for observation i, with everything smaller ignored. The ignored part is exactly zero when the quantity being estimated is linear in the distribution, as the mean is, and it can be large when the quantity is nonlinear and the group of interest differs from the pooled sample, as with the correlation in the next section. A claim “to first order” is only as good as the reason to think the ignored terms are small.↩︎
Results in statistics are proved by assuming conditions, such as independent observations, a correct model, or a large sample. “Under stated conditions” means the result is guaranteed when the conditions the authors list hold, and it can fail when they do not. It is a prompt to find the list and check each item against your data.
For pseudo-value regression with survival data, the conditions in the theory papers cited above include the following. The quantity being modeled is an average of a per-subject quantity, such as the probability of surviving past a fixed time, a cumulative incidence, or a restricted mean survival time. A simple sufficient censoring setup has independent subjects, censoring time independent of the joint event-time/covariate vector (including event type for competing risks), and positive censoring survival over the time range studied. Independence from covariates alone is not enough if censoring still depends on event time. The needed smoothness, moment, and large-sample conditions must also hold. And, as in any regression, the model for how the covariates relate to the average is adequate. When censoring depends on the covariates, pseudo-values built from the ordinary Kaplan-Meier estimate can be biased.↩︎
Here O_p(1/N) means multiplying the random error by N produces a sequence bounded in probability. It is a rate statement, not a promise that every realized error halves when N doubles. Under the stated local controls it is smaller than the root-N sampling scale, since N^{-1}/N^{-1/2}\to0. A bound for a typical observation also need not be a uniform bound over the most extreme observations in a growing sample.
Here the remainder is the leftover from the expansion above, evaluated at one observation. For a typical observation it is tiny, but it is larger for an observation with a very large influence function, because the leftover grows with the square of the influence. The code below shows this: most differences are within 0.001 in absolute value, and the largest, at an extreme point, is about 0.06 when N = 500.↩︎

title: Network inference from omics data
text: Before reading: Expression matrices, covariance, and estimands; follow influence-function links for sensitivity calculations.

title: Network inference from omics data
section: 1 Define the edge before estimating it
text:
1 Define the edge before estimating it
Let X and Y be two measured features in a specified population, and let Z be a chosen adjustment set. Three targets recur:









Edge target
Meaning
What zero does not generally establish




\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)
Marginal association across units in that population
Independence or absence of a shared driver


E[(X-m_X(Z))(Y-m_Y(Z))]
Average conditional covariance after conditional-mean adjustment
Conditional independence or a direct biological interaction


A precision-matrix partial correlation
Linear residual association after adjusting for the other modeled features
Conditional independence outside the relevant Gaussian model, or causal regulation




The normalized version of the second target is a residual correlation, not generally the average of conditional correlations. A differential-network estimand is a contrast between the same edge definition in two specified populations. State the scale, adjustment set, and feature universe before choosing the estimator. The expression examples below transfer only after the measurement assumptions for the new assay have been checked.
For Pearson correlation, normalization means

\rho=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}
{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}.

Covariance retains the measurement units; correlation divides them out using each variable’s spread. Removing a conditional mean changes the variables being related, while normalizing changes their scale. Keep these operations separate. An average residual product, its normalized correlation, and a precision-matrix entry are three different edge definitions even when computed from the same assay.

title: Network inference from omics data
text:
2 What a co-expression network is
A gene co-expression network has genes as nodes and, for each pair of genes, an edge weight that measures how strongly the two genes’ expression levels move together across samples. That last phrase is the one to hold onto. A population edge is a functional of a specified distribution, estimated from a cohort. Its estimator is not a direct measurement of regulation in an individual cell or molecule. Every property of the network is inherited from the cohort it was computed on, which is why the What is your estimator actually estimating? page applies to networks with full force.
Three decisions define a network: the association measure, whether edges are marginal or conditional, and how weights become a graph. Each has consequences for what the network can detect, how it behaves under heterogeneity, and what it costs to compute.

title: Network inference from omics data
text:
3 Association measures










Measure
Main use
Transformation behavior
Main caution




Pearson r
Linear association
Unchanged by positive affine rescaling of either variable; a sign reversal flips its sign
Sensitive to tails, mixtures, and mean shifts


Spearman \rho_S
Rank association
Unchanged by strictly increasing transformations of each variable
Subgroup shifts can change pooled ranks


Kendall \tau
Concordance
Unchanged by strictly increasing transformations of each variable
Ties and their handling matter


Biweight midcorrelation
Robust association
Uses robust centering, scaling, and outlier downweighting
Robustness depends on the definition and nondegenerate scale estimates


Distance correlation
General dependence
Translation and scalar-rescaling invariant; not invariant to arbitrary affine transformations
Population zero characterizes independence under moment conditions; finite-sample estimation still needs calibration


Mutual information
General dependence
Population quantity invariant to invertible transformations under suitable conditions
Estimated values depend on density, binning, and tuning choices


Partial correlation
Linear residual association
Depends on the conditioning variables and fitted covariance model
Zero implies conditional independence only in special models such as the Gaussian model




Two properties matter most for our work.
Invariance to transformation. Strictly increasing transformations preserve pooled ranks. A sample-specific normalization, or a shift applied only within one group, need not preserve those ranks. Rank measures can therefore change when group composition changes. Invariance to a common transformation is not robustness to heterogeneity.
Influence and outliers. Pearson’s influence function has unbounded local sensitivity, although the correlation itself remains in [-1,1]. Rank-based and robust measures offer different forms of protection, but none establishes a biological interaction or removes an incorrect population target. The next example shows a large effect of one outlying pair on Pearson correlation.


Code
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
x <- rnorm(n); y <- 0.3 * x + rnorm(n)
x[1] <- 6; y[1] <- 6                       # one outlying sample
c(pearson = cor(x, y), spearman = cor(x, y, method = "spearman"),
  pearson_without = cor(x[-1], y[-1]))


        pearson        spearman pearson_without 
      0.5722860       0.1633133       0.2163756

title: Network inference from omics data
text:
4 Marginal versus conditional dependence
A Pearson edge between genes A and B is marginal: it is nonzero if A and B co-vary for any reason, including both being driven by a third gene C, or by a cell-type proportion, or by batch. A conditional edge refers to a specified conditioning set. A full-feature graphical model conditions on the other modeled features; it does not follow that conditioning on every measured variable answers the biological question. Selection variables, mediators, and colliders can change associations. For Gaussian data the conditional edges are the partial correlations, read off the inverse covariance (precision) matrix \Omega = \Sigma^{-1}:

\rho_{AB \mid \text{rest}} = -\frac{\Omega_{AB}}{\sqrt{\Omega_{AA}\,\Omega_{BB}}}.

A zero partial correlation means conditional independence (under Gaussianity), and the graph of nonzero partial correlations is the Gaussian graphical model. Conditioning changes the estimand; it does not automatically make a network sparse or regulatory. Missing common causes, measurement error, selection, and the chosen feature universe can all change the interpretation.
“Rest” means the same specified set of the other p-2 features for this pair. If we keep only three genes, the A–B edge conditions on the third. If we add 100 genes, it conditions on a larger set and is a different population quantity. The minus sign in the precision formula comes from inverting the pair’s conditional covariance matrix: for a matrix with entries a,c,c,b, the inverse has off-diagonal entry -c/(ab-c^2). Dividing that precision entry by the square root of its two diagonal entries and changing the sign recovers c/\sqrt{ab}.


Code
set.seed(2)
n <- 500
c_gene <- rnorm(n)
a <- 0.8 * c_gene + rnorm(n, sd = 0.6)
b <- 0.8 * c_gene + rnorm(n, sd = 0.6)    # A and B share a driver C, no direct link
X <- cbind(a, b, c_gene)
cor(a, b)                                  # marginal: strongly correlated


[1] 0.661491


Code
Omega <- solve(cov(X))
-Omega[1, 2] / sqrt(Omega[1, 1] * Omega[2, 2])   # partial, given C: about zero


[1] 0.002569492




Code
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(a, b, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = "#2F80C866", xlab = "Feature A", ylab = "Feature B",
     main = sprintf("Marginal correlation: %.2f", cor(a, b)))
plot(a - 0.8*c_gene, b - 0.8*c_gene, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = "#D55E0066",
     xlab = "A minus its true conditional mean", ylab = "B minus its true conditional mean",
     main = "Shared driver removed")








Figure 1: One synthetic shared-driver example. The raw pair is associated across people; removing the true conditional means given C removes that shared component. Zero residual association in this Gaussian construction is not a general independence criterion.





In this shared-driver generator, A and B each have variance 0.8^2+0.6^2=1, and their covariance is 0.8^2\operatorname{Var}(C)=0.64. Their population marginal correlation is therefore 0.64. Subtracting 0.8C leaves the two independent noise terms, each with SD 0.6, giving residual covariance zero. The plotted sample correlation fluctuates around these population values. The conditional-independence interpretation here follows from the generator’s independent errors and Gaussian model, rather than from the label “adjusted.”

4.1 Zero covariance can hide dependence
If X is symmetric about zero and Y=X^2, then E[X]=E[X^3]=0 and \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0, despite a deterministic relationship. Taking Z constant makes this a zero residual-covariance example as well. A zero average conditional covariance can also arise by cancellation of positive and negative conditional covariances across strata. Gaussian conditional independence uses the joint Gaussian model, not zero covariance alone.


Code
x_grid <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 201)
plot(x_grid, x_grid^2, pch = 16, cex = 0.55, col = "#2F80C8",
     xlab = "X", ylab = "Y = X squared", main = "Zero linear covariance; complete nonlinear dependence")








Figure 2: A schematic nonlinear relationship with zero Pearson covariance by symmetry. A missing Pearson edge does not mean the two features are independent. Points are a deterministic grid for illustration, not a random sample for a p-value.







4.2 The p > N problem
Let X_c be the centered N\times p data matrix. The sample covariance is S=X_c^\top X_c/(N-1). Centering makes the rows sum to zero, so its rank is at most N-1. Thus S is singular when p\ge N (and can be singular earlier through collinearity): there is no unique ordinary inverse to plug into the partial-correlation formula. Three standard approaches add structure:

Shrinkage (Schäfer and Strimmer 2005; Ledoit and Wolf 2004): \hat\Sigma_\lambda = (1-\lambda)S + \lambda T for a simple target T, invertible when the target is positive definite and the shrinkage weight lies in (0,1], under suitable shrinkage estimators. Some targets have analytic tuning rules; other choices require estimation or tuning. The result is generally dense.
Graphical lasso (Friedman, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2008): maximize the Gaussian log-likelihood with an \ell_1 penalty on \Omega. Sparse result; the penalty \lambda is the sparsity knob, chosen by cross-validation, EBIC, or StARS (Liu, Roeder, and Wasserman 2010). Package glasso, or huge for a wrapper with selection.
Neighborhood selection (Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2006): regress each gene on all others with the lasso; the two directional selections are combined with a stated OR or AND rule. This and graphical lasso target related Gaussian conditional-association structures through different optimization problems; they are not algebraically equivalent.

These methods regularize the estimated covariance, precision matrix, or nodewise regressions. Their tuning affects both weights and selected edges; individual transformed edge weights need not all move toward zero. Comparing two such networks estimated with the same \lambda but different sample sizes is not a like-for-like comparison. This is a trap in differential network analysis.
Regularization makes estimation possible by introducing a target, sparsity, or another structural assumption; it does not recover an arbitrary population precision matrix from insufficient information. A nonzero penalized edge is a model-selection result, not automatically a rejection of a null with a calibrated p-value. Missing values create another issue: computing each pair on a different subset can mix populations and produce a matrix that is not positive semidefinite. State how the common population and covariance estimate are defined before interpreting the graph.

title: Network inference from omics data
section: 5 From weights to a graph, and the multiple-testing problem
text:
5 From weights to a graph, and the multiple-testing problem
An association matrix already defines a weighted network. Three common ways to transform it or select an unweighted graph are:

Hard threshold: keep |r| > c. Simple; the choice of c is arbitrary and changes every downstream summary.
Soft threshold: An unsigned WGCNA-style adjacency a_{ij}=|r_{ij}|^\beta, with \beta chosen for approximate scale-free topology (Langfelder and Horvath 2008; Zhang and Horvath 2005). This maps strong negative and positive correlations to similar positive adjacency weights. Signed variants use different transformations, such as \{(1+r_{ij})/2\}^\beta. State which network is being built; a scale-free fit criterion is a modeling heuristic, not proof of biological topology.
Significance: test each edge, adjust for p(p-1)/2 tests, keep the rejections. For i.i.d. bivariate-normal pairs, Fisher’s z=\operatorname{atanh}(r) has a familiar large-sample variance approximation 1/(N-3). It is not a reference for arbitrary measured features or missing-pair patterns.

The significance route brings the multiple-testing problem into focus. With p = 10{,}000 genes there are about 5 \times 10^7 edges. BH needs independence or a suitable PRDS condition for the p-values. Shared-edge dependence need not meet those conditions; its presence alone does not prove they fail either. A permutation calibration can account for joint dependence only when its relabeling is justified by the tested null and study design. Between-group label permutation addresses a group-comparison null; it does not generally test that an individual population correlation is zero. See the Multiple testing when the tests are not independent page for alternatives and conditions.

title: Network inference from omics data
text:
6 Differential networks
First separate an edge difference from a difference in two significance labels. Suppose the estimated Fisher-transformed correlations are 0.30 (SE 0.14) and 0.28 (SE 0.15) in independent groups. Their individual normal-reference p-values are about 0.032 and 0.062: one crosses 0.05 and the other does not. But the estimated difference is only 0.02, with SE \sqrt{0.14^2+0.15^2}\approx0.205. There is little evidence of a difference. Testing the contrast directly answers the differential-edge question; subtracting two thresholded graphs does not.
The question “do the networks differ between patients and controls” has three main formulations, in increasing order of what they demand.
Edge by edge. For two independent samples, Fisher’s z difference,

\begin{aligned}
d_z&=\operatorname{atanh}(r_1)-\operatorname{atanh}(r_2),\\
v_z&=\frac1{N_1-3}+\frac1{N_2-3},\\
T_z&=d_z/\sqrt{v_z}\\
&\approx\ N(0,1),
\end{aligned}

tests one edge. The displayed reference is for independent i.i.d. samples from nondegenerate bivariate-normal populations under the equal-correlation null. Under other distributions its variance approximation can fail; equal group means or Gaussian marginals alone do not establish joint bivariate normality. Use an appropriate influence-function or bootstrap variance, or a permutation scheme justified for the actual null. Equal correlations alone do not make group labels exchangeable.


Code
FisherZTest <- function(r1, n1, r2, n2) {
  stopifnot(n1 > 3, n2 > 3, abs(r1) < 1, abs(r2) < 1)
  z <- (atanh(r1) - atanh(r2)) / sqrt(1 / (n1 - 3) + 1 / (n2 - 3))
  c(z = z, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)))
}
FisherZTest(r1 = 0.6, n1 = 40, r2 = 0.2, n2 = 60)


         z          p 
2.32293885 0.02018244 


Whole precision matrix. Methods that estimate the difference \Omega_1 - \Omega_2 directly (Zhao, Cai, and Li 2014) or test it entry-wise with a valid multiple-testing procedure (Xia, Cai, and Cai 2015). Direct difference estimation changes the estimation problem, but still requires tuning, sparsity/model assumptions, and an evaluation design appropriate to unequal sample sizes.
Sample-specific networks (the Jackknife pseudo-values page). Construct observation-indexed summaries and define the population contrast they are intended to estimate. Cohort-derived pseudo-values share estimated quantities, so treating them as independent raw measurements in a t-test or limma is not automatically valid. An inferential argument must handle their expansion, centering, and shared estimation, in addition to the mean/variance artifacts discussed in the linked guide.
Within-group sample correlations already center and scale within each group, so different group means alone do not create a difference between those correlations. Pooled pseudo-value constructions can inherit between-group shifts, as the Jackknife pseudo-values page demonstrates. Precision-matrix contrasts, correlation contrasts, and contrasts of observation-level network summaries are distinct targets; assess each on its own definition and assumptions.

title: Network inference from omics data
text:
7 Computation
The numbers you should know before planning an analysis.
Edges scale as p^2. A network on p genes has p(p-1)/2 edges: 499,500 for p = 1000, 2 \times 10^8 for p = 20{,}000. One dense network of 20,000 genes in double precision is 3.2 decimal GB (about 2.98 GiB), before temporary arrays; the unique upper-triangle entries require about 1.6 GB. Retaining one per person rapidly multiplies that cost. Restricting the feature universe changes the target graph and tested family; outcome-dependent filtering needs an inferential justification. Prespecified pathways or streaming edge summaries can reduce computation.
One correlation matrix is cheap. cor() on an N \times p matrix costs O(N p^2) and is dominated by matrix cross-products and associated centering/scaling operations.


Code
set.seed(3)
N <- 100; p <- 1000
X <- matrix(rnorm(N * p), N, p)
system.time(R_all <- cor(X))


   user  system elapsed 
  0.029   0.001   0.030 


Sample-specific networks the naive way are N times that, and the leave-one-out recomputation is wasteful: each cor(X[-i, ]) recomputes a cross-product that differs from the full one by a single rank-one term. Update the sufficient statistics instead.


Code
# Leave-one-out correlation matrices for the rows in `idx`, from one cross-product,
# by rank-one updates. Assumes N > 2 and no constant columns.
LooCorAll <- function(X, idx = seq_len(nrow(X))) {
  stopifnot(is.matrix(X), all(is.finite(X)), nrow(X) > 2,
            length(idx) >= 1, all(idx == as.integer(idx)), all(idx >= 1), all(idx <= nrow(X)))
  n <- nrow(X)
  X <- sweep(X, 2, colMeans(X))  # translation preserves LOO correlations; reduces cancellation
  s <- colSums(X); C <- crossprod(X)
  lapply(idx, function(i) {
    s_i <- s - X[i, ]
    C_i <- C - tcrossprod(X[i, ])
    V <- (C_i - tcrossprod(s_i) / (n - 1)) / (n - 2)       # leave-one-out covariance
    if (any(!is.finite(V)) || any(diag(V) <= 0)) stop("Degenerate leave-one-out variance")
    V / sqrt(tcrossprod(diag(V)))                          # to correlation
  })
}
i <- 7
all.equal(LooCorAll(X[, 1:50], idx = i)[[1]], cor(X[-i, 1:50]), check.attributes = FALSE)


[1] TRUE


Code
# Keep this teaching benchmark small; storing many full large-feature matrices costs substantial memory.
X_bench <- X[, 1:250]
system.time(loo_naive  <- lapply(1:20, function(i) cor(X_bench[-i, ])))


   user  system elapsed 
  0.038   0.001   0.039 


Code
system.time(loo_update <- LooCorAll(X_bench, idx = 1:20))


   user  system elapsed 
  0.011   0.006   0.014 


Code
all.equal(loo_naive[[1]], loo_update[[1]], check.attributes = FALSE)


[1] TRUE


For the same 20 matrices the update version avoids repeated full-data cross-products; compare the timings on your machine rather than assuming a fixed speedup. The LIONESS network for sample i is then N * R_all - (N - 1) * loo[[i]], computed and summarized one sample at a time (call LooCorAll() with one idx at a time) so the number of retained dense matrices does not grow with the number of people. Cross-products, full estimates, updates, and temporary arrays still require several dense matrices; streaming is O(p^2) working memory, not literally one matrix. The update version is still O(p^2) per sample, which is the floor; it just avoids the factor of N from redoing the cross-product.
Permutation references multiply everything. A permutation test with B permutations costs B times the analysis. For a whole-network statistic on filtered genes this is routine; for per-edge permutation p-values across 10^7 edges it is not, and you need either a parametric reference you have checked by simulation or another calibrated approximation. Pooling edges requires assumptions about their null distributions and does not automatically solve the computational or inferential problem.
Follow the complete calculation in An end-to-end residual-network analysis, from a prespecified edge family and nuisance fits through uncertainty, multiplicity, and simulation evaluation.

title: Network inference from omics data
text:
8 Exercises
Checkpoints are completion targets for this page. Additional practice below is optional. Each checkpoint gives a completion standard, a hint, and a solution outline.


Checkpoint · NET-01 — Identify the association represented by an edge
Task type: Derivation and interpretation.
Let Z,U,V be independent standard normals, with X=Z+U and Y=Z+V. Calculate the marginal correlation and the covariance after subtracting E[X\mid Z] and E[Y\mid Z]. Explain the shared driver and why a marginal edge does not establish direct regulation. Give a dependent nonlinear pair with zero covariance. Is zero average residual covariance alone a general conditional-independence criterion?
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish marginal and residual targets and describe what the edge does and does not establish.
Transfer: What changes if U and V have covariance 0.3 instead of being independent?


Hint

Both marginal variances are 2. The conditional-mean residuals are U and V.



Solution outline — open after trying

The covariance of X and Y is 1 and each variance is 2, so the marginal correlation is 1/2. After subtracting Z, the residual covariance is E[UV]=0. Shared variation in Z explains the marginal edge. In this constructed model the independent errors also imply conditional independence, but a zero average residual covariance does not establish it in general; conditional covariances can cancel, or dependence can be nonlinear. For example, a centered symmetric normal X and Y=X^2 are dependent with E[X^3]=0, hence zero covariance; take Z constant for a residual-covariance example.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Simulate two genes with a strong monotone but nonlinear relationship (y = \exp(x) plus noise). Compare Pearson, Spearman, and distance correlation (package energy). Then add a mean shift to half the samples and see which measures move.
Generate data from a sparse Gaussian graphical model with p = 50 and N = 40 (package huge has generators). Estimate the partial correlation network with shrinkage and with the graphical lasso at two values of \lambda. Count true and false edges.
Take the LIONESS computation above and add within-group centering as a preprocessing step for a two-group X. Start with equal within-group correlations and equal within-group variances and check the group contrast. Then change the variance of one gene in one group while keeping its correlation fixed. Does centering alone still remove the artifact?
Estimate how much memory and time a LIONESS analysis of 200 samples by 15,000 genes would need if you stored every network, and then redesign it so that you store only the per-edge t-statistics between two groups.

title: Evaluating a statistical method
text: Before reading: Read What is your estimator actually estimating?; basic means, variance, and confidence intervals are assumed.

title: Evaluating a statistical method
section: 1 Evaluate a claim, not a method name
text:
1 Evaluate a claim, not a method name
A method can have a small standard error and still answer the wrong question. Before comparing procedures, write the population target \psi(P), the limit of each procedure, and the claim being evaluated: consistency, confidence-interval coverage, efficiency, robustness, prediction, or computational reliability. Those claims require different evidence.
For an omics example, a pooled coefficient, an adjusted group contrast, and a standardized population contrast may differ even with infinitely many participants. First use What is your estimator actually estimating? to determine whether a comparison has a common target. Then assess finite-sample behavior.
There are three sources of discrepancy to keep apart. Target mismatch means the procedure approaches a different population quantity. Sampling error is variation caused by which people enter a finite dataset. Numerical error arises when the implementation cannot compute its intended answer accurately. Increasing the sample size, increasing simulation replicates, and tightening an optimizer’s tolerance address different problems.

title: Evaluating a statistical method
section: 3 A precise example: shrinkage toward zero
text:
3 A precise example: shrinkage toward zero
Let independent Y_i\sim N(\mu,1) and suppose the target is \mu. Compare the sample mean with \tilde\mu=0.9\bar Y. Their limits are \mu and 0.9\mu. For the second procedure,

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Bias}(\tilde\mu)&=-0.1\mu,\\
\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\mu)&=0.81/n.
\end{aligned}

Its sampling SD is smaller: multiplying the sample mean by 0.9 multiplies its variance by 0.9^2. But

\tilde\mu-\mu=0.9(\bar Y-\mu)-0.1\mu.

The first term is sampling noise that shrinks with n; the second is a fixed displacement from the target. A smaller SE can describe the first term correctly while omitting the second completely. The bias measured in units of sampling SD is -\mu\sqrt n/9, whose magnitude grows when \mu\ne0.
Let c_n be the 97.5th percentile of t_{n-1}. Compare the usual mean interval with the naively shrunken interval,

\begin{aligned}
&\bar Y\pm c_n\frac{s}{\sqrt n},\\
&\tilde\mu\pm c_n\frac{0.9s}{\sqrt n}.
\end{aligned}

Under the normal generator, the first interval has exact 95% coverage for \mu. The second is the first interval multiplied by 0.9, so it covers 0.9\mu at 95%, but generally does not cover \mu at that rate. At \mu=0 those targets coincide. At \mu=1, the interval shrinks around 0.9 while the target stays at 1. Dividing the shrunken estimate and both endpoints by 0.9 recovers ordinary mean inference; simply shrinking the center and SE does not provide that correction.
The MSE decomposition makes a different tradeoff:

\operatorname{MSE}(\tilde\mu)=0.01\mu^2+0.81/n.

At \mu=1,n=10 this is 0.091, less than the sample mean’s 0.1. That point-estimation advantage does not establish consistency or interval coverage. For a nonzero fixed \mu, the MSE advantage disappears once n\ge19/\mu^2. Always say which loss or inferential property makes one procedure preferable.

3.1 Consistency alone is not enough for inference
Now let the multiplier approach one: \tilde\mu_n=(1-n^{-1/4})\bar Y. Both the multiplier and the sample mean converge to their desired limits, so this estimator is consistent. Its bias is nevertheless -\mu n^{-1/4}, larger than its root-n sampling SD. At a nonzero target, ordinary centered intervals can still fail increasingly badly. A multiplier 1-n^{-1} instead has bias negligible at the root-n scale. This is the same reason a semiparametric inference argument controls the rate of a nuisance remainder, rather than asking only whether it converges to zero.

title: Evaluating a statistical method
section: 4 Compare procedures on the same datasets
text:
4 Compare procedures on the same datasets
The following experiment uses the same simulated sample for both procedures in each replicate. This keeps the comparison tied to the same scenarios and permits a paired analysis. Pairing reduces Monte Carlo uncertainty when the performance contributions have positive covariance; it is not a universal variance-reduction theorem for any two algorithms. All values are synthetic, with truth supplied by the generator.


Code
set.seed(61)
n_sim <- 1000
records <- list(); i <- 0
for (mu in c(0, 1)) for (n in c(20, 100, 500)) {
  y <- matrix(rnorm(n * n_sim, mean = mu), nrow = n)
  average <- colMeans(y)
  sample_sd <- sqrt(colSums(sweep(y, 2, average)^2) / (n - 1))
  for (shrink in c(1, 0.9)) {
    estimate <- shrink * average
    se <- shrink * sample_sd / sqrt(n)
    covered <- abs(estimate - mu) <= qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se
    i <- i + 1
    records[[i]] <- data.frame(mu = mu, n = n, replicate = seq_len(n_sim),
      method = if (shrink == 1) "Mean" else "0.9 x mean",
      estimate, se, covered, squared_error = (estimate - mu)^2)
  }
}
records <- do.call(rbind, records)
cells <- split(records, interaction(records$mu, records$n, records$method))
performance <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cells, function(d) {
  R <- nrow(d); coverage <- mean(d$covered)
  data.frame(d[1, c("mu", "n", "method")],
    bias = mean(d$estimate) - d$mu[1], empirical_sd = sd(d$estimate),
    mean_se = mean(d$se), MSE = mean(d$squared_error), coverage,
    bias_mcse = sd(d$estimate) / sqrt(R),
    coverage_mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / R))
}))
print(performance, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

Each row in records belongs to one method on one replicate; the replicate ID is shared across methods within the same scenario. Summaries are computed afterwards. MCSE describes uncertainty in such a summary because the simulation uses finitely many datasets. Here bias MCSE is empirical SD divided by \sqrt R, whereas the SE reported by a method scales with \sqrt n. Increasing R improves knowledge of the method’s behavior at that n; it does not improve the method’s interval for an individual dataset.
For example, an empirical SD of 0.10 across 1,000 datasets gives a bias MCSE of about 0.0032. It does not give each dataset an estimation SE of 0.0032. This distinction matters when reporting small bias or coverage differences.


Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (target in c(0, 1)) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(15, 650), ylim = c(0.2, 1), log = "x",
       xlab = "Independent observations n", ylab = "Coverage of mu",
       main = paste("mu =", target))
  abline(h = 0.95, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
  for (j in 1:2) {
    method_name <- c("Mean", "0.9 x mean")[j]
    a <- performance[performance$mu == target & performance$method == method_name, ]
    a <- a[order(a$n), ]
    color <- c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00")[j]
    lines(a$n, a$coverage, type = "b", pch = j + 14, col = color)
    arrows(a$n, a$coverage - 2 * a$coverage_mcse,
           a$n, a$coverage + 2 * a$coverage_mcse,
           angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.04, col = color)
  }
  legend("bottomleft", c("Mean", "0.9 x mean"), col = c("#2F80C8", "#D55E00"),
         pch = 15:16, lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}








Figure 1: A smaller sampling SD does not remove target bias. At mu = 1 the shrunken procedure’s coverage deteriorates with n; the null scenario alone would conceal that problem. Bars show plus/minus two Monte Carlo standard errors.





At \mu=0, both methods have exactly the same coverage indicators in this construction: multiplying the entire interval by a positive constant does not change whether it includes zero. That reassuring null scenario conceals the failure at nonzero targets. In the right panel the shrunken estimator’s SE tracks its sampling SD, yet its intervals increasingly miss \mu=1.

4.1 Calculate uncertainty in a paired difference
Let C_{A,r} and C_{B,r} indicate coverage by methods A and B on dataset r. Form d_r=C_{B,r}-C_{A,r}, which is −1, 0, or 1. Then

\begin{aligned}
\widehat\Delta_{\rm cov}&=\bar d,\\
\widehat{\operatorname{MCSE}}(\bar d)&=s_d/\sqrt R.
\end{aligned}

A value −1 means B misses where A covers; zero means they agree; 1 means B alone covers. The variance is based on these within-dataset differences. It includes the methods’ covariance, which would be lost by treating the marginal coverage estimates as independent.


Code
a <- subset(records, mu == 1 & n == 500 & method == "Mean")
b <- subset(records, mu == 1 & n == 500 & method == "0.9 x mean")
stopifnot(identical(a$replicate, b$replicate))
d <- as.integer(b$covered) - as.integer(a$covered)
c(coverage_difference = mean(d), paired_MCSE = sd(d) / sqrt(length(d)))


coverage_difference         paired_MCSE 
        -0.63500000          0.01743786 


The same recipe works for differences in squared error, interval length, runtime, or dataset-level FDP: form the relevant pair of contributions, subtract, then summarize across independent datasets. Different performance measures require their own contributions, not a single universal binomial SE.

title: Evaluating a statistical method
text:
5 Failures are part of performance
Suppose an algorithm returns valid intervals in 90 of 100 replicates, and 86 of those cover the target. Report success rate 90/100, coverage conditional on success 86/90, and joint success-and-coverage 86/100. The last quantity treats failure as no usable covering interval and must be labeled that way; it is not a conventional coverage calculation over 100 returned intervals. Do not quietly delete failed replicates or report only the successful methods’ fastest runs.
Record warnings, convergence, nonfinite results, nuisance clipping, runtime, and memory when relevant. Prespecify retry rules and record each retry. Separate statistical failure (for example, an unidentifiable target) from numerical failure to compute a defined estimate.
If A succeeds on every dataset but B fails on the difficult ones, comparing A on all datasets with B only on its successes favors B by changing the evaluation population. Report method-specific success rates and conditional summaries, then label any paired comparison restricted to jointly successful datasets as such. Keep an attempt-level record so an absent row cannot silently become a successful fit. Runtime should include the prespecified retries and failures when assessing the complete workflow.

title: Evaluating a statistical method
text:
6 Build a useful evaluation grid
Vary the assumptions that support the claim: independent-unit count, cluster sizes, nuisance-model correctness, smoothness, overlap, sparsity, batch/design confounding, and measurement noise. Include settings where theory predicts success, settings near its boundary, and explicit counterexamples. Change one factor at a time to learn a mechanism, then investigate scientifically plausible combinations.
For the estimator in From an influence function to an estimator, compare bias and coverage while changing each nuisance model separately and both together. Record fitted probability ranges and clipping. Compare empirical variance with the known observed-data bound only in scenarios where that bound and the model are specified.
Real omics data usually do not supply the true effect or network. Agreement with another method, pathway enrichment, or reproducibility across cohorts answers a different question from simulated coverage. State what each piece of evidence can support. An empirical analysis can demonstrate feasibility and interpretation without establishing ground-truth accuracy.

title: Evaluating a statistical method
text:
7 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · EVAL-01 — Separate target bias from uncertainty calibration
Task type: Derivation and evaluation design.
For the shrunken mean with target \mu=1, derive its probability limit, bias, sampling variance, and MSE. Explain why a mean SE close to the empirical SD can coexist with poor coverage. Propose a comparison that would expose the failure, and specify how you would report 10 failed fits among 100 replicates.
For a coverage comparison on the same R datasets, define the dataset-level paired contribution and derive the MCSE of the estimated difference.
Ready to continue when: you can distinguish the target, the procedure’s limit, sampling uncertainty, and Monte Carlo uncertainty, and compute a paired performance difference.
Transfer: Would a method with lower MSE necessarily give a better confidence interval for the same target?


Hint

Compare the fixed bias with the n-dependent interval width; keep the denominators explicit.



Solution outline — open after trying

The limit is 0.9, bias is -0.1, variance is 0.81/n, and MSE is 0.01+0.81/n. A correct SE for sampling variability does not center the estimate at 1. At increasing n the bias dominates its SD. Include nonzero targets and increasing n, report bias, empirical SD, mean SE, coverage, and MCSE on paired datasets. Report success as 90/100; coverage among successful fits has denominator 90; joint success-and-coverage has denominator 100. The number covering must also be reported.
For coverage differences let d_r=1\{\theta\in I_{B,r}\}-1\{\theta\in I_{A,r}\}. Estimate the difference by \bar d and its MCSE by s_d/\sqrt R. This retains the within-dataset pairing; a formula that assumes independent marginal coverages omits their covariance.




Additional practice (optional)

Extend the paired calculation to MSE and interval-length differences. State the sign that favors each method and explain why shorter intervals should be judged alongside coverage.
Evaluate the missing-outcome estimator under one misspecified nuisance and under two; write down the predicted limits first.
Compare multipliers 1-n^{-1/4} and 1-n^{-1} at a nonzero mean. Derive their biases relative to the root-n sampling SD before simulating coverage. How can both estimators be consistent but support different conclusions about centered intervals?

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 1 Ask which conclusion depends on which assumption
text:
1 Ask which conclusion depends on which assumption
Sensitivity analysis describes how an answer changes across explicit departures or choices. Start with a fixed scientific target and name what is being varied. A different missing-outcome assumption, a different estimator of the same target, and a different outcome transformation are different exercises.
A useful record contains the target, baseline assumptions, departure parameter or alternative procedure, rationale for its range, expected effect, and uncertainty calculation. Choose scientifically defensible ranges before inspecting which ones preserve significance. Stability across several convenient fits is evidence about those fits, not verification of assumptions the data cannot test.
The group’s published manuscripts provide application case studies. When reading one, reconstruct its target and identify the assumptions that a sensitivity analysis would probe. The calculations here use synthetic or exact teaching examples so that their scope is visible.
crumbs: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 2 First distinguish three kinds of change
text:
2 First distinguish three kinds of change









Change
What is being varied?
What to keep visible




Allow a missing-outcome mean to differ from an observed mean
Identification assumption for the same full-population mean
The departure parameter and its scientific range


Change a nuisance learner or tuning parameter
Estimation procedure for a fixed functional
Training rules, diagnostics, remainder and variance conditions


Change log offsets, reference taxa, adjustment variables in a residual edge, or target population
Often the estimand itself
A separate definition and interpretation for each target


Cap inverse-probability weights
A regularized estimator
Whether it still estimates the original target and what bias remains




A preprocessing choice can also affect measurement validity or nuisance fitting. Write the actual functional rather than assigning every choice to a category by its name. The Preprocessing and the quantity being estimated page gives examples of changed scales and biological adjustment.

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 3 An observed law can support different full means
text:
3 An observed law can support different full means
Let Y\in[0,1] be an outcome, R indicate that it is observed, and suppose independent people supply W=(R,RY). Write

\begin{aligned}
p&=P(R=1),\\
q&=E[Y\mid R=1].
\end{aligned}

The observed data identify p and q when p>0. They do not identify q_0=E[Y\mid R=0] without more information. The full-population target is

\begin{aligned}
\mu&=E[Y]\\
&=pq+(1-p)q_0.
\end{aligned}

With p=0.6 and q=0.65, missing means 0.2 and 0.8 imply full means 0.47 and 0.71. Both worlds have the same observed outcome distribution if we hold that distribution fixed; the missing outcomes differ. More observations from the same observation process can estimate p,q precisely without choosing between those worlds.

Here is an explicit construction. In both worlds, draw R\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.6) and draw observed outcomes from Y\mid R=1\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.65). For the people with R=0, choose Bernoulli(0.2) in the first world and Bernoulli(0.8) in the second. An observed record has probability 0.39 of containing Y=1, probability 0.21 of containing Y=0, and probability 0.40 of containing a missing outcome, in either world. No feature of those observed records distinguishes the two missing-outcome means. This is nonidentification, not a small-sample problem.
In an omics study, the analogous issue is whether unobserved intensities have systematically different distributions from observed ones, for example because low abundance affects detection. A more flexible regression of the observed values can estimate their distribution better; it cannot reveal the unobserved distribution without further information or assumptions.
crumbs: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 4 Parameterize a departure instead of filling in certainty
text:
4 Parameterize a departure instead of filling in certainty
A simple pattern-mixture sensitivity parameter is

\begin{aligned}
\delta&=E[Y\mid R=0]-E[Y\mid R=1],\\
\mu_\delta&=q+(1-p)\delta.
\end{aligned}

At \delta=0, the two outcome means agree; that is a mean restriction, weaker than full independence. For bounded outcomes the population-compatible range is -q\leq\delta\leq1-q. This mathematical range is not necessarily a scientifically plausible range. Use external knowledge, assay limits, or substantive arguments to justify a narrower range, and state how it was chosen.
The units matter. Here \delta=-0.2 means the missing mean is 0.2 outcome units below the observed mean. With 40% missing, it lowers the full-population mean by 0.4(0.2)=0.08. The factor 1-p explains why the same assumption departure has more influence when more outcomes are missing. This linear pattern is specific to the chosen mean target and additive departure; a log-scale departure or odds-ratio restriction describes a different assumption.
Choosing a value of \delta supplies the missing information needed to identify this mean. Varying it over a justified range asks which conclusions survive those different assumptions. It does not estimate \delta from the observed records or declare that every chosen value is equally likely.
With covariates Z, a natural extension defines \delta(Z) as the missing-versus-observed conditional mean difference. For the same eligible-population target,

\mu_\delta=E\{m(Z)+(1-\pi(Z))\delta(Z)\},

where m(Z)=E[Y\mid Z,R=1] and \pi(Z)=P(R=1\mid Z). The outer average uses the covariate distribution of all eligible people. At each Z, the correction is the missing fraction times the specified conditional mean departure. MAR supplies one route to the zero-departure identification formula, with positivity on the target support. A chosen nonzero departure is an additional assumption, not something identified by fitting m more flexibly. These pattern-mixture ideas are discussed in the National Research Council sensitivity-analysis chapter and Carpenter and Smuk.
crumbs: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 5 Quantify sampling uncertainty conditional on the departure
text:
5 Quantify sampling uncertainty conditional on the departure
In the no-covariate example, estimate p by the observed fraction and q by the observed outcome mean. Hold \delta fixed as part of the assumed identification model. Different samples change both estimated quantities, so both contribute to uncertainty in \hat\mu_\delta.
First write q=E[RY]/p. The numerator is a population mean and the denominator is an observation probability. The quotient rule gives its influence function:

\begin{aligned}
\phi_q(W)
&=\frac{RY-pq}{p}-\frac{q(R-p)}p\\
&=\frac R p(Y-q).
\end{aligned}

The influence function for p is R-p. Differentiating q+(1-p)\delta therefore gives

D_\delta(W)=\frac{R}{p}(Y-q)-\delta(R-p).

The first term is the ratio-mean contribution for q; the second differentiates (1-p)\delta. It is mean zero. We require independent people, 0<p<1, fixed interior-compatible \delta, and finite nonzero contribution variance for the usual normal approximation. The bounded teaching outcome supplies finite moments. If the departure is estimated from external data, its additional uncertainty and dependence need to be included.
This also yields a useful variance check. Let \sigma_1^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid R=1). The two terms in D_\delta are uncorrelated because E[Y-q\mid R=1]=0. Hence

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(D_\delta)
&=\frac{\sigma_1^2}{p}+\delta^2p(1-p),\\
\operatorname{SE}(\hat\mu_\delta)
&\approx\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(D_\delta)/n}.
\end{aligned}

The first component is uncertainty in the observed mean; the second comes from the random observed fraction. At zero departure only the first remains. For binary outcomes, \sigma_1^2=q(1-q). With p=0.6,q=0.65,\delta=-0.375, and n=400, the population formula gives an SE of about 0.032. It quantifies sampling uncertainty if that departure is correct, without resolving whether the missing mean really differs by −0.375.
The implementation never multiplies a missing outcome by zero; it computes the residual term only for observed people.


Code
SensitivityMean <- function(r, y, delta) {
  stopifnot(length(r) == length(y), all(r %in% 0:1),
            all(is.finite(y[r == 1])), all(y[r == 1] >= 0 & y[r == 1] <= 1),
            all(is.finite(delta)))
  n <- length(r); p <- mean(r); stopifnot(n >= 2, p > 0, p < 1)
  q <- mean(y[r == 1]); residual <- numeric(n)
  residual[r == 1] <- (y[r == 1]-q)/p
  estimate <- q+(1-p)*delta
  SE <- vapply(delta, function(d) sd(residual-d*(r-p))/sqrt(n), numeric(1))
  data.frame(delta, missing_mean = q+delta, estimate, SE,
             lower = estimate-qnorm(0.975)*SE, upper = estimate+qnorm(0.975)*SE)
}
set.seed(3201)
n <- 400; r <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.6); y <- rep(NA_real_, n)
y[r == 1] <- rbinom(sum(r), 1, 0.65)
# A prespecified teaching range; scientific applications need their own justification.
curve_result <- SensitivityMean(r, y, delta = seq(-0.5, 0.25, length.out = 101))
stopifnot(all(curve_result$missing_mean >= 0 & curve_result$missing_mean <= 1))
p_hat <- mean(r); q_hat <- mean(y[r == 1])
c(observed_fraction = p_hat, observed_mean = q_hat,
  point_estimate_crossing_half = (0.5-q_hat)/(1-p_hat))


           observed_fraction                observed_mean 
                   0.6600000                    0.6212121 
point_estimate_crossing_half 
                  -0.3565062 




Code
s <- curve_result
plot(s$delta, s$estimate, type = "n", ylim = range(c(s$lower, s$upper, 0.5)),
     xlab = "Assumed missing minus observed mean (delta)", ylab = "Full-population mean")
polygon(c(s$delta, rev(s$delta)), c(s$lower, rev(s$upper)),
        col = "#2F80C830", border = NA)
lines(s$delta, s$estimate, col = "#2F80C8", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2); abline(v = 0, lty = 3)








Figure 1: One synthetic observed dataset (400 people). The line shows the full-mean estimate as the assumed missing-minus-observed mean difference changes. Shading gives pointwise 95% Wald intervals conditional on each fixed departure. The benchmark 0.5 and departure range are teaching choices, not empirical evidence for a particular missingness law.





The curve’s movement describes assumption sensitivity; its interval width describes sampling uncertainty for a specified departure. The shading is not a simultaneous band, a probability distribution over \delta, or an estimate of the missing-data law. Wald intervals may also leave the outcome’s allowed range in small samples; clipping their endpoints does not establish coverage.
All points on the curve use the same people and the same estimates of p and q; they are not 101 independent studies. With increasing n, the pointwise intervals shrink around the population curve, but the curve still moves by (1-p)\delta across departures. Better sampling precision does not remove uncertainty about the identification assumption.
The point-estimate tipping value for a benchmark c is (c-\widehat q)/(1-\widehat p). An interval endpoint crossing c is another criterion with another tipping value. Report which is used, the units, and whether it lies in the justified range. Searching for the departure that preserves a small p-value reverses the purpose of the analysis.
For the population values above and c=0.5, the tipping departure is -0.375, giving a missing mean 0.65-0.375=0.275. The point estimate stays above 0.5 for departures larger than this value. Requiring the lower interval endpoint to exceed 0.5 is a stronger statement and crosses at a different departure. A tipping point helps interpret a scientific range; it does not decide that range for us.
If an independent validation study estimates \delta with SE s_\delta, the delta method adds approximately (1-p)^2s_\delta^2 to the variance based on the main study. Shared observations require the covariance term as well. This is a different calculation from scanning fixed assumed values; externally estimated uncertainty must be propagated rather than silently treated as fixed.

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 6 Partial identification can be the honest endpoint
text:
6 Partial identification can be the honest endpoint
Without a missing-outcome mean restriction, boundedness gives the sharp population bounds

\begin{aligned}
pq&\leq\mu\\
&\leq pq+(1-p).
\end{aligned}

At p=0.6,q=0.65 these are [0.39,0.79]. Every interior value can be produced by a compatible missing mean. These are identification bounds at known population quantities, not a confidence interval. Plugging estimated p,q into the endpoints adds sampling uncertainty; confidence sets for partially identified targets require a separate construction.
The bounds are sharp because every value in them is attained by some allowed q_0\in[0,1]. Their width is 1-p=0.4. Even an infinite sample from this observation process would leave that width unchanged. Since the interval straddles 0.5, boundedness alone cannot determine which side of the benchmark the full mean lies on.

6.1 Add sampling uncertainty to the bounds
There is a simple conservative large-sample construction for this example. Let X_L=RY and X_U=RY+1-R, with RY defined as zero for a missing record. Then L=E[X_L] and U=E[X_U] are the lower and upper identification bounds. Estimate each by its sample mean and estimate its SE by its sample SD divided by \sqrt n.
Use a lower one-sided bound for L and an upper one-sided bound for U, each with error probability \alpha/2. Their union-bound construction is

\begin{aligned}
a_L&=\hat L-z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_L,\\
a_U&=\hat U+z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_U,\\
C_n&=[a_L,a_U].
\end{aligned}

Under the i.i.d. CLTs and nonzero endpoint variances, this covers the entire population identification interval with asymptotic probability at least 1-\alpha. It is conservative and uses sampling approximations, not an exact finite-sample theorem. The endpoints can be correlated; the union bound does not require their independence.


Code
observed_value <- numeric(n)
observed_value[r == 1] <- y[r == 1]
lower_contribution <- observed_value
upper_contribution <- observed_value + 1 - r
L_hat <- mean(lower_contribution); U_hat <- mean(upper_contribution)
c(estimated_L = L_hat, estimated_U = U_hat,
  confidence_lower = L_hat - qnorm(0.975)*sd(lower_contribution)/sqrt(n),
  confidence_upper = U_hat + qnorm(0.975)*sd(upper_contribution)/sqrt(n))


     estimated_L      estimated_U confidence_lower confidence_upper 
       0.4100000        0.7500000        0.3617409        0.7924876 


This wider confidence set expresses sampling uncertainty around the identified set. The pointwise intervals on the sensitivity curve instead condition on particular departures that select particular means. Neither should be labeled simply “the uncertainty interval” without saying what it covers.
The same reasoning exposes a support gap in an adjusted comparison. Suppose a target population places mass 0.3 in stratum Z=1, but group 1 supplies no outcomes there. If its supported mean at Z=0 is 0.5 and outcomes are in [0,1], its target-standardized mean is between 0.35 and 0.65. Restricting the population to Z=0 identifies a different target. Weight clipping or additional bootstrap draws do not identify the original unsupported mean.
crumbs: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 7 Use diagnostics without treating them as assumption tests
text:
7 Use diagnostics without treating them as assumption tests
Plot observation probabilities, group support, tail weights, missingness by assay/batch, and data exclusions. Compare justified nuisance learners with identical target definitions and training rules. A held-out loss can diagnose prediction, but does not test MAR against all MNAR alternatives or verify an unobserved stratum mean.
For an omics analysis, also label changes to normalization references, detection rules, cell-composition adjustment, log offsets, and feature families. Explain whether each change probes measurement assumptions, estimator stability, or a different biological target. Inspect effect magnitudes and intervals, not just discovery counts. Stability can coexist with a shared modeling error across all procedures.
crumbs: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
section: 8 Report a sensitivity argument someone can inspect
text:
8 Report a sensitivity argument someone can inspect
State the original estimand and baseline identification argument; define the departure and its plausible range; retain all planned scenarios; report the estimates and appropriately conditional uncertainty; and explain which substantive conclusion changes. Preserve unsupported or failed fits as part of the record. A useful conclusion is specific: “The estimated mean exceeds 0.5 for this stated range of missing-outcome mean differences.” It does not describe the assumptions as verified.
Use Bootstrap and resampling for statistical inference for uncertainty under a justified observation/sampling model. Use Evaluating a statistical method to assess a procedure against known targets in a simulation. Neither task replaces an identification sensitivity argument.

title: Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions
text:
9 Exercises
Try each checkpoint before opening its hint or solution.


Checkpoint · SENS-01 — Separate unidentified variation from sampling uncertainty
Task type: Derivation and computation.
For Y in [0,1], p=0.6 and observed mean q=0.65, derive the full-mean formula under missing-minus-observed mean difference δ. Calculate the means when missing means are 0.2 and 0.8, the no-assumption bounds, and the point-estimate departure at which the full mean equals 0.5. Derive D_δ for a fixed δ and distinguish its SE from uncertainty about δ.
Ready to continue when: you can construct compatible missing-data worlds, calculate a sensitivity curve, and label the identification and sampling uncertainties separately.
Transfer: How would uncertainty in a departure estimated from an independent validation study enter the variance argument?


Hint

Write the full mean as a mixture; differentiate q as a ratio and p as a mean.



Solution outline — open after trying

μ_δ=q+(1−p)δ. Missing means 0.2 and 0.8 correspond to δ=−0.45 and 0.15, giving μ=0.47 and 0.71. Boundedness alone gives [0.39,0.79]. The mean reaches 0.5 at δ=(0.5−0.65)/0.4=−0.375, within the mathematical compatible range [−0.65,0.35]. D_δ=R(Y−q)/p−δ(R−p). Its SD divided by sqrt(n) measures sampling variation conditional on the fixed departure under the stated conditions. It does not identify δ or assign probabilities to its values.





Checkpoint · SENS-02 — Name what each robustness check changes
Task type: Interpretation and diagnosis.
A workflow changes the nuisance learner, caps weights, excludes an unsupported stratum, changes a log offset, and allows nonzero δ for missing outcomes. Identify which choices can preserve the original functional, which can change the target, and which add an identification assumption. For a target with unsupported mass 0.3, supported mean 0.5, and outcomes in [0,1], derive its mean bounds. Explain what more bootstrap replicates can establish.
Ready to continue when: you can keep the estimand explicit while distinguishing an estimator choice, an assumption departure, and a changed population or measurement.
Transfer: Would stable conclusions across ten learners that all impose the same wrong missingness assumption verify that assumption?


Hint

Write the population functional after each change rather than classifying the operation by its name.



Solution outline — open after trying

A new learner can estimate the same nuisance object, with rate/variance conditions rechecked. Capping weights regularizes an estimator and may leave bias for the original target. Excluding a stratum changes the target population; changing a log offset changes the measured outcome and its mean target. A specified δ supplies a missing-outcome mean restriction for the same full-population mean. The support-gap bounds are 0.7(0.5)+0.3[0,1]=[0.35,0.65]. More resamples improve conditional Monte Carlo precision, not identification of the unsupported mean.




Additional practice (optional)

Find separately the departure where the estimate crosses 0.5 and where each pointwise interval endpoint crosses it. Explain the different conclusions.
Specify a scientifically motivated δ(Z) for an assay example and identify which parts are informed by observed data or external evidence.
Read a published group manuscript and make a table of target, key assumption, proposed departure, plausible range, and conclusion to assess.

title: Large-sample reasoning for methods research
text:
4 Core working theorems
These are the versions used throughout the guides. Each result has a particular job; a proof usually combines several rather than invoking “large samples” as a single justification. For the sample-average results, continue with the i.i.d. observations Y_1,\ldots,Y_n from a population distribution P.
Let f be a fixed function applied to each observation. We will compare the sample average n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(Y_i) with its population expectation E_P(f(Y)). The subscript P makes explicit the population distribution underlying the expectation written E earlier. For the mean example, take f(Y_i)=Y_i, so the average is \bar Y and the expectation is \mu. In the LLN and CLT below, f is fixed, rather than selected using those same observations. We will first write these results in full, then introduce shorthand for the two kinds of average.
Scope of notation and assumptions. The sample-mean notation Y_i, \mu, and \sigma^2 carries through its applications. Each theorem states the conditions it needs; these can be weaker than the finite-variance assumptions used for that example. Auxiliary variables and sequences introduced within a theorem are local to that statement, and their assumptions do not carry into the next theorem.

4.1 Law of large numbers: establish consistency
If E_P(|f(Y)|)<\infty, the weak LLN gives

\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)\xrightarrow{p}E_P(f(Y)).

The sample average consistently estimates its population expectation. Apply this separately to Y and Y^2 to begin the variance-consistency argument above. The second application requires E[Y^2]<\infty; the first only requires E[|Y|]<\infty. A pointwise LLN for a fixed f does not automatically apply to a fitted function \hat f chosen from the same data.
Under the same i.i.d. integrability condition, the strong LLN gives

\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}E_P(f(Y)).

Our consistency arguments use the weaker convergence-in-probability conclusion stated above.


4.2 Central limit theorem: obtain the fluctuation law
Applying the same fixed function f to each observation gives i.i.d. values f(Y_1),\ldots,f(Y_n). Their population mean is E_P(f(Y)) and their population variance is

\sigma_f^2=\operatorname{Var}_P(f(Y)).

If 0<\sigma_f^2<\infty, the central limit theorem gives

\sqrt n\left\{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)-E_P(f(Y))
\right\}
\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma_f^2).

Inside the braces is the difference between a sample average and its population expectation. The sample average changes across repeated studies; its population expectation stays fixed. The theorem describes the distribution of that estimation error after multiplying it by \sqrt n.
The LLN tells us that the difference approaches zero in probability. The CLT goes further: it describes the fluctuations that remain visible after rescaling. Under the stated assumptions, those fluctuations approach a normal distribution. The individual values f(Y_i) do not themselves need to be normally distributed. Their average fluctuates around E_P(f(Y)) on the n^{-1/2} scale.
For the sample mean, choose f(y)=y. Then E_P(f(Y))=\mu, \sigma_f^2=\sigma^2, and the statement becomes

\sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma^2).

When combining several sample averages, we need their joint limiting distribution. The multivariate CLT applies to a fixed vector of functions with finite second moments and supplies a normal limit with their joint covariance matrix. Those covariances matter when we subsequently transform or combine the averages.

From explicit averages to expectation shorthand. Both quantities in the CLT can be written as expectations, but under different distributions. The population distribution P describes how observations arise in the population. The empirical distribution P_n places probability 1/n on each of the n observed values, counting repeated values separately. Given the data, drawing from P_n means selecting one of those observations uniformly. An expectation under P_n therefore averages over the observed sample:

\begin{aligned}
P_nf&=E_{P_n}(f(Y))\\
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i),\\
Pf&=E_P(f(Y)).
\end{aligned}

These are exact definitions of the shorthand. In particular, P_nf includes the factor 1/n: it is an average, not an unnormalized sum. The empirical distribution P_n, and hence P_nf, changes across samples; the population distribution P and expectation Pf stay fixed. Replacing P by P_n changes the distribution being averaged over, while keeping the function f the same. Neither expression means multiplication of P or P_n by f.
The difference between the two averages can now be abbreviated as

\begin{aligned}
(P_n-P)f&=P_nf-Pf\\
&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(Y_i)-E_P(f(Y)).
\end{aligned}

Thus the full LLN and CLT statements above become

P_nf\xrightarrow{p}Pf,


\sqrt n(P_n-P)f\xrightarrow{d}N(0,\sigma_f^2).

The notation is shorter; the averages and the theorem assumptions are unchanged. For f(y)=y, P_nf=\bar Y and Pf=\mu. Use the expanded identities above whenever the compact notation hides what is being averaged or which distribution supplies the expectation.



4.3 Markov and Chebyshev: turn moments into probability bounds
For a nonnegative random variable W with finite expectation, Markov’s inequality states

\begin{aligned}
\Pr(W\ge t)&\le\frac{E[W]}t,\\
t&>0.
\end{aligned}

Applying it to a squared centered variable gives Chebyshev’s inequality. For X with finite variance and \varepsilon>0,

\Pr(|X-E[X]|\ge\varepsilon)
\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\varepsilon^2}.

For the sample mean, the bound is \sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2), which tends to zero and directly proves consistency under finite variance. Taking \varepsilon=M/\sqrt n also gives \Pr(\sqrt n|\bar Y-\mu|\ge M)\le \sigma^2/M^2, establishing \bar Y-\mu=O_p(n^{-1/2}). Neither bound identifies a normal limiting law. Later, conditional versions of this argument will control held-out empirical averages given their training data.


4.4 Continuous mapping: carry a limit through a function
If X_n\xrightarrow{p}c and g is continuous at c, then

g(X_n)\xrightarrow{p}g(c).

For example, variance consistency and \sigma^2>0 imply s_Y\xrightarrow{p}\sigma and 1/s_Y\xrightarrow{p}1/\sigma (with the reciprocal defined arbitrarily when s_Y=0). The zero-denominator event has probability tending to zero. Continuity at the limit matters: reciprocal substitution is not justified by convergence to zero.
There is also a distributional version: X_n\xrightarrow{d}X implies g(X_n)\xrightarrow{d}g(X) if g is continuous with probability one under the limiting law. Both statements extend to vectors. For two estimates converging in probability to constants, their vector converges to the vector of constants, so continuous functions of both have the corresponding limit.


4.5 Slutsky’s theorem: combine a limiting law with consistent quantities
Let Z_n and B_n be sequences of random variables satisfying Z_n\xrightarrow{d}Z and B_n\xrightarrow{p}c, where c is a constant. Here B_n is a new sequence whose required condition is convergence in probability to that constant; no sign or moment assumptions are added. Then

\begin{aligned}
Z_n+B_n&\xrightarrow{d}Z+c,\\
Z_nB_n&\xrightarrow{d}cZ,\\
Z_n/B_n&\xrightarrow{d}Z/c\qquad(c\ne0).
\end{aligned}

The theorem works because (Z_n,B_n) converges jointly in distribution to (Z,c), after which continuous mapping applies. Independence of Z_n and B_n is not required. This is why we can use the sample mean and sample variance calculated from the same people.
For the mean, set Z_n=\sqrt n(\bar Y-\mu) and B_n=s_Y. The CLT gives the first limit, and variance consistency gives the second with c=\sigma>0. Division yields a standard normal limit. Replacing a population variance by an estimate therefore needs a consistency proof, not an assertion that the estimate is “close” in one dataset.
Slutsky also removes a negligible remainder. If Z_n\xrightarrow{d}N(0,V) and A_n=o_p(1), then Z_n+A_n\xrightarrow{d}N(0,V). This is the step used after proving \sqrt nR_n=o_p(1) in an estimator expansion. If the added term is only O_p(1), it can change the limit. Likewise, two separate nondegenerate distributional limits do not by themselves justify multiplication or division; their joint behavior matters.


4.6 The delta method is the same first-order idea
The function f above acts on each observation before averaging. Here a function g acts on an estimator after it has been calculated. For a transformed population mean, the connection is

\begin{aligned}
\hat\eta&=P_nf\\
&=\bar Y,\\
\eta_0&=Pf\\
&=\mu,\\
f(y)&=y.
\end{aligned}

For example, g(u)=\sqrt u gives g(\hat\eta)=\sqrt{\bar Y} as an estimator of g(\eta_0)=\sqrt\mu when \mu>0. Transforming an average generally differs from averaging transformed observations. We use a separate letter g to distinguish these two roles. The general result below also applies to estimators that are not simple averages, and allows \hat\eta and \eta_0 to be vectors.
If \sqrt n(\hat\eta-\eta_0)\to_d N(0,\Sigma) and g is differentiable at \eta_0, then

\sqrt n\{g(\hat\eta)-g(\eta_0)\}
\to_d N\!(0,\nabla g^\top\Sigma\nabla g).

The gradient is evaluated at \eta_0. A first-order Taylor expansion gives the leading term \nabla g(\eta_0)^\top\sqrt n(\hat\eta-\eta_0); differentiability and the root-n rate make the remaining scaled error negligible. Continuous mapping and Slutsky then give the displayed limit.
For a positive population mean \mu and g(u)=\sqrt u, the derivative is 1/(2\sqrt\mu), so

\sqrt n(\sqrt{\bar Y}-\sqrt\mu)
\xrightarrow{d}N\!\left(0,\frac{\sigma^2}{4\mu}\right).

If measurements can be negative, consistency and \mu>0 ensure that \bar Y>0 with probability tending to one; the transformed estimator can be defined arbitrarily on the remaining event for this asymptotic argument. A feasible delta-method SE is s_Y/(2\sqrt{\bar Y}\sqrt n) on positive sample means.
For a ratio or correlation, the delta method propagates the joint covariance, not just separate standard errors. Dropping covariance between components can give the wrong uncertainty. If the gradient vanishes, the displayed first-order limit may be degenerate and a higher-order analysis may be needed.

title: Quantiles and local expansions
section: 2 Derive the population path derivative separately
text:
2 Derive the population path derivative separately
For a bounded, mean-zero-score path dP_t=(1+ts)dP, let F_t be its CDF and q_t its quantile. At a fixed endpoint u,

F_t(u)=F(u)+tE[1\{Y\le u\}s(Y)].

The identity F_t(q_t)=\tau changes both the distribution and the endpoint. Differentiating at zero gives

0=E[1\{Y\le q\}s(Y)]+f(q)\dot q.

Solving and using E[s]=0 yields \dot q=E[\phi_q(Y)s(Y)], with the same \phi_q as the sample expansion. The path derivative is a deterministic sensitivity calculation for populations. The empirical-CDF lemma above was the extra step needed for the random sample quantile.

title: Quantiles and local expansions
text:
3 Obtain and interpret uncertainty
Because 1\{Y\le q\} is Bernoulli with probability \tau, E[\phi_q]=0 and

\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\phi_q)&=\frac{\tau(1-\tau)}{f(q)^2},\\
\operatorname{Var}(\hat q)&\approx\frac{\tau(1-\tau)}{nf(q)^2}.
\end{aligned}

The first is the limiting variance of the scaled error; the second is the estimator’s first-order variance. A feasible SE can use \sqrt{\tau(1-\tau)}/\{\sqrt n\,\hat f(\hat q)\} if the density estimate at the fitted quantile converges to f(q)>0. Such consistency needs an appropriate density estimator and its own conditions; another justified quantile-uncertainty procedure is also possible.
The influence contribution is bounded under the stated positive-density conditions, so this CLT does not require the raw outcome to have finite variance. If the density is zero at q, or the CDF has a jump there, the displayed inversion and regularity argument must be reconsidered. Nonsmoothness of the sample equation alone is therefore a different issue from failure of the population derivative or local empirical control.

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
section: 3 Counts, realized fractions, and error rates
text:
3 Counts, realized fractions, and error rates
Let D be the total number of discoveries and V the number of those discoveries whose null hypotheses are actually true. Both vary with the sampled dataset. Define

\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{FDP}&=\frac{V}{\max(D,1)},\\
\mathrm{FDR}&=E[\mathrm{FDP}],\\
\mathrm{FWER}&=\Pr(V\ge1).
\end{aligned}

The false discovery proportion (FDP) describes one list. It is zero by convention when nothing is rejected. In real data, we know D but generally do not know V, so we cannot inspect the list and calculate its true FDP. Simulation gives us that opportunity because we supply the truth.
The family-wise error rate (FWER) is the probability of making even one false rejection. It is useful when a single false claim is costly. The false discovery rate (FDR) averages the false fraction over repetitions of the entire procedure. It can suit an exploratory discovery list, but it allows some individual lists to have much larger false fractions than the target q. Neither criterion is automatically right for every confirmatory or exploratory analysis; choose from the consequences of the claims.
An expectation of fractions is different from a fraction of expected counts. Imagine two equally likely outcomes: a list with (D,V)=(1,1) and a list with (D,V)=(99,0). Their FDPs are 1 and 0, so FDR is 1/2. Pooling the lists gives one false claim in 100 discoveries, or 0.01. That pooled fraction weights large lists more heavily and is not FDR. In a simulation, average one FDP per dataset.
Under the global null every discovery is false. FDP is then 1 if there is any rejection and 0 otherwise, so FDR equals FWER. Away from that special case, the two criteria ask different questions.

title: Multiple testing when the tests are not independent
section: 8 Permutation resolution is a separate limitation
text:
8 Permutation resolution is a separate limitation
With B random permutations and the plus-one formula, the smallest possible p-value is 1/(B+1). That floor says nothing about whether the permutation scheme is valid, and reaching a cutoff does not imply precise tail estimation.
For marginal permutation p-values followed by Bonferroni, the floor must satisfy 1/(B+1)\le\alpha/m before any rejection is possible. Thus B+1\ge m/\alpha. With 1,000 tests and \alpha=0.05, this requires at least 19,999 permutations just to reach the cutoff.
For BH the relevant threshold is kq/m, where k is the last passing rank. At m=1000, q=0.05, and B=999, the minimum p-value is 0.001. One isolated p-value at that floor cannot pass rank 1, but 20 p-values at the floor pass at rank 20, since 20(0.05)/1000=0.001. The smallest BH cutoff is therefore a limitation for a sparse discovery set, not an unconditional requirement for every possible rejection. For 10^5 tests, reaching rank 1’s 5\times10^{-7} cutoff requires about two million permutations.
The maxT adjusted p-values also have the 1/(B+1) floor, but they are compared directly with \alpha, because the maximum already accounts for the family. Pooling tests or fitting a parametric tail changes the calibration argument; neither is an automatic cure for limited permutation resolution.
