title: Evaluating a statistical method
section: 2 Choose measures that answer the claim
text:
2 Choose measures that answer the claim
Suppose a scenario has fixed population truth \theta and produces R independent datasets. For replicate r, retain the estimate \hat\theta_r, reported SE \hat s_r, interval I_r, and fitting status. Then the main summaries are

\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\operatorname{Bias}}&=\overline{\hat\theta}-\theta,\\
s_{\rm emp}^2&=\frac1{R-1}\sum_r
(\hat\theta_r-\overline{\hat\theta})^2,\\
\overline{\operatorname{SE}}&=\frac1R\sum_r\hat s_r,\\
\widehat{\operatorname{MSE}}&=\frac1R\sum_r(\hat\theta_r-\theta)^2,\\
\widehat{\operatorname{Coverage}}&=\frac1R\sum_r1\{\theta\in I_r\}.
\end{aligned}

Bias measures the average signed error; positive and negative errors can cancel. MSE averages squared errors, penalizing both bias and variation. Empirical SD measures how estimates vary between datasets. Mean SE summarizes what the method reports within datasets. Coverage asks whether the intervals actually include the common target at the advertised frequency. Comparing interval length is meaningful alongside coverage: very short intervals are easy to produce if they miss the target.
For testing, rejection under a true scientific null estimates Type I error; rejection under a specified alternative estimates power. For a family of omics hypotheses, estimate FDR by averaging one false discovery proportion per dataset. Genes and edges from the same dataset are not independent simulation replicates. See Multiple testing when the tests are not independent for that distinction.
For the formulas above assume all fits return usable results; the failure section below explains the denominators when they do not. If truth changes randomly between replicates, also state whether the summaries average over that random-truth distribution or concern one fixed parameter. Those are different evaluation claims.

title: Reporting a statistical methods study
section: 5 Choose displays that answer a question
text:
5 Choose displays that answer a question
A single estimate and interval can be reported clearly in a sentence. Use a plot when its structure reveals something the reader needs to assess: heterogeneity across features, bias as n grows, failure under a changed assumption, or a tradeoff across methods. A graphic that only repeats two numbers from the surrounding sentence adds little.
For example, the balance-by-mean-shift plot in Simulation studies for methods research reveals an interaction that a single rejection rate conceals. Its caption must distinguish the true equal-correlation null, the simulated datasets, the changing mean shifts, and the binomial reference band. The curve in Sensitivity analysis for assumptions and research decisions instead varies an assumption on one observed dataset; its shading represents conditional sampling uncertainty. Calling both shaded regions simply “95% uncertainty” would hide different meanings.
Label a reference line as known simulation truth, a hypothesized null, or an estimated benchmark. A full-data or external estimate is not an oracle; it has its own sampling variation, target, and possible measurement error. Captions should also state whether features were prespecified for display or selected after seeing results. A reader should be able to tell what comparison the figure supports before reading a conclusion about it.

title: From a research question to an identified estimand
section: 8 Distinguish structural absence from a small sample
text:
8 Distinguish structural absence from a small sample
No observations in a sample cell need not mean its population probability is zero. With positive population support, an empty finite cell is an estimation difficulty: more suitable observations may supply information. A structural zero is different. If outcomes are never observed in a needed population stratum, even an infinite sample from that process leaves its outcome mean unknown without additional restrictions.
For the exercise below, both groups still occur in both Z strata. What becomes zero is the probability of observing an outcome in group 0 at Z=1. Its full-population conditional mean is therefore a defined quantity, but the observed record contains no outcomes that reveal it. Keeping group membership and outcome observation separate makes the nonidentification argument precise.

title: Residual covariance and nuisance-estimation error
text:
10 Exercises
The checkpoint is this page’s completion target. Additional practice is optional. Use the missing-mean argument as a reference, but derive the covariance remainder rather than assuming it is unchanged.


Checkpoint · COV-01 — Separate nuisance bias from held-out fluctuation
Task type: Derivation and rate reasoning.
Let m_X(Z)=E[X\mid Z], m_Y(Z)=E[Y\mid Z], and \psi=E[(X-m_X(Z))(Y-m_Y(Z))]. Hold training fits fixed, with errors \delta_X=\hat m_X-m_X and \delta_Y=\hat m_Y-m_Y. Assume the variables and fitted means have finite second moments.

Derive the population bias of the residual-product formula and of the difference formula E[XY]-E[\hat m_X(Z)\hat m_Y(Z)]. Which formula removes the terms involving only one nuisance error?
Take both errors to be the positive constant n^{-1/5}. Calculate the residual-product bias and its size after multiplication by \sqrt n. Would evaluating on held-out people remove it?
State a sufficient product-of-L2-errors condition for negligible root-n bias. Identify the separate fitted-minus-true empirical term and variance conditions still needed before reporting an influence-function SE.

Ready to continue when: you can derive the covariance nuisance-bias remainder and distinguish its rate requirement from cross-fitting and variance consistency.
Transfer: If one conditional mean is exactly correct and the other is misspecified, what happens to the population bias? Does that alone establish the efficient-SE argument?


Hint

Write each fitted residual as its true residual minus \delta. Condition on Z to remove the single-error terms in the residual product. For the rate comparison, multiply the product bias by \sqrt n before judging whether it disappears.



Solution outline — open after trying

Writing U_X=X-m_X(Z) and U_Y=Y-m_Y(Z) gives

E[(U_X-\delta_X)(U_Y-\delta_Y)]-\psi
=E[\delta_X\delta_Y],

because both true residuals have conditional mean zero given Z. The difference formula instead has bias -E[m_X\delta_Y+m_Y\delta_X+\delta_X\delta_Y], which generally includes single-error terms.
With both errors equal to n^{-1/5}, the residual-product bias is n^{-2/5} and its scaled size is n^{1/10}, which diverges. Cross-fitting does not change this population expectation.
Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the bias by \|\delta_X\|_2\|\delta_Y\|_2, so a product o_p(n^{-1/2}) is sufficient. The held-out empirical term is (P_{n,k}-P)H_k, where H_k is the fitted-minus-true residual product. Its L2 size must vanish under the stated fold conditions. A CLT for the true contribution and consistent estimation of its finite, positive variance are also required; L2 consistency of the mean fits alone need not control their product’s L2 size.
If either error is zero, the population bias is zero. The remaining fit can still change the leading contribution and its variance, so this alone does not establish the efficient-SE argument.




Additional practice (optional)
These exercises extend the ideas through further derivations, simulations, or applications. Choose those useful for your work.

Show that the variance \sigma^2 = E[(X - \mu)^2], viewed as a formula with nuisance \mu, is Neyman orthogonal in \mu. Then show that the formula E[X^2] - \mu^2 is not. Check both numerically by inflating \mu by 1 + \varepsilon.
In the orthogonality simulation, replace the inflation error with an additive error m + \varepsilon(Z - 1/2) and predict, before running, the leading term of each formula’s bias.
Change df in the cross-fitting example to 5 and to 40 and re-run at N = 200. How do the two biases change, and which grows faster with df? Then replace the smoothing spline with an average of 20 deep regression trees, each grown on a bootstrap resample (rpart is a recommended R package; use rpart.control() with cp=0, minsplit=5, and minbucket=3). Compare the in-sample and cross-fit biases. Why does a deep tree fit its own noise?
The residual correlation is \psi / \sqrt{\psi_{XX}\,\psi_{YY}} with \psi_{XX} = E[\operatorname{Var}(X \mid Z)]. Write the orthogonal estimators of the three pieces and combine them. What does the delta method say about the standard error?
